_childDocuments_.review: Of all the games I've played in 2024 so far, Bakeru is easily my game of the year. No other game has brought me this much genuine joy without any strings attached. It's just a pure, fun, polished, inspired action platformer that wears its Japanese heritage and influence on its sleeve. The premise is straightforward. The game takes place in a version of modern Japan where all its folkore are real, and stars a shapeshifting tanuki boy named Bakeru, who must travel across the country to save it from the power Oracle Saitaro and his festival troops. Armed with a pair of traditional drum sticks, Bakeru beats enemies like a taiko drum and can even shapeshift into one of four forms to aid him in his quest. The story is fairly straightforward, but there's a good cast of characters to keep things lively the whole way through. The banter between Bakeru and his travel companion Sun, as well as the other fairytale heroes they meet along the way, help give the game plenty of personality, charm, and even franchise potential. It's a very well-realised world that could easily be revisited with future games. The gameplay of Bakeru combines linear 3D platforming with beat-'em-up combat. The player must navigate Bakeru through a series of obstacle courses set in various parts of Japan (often exaggerated fantasy versions of their real-world counterparts), destroying three magic lanterns along the way to gain access to the goal at the end; one of Oracle Saitaro's mind-control towers operated by a drum. Levels tend to be very spacious despite their linear structure, and while this makes for less-difficult level design than platforming fans are used to, it tends to accommidate the large groups of enemies you encounter, allowing for a decent-sized battlefield in any given situation. There are plenty of secrets to find off the beaten path, and while most are easy to uncover, they all do a good job of both extending the playtime and giving levels even more purpose than to just be rushed through. There are three souvenirs to find in each level, usually pertaining to the location they were found in. And also five pieces of trivia given by the character Scoop, which range from trivia on whatever part of Japan you're currently in, or even something as universal as human biology and health tips. Both collectibles ad a lot of novelty and character to the game, and it was always fun to read the descriptions of the souvenirs or the various Scoop trivia. If I could compare Bakeru to other games, it's basically what you'd get if you combined Super Mario 3D World with Ape Escape 3. 3D World for its linear level design with optional collectibles, but Ape Escape more so for how its combat is handled. You won't be catching monkeys in this game, but like Ape Escape, you attack using an unconventional button scheme. Instead of a dedicated attack button, pressing the left or right bumper on your controller will make Bakeru attack with the corresponding drum stick. Holding one or the other down yields a different charged-attack, as does holding both down, and this applies even to three of his four transformation abilities called Henge, where the biggest Ape Escape 3 comparison can be drawn. In addition to this, you can block and even parry attacks by guarding at the right time, and counterattack by dodging before an attack lands.After defeating one of the three fairytale heroes, said hero will grant you his Henge license, allowing Bakeru to transform and use the associated ability. Kintaro's is a close-range ability that can deal hard-hitting heavy attacks ideal for bosses and enemies that normally take multiple hits to defeat. Urashima Taro flings fishing rods at enemies with a good midrange distance, perfect for crowd control. And Momotaro (admittedly the most useless one, I found, due to its weak damage output) can use two pistols to fire at range (y'know, like Momotaro was known to do). You get an early Henge ability at the start of the game; Sun's, which allows Bakeru to shrink and enter small spaces he otherwise couldn't, at the cost of his ability to attack. Using Henge depletes a meter, which can be refilled by collecting essences from defeated enemies. The transformations aren't created equal, and Sun's especially feels very situational. In fact, I don't think any of them are mandatory to beat the game. But I do appreciate the game letting me use them at my own discretion, and figuring out for myself what situations best suit them. The Steam version of Bakeru actually awards you achievements for defeating bosses without using a henge ability. In addition to the typical platforming stages, you also have racing sections help add variety to the gameplay. They're quite easy when you get used to the controls, but they're a nice change of pace. The on-rails shooting sections fair a bit better though, with a rechargable beam and three bombs at your disposal, as you mow down enemies like a Starfox game. Only thing that could improve it would be an aiming retical for better accuracy.Lastly, there's the giant robot battles, in which the ship you travel around in (basically a giant tea kettle) transforms into a fighting robot to face off against one of five bosses. While I'm not the biggest fan of how slow the robot is, it's still a fun time landing hits on the enemy till they fall, as is using the special attack on them when their guard is down. The gameplay isn't too disimilar to that of the regular combat, with the robot's arms corresponding to the left and right bumpers respectively, as well as dodging and guarding being mapped to the same buttons as usual (though you can't parry or counterattack this time). While neither the combat nor the platforming mechanics are great on their own, when combined they compliment each other, and the additional genre-shifting gameplay sections result in a game that's greater than the sum of its parts, all set in imaginative takes on various Japanese locales.The enemy variety on display deserves mention as well. The Festival Troops take on a variety of different forms, most of which are people or creatures wearing goofy-looking Hyotyoko masks. They range from kendo swordsman to nara deer and one of three-coloured oni. The weaker enemies introduced early on can be dispatched with one hit, while later ones will take several and incentivise counter-attacks and parries to get the most hits in before they deal damage. Enemies also drop golden ryo coins (old Japanese currency), which can be spent on healing and other consumable items, permanent health upgrades, various masks Bakeru can wear, and upgrades to the robot.The music in Bakeru is superb. A mixture of traditional and modern Japan that creates the atmosphere of a jolly summer festival. Ironically enough though, one of my favourite tracks is the end-level theme, as you must beat away at the drum connected to the Oracle tower to claim it as Bakeru's. This is punctuated by the satisfying thuds of the drum along with the rising meter as it reaches closer to the top. Then as the victory jingle plays, Bakeru hits the drum two or three more times in rhythm with the music. It's stylish, and makes an already satisfying game even more rewarding to beat. While the visuals won't wow you on a technical level (definitely lower-poly models being used to accomidate its original Switch release), its artstyle does most of the heavy lifting. Colourful, vibrant areas to explore, gorgeous scale-like patterns in the sea, and flashy effects punctuating the on-screen action make it no surprise that its developers, Good Feel, previously worked on Nintendo platformers. It's a gorgeous game to look at, and runs phenominally on PC at max settings with an uncapped framerate.There's a lot more I could say about the game, but at this point, you should probably get it yourself. I cannot recommend it enough, especially given how much content is packed in.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first review ever because I feel like this game is flying under the radar so I want to do my part to get more people to play!Goemon's Great Adventures was the first game I owned on the first console I owned. I LOVED it. So for years I've been trying to chase that dragon and I think Bakeru comes as close as any game ever has. Obviously it's not a 1:1 (there's no towns to roam which is a slight bummer, but that's just a gripe on my part and in no way a negative overall) The stages are beautiful and creative which is impressive because there's a lot of them. It's easy to get repetitive but I feel like Bakeru does a good job with keeping it engaging. The little trivia poops and trinkets you can collect are fun too! And of course Giant Robot Boss Battles >:)It's a great 'brain-turn-off' beat em up. Can't recommend enough!
_childDocuments_.name: BAKERU

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem. All of the other reviews praising this game are no joke. This game might sincerely be one of my favorite 3D platformers I've played in a long time. There's a lot of things this game does right.The general gameplay is pretty simplistic but extremely fun. It reminds me a lot of playing Nintendo titles like Kirby or Mario. It also has combat that feels similar to DMC, but it's much simpler and still feels nuanced. The level variety is also incredible. This game has A LOT of different level types. You have standard levels like I just described as well as levels that involving, racing, shmup levels, boss fights with a giant mech, etc.The game also has a phenomenal soundtrack. I found myself constantly humming some of the songs from the game in my head. The level theming is also great. It feels like you're getting to explore parts of Japan as you play the game and the levels feel very fun and charming, for the most part. Last, but not least, there's the collectibles. The collectibles are very different from what I've seen in most games. You have 5 pieces of trivia you can find in each level as well as 3 souvenirs which are usually objects that seem to be from Japan. Roughly, by the time you beat the 3rd boss you also unlock one more collectible that only pops up in certain levels of the game.If all of this sounds good to you then please buy this game. This game is worth the price. I bought it when it was on sale for $35 but this is easily worth the normal asking price. Also at least the initial release in Japan seems to have been a failure, and it's not clear if it's faring better internationally. Support this game if you want to see a Bakeru 2.
_childDocuments_.name: BAKERU

_childDocuments_.review: A light-hearted adventure with fun and engaging gameplay through and through.The battle system is fairly simple and permissive, allowing you to play as relaxed or "sweaty" as you want; the combos are nice and fast, keeping the pace up both in exploration sections and boss battles, also featuring blocking, parrying, dashing and counter-attacking.The platform is pleasant as well, with the difficulty ramping up a bit towards the end as hazards and dynamic elements come more and more into play.I enjoyed exploring the levels, which have various collectables hidden all over them, these being a mix of mostly japanese trivia and references to different areas of Japan. Thematically, visually and musically, I find this game to be a gem; I couldn't help but to smile and laugh as I played it.
_childDocuments_.name: BAKERU

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely charming characters, world, and game. Just fun to play, plenty of secrets to find, one of which tells you fun facts (mostly about Japanese culture) each time you find him, which I love. A lot of content for the price, 63 levels, a few of which are kart/boat racing or shoot em up to mix things up. The soundtrack is really good, reminds me a LOT of Okami's. Strongly recommended for 3d platformer/beat em up enjoyers.Runs well on Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: BAKERU

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just plain fun.A lot of other reviews will probably bring up Goemon, but outside of Legend of the Mystical Ninja on SNES I have no nostalgia for the franchise. Though looking at this and it's artstyle it does seem reminiscent I think this game does it's own thing well enough to stand apart.It's a definite throwback to the N64/Dreamcast/PS2 platformers, but the platforming itself is kind of sparse. Maybe that opens up a bit and I get new moves opening it up later, IDK, but it's not a big deal. Running through the areas, beating baddies, and finding collectibles is fun and the controls are buttery smooth. Bosses so far have been fun too. This was originally a Switch game, but this port definitely pulls off a better look on PC. It's really a pleasantly charming game to look at. A lot of the humor is funny as well. I found myself really enjoying the characters even if the story is kind of basic and straight forward. From what I'm seeing it looks like a max 10hr romp so I look forward to playing this and probably beating it over the weekend.EDIT: Took a lil longer than 10 and I didn't collect everything. Probably 80% complete. This game never bored me. It seemed to keep coming up with interesting things to throw at me just as soon as I thought I'd seen it all. I could say in terms of action it's a bit repetitive, but never really dull. All in all a fun game!

name: Gimmick! 2
detailed_description: A Classic Challenge Modernized In Gimmick! 2 , you once again meet the green little yokai Yumetaro. Decades after his first adventure he now sets out on a new quest in a world packed with interesting challenges, dangerous enemies, and hidden treasures. The game can be played in either a friendlier assisted mode, or if you’re up for a challenge play in the true-to-the-original “Gimmick!” mode! Star physics As a yokai, Yumetaro has the ability to summon and throw a powerful star that not only bounces, but also keeps the momentum of his movement. The Star can be used to activate switches, defend against enemies and even be ridden to get to those hard-to-reach places while exploring the secrets of the world. You can discover treasure, find shortcuts or set speed records by mastering the star's bouncing physics. Experiment with it to unlock its full potential. This is a game with true star power! A Legendary Soundtrack The composer David Wise hardly needs any introduction. In his work on the Gimmick! 2 soundtrack, he has both written completely new melodies and remade old classics. The soundtrack was creatively directed by Pelle Cahndlerby and recorded live in Sweden together with Joel Bille. Blast from the past The original Gimmick! game was released for the Famicom™ in 1992. It was localized and released in the West - but only in Scandinavia. This, combined with the fact that the game's physics and gameplay mechanics were far ahead of its time, made the game both fabled and beloved. With Gimmick! 2 , however, there is no longer any doubt: this is a game that the whole world should have the chance to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a speedrunner and a big fan of the original Famicom Gimmick!, and I thoroughly enjoyed my first playthrough of this game.Some people may feel like Gimmick! 2 doesn't capture much of the essence of the original Famicom game, and I can see where they're coming from. This isn't so much a direct sequel in the classic sense, rather it's more of a modern reinterpretation of the original essence. But I'd argue the original game essence is all still there and expanded upon.Gimmick! 2 puts a slightly bigger emphasis on puzzles, which I think works out really well in bringing out the extent to which you can use the Star mechanics, which are still as fun to make use of as they were in the original game (albeit they're different in a significant way). Platforming segments are still plentiful, too.If you're looking for a simpler experience, most of the game's main path isn't too difficult. However, if you are interested in achieving the True Ending, then you can expect to have your Star abilities challenged in a major way.Additionally, there are plenty of hidden collectables scattered throughout, some of which are required for the True Ending, so you can expect a pretty big exploration element too, if that suits your fancy. Some of these secrets can be pretty highly rewarding to collect: more than one time I have exclaimed something along the lines of "this game is sick" after solving some brilliantly crafted puzzles.Gone is the whole lives and continues system from the original Gimmick!, and in its place we have fairly abundant checkpoints and infinite retries. I think when it comes to NES-era videogame enthusiasts a lives system tends to be seen as more of a positive, but I think particularly when it comes to a game of this style, this checkpoint system is much more enjoyable and should also allow less experienced players to enjoy the game.I wasn't too convinced of the art style at first, but the more I looked at it, the less I ended up feeling like it was reminiscent of "cheap mobile games". I enjoy how colorful and vibrant everything looks.The music is fantastic too: you can tell David Wise was on the team. It reminds me a lot of Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze's OST, with it being a little more on the ambient side and adding to the immersion to the environments.The one (minor) critique I'd make of this game is that the levels can get pretty long. This is particularly noticeable when trying to find missing collectables: you end up searching pretty wide areas when trying to look for the few things you know you missed in a given level. The levels are definitely still fun to me however.Overall, I can confidently say I am very satisfied with the game. I was not expecting the 1992 Gimmick! to ever be given a follow-up title, so it was certainly a surprise when Gimmick! 2 was announced earlier this year, and I am very pleased that the game was as fun to play as it is for me. I could feel some true passion in the making of this title.Thank you Bitwave Games for creating this wonderful game. Now if you will excuse me, I have a new speedrun to route...
_childDocuments_.name: Gimmick! 2

_childDocuments_.review: two swings and two misses for bitwave's handling of gimmick. this is an absolute base-level fundamental misunderstanding of everything the original title has to offer.i do not like leaving bad reviews, but this feels personal.first, a boring technical note: horrible input latency. even with vsync and fullscreen windowed mode, it feels like i'm playing via a radio broadcast from another planet. i'm exaggerating, but this is at least a few noticeable frames, which is far too much for a "hardcore" (lol) game. the star recall mechanic is absolutely miserable, often resulting in cancelling stars you needed to keep. disabling this mechanic of course kneecaps the game in a new and exciting way: stars will stay active offscreen for *ages*, so you can't just wait for one to leave before recalling. this is especially troublesome with the "star-lock" """"puzzles"""" littered throughout.the window for being able to land on a star after it hits a wall is terribly poor. the whole deal with gimmick is that as soon as a star exists, you can interact with it. being forced to be [x] distance from the wall or wait [x] amount of time before getting on the star just makes the whole thing feel like an ordeal.the levels are over-long and nothing happens. the traps and tricks all operate on tripping the player up through ignorance of the setpiece rather than inviting the player to actually learn anything. nothing here feels like an "aha" moment, just "wtf am i supposed to do?" followed by "ok, sure, whatever." it takes great joy in just dropping enemies on your head for no discernable reason, even if we are to include comedic gags at the player's expense - which the original gimmick has a few of. i do not feel invited to laugh *with* this game, however.as i mentioned in my gimmick special edition review (see: , i have reasonably intimate familiarity with gimmick, having played it for many years, owned a cartridge, having one-life-cleared it several times, etc. tomomi sakai's design work on that game continues to impress me hundreds of plays later. i cannot emphaisze enough that "gimmick 2" is as close as you can get to missing the point, and that is heartbreaking. i do not wish to spend more time with this. if it gets better, so be it. it should not need time to "get better" and i should not be spending nearly 30 minutes in the first nothing-stage solving nothing-puzzles and being hit by nothing-traps only to fight an extremely nothing-boss.to move beyond the gameplay, this game is not particularly easy on the eyes. another review called it "peggle 2" art and i am inclined to agree. it is just unappealing across the board, with the exception of the checkpoint character, who is adorable. it bewilders me that a famicom game released in 1992 with graphics by a single person has more character than this.the audio merely exists. the music is passable, but why this? why this cutesy chamber band stuff? i am 100% onboard with shaking up a formula, but the thing is that gimmick barely had the chance to develop one in its very short original run time. wouldn't it make more sense to continue to explore that? there's so much lovely jazz (as you would expect from a sax player) completely left on the cutting room floor here in favor of... i'm not even sure what. it's so limp, so simple, so acceptable, and utterly boring.i completed a single stage of this game before deciding that there is no way this can be worth my time or money. not recommended in any way, shape, or form. i will likely never write something so scathing about a game again in my life.
_childDocuments_.name: Gimmick! 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fine enough game, I just can't really recommend it in good faith to anyone. Platformers are my absolute favorite genre of games and I absolutely love me a good 2D platformer, but Gimmick 2 is kinda just. Just okay. It definitely does feel like Gimmick, the physics and the star bouncing feel as clean and fun to utilize as the original in my opinion, but that's kind of where the Gimmick-isms end. At it's core, Gimmick 2 is just a very safe game. When Gimmick 1 is so bombastic and full of energy in it's environments and soundtrack, it makes it very hard to look at Gimmick 2 and feel like this is supposed to be a true sequel. The aesthetic of Gimmick is kinda what made it stick out to me so Gimmick 2 having absolutely none of the sauce is upsetting. There's a few times where they do remix music from Gimmick 1 (the intro did make me smile), but having these songs here honestly detriments the game by just showing how BORING the rest of the soundtrack is. It's all serene soothing environmental tracks that all just kinda blend into one another, I can't say I remember a single track, but every song in Gimmick 1 stands out in my mind. I think the closest this game got to feeling like Gimmick 1 in personality was the lava factory level. David Wise is an excellent composer but he just wasn't the right pick for something like this. It's a cult classic and very niche game that's most known for how far it pushed it's soundtrack on limiting hardware. The peaceful music is good it just. It's not Gimmick. It's not. Spoilers for the true ending too but  But the OST of this game kind of represents everything that's wrong about Gimmick 2. Like I said, having songs from the first game kind of hurt the rest of the OST, and the same can be said when you just compare 2 to its NES predecessor. The environments in 2 are just the boring grass jungle ice fire etc etc. The fish factory and the final level were pretty interesting visually though I'll give them that, but the rest kinda just lacks any originality. There's a lack of any flair or twist to stages that made basic environments in Gimmick 1 feel fresh (especially with it's soundtrack backing these locations up). It all feels safe, derivative, and that's everything but Gimmick.There's only a handful of levels too which for $25 is like... okay... but they're all like 20-30 minutes long on your first go. I wasn't expecting them to be so long given the fast paced nature of the first game, but I get that this game wanted to try something new. It just. didn't land for me. The levels are tough, but there's a lot of cheapness to it. A lof of rooms with tiny blocks with really annoying enemy placements or like "this enemy auto aims at you have fun" (it's not fun!). The last level is especially guilty of small platform jumps it's just so cheap of a solution to making "difficulty." I think Gimmick 1 had a lot of cheap moments like that too but at least those levels are short. These levels being long was just not the right call for a game like this. Not to mention there were a lot of leap-of-faith moments which are also never fun. A hard platformer needs to let you know what's coming up, Celeste even gives you binoculars in bigger rooms to give you an idea of what's coming up. Gimmick 2 feels like it actively hates you.The best part of the game are the secret bonus/treasure rooms. They use a song from Gimmick 1 so that's a plus but good luck finding them. I played before any patches so it may be different now but it still soured my experience that so many bonus rooms were just impossible to find. A lot of the time they had no hints, no changes in the environment, and placed somewhere you'd avoid (the pirate ship was especially guilty of this, those secrets were total garbage to find). I'm sure now with the updates they're better, but that doesn't save you from the rest of the game just being kinda whatever. It's just not super fun, I can't seem to play more than a level at a time because I feel so slogged or whatever by the end of one. It's insanely different from Celeste where it's longer level format has the levels evolve and change and grow (not to mention, it just has a good OST and presentation). The levels here feel like you're just playing a really long. hard level. that's it. that's all there is to it.It's kinda sad when the most this game has going for it in sauce for me is the menu UI. I like that a lot. I thought it was also cute that to pick the difficulty setting you had to make a bunch of tight jumps too, But.... yeah...It's just a very forgettable, very safe game, I applaud Bitwave for caring so much about a cult classic but it REALLY shows that they didn't reach out to the original developers of the first game or anything. It doesn't just not feel like GImmick 1, it just doesn't feel like anything at all. I can't say I got anything out of this game. It's fine enough platforming there's definitely worse out there but there's nothing special I can really say about this game other than that "wow we really have Gimmick 2 now."I'm happy that many people seem to enjoy this game, I just don't think it's something I can recommend when a game like Celeste is like $5 and infinitely more valuable of an experience.

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD:-Physics, difficulty level, and puzzles seem to be on par with the original.-Cosmetics are a neat addition that adds some replay value-Yumetaro squeaks like a squeaky toy when hurtTHE BAD:-"Peggle 2" shovelware art style-Has all the stylistic trappings of an indie Xbox 360 game from 2008, which would be fine for back then, except it's 2024 now.-David Wise's soundtrack, while cute, ends up coming off a bit mawkish, and does not at all capture the edgy, jazz-fusion spirit of "Gimmick".THE UGLY:-I experienced input lag to a degree which I have never encountered before on any game I've played on my PC. I'm talking about an entire  between me pressing the jump button and the character on screen jumping. This is with a gaming monitor, beefy CPU and GPU.-The game crashed on the first level when I tried to change the resolution in the pause menu. It no longer boots at all. I have to refund it.-This game made a bit of a stink on social media due to its "mobile game"-like presentation, along with the fact that its devs did not make any effort to consult the original producer of the game, Tomomi Sakai, during any part of development, despite him being very active and accessible online. As a result, a number of the original's fans feel that this sequel was mishandled.

_childDocuments_.review: Terribly Disappointing gameIt`s obvious that the project was handled by people who were simply given the task of making a game, and who were not interested in the project itself. It's looks like poorest copy of they previous game - Wunderling DXSince only the mr.gimmick name remains from the game.Unusual situations, traps, various eccentric creatures, some of which do not even attack you, a surreal fairy-tale world and soulful music. All this is not here.Absolutely random poor locations, with backgrounds like in mobile games. A reduced bestiary of enemies, in the original even the black creatures had different sprites and abilities, here the same opponents will run throughout the game without even a drop of creativity, boring bosses - one of which is an ordinary enemy from the previous game, who was made the boss here in first level. =/The original surprised by oddities, because it was not focused on one thing, in one moment we can solve a puzzle, dodge traps, but in second moment we are just peacefully floating on the head of a pink dinosaur, who can also start attacking us if you hit him.In the sequel, everything is focused on fast jumps and solving "puzzles" using an asterisk, the locations in such cases are not expressive and are more reminiscent of randomly generated levels with the goal of leading your character from point A to point B.They are trying to attract the player's attention with a huge number of secrets, but this is just stupid cosmetics that does not bring anything interesting to the game.It is not clear for whom the sequel was created, the game has a very small audience, and given the course the developers have chosen, this will alienate some of the remaining fans.

_childDocuments_.review: im only one level in so far (will be explained later) but this really is a great gamethis is the sequel to a notoriously tough Famicom game and though there is an assist mode the normal mode pulls no punches BUTIt has great physics and controls to where you know when you die in a level it's your fault, and the checkpoint system is very merciful even in normal modeit's less frustrating and more "i wanna keep playing", kinda how hotline Miami wasthe art is beautiful and the sound and music by legendary composer David Wise is fantasticim very happy to get to play this, ill have to get through more to decide but it might be my GOTYit's only $25 too, get it!

_childDocuments_.review: It's not clear whether it was intentional or not, but they somehow missed what made Gimmick Gimmick.I wouldn't say the music is bad, but it's a big contrast to the original's upbeat style. The style they've chosen for this sequel just doesn't fit for a Gimmick game.In terms of gameplay, I think Gimmick controls pretty much the same way as he did in the original. That's about all the positives I can think of though. The levels, enemies and bosses are pretty uninspiring, and most of the challenging sections in this game feel a bit cheap. More often than not such sections are just filled with things like multiple enemies that shoot across the room or other cheap tactics to make the game appear difficult. The original game didn't have anything like this and still managed to be challenging in it's own way without the tediousness.Another huge shame in my opinion is the art style they've chosen to go with here. As others have already said, it just looks like your average cheap mobile game. Given that Gimmick on the Famicom was one of the best-looking games on the entire system, makes this hurt even more.I say, if you really, really liked the first game maybe give this one a try and just refund it if you don't enjoy it.Personally though, i wouldn't really recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Gimmick 2 takes the premise of Gimmick, strips away much of the game's original mechanics (score, lives, items) and instead chooses to focus purely on the Star Throw mechanic. The star's physics have been changed to make the mechanic more accessible, but not in a way that compromises the game feel. The game controls very smoothly and with the precision necessary to enjoy its often VERY challenging platforming sequences. In particular the game's secret areas are completely delightful, and I recommend doing all of them. Solving these complex platforming puzzles and then executing on their mechanical challenge is deeply, deeply satisfying in a way that 2D platformers can rarely manage.All that said, I do think that that the original Gimmick has a je ne sais quoi that isn't captured here. There are lots of small differences, the first world being a standard, platformer grassland is a big let down. The boss fights are much less organic, the world isn't as cohesive, the game's story feels like an afterthought. Lots of environmental assets don't feel like they really belong in the game's art style, and at worst some of them look like they might be reused from a different project.Gimmick 2's large scale level design is much more comparable to Super Meat Boy than Gimmick 1. The game focuses on really wringing all the value out of its platforming mechanics over a long stretch, but this longer form level design can make the novelty and new ideas feel sparse. This is a really noticeable problem for Gimmick 2, since the original game was just non-stop creativity.I felt it was important to share these gripes to be clear that Gimmick 2 is not an entirely faithful sequel. Despite that, I still enjoyed the game. Even if it heavily departs from the original, it succeeds in its new direction. Purely as a precision platformer, I recommend the game highly.

_childDocuments_.review: I have never made a serious review in my 9 years on Steam, but Gimmick is important to me and I felt this is warranted. I wish I could choose a "maybe recommend" option because this game has a lot of things going for it, but I'll say I'd recommend it because of what it has going for it. Turning Gimmick into a puzzle, precision platformer was a good idea, but I believe that it was handled poorly.Let's get the good out of the way:- The physics and gameplay are enjoyable enough and reminiscent enough to the original Gimmick. Platforming is fun and a lot of the challenges are interesting, especially in the secret areas. Some parts take deep thinking and usually there's different ways to solve the same problem. After beating the game I looked at how some people tackled some sections and it was totally different to how I was doing it. I find that interesting and speedrunning-wise has a lot of appeal.- Being able to get rid of your star was such a good quality of life improvement. Not needing to hold the button to form a star was also a good control change. I also believe that using the star ability to its fullest potential with puzzles based around it was the right direction to go in.The mediocre:- The soundtrack is pretty plain. Some songs incorporate the main theme in there somewhere, sorta like Super Mario World's soundtrack, and it works pretty well. The problem is the soundtrack is just uninteresting. David Wise has worked on some pretty incredible game soundtracks. This is not one of them and they have the balls to use his name as a selling point.- Some secrets are so beyond cryptic that I had to use a guide to figure them out. How was I supposed to know that one unassuming wall can just be gone straight through for a secret? How was I supposed to even consider that bringing the frog somewhere completely different would reveal a pipe in the ceiling? Any other time I brought the frog off the beaten path, I got nothing. I find that "go through the wall" secrets work best when there's a subtle indication that you can actually go through the wall. In a lot of cases, there is no indication, but sometimes there is. It's just so inconsistent.The bad:- The levels have good ideas, but when those ideas drag on for 20 minutes it becomes boring. A Mega Man or even an original Gimmick level is like, what, maybe 5 or 10 minutes? You get bite sized ideas in a short, condensed level that doesn't overstay its welcome. Everything in this game felt like it dragged on forever. The bosses, the levels, the puzzles. Halfway through each level I was just kind of waiting for it to end. At least the game saves on checkpoints so I could come back to the lengthy misery a bit later. Instead of like 5 levels that are 20 minutes long I would've much preferred 10 levels that are 10 minutes long.- Where are the items that enemies drop? To me, that was an integral part of the original Gimmick, and they just don't exist here. I understand that score doesn't exist in this game and that's how item drops were determined, but they could've made it luck based or have a secret score or something. These items could've offered a few more ideas within levels, maybe having them out in the open to use like the frog or be used for secrets.- The artstyle is horrible. I'm not going to sugarcoat it because it genuinely looks awful. In-game there appears to be no real anti-aliasing, and on my 1440p monitor every environment has awful looking jagged edges. So, not only is the style itself similar to those bootleg Mario elf games on mobile phones, it looks even worse due to jagged edges. Since Ufouria The Saga 2 went for more of a fabric, a la Yoshi's Woolly World, type of feel I was thinking maybe a potential Gimmick sequel would have a similar style; or a claymation style like the original Japanese box art (which would've been awesome).A few misc. notes:- Some people talked about input delay being bad (up to half a second!) but I experienced nothing of the sort. This is coming from someone who practically always needs to use a CRT TV for platformers. I mean that's what I beat the original Gimmick on. I also don't have a low lag monitor, so I don't know what problems people are having.- If you haven't played the original Gimmick then play that first. In my eyes, you can't appreciate what this game is trying to do without playing the original first.Comparing this to Ufouria The Saga 2, I think this game has a lot more ambition and a lot more ideas. The issue is the game is inconsistent with these ideas. I hope my thoughts are taken into consideration for a hypothetical Gimmick 3. I personally enjoyed what the game was trying to be; a puzzle platformer, but I think it wasn't executed correctly and could use some polish for a third game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a game so thoroughly that I lost track of time & didn't want to stop.I don't usually write reviews, but I hope this is helpful to anyone afraid this looks too hard. I can't recommend this game highly enough. Played on Steam Deck OledDifficulty: Gimmick  (I think assist just lets you take 2 more hits before respawning at the last checkpoint.)This is one of the best games I've ever played.  Level design is perfect. Pacing from room to room feels great slowing down for more pensive puzzles & picking up for some quick sprints.  It never feels repetitive, always engaging. I've only seen the first 2 levels, but only had to watch play footage for 2 very well hidden secrets in order to 100% both.Retry is quick. I never became frustrated repeating attempts to alter how I was throwing the star, retrying a very tight jump, etc.Controls are perfectLevel design feels perfect; watching other people play, it's great to see there are multiple ways to solve some rooms, allowing for player creativity (rather than forcing the player to memorize a series of strict inputs like a human TAS player.)I'm not great at hard games; don't play for long sessions to grind levels out. Love the idea of Kaizo, but can't beat even the easiest ones (control and speed seem to be my issues). I've only played 2 days and I was already able to 100% the 1st 2 levels, but there were 2 secrets I had to find through watching others' playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: Gimmick 2 is overall a great platformer and in my opinion a worthy followup to the original cult classic NES game. Though if you're expecting it to be the exact same as the original with more levels and prettier graphics you may be slightly disappointed.Gimmick 2 is much more of a precision puzzle platformer compared to the original, featuring frequent checkpoints and quick respawns. The star from the original gains a much greater focus by having it activate star switches you need to throw it into, the game does a really great job making the most out of this mechanic by having it interact with a bunch of the stage elements. The level design in general is really good, I especially liked all the setups with the enemies in combination with the star platforms/pipes.One thing I'm still a bit unsure about though is the instant star cancel, it makes sense that you can instantly recall the star when it's locked inside of a switch but not being able to charge up a second star while your first one is out made enemy encounters feel awkward at times, I did get more used to it as the game progressed though.One thing I really liked about this game was the secrets, the main path doesn't ask anything to complex of the player but if you want to get to the secrets you'll really need to get good at using your star as a platform, especially the secret treasure areas will test your platforming abilities and I found them to be a lot of fun to beat. The amount of secrets present helps a lot as well, the original hardly ever asked you to get good at using your star despite it being a central mechanic which made it feel underutilized, I think the sequel does a good job of addressing this by adding tons of optional stuff without destroying the overall flow of the level. I ended up liking the customization features you get from these secrets a lot more than I initially expected as well, they're a great motivator.This ended up being addressed in an update woo! Something I think is lacking compared to the original is the stage themes, the original did a great job of featuring thematic progression inside of the levels that made a each stage feel more like a full world you're exploring. This game still features some of that but to a lesser extent and some levels more than others, stage 2 for instance is a mostly nondescript jungle/temple area and felt bland as a result. This is in contrast to stage 4, which ended up being one of my favorite levels. I believe it's the longest stage in the game but the thematic progression here kept everything extremely fun and interesting. Similarly, the amount of memorable setpieces is more lacking compared to the original as well, that's not to say they're not there, they're just taking a pretty big backseat in favor of the gameplay and level design.Adding onto this, I don't have too much to say about the visuals, they look colorful and nice and they do their job well. The music is also really nice, I'm not totally sure if David Wise was the best fit for a sequel to Gimmick but I can appreciate his work knowing that this game is simply going for its own thing.A last couple of minor gripes I want to get out of the way, I do feel the enemy variety is a bit lacking and the bosses aren't as dynamic compared to the original,  (this got addressed as well). Also, the lack of items like in the original feels like a huge missed opportunity since the consumable attacks would've been much more interesting to use when you're unable to use your star. Still, I think despite all this the game really excels at the aspects it ended up focusing in on and I thoroughly enjoyed it for what it was.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, great sequel. I wish the levels could have been shorter - I'd prefer more levels with less collectibles as the longer 30-40 min stages start to drag after a while. The secret item rooms were fun and very challenging, the game definitely stays true to the difficulty of the original. The final level was also really cool - they really go all out with the star projectile puzzles. A lot of love was put into this game and it shows I recommend Gimmick 2. There are a lot of games that are cheaper than this so If the price seems like too much I'd get it on sale. If you're a huge fan of the OG this game is a must-play!

_childDocuments_.review: Now before 2024, if you told a gamer that a sequel to Gimmick! is coming and composed by David Wise, 99.9% of the listeners wouldn't believe you.Here we are.So I have beaten everything(?*) and here are my thoughts.Is it brutal?Not always but at times it can, this is especially true when hunting down secret treasures in later levels and the boss fights in the last level, those parts I can easily say were harder than Gimmick 1.Fortunately this higher difficulty is somewhat remedied by using the more forgiving checkpoint system and having infinite lives, trust me if this level design was a thing in the 90s with limited lives, no passwords, etc, it would've been a super duper tough game to beat.Is the music great?Yes, there's fewer remixes from the first game than expected but the new tracks really fits the puzzle platforming aspect well. Tadpole Temple at the start has DKC Tropical Freeze vibes (David Wise composed that game and this one btw) and Fishy Factory's Warehouse segment is one of my favourites as you get to hear that sonar like sfx you probably heard in Goldeneye N64's pause theme.Length:Much longer than expected as well. The size of each map per level is roughly 10-15 times longer than the original, part of this is thanks to an extra task for 100% completion, finding all cosmetic treasures (over 10 per level) that can alter Yumetaro's appearance from skin colour, horn design, hat design and star colour, some of them are easy to find, others will have your head scratching for a while. Another big contribution to the overall playtime it takes to 100% is trying to collect a late game secret treasure for the first time. For example, the last two secret treasures can easily take 30-40 minutes if not a lot longer depending on your gaming skill in general. I'd say these parts were still brutal on the easier "Assist" difficulty, perhaps add some extra platforms or some checkpoints in those areas, I don't think many younger players will have the mental patience on completing those levels.Game mechanics:Easy to learn, hard to master feel is still there but gone are the secondary items including HP potions, that's still okay as Assist difficulty gives you 5 HP whereas Gimmick difficulty only gives you 3 HP.Overall, this is a "better than expected 2D platformer". Yes there will be some difficulty spikes when figuring some stuff out but in most cases, you'll be very satisfied when you finally figured out the solution that has been blocking you for quite some time.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the original, I'm really enjoying this so far having completed the first two levels! There are some little vignettes between challenges which I appreciate but it doesn't go as far as the original did, but I think that is understandable given how much emphasis the game's mechanics were given here compared to the original. _childDocuments_.review: I love the original Gimmick! on Famicom, and I always thought that the star mechanic, which acts both as an attack and a platform, was genius, yet underutilized since we had only one game. Until now! I was pleasantly surprised to see a sequel pop up this year!So, how does Gimmick! 2 fare? Gameplay-wise, the star mechanics feel just as good as the original, with all the different speeds and angles you can throw it with. Gimmick! 2 invites you to experiment with these too, with well-hidden secret areas that will test your skills to the limits with some extremely well-crafted levels that genuinely surprised me. Solving and completing these secret levels is very satisfying.There are more uses for the star, which includes throwing it into these star gates. These activate platforms, spawn enemies, or cause other changes depending on what the level throws at you. It's versatile, yet builds on the original mechanic and adds more puzzle elements to the game. A nice quality of life feature this depends on is the ability to recall the star at any time. In the original game, you had to wait for the star to disappear, which left you vulnerable in the meantime. Instead of lives, Gimmick! 2 opts for a Rayman Origins-esque approach with checkpoints at each section, allowing you to retry as much as you like....However, that's about all Gimmick! 2 stands out in. What it's lacking is the essence and energy of the original game. Aside from the excellent (!) remixes of some of the original music tracks, I'm disappointed that none of the music really stood out and was more ambient instead of action-packed. The world themes were visually also more generic, with a grass plain world for the first level.On top of that, I felt the levels were too long. The first level took me 30 minutes to complete, with some others taking even longer. I would have preferred shorter levels that are more concise and challenging, closer to the original game. The only difficult part of some sections would be a pixel-perfect jump or some inconvenient enemy placement, which I found frustrating more than challenging.The length of the levels also exasperates finding collectibles. One very nice thing is it shows which general parts of the level (split up into numbered checkpoints) you're missing a collectible in. However, I feel there should've been a way to jump to each numbered checkpoint from the menu because I found it inconvenient to restart the level or trek through the rest of one area just to go to where I want to be.The level that I think the rest of the game should've followed was the , which involved concise, difficult sections that naturally progressed....The graphics are good, and they somehow managed to make the Ohagis adorable! The menus are actually so beautiful that it's a wonder the developers put so much effort into them when there are only a few across the whole game. Parts of me wish Yumetaro still had his "sliding" walking animation from the first game.So, overall? I would recommend Gimmick! 2, but I would say don't play it expecting a true sequel to the original game. The parts it does well are done superbly, and I think it's a great experience regardless.Here's hoping to more Gimmick! in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Gimmick! 2

_childDocuments_.review: A fun-puzzle platformer that stands well on its own, but overall pales in comparison to its predecessor.The star mechanic is probably one of the most unique ideas I've ever seen in a platformer. A star is pulled out, thrown, and must be used to destroy enemies. Sounds simple enough, but it also has a complete physics system behind it that allows it to bounce off walls, objects, and at times must be used as a platform to reach higher, secret areas. Some QOL improvements were made to this including the ability to "recall" the star, instead of waiting for it to run out and be a sitting duck. Not having to worry about number of lives remaining is also nice as game-overing in the original booted you to the beginning of each level, and also prevented you from seeing its true ending...If there is a single word I can use to describe the level design, it would definitely be "safe". The star switch puzzles are simple, creative, but get tedious and repetitive when you realise how egregiously long the levels are. Just going along the main path can take upwards of 15 - 20 minutes; longer if you decide to go for secrets. The bolder and more creative designs are reserved for the big secrets that are required to unlock the final boss. I wish this carried through for the main path as the original wasn't shy to throw every creative trick it had at you, whether it be an environmental obstacle, a strong enemy, or even requiring the star to be bounced and ridden on in a specific way. One could even call these designs unfair and "kaizo" at times, but I also feel encompasses what made Gimmick! Gimmick! The game may as well be called "Fair!"Bosses in this game are surprisingly dull, save for the True Last Boss (TLB). The first few are easy and fair, but the ones later on aren't even fights but rather surviving some enemy spitting contraption, an auto scroller, or just surviving being chased by multiple rolling rocks. The original had you fight a pirate, a snail, a newly hatched bird, and a deadly robot spider. One of the minibosses (soldier with shield and wand) in the original was "upgraded" to a boss, yet this fight I would say was even easier since there are only one of them, and the harder phase just lazily spawns enemies and arrow shooters. I think the only memorable boss fight was the TLB with its multiple phases. Music.... I'll be honest, I don't really like it. As legendary as Dave Wise is, the music for the game is really ambient, atmospheric and relaxing; which is nothing like the original where the music was very up-beat, melodic, and complemented the hecticness, and dynamic gameplay. The original intro theme was one of the best and most recognizable themes on the NES, and the remix for it seems mellowed out and less impactful. There were a few good tracks such as "Lava", but for the most part I feel like many tracks feel out of place and is something you would find in a game like LittleBigPlanet.Aside from that, I think the game overall stands well enough on its own and can be enjoyed by a modern audience. The star mechanic alone is what sets it apart from other platformers. I would also suggest trying the original if you haven't already, yet I would also exercise caution for some of its brutally difficult gameplay and bold level design.

_childDocuments_.review: Charming platformer with a great gimmick (ha) and deceptive difficulty. Levels are well designed, and the design space of the central ability is nicely utilized even if it's not quite as polished as some of its peers (Celeste). Excellent game for those who like learning through brute force (i.e. dying quite a lot), and I mean that as a compliment. I'm sure speedruns will look bananas.
_childDocuments_.name: Gimmick! 2

_childDocuments_.review: Gimmick 2's creative use of the star eclipses the original.While they're both great games, I really appreciate that they leaned into the star mechanics for the sequel. The star switches, frogs, breakable ice, these new ideas fit in so naturally I couldn't believe they didn't think of them for the first game.They did a great job getting the player comfortable with using the star, after a while you'll be doing crazy jumps and skips without even thinking about it.The levels themselves also have great variety, you go from fast platforming, to combat, to puzzle solving, and even borderline kaizo challenges all in one level. It gets difficult, but the frequent checkpoints keep you encouraged, and the hidden collectables and secret areas keep you engaged.I never imagined we would get a sequel to Gimmick, and the fact that 30 years after the original's release we got one that's as great as this is a dream come true

name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate
detailed_description: Grab your friends, pick your favorite Turtle and jump into a roguelike adventure to save Master Splinter from the foot clan! Master ninja skills, unite in bodacious online and local co-op gameplay, and conquer iconic NYC locales. In In TMNT Splintered Fate, brace yourself for fast-paced, roguelike action where no two runs are the same. With randomized power-ups, room layouts, and boss modifiers, the excitement never ends. Take control of all four Turtles, each wielding unique powers, and team up with friends for bodacious co-op gameplay. Explore iconic NYC locations, upgrade your Turtle powers, and prepare to face off against formidable enemies. Master the powers of water and fire, utrom and ooze, light and darkness, and -most importantly- Ninja to create unique and bodacious builds for your Turtles. Every run brings new challenges and opportunities - explore and perfect your favorite builds, and combine them with allies to conquer your enemies. When Splinter is kidnapped by Shredder, mysterious portals simultaneously appear across NYC. Be ready to restore peace to the city!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid roguelike action game for a licensed IP. It borrows a lot from Hades, in a good way, both in combat and how characters interact and how the story is delivered. Personally I think it's awesome, specially if you're a TMNT fan, there's some very interesting / funny dialogue between the whole cast.Don't expect the same level of challenge that comes from playing Hades btw, Splintered Fate is doing its own thing at the end of the day. I think meta progression and stats values (unfortunately at times, when enemy hordes with armor and excessive AOE attacks get out of control) plays a bigger role in combat here compared to Hades, it's a fun time nonetheless if you manage your expectations. It takes inspiration from Hades but it doesn't need to be a 1:1 copy of the game.Also there's 4 players local couch co-op support and that alone will always deserve an easy thumbs up in my book in this day and age. It kinda scratch that Marvel Ultimate Alliance / X-Men Legends itch in a way.Last but not least, the soundtrack goes HARD, the voice acting is amazing and the artist who drew the characters did some top tier job.Overall it's a solid game, nothing mindblowing tbh but pretty good stuff anyways. The developers announced a roadmap with plenty of new content that's coming in the future, very promising stuff imo bc I feel like this game has a lot of untapped potential to be one the best games in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate might be one of the better TMNT games out there, but it does lack in a few areas and has A LOT to talk about.First, the gameplay in run upgrades. It's very similar to Hades in that regard. You pick your turtle, each one having their own weapon with a special ability, and a tool. The tools and special abilities charge based on damage, and in a run you can swap out your tool if you see fit. There is an okay amount of build variety with upgrades. You have damage overtimes with flame, ooze (poison), ultrom (shock), and more. You have your simple upgrades of damage, attack speed, etc, and even health upgrades. While the turtles all have different moves, they also have different 'inspirations' which act as passive buffs in a run. Raph has higher crit chance and damage, Leo lets you have two charges of special, Mikey has higher multi-hit chance, and Donny restores HP when entering a room (which is nice in the early game), but you can still gain other turtles inspirations in the run which makes the turtles less unique. I find myself enjoying Raph and Mikey the most because of their movesets. Those are upgrades in a run, they're fine. The combat is kind of simple and the enemies never really change mid run besides getting stronger, which isn't that big of a deal. You have four biomes, all ending with a boss and having a miniboss, shop, and regular encounters. While that is fine, it doesn't seem to have much inspiration elsewhere and the runs become a bit monotonous towards the end as it's just a crazy amount of enemies, and some of them have WAY too much armor. Regular rooms are harder than mini bosses in the third and fourth (mostly fourth) biome because enemies can take a solid 30 seconds to kill because armor. The bosses aren't that bad, they're fun to play against, and a little tanky, but you can get a busted build to melt them, but armored enemies is just straight up terrible, even with the upgrade to do more damage to armor. So, combat as a whole is solid, but can feel a bit boring after a handful of runs.Now where the game struggles and shines at the same time is meta progression. In your runs you gain dragon coins and dreamer coins. Dragon coins upgrade the turtles with every basic upgrade. Health, speed, damage, crit chance, health restored, being able to find health mid run (very important to get), attack speed, you name it. Bascially EVERYTHING is upgraded with Dragon coins, everything that will make runs easier, and that is just kind of bland to me. I don't mind meta progression in a game like this, but it just feels so uninspired, and with that normal runs, and especially difficulty enhanced runs won't feel too winnable until X amount of upgrades. A bit unfortunate but it is what it is, you still have more meta progression with dreamer coins. These allow you to upgrade artifacts you can find (buffs in a run, kinda like keepsakes in Hades), and upgrade more economic benefits. Starting a run with more scrap, higher chance for higher level upgrades, that type of stuff. I like the Dreamer coin upgrades more in terms of they feel more inspired, but Dragon coins are definitely more valuable.Last I want to talk about difficulty. A big one to a lot of people. This game is VERY easy, or very hard. you unlock difficulty enhancers by clearing the game once (took me about 7 hours), and the enhancers aren't that bad. You can go through a portal in certain levels to add a difficulty enhancer for the run and gain more dragon/dreamer coins. These are okay, and some of the enhancers are well thought of. Certain enemies do more damage, less upgrade choices, shops cost more, etc. Those are fine and can definitely up the difficulty of a normal run, as a normal run is VERY easy up until chapter 4 (for me atleast now that I'm 12 hours in as of writing this). The only chapter 4 issue is armored enemies. Base runs are kinda easy once you get into the meat and bones, but one thing that REALLY gets hard is boss fights, they straight up feel unwinnable with these enhancers. Once cleared a run, every boss and miniboss can be turned into a gauntlet for added difficulty, and the minibosses, they aren't too hard. Adds a good challenge most of the time without feeling totally unfair with enemies all spamming lasers and shurikens at you, but the bosses... holy god man/ I've only cleared the first boss with a gauntlet mode and it was just straight up terrible. I lost both of my revives, the boss was SUPER tanky, and spawned CONSTANT enemies throwing down AOE's and spamming poison rats at me. It felt like it was hard just to be hard and not to have any fun. There is no in between from a super easy boss fight to unfairly hard which is disappointing for me. At the end of the day I do think this is a good game and I'd recommend it. It's a very nice TMNT game, and a nice change of pace from the typical beat em ups. I do think their is a decent amount of balance issues with armored enemies, gauntlets for bosses, and meta progression feeling so uninspired, but at it's core, the gameplay is well done and I've enjoyed my time with it. I fully want to beat it and hopefully will have the time to. Even if I stopped playing today at 12-13 hours in, I'll say my purchase was worth the moneyEDIT*Forgot to mention this game does have multiplayer outside of local co-op. I only played it for about 30 minutes, but it ran well with two random people. I noticed the difference in attacks instantly because of delay, but once you adapt to it the game runs VERY well for co-op. Good to play with friends if that's your style! (and you all get your own upgrades, meta progression, etc)

_childDocuments_.review: Played this on switch and loved it, had to pick it up for PC to play with my PC buds. Its a simple to pick up Rougelike but has a really fun skill ceiling. I would say if you are looking for the complexity of Hades or Dead Cells you are not going to get it, but if you want a fun arcade style beat-um up Rougelike than this is a good option. Its not super hard like I said but its fun all the way through and builds are unqiue enough to be fun. Give it a try if you are a fan of Rouges or Beatum ups. Also makes an amazing couch co-op game.

_childDocuments_.review: -Many different perks and upgrades that can be combined to a new one.-Many cameos of characters from the whole TMNT universe.-Graphics is okaaay, but there is no support 21:9 resolution (new release and again).-many bugs, much more than on the iPhone’s release.-the game supports playing with a keyboard and mouse, but it feels very poorly and buggy, so for comfort experience play on a gamepad only.-added a searching for a OPEN game (on the iPhone you could only play with friends by invitation), and now there is a crossplay.-you can play with 3 friends, but if you are from different regions, instead of lags, the game will slow down accordingly, and it feels like you play at 20 fps. While when playing from the same region - everything works quite well.-the difficulty scales very strangely when playing online: if when playing in two, the health of enemies is not greatly boosted, but when you playing full party, enemies become just sponges for damage, and bosses goes absolutely nightmare.-not enough content: the same bosses (4 ) every time, the same locations (also 4), all it gets boring. Although the conditions, boss variations and leveling up will be different each time, but this does not save the situation much.-$30 full price? That’s to much, worth it only if you fan of TMNT. Other way - $15 will a good price for game with all this contents. But I’m fan and complete this game and on Apple Arcade and on Steam.   There are achievements that depend on the difficulty of the run, but this can be solved by global leveling up the characters, For the normal passage of the most difficult run I needed complete about 40 runs in total. The only one achievement with “right” suicide can be problem, but at the end game you will understand how to do it for unlock by yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Once again Steam needs more then thumbs up and thumbs down.The Game is absolutely playable.  there is a decent section of abilities and upgrades that they seem to have put more thought in then just numerical changes.  The game play feels decent and there is a legitimate challenge.THAT BEING SAIDThere is such a ridiculous lack of polish for a game that thinks its worth $30.  Text wont fit in the frames they provide for it.  Pressing the button to get more information or to compare upgrades makes too many additional windows.  Pop up windows to explain things not going away.  Sometimes in multiplayer one player wont be able to access the shop or artifact select in a shop room.Is the game fun?  Yes, absolutely.  Me and a couple friends will probably sink 20-40 hours into this game before moving on.  But how does the game stand up to its peers at this price point?  Honestly not great.  You are paying a lot of money for the TMNT IP.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the better TMNT games out there besides Shredder's Revenge, Mutants in Manhattan was decent too but no longer on Steam, Splintered Fate does lack alot of depth compared to other rogue likes in the genre, but the story isn't too bad albeit slighly short and repetitive but most rogue likes don't even have a story anyway, the grind for permanent upgrades is addictive and it does give a sense of a huge power creep once fully maxed in everything, tons of build variations to mess with, there is Meta builds going around, Shurikens/ Dash builds, if you know you know but there is still alot of build variety, if you mix and match specific elements you can get a chance at a legendary in the upgrades screen, Astral/Water will give you HP back on hit for e.g, google the rest of the combos, it'll help alot in your runs, personally I'm grinding to max out everything in order to help others online which is endless replayability to me, others I've seen drop the game within 2 hrs or so which is not enough time to give it, you have to beat Shredder I think 7 times or more, each time you do the game changes up Spawns, you'll encounter Mystic and Shadow versions of bosses changing up their attacks/patterns, you'll get access to Portals with negative modifiers for 10% Currency gain, Gauntlet versions of bosses, all unlocked after beating the game, if you're huge TMNT fan don't drop it within 2 hrs, keep grinding the game gets better the longer you play, there is also a roadmap for future DLC via, new playable characters,levels,enemies,bosses, story & more, catch you in game, Cowabunga dudes!

_childDocuments_.review: You'll keep hearing this game is TMNT mixed with Hades and this is mostly right. The game may seem short but the runs will have completely new powers and gameplay variations. The element system is cool and the voice acting is great which is often hit or miss in TMNT games. Online co-op and the promise from developers that more characters and environments are on the way justify the overall package.
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate

_childDocuments_.review: Had alot of fun playing this as a fan of Hades and TMNT in general. The biggest selling points are multiplayer and the unique abilities of the turtles. As it stands right now, this game is basically alot more simplified in terms of how you get stronger: As you do maps, you get Dragon and Dreamer currency to buff up. Eventually, the price gets too steep or requires you to do challenges to unlock more powerful stuff, but the important thing is that once you unlock enough stuff early on, the game becomes much easier without the challenges. Story-wise, the game surprisingly is taking a much longer route than other games. Once you expect to beat the boss, you then realize the post-game content is actually where the meat of the game heads towards and is actually where the heart of the game goes. You can breeze through the story once you're familiar enough with the game and bought enough buffs (Or you can just play Easy mode. Definitely not a bad option) you can proceed to just finish the story in it's natural state and continue the cycle of buying buffs and testing them to your heart's content. The game offers alot of powerful purchases afterwards and I had alot of rewards seeing just how strong the turtles become.Another factor that I enjoyed personally about this game is the story taking pages from IDW Turtles. Not many people know IDW turtles these days and this feels like a great refreshing take on the characters we see and if the DLC that's coming is true, i'm hoping that they introduce us to much of the IDW cast. (Alopex, Mutanimals and Koya/Bludgeon, i'm looking at you!)All in all, a very solid game. It maybe compared to a Hades clone, but it's actually a very solid, if also simple game for your money. Hoping for some good things in the future with this series.
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate

_childDocuments_.review: A decent attempt to make a TMNT themed Hades-like that misses the mark. I think it could be great, but there are just so many little issues impacting the experience:- The dash isn't responsive enough. Could learn from the tweaking Hades 2 did.- Sub-optimal UI decisions (why make me scroll to see various upgrades when they could all fit on screen)- Dodging lingering effects when the rewards come up will accidentally select the first upgrade item- No stats to learn from and/or compare in multiplayer. That's part of the fun!- Poor enemy attack warning coloring. Just show them all as RED and differentiate friendly vs. enemy projectiles!- Unnecessary darkened screen reducing visibility when defeated and watching your friends- Poor camera can block your view of the action. Please make things transparent when behind them!- Bugs impacting multiplayer progression. Resuming a run because of them causes non-host players to lose all of their upgrades and currency.- Need to enter a code to join a friend's game vs. joining via Steam friends like every other game!- Copies a lot of the Hades concepts/flow while slightly missing the point of what makes those systems work in HadesAs a fan of action roguelikes and every TMNT beat-em-up before this, I really hope these things can be fixed/improved! As it stands, all of these issues result in an experience that isn't quite fun. I refunded for now, but I hope to come back.
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a brawler but a very stressful, very demanding, coop-focused, turtle-themed rogue-like. So, know what to expect here or you'll be very frustrated and disappointed. Always buy additional dashes and splinter revives first.Always watch area damage and special counter or game-over will pop up faster than you can say "Cowabunga, dude!".
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate

_childDocuments_.review: If this was $10, sure; but this is not a $30 game.  If you want a TMNT game, play Shredder's Revenge; if you want an action roguelike, play Hades.Once again I wish Steam had a "meh" rating.  TMNT:SF is fine, but the conversion from mobile to desktop has not gone smoothly.  Here are some of the issues:- Hope you don't dash everywhere, because you're going to end up buying something you don't want when the jump scare store pops up.- Stores don't make sense.  Say you buy something for 100.  It then goes up in price to 200, but you can't buy a second.  Even though you can click on it and it plays the purchase animation again.- Menu systems are a mess.  Overlapping text, select boxes jumping to the top of the list instead of scrolling down, and items that can't be purchased.- Enemies can get behind scenery so all you can see is their health bar.  Good luck dodging something you can't see.- Game has a tendency to not load the next area.  Softlocking your run.There are MANY more bugs if you look at the community discussions, but I haven't experienced those.
