_childDocuments_.review: Single Player:Story spoiler:It's Half-Life 1 how do you not know the story? Seriously? Fine. The story takes place at the Black Mesa Research Facility in New Mexico. You play as a theoretical physicist named "Gordon Freeman". You are heading off to your normal day of work and to nobody's surprise everything goes to hell. You are then sent throughout the Black Mesa Research Facility against both the U.S. Military and aliens alike, starting your adventure in the Sector C research labs, making your way through the offices of Black Mesa, the railway transits, hell that is known as the surface, and then the lambda complex. (To be Continued: Xen.) The game is basically one long "Get from Point A to Point B" with a bunch of puzzles, confusing level design (To new players), and some small boss battles along the way. But with the twist of the design forcing you to plot how you will play the game through, make you conserve your ammunition, and at some points question your mental sanity and wonder how the hell you're supposed to get through that room with 3 health and no armour left at all.Level Design:Can you really count "Level Design" since it's a remake? Damn straight you can. A lot of small and large changes were made to the game's levels. Even adding some new areas to the game. Some of the more noticeable changes are the scenery during the introductory tram ride, sector C laboratories, and the surface areas. It's just enough of a difference to keep the game going without making it feel like you're playing something that isn't Half-Life 1.Downside in the level design: The "Vent maze" and the "Tram maze" were cut from the Steam version of the game as the developers said they don't feel they were made to their standards. A user has re-uploaded them from the mod version to work compatibly with the game on the Steam Workshop.(On a Rail Link) (We've got Hostiles Link)Cutscenes:The game has been given a much more dramatic feel with more voice actors, facial generation, and quite a few added little cutscenes and dialogue. For example in Half-Life 1: "What the hell are you still doing here? Get topside I hear troops are coming to rescue us." Almost every guard or hiding scientist has their little story to share when you find them. All the existing cutscenes in the game have been overhauled amazingly well, one of my favourite being the "Tentacle Scene" in the rocket firing chamber. which has seen some rather nice improvement in visuals and sounds from the mod version. Also the new voices for the HECU soldiers in the Steam version are a ton better than the original mod version's in my opinion.Gameplay:The game itself plays relatively similar to Half-Life 1 with added physics, but controls and moves as if it were Half-Life 2. You have the option in the "Black Mesa" section of the options menu to make your character always run, more like Half-Life 1 was. Holding sprint in either mode will make the player run significantly faster and play an animation on all weapons other than the crossbow and the satchel charge. The weapons all function the same. Satchels explode on command, grenades have their same insane movement influence in gravity.Soundtrack:Joel Nielson did an amazing job. Damn near perfect. (My personal favourite song being the first On a Rail segment) The soundtrack seems to fit amazing with the ambiance and progression of the game and it's story. The combat music is some of the better sides (Questionable Ethics #1 being an exceptional example) and fits very well into the Half-Life feel of the game. I truly imagine this mod would not have made it as far without his works added to the game.Other:The visuals, sound, and AI for the game have been extremely improved upon. (AKA HECU and scientists no longer run into grenades.) The visuals to the game are extreme. Quality you'd expect from an actual game studio. Albeit limited due to the source engine. The sound design is superb, meant for modern systems with surround sound providing an extremely immersive experience.A few smaller new features were added to Black Mesa, such as an auto-crouch jump (This can be turned off from the "Black Mesa" section of the options menu). Which I can only feel was added solely because of DSP.Multiplayer:Note: The multiplayer is incomplete as of the current time this review was written and has some changes planned to be made. I will keep this section bound to core elements only.Gameplay:The game in multiplayer plays near parallel to Half-Life: Deathmatch's. And yes, crossbow bolts explode again. The multiplayer maps are being remade and modified to Black Mesa's play style and completely overhauled in visuals. It feels essentially like Half-Life Deathmatch but with an HD remake overlayed over it, but with changes in all the right places.Levels: (?)The multiplayer maps have to be downloaded from the Steam Workshop. If I have to guess this is so the developers can easily update a map without having to release an update for the entire game. As of the current time there are the following maps available from play officially from the BMS team: "dm_rocketfire, dm_tension, dm_office, dm_rail, dm_shipping, dm_boom, and dm_power". Adding up to seven maps currently.A list of the good, and the bad:Good:- Complete Overhaul. Not much more needs to be said there.- Balanced and fun to play multiplayer which will have more features in future updates- Just holy hell that soundtrack.- Plenty of little Easter eggs, inside jokes, and references to find everywhere.- More improvements than the free mod versionBad:- The AI can still show it's typical for the source engine at times (Several times I've walked up to HECU Soldiers and they did not do anything but stare at me with their gun practically in my throat.)- Being on Source, you can expect both good physics, but at the same time physics that will break at a moments notice and likely injure or damage the player.- Just holy hell, the human assassins will swarm the player and just spray away with their guns, making it extremely difficult to kill them without explosives or wild gunfire before dying. (You have about 5-10 seconds on the medium difficulty before they kill you.)My "Overall" rating would be ultimately a  9.4 out of 10.The game itself is very balanced in both singleplayer and multiplayer aspects, the game plays and runs fluently. I've got no real complains outside the human assassin's tendency to swarm the player.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rather difficult recommendation to write without quite a few asterisks.On the surface, it's certainly a nice visual upgrade to the original 1998 Half-life that we all know and love, with a handful of additions from Half-life 2 present as well. The facility makes a bit more logical sense accessibility-wise, with more doors and walkways placed around to show how someone would actually get to certain areas, bits of story that weren't elaborated as well from the original (such as the vortigaunt's status in the Xen hierarchy) get their proper spotlight this time around, and there's a more diverse set of models for the scientists, security, and zombies that inhabit this world to help it feel lived in. I do wish the forklift driver would've also made the leap to this version, if for no other reason than to have other jobs appearing in the facility. You probably also noticed I left out the military from that last part, that's because they don't have their own models in this one, they share the aforementioned ones but are covered in most of the military gear seen in the original... most. With all the new faces in the pool, I think sectioning some of them off for use as one or the other would've been a smarter decision here. Might not make a difference to most people, so take it as you will.One of the largest barriers for my complete recommendation however is in the gameplay. Now of course these are going to be subjective for each player, so I'm going to try to list everything that might sit in the back of your mind.Let's start with the positives:+ Enemies for the most part do higher overall damage, they can hurt a complacent player quite a bit and are more active in their attacks (usually). Some alien enemies even have new attacks... particularly Nihilanth+ There's been some ammo capacity rebalances to encourage the full use of the kit you have available+ NPC interactivity, be it from an ally reminding you that you should probably reload, acknowledging a kill, or just hearing the differences in environment-specific chatter from bringing them along with other allies, the fact they don't feel like they're on a loop is a nice bit of detailing work. Guards took a more active role in defending me in some situations, running to my aid and saving me from damage+ The struggle between all the factions involved in the game's events feel a lot more defined than their counterpart. The HCEU taking heavy losses from the Xen invaders in "Surface Tension", the Gargantua encounter in "Power Up", all have more impact this go around+ The new scripted ambushes and encounters shake up the pacing a bit, ranging from exhilarating at best to fairly inconsequential at worst. As for the negatives:- HP and Armor are WAY too generous by design in this iteration from both item pickups and recharging stations. They are largely identical to how they became in Half-life 2, albeit minus the semi-randomness from supply crates that kept you from getting too much of any one thing. Difficulty does not affect the values like it did in the original, which will probably leave some players constantly topped off even after a poor combat decision / execution. The balancing in the original Half-life is vastly superior in this regard. I never felt pressured at any point during my playthrough on hard- Deafening music. Look, I love a good track as much as the next guy, but this stuff is insanely loud by default, easily drowning out NPCs and key environmental audio cues (like enemies teleporting in or grenades being thrown at me). The fact I'm even devoting a bullet point to this should indicate on it's own how out of place this is. The direction with the new music might be off-putting to some players as well.- I was able to softlock myself in a few different areas, specifically outside of the big fan room in the "Blast Pit" chapter, and perhaps most egregiously, in the teleporter room we use to make the jump to Xen.- Some chapters had a few too many liberties taken with their new design compared to their source material... yes even the long awaited Xen- Enemy durability is noticeably lower to the point where it almost feels like they have half the life, this is quite a problem when it comes to what should be more dangerous enemies like icthyosaurs (the alien sharks) being killable before they even get in range. - Enemy explosives have some very unusual damage numbers and radii. Human grunt SMG grenades, helicopter rockets, mortar fire, all did what felt like chip damage at ranges that I know I should've taken more from. Significantly more in fact.- Some alien attacks didn't feel balanced properly either, an alien controller throws a boulder at me, I take 50 health and 100 points of armor damage... understandable. Nihilanth throws cars at me, I took 1 point of armor damage... what.- Environmental hazards are not coded properly, full stop. Trying to squeeze past the slowly rotating gear in the "Residual Processing" chapter for example was actually a chore. The original would just push you along with it. This one will rapidly drain your health in a second if you even brush up against any part of the gear, likely killing you at least once or twice with it's puzzling precision despite being the exact same design. Meanwhile things like drowning only do 2 hp a tick this timeOverall, it was a very mixed bag for me. I did still enjoy the experience, but it's one I probably won't return to for seconds.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a faithful, 1:1 recreation of Half-Life with some modern tweaks thrown in. The VAs are excellent in their roles, levels are gorgeously well crafted, and the small easter eggs that remind you that you're in the Half-Life/Portal universe makes it hard to believe this wasn't from Valve themselves.Gameplay is a huge step up from the original. Part of Half-Life's difficulty simply came from everything being hard to do. Movement feels more responsive and smoother. I'm not sure what they did with the gunplay, but  weapons just feel much better to navigate and use. The levels have a lot of detail to them and I never felt like an area didn't serve some purpose.A few issues. Since this is Source, there are save/physics issues that happen. Getting stuck in objects and going into death loops were the major issues for me.Toward the end of the game I began having frame drops as low as 40. Not terrible, but noticeable when everything up until that point had been at 60 fps.A few times my weapons would randomly fire. I just reloaded my save until it stopped.Black Mesa suffers from an issue from the original: things are too ambiguous. Puzzles have ambiguous solutions, paths to progress are not clear, and often times I'll spin around a room for 5 minutes before finally seeing the innocuous solution to my problem. Or I'll solve a puzzle and spend the rest of the game thinking "That was dumb, what was the  solution?" (Maybe it's just a me thing, so take with a grain of salt)The game overall is amazing, but it feels too easy on normal due to some of the QOL changes. It seems that enemies have less health than in the original. Combined with the use of sprint resulted in me feeling like Doomguy, not a nerd in a hazmat suit. I recommend hard mode if you want a challenge.Overall, Huge props to the developers, you've created something special.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, they really fixed this one up. I played it a couple times back when it was a free mod and while there was plenty of potential there was just so much "off" about it. The soldiers were way too OP, the weapons handled like crap and it was too hard. Not in a challenging way, but in a cheap way. It was garbage.However, lately I had been on a Half-Life binge and figured I'd give the mod another go, so I forked over the new $20 price tag.I don't know if it was Valve's intervention or community input but good lord did they turn this game around. Not only does it finally meet the original Half-Life's standards, it goes above and beyond them. The remodeled Black Mesa looks fantastic. Everything else has been upgraded as well: weapon models, characters, enemies, there are even some new nooks and crannies to be discovered. It feels just like it should: a fresh new take on an iconic classic.First and foremost: Pathfinding. Since all entities are based on the Source engine, NPC's no longer get stuck on boxes or corners; they go AROUND. You almost never have to look over your shoulder to make sure they've got your back. Likewise, not only are the new marines more fun to fight, they have combine AI which means no run-stop-fire-run-stop fire; these guys run AND shoot. They actually look and sound like real human beings too, in fact I found them incredibly sympathetic and even started to feel sorry for them as their mission began to fall apart one platoon at a time. The new military PA system is incredibly threatening, as are the new turrents. And don't get me started on the Alien Grunts, who resemble some sort of angry Nazi Super Soldier.All of the weaponry is a pleasure to use. Most of the set-pieces from the original have been redesigned to pay homage to the original game while adding little twists to keep the player on their toes, giving you a sensation of both nostalgia and apprehension that is hard to capture. In the level Office Complex, setting zombies on fire using flares causes the sprinkles to go off and alarms to activate. The military base at the end of Surface Tension is now elevated and riddled with sewer pipes, forcing you to engage with marines vertically instead of horizontally. During the famous cliff descent, bombers fly overhead and obliterate distant targets on the horizon. Late in the game you come upon a tank moving down an alley firing sideways toward overwhelming hordes of Xen fauna. Do you intervene, or wait to engage the victor?There are the usual Source quirks. The game skips from time to time, especially when using the flashlight. I found grenades extremely difficult to aim; they would often fly off to the right of my crosshair, bouncing off the rims of doors and other openings and landing back at my feet. You can dodge the Vortigaunt thunderbolt now, which seems like kind of a cop-out; in the original, staying out of sight before their "charge" sequence finished required on-the-fly tactical maneuvering. Now, their most unique and memorable trait has been nerfed. I only encountered a few glitches; some corpses float in the air, and the same with some objects during outdoor sections. Some marines seemed too slow on the uptake later in the game, and I was infuriated at monsters would automatically rush me and me alone during three-way firefights.These are small issues compared to the bigger picture, which is impressive. This game is clearly a labor of love nearly a decade in the making, and will only get better when Xen is (hopefully) released later this year.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to overstate just how much of an amazing achievement Black Mesa is. Even saying that it started as a mod for Half Life 2 (which it did) is almost a disservice. This is a fully fledged game whose HL 2 roots are only barely visible. Every single thing appears to have been hand crafted from the ground up, and in a manner that stands tall and proud among even the AAA releases of the last few years. An important thing to keep in mind; this is not "Half Life in the source engine". This is a remake in the same way that say, Peter Jackson's King Kong was a remake of the original. The plot beats are the same, but specific paths between them, the effects, everything else is brand new. This extends to a lot of the game play and level mechanics... for better AND for worse. The good parts first: this game is GORGEOUS. The first half offers little more than underground science labs and industrial complexes, but once it gets to Surface Tension- and Xen- it's downright jaw-dropping. Xen in particular offers a visual feast that's frankly on par with the offerings of Doom 2016 and Eternal's visions of Hell. The attention to detail striking throughout the game as well, and makes even Half Life 2's world seem positively empty. On a less pleasant note; by and large, the combat is great, but there are some questionable decisions, such as the Quake 2 style recoil on the SMG, or the heavy leaning into the use of the  beam weapon in the latter half of the game. Some of the puzzles and navigation gimmics in the later levels can also range from overused to flat out irritating. Then there's the HECU marines, who consistently have godly aim and rarely have a break in their firing pattern. Lastly; some of the equipment sounds , while of high quality, are not as punchy as I would have liked. There are mods that solve the sound (and weapon) issues, but those problems do exist. How much they might bother anyone else will vary. With all of that said; the adventure itself is great, and is an overall much improved way to experience the original Half Life story. If one were to go into a Half Life adventure marathon in sequence, I would easily say that playing this INSTEAD of the original would be a good bet, the only caveat being that I suggest doing so with the aforementioned mods.

_childDocuments_.review: It's impossible to overstate how much of a game changer the original Half Life was at the time. The opening 15 minutes consisted of a monorail ride through the expansive Black Mesa research facility and small talk with the coworkers. By this point, before anything of any significance had happened, I was all in. FPS games had been around for nearly 10 years, but none had introduced storytelling beyond 'shoot the bad guys' and maaaaybe 'find the blue key.' But Half Life introduced an actual plot and story line: at a top secret research facility in New Mexico, an experiment goes awry and opens a rift with another world and you, playing scientist Gordon Freeman, are one of the few survivors. You need to try to escape the facility while avoiding a government containment and clean up team.But alas, Half Life got old and it *felt* old. The story was still stellar, but the graphics were stuck in the late 1990s. That's where Black Mesa was born. Black Mesa isn't really a reboot or a remake, it is more like a digitally remastered Blu-ray release of an old movie: sharper picture, better audio, maybe some deleted scenes, but by and large the same story nearly scene-for-scene.The graphics in Black Mesa aren't GREAT, but they're certainly several steps above the original and they're enough to make the game feel modern enough. I got those same tingles on that opening monorail ride and had a wide smile on my face when re-encountering familiar chapters I'd played 21 years before. And the 'Zen' maps, depicting an other worldly planet that Freeman encounters later in the game are oftentimes downright gorgeous!That said, Zen is also the only knock on the game for me. I'll admit, I wasn't a big fan of the Zen chapters in the original Half Life. I liked the familiarity of the earth-bound Black Mesa research facility and jumping to another astral plane with different gravity, toxins and creatures just felt like too much of a hard turn for me. I emphasize the 'FOR ME' there, as I realize it's subjective. While the Zen levels in Black Mesa are truly beautiful, it feels like they're also significantly longer than they were in the original game. I'm going off of memory here but it felt like Half Life, the research facility chapters made up about 70% of total time spent in the game while Zen chapters made up the remaining 30%, while in Black Mesa I spent about 10 hours each in the research facility and the Zen chapters. For someone not all that keen on Zen to begin with, more Zen did not make Black Mesa a better experience. Finishing the 'Interloper' chapter in the Black Mesa remake was more of a laborious chore than an exciting adventure. It was a very lovely laborious chore though.All in all, Black Mesa is a nice way to enjoy the original 1998 Half Life experience through the eyes of a 2012-ish computer engine, and if you've not played the original Half Life then Black Mesa is definitely a game worth acquiring.

_childDocuments_.review: Years ago, I wrote a review for Black Mesa saying "Really hyped for Xen, I have full trust that Crowbar Collective can make it work better than it did in the original game." And here we are, the absolute madmen actually pulled through with it, what a journey it's been.Black Mesa is hands down one of the best remakes and likely the best fan game ever made. It's everything Half-Life: Source should've been, and much more. It modernises many mechanics and elements from Half-Life 1 and 2, such as a sleek UI and infinite sprint/stamina, and retains the core elements that made both games amazing. Fast-paced combat with lots of room to improvise use the environment to your advantage has never felt better in the series. The combat sections are intertwined well among more moodier, quieter areas and different puzzles, utilising Source physics when appropriate.Most of the level design has stayed true to its source material, changing things around and removing 90s cliches like unnecessary mazes. Crowbar Collective has embraced the Valve style of level design extremely well, subtly guiding and teaching players new mechanics and enemies without saying a word. This is easily noticeable in Xen.Black Mesa's Xen is a complete reimagining of what the original could've been. It's been expanded to terrific lenghts, introducing new enemy types and expanding on the Half-Life lore of the Lambda team already having explored some of Xen. The boss battles are also incredibly intense, being some of the most fun I've had in an FPS in a while. With Xen, the game now looks better than a Source game has any right to. It is astonishing what Crowbar Collective have accomplished.Joel Nielsen's music has to be mentioned here as well, his soundtrack may not perfectly sync with every moment but every track is memorable and amazingly composed, whether it's ambient or combat music up to 11. And it only gets better in Xen. The voice acting is also all redone with different people. I don't know what black magic was used, but they all sound extremely alike to the classic Half-Life voices of every character.This was the first Steam game ever Greenlit, and it's probably the last that was fully released. Poetic, in a way. It is my favourite Half-Life game, and a near perfect game for both newcomers and veterans of the franchise. No matter how many times I finish the game from start to finish, I always come back later for the gameplay and the nostalgia. It is an unforgettable experience.

Some great songs either started too early or ended too early. Hopefully their next endeavor takes a bit more inspiration from Doom's sound design.- Xen felt a bit too padded, and could easily have been trimmed down to be about an hour shorter.- Max texture quality is still a bit dated for 2020, and I had random performance hiccups even with a 2060 Super but usually ran fairly consistent.- Menu UI a bit janky looking.- Quick-loading a bit annoying even with an SSD, can sometimes take a decent pause to get back to a point even in the same area.Great things to balance my nitpicks:- Great visual update especially for weapons and environments (particularly Xen).- Didn't change too much about how the game feels and handles.- Eli and Kleiner look unique and closer to their HL2 appearance.- Pretty good lighting design, art direction in general is great.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an auspicious omen that a mod- in development for nearly as long as the rumored Half Life installment, and given the blessing of (and rights to cash in on) Valve's golden child IP- should be released in the same month that the Half Life Saga resumes. The stars sometimes align.Black Mesa has been finalized with that love of artists who look at the totality and depth of their vision. Standing alone, it's a theatrical piece with a last act that works you in awe over every hour. Standing in the shadow of the original's design, it's both faithful recreation and brilliant retelling. As someone who was far too familiar with the twists and spaces of the original game, seeing the echoes of the original designs revealed just how much attention the team put into story boarding. Nothing about this feels like what you would call a mod.What sometimes feels new, is in its DNA an exact examination of the original impulses: a bizarrely textured crawlspace illuminated with floating red particles; a series of helices that intertwine above an infinite pit; mud huts and belts of refinery gangways. The direction of every conveyor, and the movement of the action, is on the same compass of the original. But where there are some cuts, there are also expansions giving life to the ideas barely expressed in the original (it was a rushed process, with a regretted series of chapters); everywhere the developers are witty, imaginative, and thorough- they've really taken something, and made it into their own. Much as the original Half Life was praised on the (then groundbreaking) tenet of making you feel like you were in a movie, so has the Black Mesa team put in the love and artistry to make this game feel like a blockbuster.

_childDocuments_.review: 'Minor lacerations detected. User death imminent.'It’s been more than twenty years since I first heard a robotic voice coo those words into my ear. Hearing them recently ferried me back to 1999 when I first played 'Half-Life' on a PC with about 6 gigs of hard drive space.'Black Mesa' is a painstaking recreation of 'Half-Life' with modern-day graphics and extensive level design tweaks. It’s a perfect complement to my rose-tinted memories, which is to say that it passed my personal test of being close enough to its source material that the visual overhaul did not strike me as jarring.'Black Mesa' doesn’t modernise the antiquated design – but then, it wouldn’t be 'Half-Life' if it did. As it is, it’s the best way to play Valve’s original design if you haven’t done so before, and it’s a brilliant way to retread those old ventilation shafts, if you have.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome back to Black Mesa, I guess.It's Half-Life 1 but honestly the people who made this put way too much attention into making it. It's an odd feeling, but not an unpleasant one. You can just kind of see it in the way they loaded up every level with SO much stuff. Like seriously, the attention to detail is unreal. This is one of those Source engine games that really does kind of try to differentiate itself as much as possible from the Source engine, and it really shows.While I guarantee you Half-Life (or Half-Life: Source) absolutely still hold up to modern video game standards today, Black Mesa is an update that would probably make the game more easy to stomach for people who have difficulty playing games older than they are.This isn't a strict retexture or even a remaster of Half-Life, this is in fact a remake. If only because, they have put some effort into redesigning some of the levels. For instance, the first chapter or so of the game is almost completely different. They kept everything from Half-Life, but they also add a lot of new things. _childDocuments_.review: "Do you recommend Black Mesa?" is kind of a weird question to answer because, well, it's Half-Life. Most of what was great about Half-Life is as great or almost as great here, so Black Mesa is a very good game. That's the trouble, though: as long as some parts of it are only "almost as great", it's difficult to justify choosing Black Mesa over Half-Life. Half-Life is old and you can tell - all the models are ugly and polygonal, the textures are low resolution, the physics are primitive and janky, it doesn't have fancy dynamic shadows or anything like that, but it's a masterfully paced adventure that is dripping with atmosphere, and it has rightfully earned its place as a piece of gaming history. While playing it, you can feel how it moved its genre forward, because it sits in the perfect balance between the pure gameplay of the shooters that came before, and the more set piece driven experience of the shooters that came afterwards. It has fights with aliens, which fit mostly in the traditional shooter mould of constantly moving and dodging projectiles. It has fights with soldiers, which are more about using cover and flanking to get the upper hand. It has environmental puzzles, and it has memorable scripted moments. It weaves effortlessly between all four modes of gameplay. It's a masterpiece. All of that good stuff is here in Black Mesa, but with some niggling annoyances. The gunplay isn't quite as nice. There's a weird delay on some of the guns, particularly the shotgun, where if you try to reload-cancel it, the input buffers and you can end up shooting a full second after clicking the mouse. The AI's kind of annoying - it's the sort of AI where you walk into a room and every enemy immediately knows your exact position and starts firing at you, and they will track you through walls with ease, so you really don't have the ability to outflank them or anything, even though the combat areas are clearly designed with that in mind. This is particularly egregious with the tank in Surface Tension, which will immediately one-shot you with its cannon as soon as you poke your head out of cover (I beat it with god mode, and I'm not ashamed). There's really major aimpunch any time you get hit, making precision weapons a pain to use. Hitboxes for obstables are awful - you can aim straight at an enemy and fire a full clip of SMG ammo at them, and it will all miss because there's a rock "in the way", despite your gun pointing multiple feet beyond its visible edge. Voice acting is quite poor - it wasn't exactly brilliant in the original, but in Black Mesa the voice lines are delivered with a dull passsionlessness that doesn't even leave room for it to be endearingly bad. The soundtrack is totally different, and a lot of it's that kind of djenty stuff that every FPS has had to have since Doom 2016, which isn't as good a fit for the tone of the game compared to the original techno bangers. And then... there's Xen. Most people who played the original Half-Life will tell you it's the worst section of the game, so I don't think anyone had any complaints when the guys at Crowbar Collective decided to overhaul it. Unfortunately, I don't know if I can say they managed to meaningfully improve it. It's "better" in the sense that it's more interesting to play than the original Xen, but it's still the worst part of the game, and now it's three times as long. The biggest issue with Xen was the way it killed the otherwise excellent pacing of Half-Life, and Black Mesa actually makes that worse. Rather than being an unfortunately awkward and annoying final chapter, it's an utterly tedious slog that makes up almost a quarter of the game. It's full of repetitive puzzles - puzzles that take a single idea and build on it can be great, but Xen's puzzles never progress beyond "you need to find the right object that's hidden somewhere in the environment". There's lots of first-person platforming, which is better than it was before, but I still don't want to do it. There's a stark difference between Crowbar Collective's completely original combat encounters and those they adapted from Valve. The new ones have an amateurish feel, like a novice messing around in the Hammer editor, they tend to consist of just throwing a tonne of enemies at you in a big open space. Rather than a throwaway boss fight, Gonarch is now a level in itself, a huge multi-stage fight where you chase her, then she chases you, then you solve some puzzles and chase her again, then finally actually fight her. I think if you ask people "what didn't you like about Xen in Half-Life?" You're not going to get a lot of people answering "I wish there was more Gonarch". Xen just kind of sucks, which is a shame, because there's clearly been a lot of effort made in creating a visually striking alien world, and filling it with environmental details that add context that wasn't there in the original. There's a whole section where you go through this alien industrial complex manned by vortigaunts, and you learn that the zappy boys you've been mindlessly blowing up are slaves, and that's all new. It's really cool! But, at the same time, it's kind of tedious to actually play through. Black Mesa is neat. If you've already played Half-Life to death, it's fun to experience a slightly different take on it, and see all the amazing set pieces lovingly re-created with modern high fidelity graphics. Maybe if you truly can't stomach the graphics of the 1998 original, it's better to have played Black Mesa than to have not played Half-Life at all. Half-Life is ultimately the better game, though, and it's half the price, so my answer to "do I recommend Black Mesa?" is "play Half-Life instead."

_childDocuments_.review: The original Half-Life blew my mind decades ago like any other young gamer back in the day. I found the gameplay difficult back then, and I was just as immersed in the atmosphere. The same thing happened with Half-Life 2, so when a group of fans announced the ambitious Black Mesa project, I felt excited of experiencing a true remake of the original.I waited for more than ten years, not even touching the mod or the game until the whole thing was finally released in full, from the tram ride at the start to Xen at the end. Black Mesa was so freaking worth it. I took my time exploring every little detail, hanging around the NPCs, and looking through every nook and cranny. The game blew my mind AGAIN at just how far the dev team went in recreating the HL1 experience. In an era where video games are being remade or remastered with the latest tech, this is how a remake is supposed to be. Barely anything was cut. I've read that some parts of Surface Tension and On a Rail were cut out, but honestly I didn't really feel much. The only thing really "new" was Xen, and it was visual eye candy everywhere. There were also a lot more ichthyosaurs than the original, and it got to the point where I was wary of every body of water I came across after the enemy's first introduction. Difficulty of gameplay is pretty good. It's not that frustrating, though I've had my fair share of repeated quick-loads during combat against the marines or that last section in Interloper, and I actually had to flee the assassins encountered right before entering Lambda Core. The Nihilanth fight at the end actually felt like a final boss, unlike the original. Only tip I have is to not get used to quick-saving every often.Overall, wonderful game. The best way to experience Half-Life 1 now.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Mesa

_childDocuments_.review: Exactly how remakes should be done. Stays very true to the original Half-Life but with much improved physics, graphics and pretty much everything else. Some areas feel a little unpolished and glitches happen somewhat regularly but the game still has a good feel to it. It's amazing what such a small development team can do. Shame that the Xen levels are taking so long to come out though.[EDIT] Changed to would not recommend.The developers are still seemingly sitting on their hands when it comes to the Xen levels. For a game that came out in 2015 that's ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this back when it was still a free mod, and it was my introduction to the Half-Life series (outside the Portal games). I don't know how much of the level design has changed relative to the original version, but as someone who had never played a real FPS before Black Mesa, I can say that this is an incredible experience. Simple but fun gameplay, masterful level design, truly immersive first-person storytelling, clever puzzles, cheesy/funny dialogue, and some spectacular setpieces. Definitely the best way to start with the HL franchise, since it brings it in-line with Half-Life 2 and its episodic sequels in terms of production quality (and honestly it looks/sounds even better).

_childDocuments_.review: Black Mesa is the definitive way to experience Half Life.Just to preface this I wouldn't recommend playing Black Mesa before Half-Life 2, just to get better acquainted with the Source engine and properly recognising some characters is also a nice detail. Also, while I do think that Black Mesa is a better game than Half-Life, I do still think there's a lot of value in playing Half-Life first just to appreciate how much has been overhauled and changed while still staying recognisable.With all that said, this remake is phenomenal. It is an upgrade to Half-Life in almost everything.The presentation is the obvious thing to highlight. Its visually stunning the entire way through from the opening Tram Ride to Xen. The updated visuals however serve more of a purpose than just to be jaw droppingly gorgeous, but it enhances the environmental storytelling in ways that the original couldn't with the far more detailed world. It’s a vivid reimagining of Half-Life, while still maintaining the original’s tone and atmosphere. The sound design is also incredible with all the weapons being very satisfying to fire and couple with a soundtrack that’s just AWESOME!The gameplay has seen a bit of an overhaul too, the gun play is still very solid, enemy encounters are a lot more dynamic and the overall level design I’d argue is much better paced than the original, cutting down on some of the more tedious sections and focusing more on its set pieces and the original’s highlights. Finally, there’s also of course the completely reimagined Xen, which is just an incredible spectacle to play all the way through.All in all, Black Mesa stands out on its own as a brand-new experience while still being faithful to the original game. It is one of the best remakes of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Black Mesa

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Very good reimagining of Half-Life with many unique features that separate it from the original and make it worth your money.If you're looking for a faithful remake of the original game, this is not the place. Black Mesa is first and foremost a reimagining of Half-Life, and I have to applaud the developers for doing such a great job of such a daunting task.I felt that the game tended to pace better in comparison to the original Half-Life, and to me felt as if it paced closer to Half-Life 2 and even some newer games outside of the Half-Life franchise. This was thanks to many different changes such as removing areas that may previously slow the player down and shortening certain areas of the game here and there to create a better balance between puzzle-solving and action.However, whilst areas were removed, the best were left in and new concepts and areas were added to really bring the game up to standard as if it were a game released today. In Unforeseen Consequences for example, you are faced with more puzzles until you reach the end of the chapter - this lengthened the chapter to be closer to the rest of the game and serves as a great introduction to the fundamental changes that Black Mesa has to offer.With this game being based on the more physics-based Source Engine, the game makes heavy use (especially in Xen) of physics-based puzzles. In particular, I found that the power plugs first seen in the beginning of Half-Life 2 are largely utilised for puzzles in the game, alongside fire spreading to unblock certain pathways.With this being a modern reimagining of Half-Life intended for the modern audience, you would expect the graphics to be improved. I cannot believe to imagine the amount of effort that the art team has put into this game - the graphics feel on par with if Valve had made it themselves. Furthermore, new graphic details such as lens flares have been programmed into the Source Engine, further enhancing the appearance of the game. Especially during the Xen chapters, I found that the technology seen in Xen appeared closer to what we eventually see from the Combine in later Half-Life games, sharing similar designs and color schemes. I felt this was a detail I almost didn't expect and ties the events of the first game in closer to the subsequent games in the series, which may be a good thing for newcomers to the series seeking to move through every Half-Life game in anticipation for Half-Life: Alyx.The largest selling point of this game for me, personally, is the newly released final Xen chapters. I completely understand why these chapters have taken so long to be released as they are complete reworks of the final chapters. I felt like only themes were carried over, and this was for the better. It means that for the final four chapters the game is almost entirely unique, and this paced a lot better and played a lot better than the original Xen. Compared to the rest of the game, it feels much more similar though the more open-environments change it just enough to generate the same initial feeling as the original game. I found that the changes that were made to Xen made me wish for an entire game set within the Crowbar Collective's interpretation of Xen.I'll be the first to admit I have a small mind, and this has influenced my next statement: I believe that some of the puzzles and routes in Xen should have been more signposted. While not a major issue, I did have to personally resort to walkthroughs on the odd occasion. I'm sure people with more awareness of their surroundings wouldn't have too much of an issue, however.The final boss fight has undergone an entire rework, and has become very closely linked to the weapons that you utilise throughout the game - I found myself only really needing two weapons to complete the fight, which the game usefully provides ammo for throughout the fight. However, whilst it felt like a boss fight - like a being more powerful than anything previously seen in the game - I felt as if in certain places it was easier to tackle than some of the other situations you find yourself in during the game against weaker forces. I will say, however, that I believe that I was very lucky not to die during the final phase of the fight primarily due to the way that I approached it.Overall, I very much enjoyed Black Mesa (though I cannot comment on the Multiplayer section), and cannot wait to see the improvements that the developers will make to Xen in the coming months after it's release and perhaps other areas in the game in response to feedback.

_childDocuments_.review: Black is a fan-made remake of the critically acclaimed and groundbreaking Half Life 1 which ports over the landmark game to the Source engine. If you have never played Half Life 1 before, then you should buy Black Mesa right now without going further in the review. For a current day gamer, it is going to be difficult putting up the nostalgic tinted glasses and play the original version of Half Life without him thinking why is this game highly regarded.That is where Black Mesa comes in. Unlike the half hearted remake by Valve, Black Mesa provides a fresh and different experience from the original game. It not only enhances the visual level of the game but also includes a few tricks of its own. Half Life is considered one of the best FPS games of all times and it stands the test of time in terms of its gameplay, excellent storytelling and some thrilling and haunting set pieces.If you have played the original game, you would remember some of the incredibly creepy enemies and the sequences of scientists getting dragged up into the vents. The environments in the original though felt bland and added little to the narrative structure there. But due to enhanced visuals and some remodelling and repainting of the environments, Black Mesa feels like a haunting structure where Gordon does not know what exactly is he dealing with.Unlike the modern tropes of handling over the game to you, Black Mesa requires to figure out each and everything through travelling and observing the environment. Even though there are times where it feels like the game is padding its game length, it is much better and satisfactory to figure out a path on your own than someone holding your hand to it. It is a far cry from what we see today and is a good throwback to the games of old. But just like the achievements of Half Life, it also carries the downsides of the original which become far more apparent today than they were when it was released. The most frustrating aspect of the game is the constant respawing of enemies out of nowhere. You can clear out a path and come back to it a couple of minutes later and it will be filled again with enemies. These enemies are the Zubats of Half life and while you know they cannot harm you, you still have to plod through them. The game also seems to be over reliant on puzzle solving at times and there are a few where I got absolutely stuck with zero idea where to go next. Being in early access it is expected to have bugs and Black Mesa does not disappoint. The enemies simply ignore you at times and will clip through the environments. It has very frequent and long loading times breaks the immersion and things like sudden crashes or freezes are easy to come by. While it is yet to get out of early access, it needs a good amount of polish before it comes close to the original’s legacy.While Black Mesa is a far cry from the flat out ugly models and environments present in the original, it comes nowhere near one of the modern games. It is limited by the source engine and while the team behind Black Mesa has done an incredible job in creating the environments, the character models still look very stiff and the movement is still incredibly clunky. Though Black Mesa does increase the impact of some great sequences of the game, do not expect it to be a visual masterpiece. But it is the best way to experience the original Half Life despite its visual limitations.Black Mesa features an all new soundtrack and some new voice acting. While the soundtrack itself is excellent, the voice acting can be a hit and miss sometimes. The sound effects are excellent and help in building a top notch strange atmosphere. Even with a few mistakes, the overall sound package of Black Mesa is excellent.If you have never played Half Life before, Black Mesa is the best option to experience the game and it is a game which deserves to be played. It holds up very well even today and even if there are certain problems with the game in its current state, it is a journey worth taking. Even if you have played the original before, Black Mesa provides just enough freshness that it is worth playing once more even if just for experiencing the story again. It is priced right and there is no real reason aside from some bugs which should prevent you from buying this gem of a game.This review was brought to you by .

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game. After playing Half-Life, I wanted the same experience but something more. This game satisfies that itch. Everything from the movement, to the combat, to the level design are all delivered in high quality and effort. The music is one of the most attentive editions in any game. For example, after entering an area, music will start playing - but it will not finish playing; the music will loop over some movement. Only after the player continues to a new region (where the combat becomes intense), the music will stop looping and continue to the next movement, usually amplifying its composition. This makes firefights more engaging. Personally, my playstyle is to snipe enemies at a distance, but when the music kicks in, it makes me want to fight head-on and utilize all my weapons. The only complaint I have is that my favorite chapter, "On A Rail", was lacking the things that made it fun to me in the original game. Before, it was like a labyrinth and you could shoot the arrows up ahead to change the direction of the tracks. Now, the train only goes in one direction. It is more linear in comparison. Overall, this game is amazing and it is almost everything I wanted from a remake of Half-Life. I highly recommend playing the original before playing Black Mesa. That way, you can appreciate all the little things this game has done.

_childDocuments_.review: Black Mesa is an excellent re-imagining/remake of Half Life in the Source Engine. Rather than a mere graphical update to the game or the piss poor source port offered by Valve, this is a true re-engineered take on the game with many  small changes that make the game feel like a polished touch up port, without straying from the feeling and general layout of the original. As a brief summary of the game, it is a strategic and narrative first-person shooter, which tasks you in surviving and escaping a high-tech science facility after a failed experiment results in an alien invasion of the compound. All of this is done from the viewpoint of the player, without any third person cutscenes, player character dialogue, or exposition dumps.  Unlike earlier fps games, combat is not run and gun but rather strategic; as all encounters can use your environment, planning, or proper weapons usage to your advantage.  Head on fighting will make you barely scrape by. The real joy of combat comes from planning, predicting, and outsmarting your opponents, even when they clearly outgun you, as well as certain aspects of enemy movement and AI. It is a spectacular feeling few other games have tried going for. Unlike Half Life 2, which was also on the source engine, combat retains its hard, gritty, and satisfyingly chunky feeling with weapons and gunplay. Not much is changed from the original here, which is good. The difference and improvement  in combat gameplay is the removal of many hard to see or pinpoint traps and enemies, leading to fairer encounters when playing smartly. Rushing in blind to all combat situations will still kill you quickly. Most ‘boss’ encounters have also been redesigned and are substantially more interactive and challenging. Visually the game is a major improvement from it’s 1998 graphics, with much less muddied textures and larger, more technical and creepy settings. The final few sections of the game really highlight this. A lot of detail can be seen in each environment and model. While it has less charm compared to the original, the new visuals help convey the atmosphere and setting better. It makes the Black Mesa compound feel like SCP Containment Breach with a focus on combat instead. Levels are the exact same from the original game, but are edited, expanded upon ,or remove sluggish features and design structure. In addition, nearly all the specific scenes and memorable moments from the first game are included in Black Mesa, often with better design or improved functions. In particular, the physics of the Source Engine allow for more creative puzzles and new ways to approach combat and level traversal. The story, cutscenes, and characters of the game are the exact same, with brand new voice acting and music accompanying them. The VA’s sound very similar to their original counterparts, giving it a fair passing grade. The new music tracks sound great and fit the tone of the original sound track, although the lack of any tracks from the first game is noteworthy and a disappointment. Performance wise, the game loads much slower than the original, even when playing on a Solid State Drive. During a loading  sequence  my game crashed, and one of my quick saves became glitched. In the last area, frame rate was abysmal despite never tanking before. Overall, this is the definitive way to experience the first Half Life, although the original game is still a fun experience. Unless you have massive nostalgia for the original, love 1998 era graphics, or simply want to experience the first in its entirely, this is the best way to experience the Black Mesa compound and it is a real treat. 8.5/10, with half a point off for performance issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Black Mesa is much much more than just a remake of the original Half-Life. It's a whole new game with the level design and gameplay quality which one would only expect from an actual modern Valve release. Crowbar Collective didn't just remake all the levels and assets -- they added new levels where the original game fell short, re-engineered large parts of the Source Engine to enable new graphics technologies, and completely scrapped the rushed mess that was Xen in the original release and replaced it with a game world like I've never seen before.It is incredible that CC had the perseverance to bring this project to a full release after 14 long years of development with probably only minimal resources, and I can only recommend for everyone to give this game a try, Half-Life fan or not, as it certainly become one of my all-time-favorites.

_childDocuments_.review: From the faithful recreation of the opening tram sequence to the complete overhaul of the last leg of the game, Black Mesa is a buffet of classic FPS gameplay and impressive visuals that is worth experiencing for both returning fans and new players. For fans of the original Half-Life, this is simultaneously a fresh experience with new tie-ins to later games and a nostalgic romp through the re-imagined concrete corridors and surreal alien landscapes of the original game. For new players, this is a glimpse into what classic FPS gameplay was like, before all the bells and whistles. It's just you, a bunch of different weapons, and hundreds of aliens and enemy soldiers that have far too few holes in them. The only remotely negative thing I can say about this game is that it has some minor optimization issues at specific areas, and I say remotely negative because it's still impressive how few issues this game has, given the fact that it's built on top of software that's roughly twenty years old. On paper, a remake of Half-Life 1 that's done by fans sounds like a nightmare, since we've been burned by fan projects before, but Black Mesa is a lot more than a simple fan project. It is a testament to what fans can achieve when they are both passionate AND skilled. Crowbar Collective has done an excellent job at bringing this all-time classic into the modern standard.

It does all of this without sacrificing anything we loved about the original:  There is SO much more great content, especially in Xen, that it's incredible the price is only $19.99.If you've never played Half-Life before, ignore the original game and play Black Mesa instead. It's THAT good.

_childDocuments_.review: A fan remake of one of my favourite shooters. Very much fantastic but got a few issues to work out.For those who don't know, Half-Life 1 is an FPS game where you play as scientist Gordon Freeman who works in a supermassive Black Mesa research complex, a character unto itself with it's many scientific and industrial environments and OSHA violation hazards. During a routine experiment things go wrong and everything goes up in flames as otherworldly creatures invade and facility's already unsafe infeastructure begins to crumble. You have to use your wits and your brawn to set things right. Then military comes in and they also want you dead to cover up whatever shady things BM was researching. Then you go to Xen, the alien world that was rather underwhelming yet still strange in HL1, but that's fully remade and straight up amazing in Black Mesa.The level design is very similar to original vision but the visuals are updated to mdoern standards, from enemies and allies to locales, the somewhat surreal layouts of original game look pretty convincing and logic here. The weapons act pretty much the same as in original game with some minor tweaks at best, and the soundtrack absolutely amazing and perfect for each ocassion it plays in. Everything's great, really.I only have two complains - one is minor and a matter of taste, other serious - first of all, they changed vortigaunts from guaranteed hitscan to inaccurate hitscan and gave them a dodge - while it's cool I feel like original version demanded greater enviromental awareness where you'd need to maneveur in ways that guarantee you'll have cover, meanwhile current ones can be beaten with mere straffing. The other concerns is that quite some Xen areas, including real tough ones, have major FPS drops that don't seem to be fixable trough mere settings changes or other tweaks, making them extremely tough to beat. Hope that gets patched, I really struggled in some Gonarch areas and the finale of Interloper over this.Nonetheless it's a great fan remake and I wish more game remakes would be as good as this. Totally recommended to anyone new to or familiar with Half-Life.

_childDocuments_.review: -An epic story, mostly told by 'showing' rather than 'telling'-Fast, fun and engaging gameplay on par with, and at times surpassing, Half-Life 2-Stunningly gorgeous visuals-Immersive environments and locales-Interesting human and alien enemies that range in difficulty from effortless to very challenging-One of the most phenomenal video game soundtracks of all time-Well, uh...it's Half-Life!Why WOULDN'T you get this game?Seriously, though, this is probably my favorite game of all time; there is just no way to convey the experience I had playing the entire thing start to finish in one sitting. It's an epic in the truest sense of the word; one lowly scientist, who has likely never held a gun before in his life, working his way through hundreds of aliens, soldiers and environmental obstacles, from the secret research complex Black Mesa to the gorgeous, otherworldly alien planet Xen, to ultimately defeating a being that may as well be a corporeal, tangible god. With stunningly beautiful graphics and environments, simple-yet-fun shooting mechanics and a digestible yet unforgettable story...there is nothing like Black Mesa, and this game deserves to go down in history as a shining example of exactly how to remake a beloved classic.

_childDocuments_.review: We've been following Black Mesa's progress for several years. Some said Crowbar Collective wouldn't manage it, but I was adamant this game would be finished, because the passion behind it was obvious.My expectations were not just met, they were completely blown away. Not only was Crowbar Collective careful in preserving Half-Life's spirit, but they also looked at it through a crititcal lens and came up with great new content, and I'm not even talking about Xen!The final chapters, however, were worth all the wait: the original Xen bit was rather short and monotonous, but held much potential. Black Mesa unearthed it, fleshed it out and polished it, making Xen astonishing. It could make a fantastic game on its own!I want to mention Joel Nielsen's work separately. I am a big fan of game soundtracks, and his music captivated me back when I was playing an early version. His Xen tracks are a perfect match for the final chapters: alien, out-of-this-world beautiful and haunting.Overall, it's far more than just a retexture or a simple remake. Black Mesa is a well-thought reimagination, a proud example of mixing a legendary game with great new ideas, talent, hard work, and sincere love for the source material.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're a fan of Half Life 1, then you simply NEED to play this game. It's without a doubt a masterpiece on its own. Toggle on "Always Run" in the games settings, since the higher movement speed in water, vents, and of course on foot suits Half Life 1's style more than the default Half Life 2 style movement.The quality of the game was already high throughout, but its obvious that Xen is definitely the best part of the game right from the start of that section to the end, and on it's own makes this game worth the buy. Xen goes from being a short, forgettable and trypophobic experience from Half Life 1, into a much longer, more enjoyable section. Xen is downright beautiful which slowly turning terrifying, with excellent pacing and level design which makes you never feel lost. Gun animations are redone and top notch, and the game is one of the most impressive Source engine games in terms of visuals. Sound design is also really well done, but some of the voice actors such as the one for for Eli Vance tend to miss the mark in terms of authenticity to the original game.Movement is also very fun, the game introduces a sliding feature, and when combined with Always Run on allows incredibly easy bunnyhopping, almost like Slide Hopping in the Titanfall series. This makes sections with large open areas incredibly fun to traverse, and I can only imagine how speedrunning can take advantage of this. Some minor issues I've encountered include some physics objects that are required to progress sometimes disappear when loading a quicksave, such as rotating wheels that control doors. Some specific areas cause the framerate to absolutely tank, such as outdoor scenes with large amounts of grunts. There was one particular section in Xen which caused my framerate to drop down to 5 FPS when looking at a certain area. Which is concerning on a system with a GTX 1080 and a Ryzen 5 2600. Finally, one issue that really bothered me was overuse of Houndeyes. Where Half LIfe 1 would spawn 1 to 2 houndeyes in an area at a time, Black Mesa likes to quadruple this number. You get over run by 6-8 houndeyes at a time when they're introduced multiple times over the course of the game, and it tends to get frustrating, even on Normal difficulty.buy the game lol stop reading this and buy the game already

_childDocuments_.review: Black Mesa is a 2020 first-person shooter game developed and published by Crowbar Collective. It is a third-party remake of Half-Life (1998) made in the Source game engine. Originally published as a free mod in September 2012, Black Mesa was approved for commercial release by Valve, the developers of Half-Life. You are Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist at the Black Mesa Research Facility. When a routine experiment goes horribly wrong, you must fight your way through an interdimensional alien invasion, and a bloodthirsty military clean-up crew in order to save the science team... and the world!

_childDocuments_.review: While Valve's Half-Life: Source was merely intended to show how easy it was to port GoldSrc games to their new engine, the Crowbar Collective have gone above and beyond to provide a proper, full fledged, remake.Originally developed as free mod, Black Mesa was approved by Valve for a commercial release. You may be able to find the mod version online, but note that it does not include the final chapters of the campaign or the multiplayer, and it runs on an older version of the Source engine. This standalone version includes the full game, and has numerous bug fixes and improvements over the mod version. It also has a chapter select menu with all the chapters available to choose from at the start, a great quality of life feature.I found the performance on Linux to be acceptable with OpenGL. Though it's possible to utilize Vulkan with DXVK. On Linux, simply force Proton. On Windows, DXVK can be manually installed, and may yield better performance than Direct3D.More info here:

_childDocuments_.review: is how remakes are done: This game took Half-Life's story and gameplay principles and took the to our time, mainly from a graphical standpoint. The game closely follows HL's story closely and mainly uses its basic level structure, it may, on some occasions catch you off-guard by reinterpreting an area in a completely new way (like Xen probably if it ever comes out). Gameplay-wise, I did not see any problems and there only exists one flaw where the game will crash if you hurt its feelings by using the wrong graphics settings.Black Mesa's gunplay is pretty fun, no weapons feel too weak or too strong; other than that, there's not much to say except that it follows old FPS traditions instead of having a 2-weapon-limit.The game lets you interact with the NPCs which either help you fight or give you access to some secret or crucial areas (and while I do know that they are basically just numbers in my RAM, I always want to rescue all of them).TLDR: This might just be the best way Half-Life could be remade and if you liked HL1, play it; if you didn't ever play HL1, play that first and then appreciate how far we've come in PC graphics (and voice acting, Michael Hillard is just so great).Edit:Xen is an improvement over the old Half-Life's, however it feels very long (I think it was another 4 hours) and sometimes very annoying. Still, while being kind of an anti-climax (and some might just want to skip it) it is still worth playing through.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:If you'll never play the original, play this without guilt. Otherwise, play them in order. Either way you should buy it. I played the original Half Life with a clear understanding that it had to be taken in with context, especially because I was playing it over two decades after it released. It was amazing in 1998, but Black Mesa is amazing in 2020.Gameplay is smooth, animations are fantastic and the story and environments have been enriched in every possible way. Having played the original a lot carries over. It's not an HD pack or a remaster, it's a fully re-imagined experience in the best of senses.Here's some Pros and Cons:Pros:- Much better checkpoints, most of the times I found myself saving I was just being extra cautious, I was never infuriated.- Much nicer flow, a lot of busywork and frankly not fun vent diving was streamlined in this version.- Better graphics. (duh)- Amazing music.- Better character movement and AI.- Xen, it's actually good. I'd say it's one of the best parts of the game.Cons:- Performance can sometimes be spotty, I had well over 100 FPS for most of the time, but some sections especially near the end of Xen the game stuttered and dipped well bellow 50.- In a few occasions I did not recall the solution for a puzzle I would end up slightly stuck, but it never took me too long to figure it out.I think the game is really worth it. Don't wait for a sale, tip your hat to Crowbar collective and enjoy one of the best remakes of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what you would call the opposite of a 'Pacifist Run' but I thoroughly enjoyed doing that on my first play through. I would role-play Gordon Freeman as someone who had been trapped by the scientists in Black Mesa and forced to perform dangerous experiments and dance on command against my will. This would perfectly explain why Gordon was forced to start the resonance cascade by hand at the start of the game, when this could have easily been performed by robotic arm. Gordon's least favourite humiliation he suffered at the hands of the mad scientists was 'The Mime'. This was were Gordon was forced to mime all of the safety protocols to new Black Mesa employees while dressed up like Daisy Duke. If he made any noise or complaint, he would be forced to start over from the beginning, and his rations would be halfed until his captors felt he had been sufficiently punished. This is the root trauma behind Gordon Freeman's muteness as displayed in Half Life 2. As the story progresses Gordon sees the scientists for what they are. Loathsome cowards. As he single-handedly defeats not only the US Military and a whole host of unknown lifeforms, he sees nothing but cowardice from the scientists and incompetence from the security forces that would enforce all physical punishments deemed necessary by his captors. This does nothing but fuel his hatred. As he unloads his shotgun into the faces of tormentors turned tormented, he finds his scars will not easily heal, which enrages him further. Not until Gordon Freeman is the only living creature on Earth and beyond will his blood lust be sated.The final irony being that as he frees himself from the bondage of his captors to finally become a Free Man (see what I did there), he only succeeds in delivering himself into an even more menacing and manipulative force. Or at least this is what I imagined would have been going through Gordon's mind throughout the game.

_childDocuments_.review: My conclusive review on Black Mesa, the (almost) complete remake of the original Half Life:Pros:- Completely new textures- New environments (although similar to Half Life's, obviously)- Completely new voice clips and lines for characters to say that are surprisingly close to the originals, but much higher in quality.- New music- Movement is less slippy- Option to go back to the original movement system if preferred- Guns are more refined and less weird to use- Greatly improved visuals and physics courtesy of the Source engine- Stays quite faithful to the source material while adding new and interesting areas and challenges.Cons (Keep in mind, most of these things are very minor anyways so they don't detract from the game much and will probably be ironed out in the full release):- (Medium Importance) enemy A.I. doesn't have the complexity that the A.I. from the original game did, most notable in the Marines, who would flank and try to flush you out of hiding spots with grenades in the original game, and Vortigaunts, who are more cowardly in the original game and will run away if damaged. For a demonstration in the absurd complexity of Half Life's A.I., see this playlist: - (Low Importance, probably will be fixed) There's a couple of little mild immersion-breaking bugs such as the auto run feature not auto-running after a loading screen until pressing the key to go slow once, and then in the chapter "On a Rail," when going up a slant in the beginning of the level it will slide you to the back of the train for seemingly no reason instead of just keeping you at the front of the train.- (Medium Importance) In most areas, the level design feels flush and polished in terms of both looks and gameplay. In certain areas though, it feels ever so slightly as if it was designed more to look pretty and to cater to more advanced players that already know what they're doing rather than serve an actual purpose or be friendly to newer players and therefore isn't as fun as the rest of the game.- No Xen yet :(Welp, that was it I guess, My Final Verdict:Very Highly Recommended for anyone who likes Half Life and even people who just like FPS games in general, just don't come in expecting Valve's level of polish to every single thing like I did, Crowbar Collective did a very good job with this though :).

_childDocuments_.review: Black Mesa is a fan (Crowbar Collective) remake that took 15 years-ish to make of the 1998 globally successful first-person shooter (FPS) Half Life. Many a PC gamer will attest to how much of a masterpiece Half Life is - I've never played it. Before coming here I took a gander at the games Steam forums and negative reviews to see what's the script... yeah people are crazy. You see, this game shouldn't and doesn't (at least from myself) get any brownie points for being THE Half Life remake. A copy of a good thing is just that, a copy - although this time round it seems, the naughty school boy (Crowbar Collective) not only copied his homework but also decided to crank out the old thesaurus and actually put in effort.People seem really hung up on Chapter 15 aka Xen. Xen has a troubled past in regards to Half Life with people seemingly hating it. I can't help but think it purely based on the mentality that they just wanna shoot more stuff in a military base and/or science lab. At the time of writing there's a guy literally describing the Xen levels (3 chapters) as a walking simulator in the Steam forums - clearly that guy has no idea what a walking simulator is or consists of - last I checked, gun fights with mind controlling flying aliens to mention only one thing tends not to be in walking sims. Why do I bring this up, some may ask. I bring this up because the games Half Life and Black Mesa have either been out for a long time or been getting made for a long time, plus people know the Half Life series before buying into the games. The only real thing - I guess - that'll put you off this title is the negative reviews. Between the forums and the Steam reviews, I've seen plenty of stuff so sharp I just knew that the author of those reviews etc had cut themselves typing stuff like, "xen can ♥♥♥♥ off" so I thought I'd clear the air a little.Okay fair enough, admittedly, xen at times is like American McGee's Alice had a baby with Metroid and named it Xen but hey, it works. The area has loads of environmental plot, gun fights, puzzles and bosses if you count chapter 18 (something people seemingly don't do) i.e. Xen has everything chapter 1 up to and including chapter 15 has.So here's the simple truth, Xen is dislikeable sure, absolutely - to some - and I'd put it down to the simple reason that it's a different pace from the first 15 chapters. I honestly think it's too different for some.Next reason to not buy the game would be it has a "very invasive information gathering policy". Yeah so basically, buy the game and every piece of info your computer gives the game such as your email address etc could be sold. The copy I own via Steam, does not have an opt out option. Does this bother me, nope. It doesn't bother me because I'am a nobody typing a "review" on Steam. I hold no claim to a mansion, private jet or Pamela Anderson sex tape copyright. I'am just a standard guy having a standard life. I couldn't care less that a company wants to buy my "interests" and browsing habits to figure out what type of tooth paste I'm more willing to buy. I've never bought any guff advertised to me in my life. That ain't gonna change because Black Mesa has my info.Here's the real deal, there are holes in this games armor, two examples are:* Everyone has a small variation of the same face* Everyone sees the protagonist Gordon Freeman kicking ass and escaping this or that yet, no one wants to join him. It's small silly stuff like that. That said, this is a fantastic tight as your mum in her prime years FPS game with a plot that's continuously hinted at but never really told outright. Intrigue is always at an all time high when needed, the set pieces are fantastic and the music.... offt, it's good. It's goooood.I suggest you ignore the reviews that are trying so desperate to be a one time wonder of a meme by copying and pasting an already existing meme (that died years ago) and give this a try. All the Half Life games are on sale regularly, perhaps - like myself - wait until they are all on sale and scoop them all up.
