_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus takes the journey from snowy and radioactive Moscow and its dark tunnels, to the vast, diverse and beautiful Russian far east. Enhanced version is the way to play, if you can run raytracing. While gamma correction is a bit off, causing some areas too bright or too dark, and there are occasional glitches, enhanced version has much better ambient illumination, less image noise and the ability to turn off motion blur completely and adjust FOV.Metro Exodus not only has great stealth and excellent gunplay, but also an enjoyable amount of realism, such as the need to prioritize stealth and avoid combat as resources are scarce in a post-apocalyptic world. Weapons also start to wear out with more dirt and mud covered, causing jamming and damage and accuracy loss (the game provides a hardcore realistic difficulty as well). Additionally, the ability to customize weapon parts automatically wins a score from me. However, some design choices of the game are not to my liking (they are not bad) and some are just plain bad.Metro Exodus has a unique approach to characterizing. The game often has five to ten minutes of just people talking to fully immerse players into the role of listener, from which you can learn valuable insights of the characters: their pasts, motives, traits, stands and thoughts, fully fleshing out the characters and forming a connection between them and players. Some of these stories are very entertaining with clever sarcasm about real-life social phenomena, and I totally respect this immersive way of characterizing. However, as a psychopath who always watches videos at 1.5x speed, I find these conversations too lengthy and I prefer something shorter and more condensed.The moral point system dictates a good or bad ending in the Metro series. Previous games have harsher requirements such as listening to every lengthy dialogue. Fortunately, Metro Exodus does not require it, but you still need to take a non-lethal approach in many missions, which handicaps players. It is not just me being a blood thirst maniac wanting to kill everyone, it effectively strips away lots of approaches on dealing enemies taking away many gameplay features, and you have to read walkthroughs a lot. While it can be frustrating, the good ending is so beautiful and all seem worthy.Let’s dive into the bad side. Though Metro Exodus is a good game, the pacing is far from being good, and the lack of long and consecutive levels is the root cause. With levels being relatively short, after finishing one level, the game tends to put players through long story sequences or require them to traverse a long distance in the open world, before they can have another short-lived level of action. The open world session pacing is the worst, with the much better and tighter pacing in late-game linear sessions and DLCs. It feels like the developers didn't have enough content in the middle of the game, so they stretched out what they had for far too long.Metro Exodus changes to a semi-open-world-semi-linear structure, marking the first open world title in the series. However, the open world is the weakest part of the game. It is partially to blame for the sloppy pacing as reason mentioned, and it is vast and empty. Though the emptiness fits in the post-apocalyptic setting, it doesn’t justify the emptiness itself being lackluster in terms of gameplay. In fact, I really think the open world is unnecessary. Extra exploration for upgrades in the open world can easily be rearranged as linear levels, which not only paces the game better but also addresses the lack of long and consecutive levels to some degree. That said, it is at least better than those mundane checklist open worlds created just for the sake of making the game longer.The story of Metro Exodus is based on a premise I find hard to believe (I didn’t read the novel), that there are people outside Moscow but was kept as a secret for years. From what I can recall, previous games did not foreshadow this, and it makes events in the last game look like a joke. The transition between knowing the truth and accepting it is also stiff and awkward, but it pales in comparison to the laughable silent protagonist.The last two Metro games both have a silent protagonist, which was popular in the last two decades. I never found it jarring in the last two games, due to writers taking such good care of the fact that Artyom (protagonist) doesn’t talk, hence they never put him in a position being asked for a direct response. But the writers of Metro Exodus did not have such a heart. There are numerous occasions someone on the radio asks something like “Artyom, what is going on”, and Artyom responds with nothing but awkward silence, which completely breaks the immersion. This game goes the extra mile for immersion and realism in gameplay and storytelling, but somehow, they screwed up something so prominent. In stark contrast, DLC protagonists can talk, and you can immediately tell DLCs have a much more immersive presentation than the base game.From the resource management focus combat to the bold storytelling design that might not win everyone’s favor, Metro Exodus is a slow burner compared to traditional FPS titles that are usually fast and thrilling. It suffers from poor pacing and a mediocre open world and is flawed in story and writing, but I still think it is a unique and excellent game after all. Two DLCs are also of high quality, with emotionally contagious plots, good level design and new weapons and parts (you only get the silent sniper rifle in DLC). These two DLCs are must-play as I think they even transcend the base game in many aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: Neat Metro 8/10 so far, a change in pace to previous metros in the open world-ness and advanced crafting that requires you to make your own supplies. If you liked the previous Metros you will probably like this one.Note: If you played previous Metros on Ranger Hardcore this one is much rougher;- Most enemies, such as bandits, can literally one shot you at full health and you run *entirely* out of ammo in early game quite often.-The stealth detection in this one is also pretty hit or miss, more than previous Metros enemies can *sense* you nearby or see you out of the corner of their eye when you swore you were hidden. The stealth KO has also been wonky on more occasions I can count, leaving me sitting there mashing E while an enemy slowly turns around to Kurt Kobain my brain.

_childDocuments_.review: So at this point I've beaten the game, and I just wanted to update this a little bit. The bottom parts still stand (still V1) but I figured final thoughts would be in order, if you haven't read my original thoughts skip down below and then come back.- The Story, its good, not masterclass, but good. The story kept me coming back, and held me until the end. Some side-stories / characters need fleshed out more, the ending jump is kinda interesting too. So... Maybe DLC & game 4?! It's worth experiencing regardless.- I either stopped noticing the mechanical issues as much (outside of the broken menu...) or the game actually became more polished the further into it I got (which is a true oddity as usually the reverse is true). All of the below is still true, but its less apparent late game. Actually the more "metro" the level is, the better the game plays, the more open the area, it suffers.In the end what kills me is this is a 7/8 out of 10 game, stuck at the moment at a 5/6 out of 10 because of the below. I hope in time it will get the polish it deserves and reach its true potential.Original Review--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------So I've been playing for a little over two hours at this point and I don't understand the praise / positive reviews. Completely ignoring the Epic Store vs Steam controversy this game feels extremely unpolished / unfinished at least on PC. Before I explain my thoughts on the game let me tell you my system specs / the settings I played on.--PC Specs--CPU: i9-9900KRAM: 32GB - 3000mhzSSD: Samsung 970 EVO (M.2) 1TB  GPU: Nvidia 2080ti (x2/SLI)--Game Settings (roughly)--Resolution: 3440x1440 (ultra-wide)Vsync: off (I have G-sync)Details (there's literally one slider for this): UltraRTX: OnDLSS: (On/Off) I tried both with negligible effectsHairworks: OnAdvanced PhysiX: OnFiltering: 16x So TL;DR. If you haven't bought the game yet, (here or on the Epic store) consider yourself lucky, the game needs quite a few updates to be PC ready, if you're extremely lucky it will be worth playing in a years time when it becomes available on Steam again.Now to explain why I feel the above is true:- Many sounds and voices are not synced up with their actions. At the very beginning of the game (maybe 10 minutes in) I watched one of the Spartans clap, and then 3 seconds later heard the actual clap sound. Sometimes voices play before or after the characters mouth has moved while you're looking right at them.- Movement in general, especially QTE movement, is extremely janky, like animations are missing or just forgotten so you basically teleport forward, up, down, just everywhere. It's. so. weird. You feel like your skating around or 600 pounds. Its clunky and just doesn't appear to work right on PC. (The mouse sensitivity to start is also unplayable, there's an extremely noticeable delay in your mouse movement to when the character actually moves unless you turn up the sensitivity to over 60%, by default its at like 20%. - Jumping & Falling are completely broken, jumping is like, you lift a foot off of the ground and go "I jumped" and then if you run too fast (sprint) over a small slope the game will fling you forward and kill you. Falling more than 2 feet is an instant death and you have to go back to you last checkpoint. UNLESS it's a QTE or scripted fall. In which case you're fine. - The game is "semi-open world" but really isnt, if you stray off the path beyond what the game expects it kills you OR teleports you across the map. Fall off the boat not close enough to land, or jump on ice that really isnt ice? you fall in the water and then get teleported either back onto the boat or if thats not possible somewhere extremely far away. I was on a boat in a tunnel, and slid off trying to pick one of the green mushroom things, game teleported me about 250 yards away no where near where I was, theres now no way to get that boat back, completely screwing me in the first "semi-open" area.- If you have an ultra-wide monitor, GG, because the menu's are broken. You'll spend about 20 minutes like I did trying to figure out how to get into the gun menu just to realize the icons and the actual click target aren't in the same place because the developers seemingly didnlt expect ultra-wide monitors (but allow it) so the icons get pushed far to the right, but the click targets are where they are suppose to be? Its extremely annoying, and an unbelieveable oversite. Honestly I feel like a lot of my problems above may be related to playing in ultra-wide but even if that is the case (I may do some testing here shortly) why. even. let. me. select. ultra-wide. then. - The voice acting is worse than I remember for some characters in the previous games, and the audio / talking of characters overlap each other sometimes so I can understand / hear nothing of value. BUT HEY, THEY GOT TOM FROM TOONAMI FOR ONE OF THE VOICE ACTORS, USING HIS TOM VOICE. SO UHHH THATS WORTH SOMETHING RIGHT?! (Seriously it makes no sense, every other character at least attempts a Russian accent, to varying degrees of success, and then there's just good old regular Tom from Toonami. Like hey whats up guys? Wtf?)- The story / plot could be good, but the execution just isn't there. Like I get the direction they are trying to push me in and its really the only reason I want to play, but again it doesn't really pull me in, I feel like the writers took a "how to write a video game story" class from the late 90's to early 00's its campy, unpolished, and just doesn't let you get immersed in the game & world. Artyom also still can't talk (even though he still does in the loading screens) BUT CHARACTERS STILL TELL HIM TO TALK, CONVINCE, ANSWER, other people. It makes. no. sense. Like in one scene they tell you to convince the commander to do something, you sit down next to him, he talks, you clearly say and do nothing, other people come in the room, talk, and the commander says alright we can do the thing. THEN EVERYONE CONGRATULATES YOU FOR YOUR EXPERT DIPLOMACY AND SPEAKING SKILLS. I actually started laughing it was so ridiculous, because the game takes itself EXTREMELY SERIOUSLY.  - The A.I at least on normal are completely brain dead, they don't notice you when they should, their animations are ehhh, more so the monsters than humans but its all over.- The visuals, are interesting. Sometimes the game looks incredible, like some of the best environmental & texture work I've seen in a long while. Then (again within the first 30 minutes of the game) I get thrown in a room with explosions, and you see flame textures everywhere that look like they are straight out of the original doom game. Like basic 2D 5 second sprites on a loop, and you just sit there, laugh, and go WTF.Look, I've played both the original Metro 2033, and Last Light. I loved them both, they are great games. I *wanted* to love Exodus, I still *want* to love Exodus and i'll probably power through and finish it. I do love the *concept* for this game, the execution though, at least right now is just way to lacking. It needs more time, attention, and polish, at least on PC. If the previous games are any indication 4A will (probably) fix a lot of the technical issues over the next few months and it will be what it deserves to be. Because there is good stuff here, the environment like I said can be beautiful. The weapon system is extremely interesting. The mechanics from the previous games are still here and as good as ever. The premise of the story is truly interesting. There is a good game in here somewhere, trying to get out. Which make this initial release that much more painful. Hopefully someday I can come back to this game and change this review, if you can call it that, to a yes, I recommend this, but for right now. Its a no for those of you on the fence who haven't bought it yet, just wait.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, hear me out......The game is, story-wise, amazing. It continues with the story of Artyom, Anna, Miller and company, in a way that feels much more human even though Artyom never actually says a thing. Every interaction between the characters feels grounded, and since it is so "organic" ala Half-Life, nothing feels forced (though there are a few scripted sequences which honestly didn't bother me). The feeling of staying just a little bit longer just to LISTEN to what someone has to say is not something to be understated, specially considering I'm the type of gamer who may even skip cutscenes if he's not interested.. 4A Games really have stepped up their game in terms of narrative and character development. Obviously Dmitry Glukhovsky's work shines through as well.Graphically speaking..... DAMN, the game is simply stunning. Their implementation of Ray traced global illumination brings the levels and characters to life, with a lightning system that is mind blowing. Sure, its performance takes a huge hit if you're not running an RT enabled card, and even then you won't be running the game at 4k 60 unless you have the best of the best, but trust me, that alone is worth the effect.Gameplay wise, the game is defined as "open world" for a reason. While the game is divided into sections, these sections are open enough to let the player explore the world and get lost in its visual storytelling, as well as finding emerging gameplay such as imminent threats, a secret that can help with the upcoming battles, or sneaking (with a rudimentary system mind you) through an entire camp which really put your skills (and looting) to the test, since ammo is scarce, as well as medkits.Sadly, the gameplay is marred by some very wonky controls, which give off the feeling of floating around constantly, to the point where I wouldn't even recommend sprinting while going over an incline, as you'll just... fly out. I'm guessing it's something to do with Artyom's acceleration... Too much radiation perhaps?Controls are not the only negative however, and this is where the game almost made me rage quit and ask for a refund even though I was on my 25th hour of gameplay, and that is the HUMONGOUS amount of hard chrashes which forced me to reboot my computer. At some point it got so bad I couldn't even advance a few meters without one. Eventually, I had to disable pretty much every overlay possible, as well as disable any and all Overclocks I had (even though they are rock solid), and even then crashes would still occur, even in the ending credits.What really pissed me off about that is that the game is definitely not new, and its story and gameplay are really really worth it, but DAMN the amount of issues the game has, and the fact that the devs didn't even bother fixing them is a big screw you to the consumers who just want to enjoy this incredible story.So... Would I recommend the game? Sure, at its core the game is incredible, but the amount of crashing alone can cause enough frustration to uninstall it before you finish. Be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is an excellent entry in the post-apocalyptic series, combining a new direction of sandbox level design, with the gritty setting of the irradiated Russian countryside. The levels remind me of Far Cry 2 with the ability to spot and identify targets from afar, and choose your point of entry with each engagement. The levels also hold true to the design of the previous games, with alternate paths tucked away leading to advantageous positions for engagements, or a cache of weapons, ammo or resources.The modular nature of the weapons in Exodus offer a huge degree of adaptability, with is very refreshing for the franchise, as you are no longer confined to modifying at trader shops located exclusively within a handful of metro stations. The weapons also feel great, with awesome new improvements to classic weapons like the Tikhar and Helsing, as well as some new additions. Some fan favourites like the Duplet and (my personal favourite) the VSS are missing. Fortunately with the existing weapon list, you can modify other weapons to replicate these missing classics.The visuals and graphics are simply amazing. Considering how the series looked not too long ago, the team at 4A have made great strides in improving the look and feel of their games, and I hope this series can continue to reach an ever expanding fanbase. I understand that people are upset at the Epic Store exclusivity, and I can't blame them for that. However, this was decision made by the publisher Deep Silver, not 4A. Once this period is up however, I would recommend anyone who has an interest in this game to pick it up, it is excellent and I am currently eagerly awaiting the DLC expansions. I have played it 3 times through at the time of writing, and I still thoroughly enjoy this game.

The maps are gorgeous and well designed so that I felt compelled to explore and find new things without it feeling repetitive. It's games like this that give me hope in single player experiences and I look forward to future instalments of the series. Hopefully with less internet drama next time though.Also, if you don't play this on Ranger Hardcore you're doing yourself a huge disservice. Dunno why 4A even bothers with the other difficulty levels.

_childDocuments_.review: I prefer to leave "Neutral" as recommendation but since its yes or no I'll just leave it at yes.Let me get this out of the way first.This game has MANY issues when it comes to its gameplay I will talk about it after all the good things about it.This game is a mix of between Linear and open world experience, you'll be thrown into this "world" tackling a lot of side missions and you're free to do them in any order you wants but the main story will drive you along in a linear path.They really puts a huge amount of efforts getting the players to immerse in this world everything the player does the world take notes about it and reflect about them through NPC's dialogue and the main character's diary. Every interactable objects are part of the world itself ... they may go a little too far in this department but I'll talk about it in the gameplay part.Graphics .... is an icing on the cake for this believable world. It is gorgeous on High settings, lower than high and it starts to get blurry which is not ideal but seeing the game engine itself is very well optimize most PC should be capable of running this game in high settings.Now here is where it all fall shorts...the gameplay.Starts with character movement slight incline low or high they are potentially lethal to the player. High inclines slows you down maybe that is how it works in real life but then you notice this happens with every small hill and everytime it happens you'll hear that sound effect which appears to be a character sliding sound effect. Try your very best to approach low inclines slowly otherwise you'll notice you get a lot of air time by simply running off them highly lethal in some area.Weapons now jam when they gets dirty ... awesome this is a fine system until you realize that it doesn't just jammed. When the weapons get dirty their performance also drops so it doesn't matter how buff your gun is if it gets dirty it won't delivers what you wanted it to do combine that with weapon jamming and you get the idea of this mess. Its like they don't want the players to use any of these cool looking metro design firearms.Objects interaction...I'll just refer as "animations"A lot of the objects in the world can be interact with....all of them has mostly the same animations and it is not a fast one. Sure for the very first time the character has to interact with the object they have to inspect it closely that explains the time it took for the character to do his things BUT some objects like Electric Motors and a Generator the character interacts with them all the time and when there's an enemy making all the noises and in some cases RIGHT IN FRONT OF THE CHARACTER and he doesn't show any sense of urgency to...you know FINISH whatever he's doing FAST to respond to life threatening situation !?Yes this is about "muh immersion" but this can ruin anybody else's when there's a disconnection in the subject of "realism"Vehicles....ESPECIALLY the boat.Yes the players get to drive around in a vehicle in this game but whatever you do try to spend as least amount of time as possible on a boat. The boat moves SLOWLY.... make sense considering the player is basically rowing it until you realize that there are enemies you have to fight on that small of a platform. To make matter worse the enemies you're fighting are the one that do RANGE ATTACKS which if you happens to be on ... I don't know A BOAT IN THE MIDDLE OF THE RIVER ? Have fun.The game has a moral system for you guess it.... them endings.From my experience it doesn't really force the player to play the game in "the only way possible" as many would implies.The player can approach the game with "If its hostile, you kill it" mindset but remember NOT everything is hostile.This way you don't have to force your way to play the game "the only way" which happens to be stealth.Still it could've been better I don't like the idea of "Do good deeds to be rewarded" as this is not a good mindset for anyone.That's all I have to say some may notice that I did a review for the game not too long ago but I see it as a full negative reviews which is unfair towards the game with this amount of effort put into it so here it is a hopefully a better one.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I ended up picking this game and the other three in a bundle back when it was on sale due to a friend's recommendation, and I must say I am not disappointed in the slightest. The previous two games in the series have managed to keep my spastic attention span in an iron grip with it's amazing story, setting and gunplay, and Metro Exodus has not failed to follow up. I have enjoyed this game more than any other single player series in the last few years. As somebody who is a sucker for this style of story (Post apocalyptic wasteland survival with a good story thrown in) it's hard to find a game or game series that manages to do it well. I ended up playing through the previous two games on the hard difficulty, and I made the choice of amping things up by running Ranger Hardcore with the "deep dive" hud, which is to say I had basically no hud whatsoever. There were times that it was frustrating due to not knowing how much ammo I had unless at a workbench, but in the end I'm glad I did it; it certainly added greatly to the experience, and it really felt like I was playing through the eyes of Artyom. If you're willing to deal with some trial and error, I would recommend this as the way to go. To wrap this already long review up before it gets any longer, I would highly recommend you give this game a try if you've played the previous in the series. I was very satisfied with how the story resolved itself, and in my opinion this is one of the best games I've ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: Ten years ago Metro 2033 was an unexpected pleasant surprise. It was a scripted linear stealth FPS that cared about its storytelling, its world and characters more than about making you feel cool, something that was commonplace for the tightly scripted big budget titles of the time. It was as if Escape from Butcher Bay was based on a Russian post-apocalyptic sci-fi novel. And despite a lot of its issues, it was unforgettable and wonderful.Ten years from then, Metro Exodus is trying to turn Metro 2033 into Far Cry. Results are far less disastrous than one might expect.I simply do not understand why anyone thought that basing Metro Exodus almost entirely on gameplay would be a good idea, without rethinking said gameplay completely. But that is what happened. Exodus has several story sequences/levels that work almost exactly like the previous games - highly scripted stealth FPS with forced action moments. And then most of game is set inside open maps/open levels which are essentially tiny open world locations with several locations for you to explore at your own pace. Except, most of those, if they have any kind of quest attached to them, work exactly like what I've described with the older games. Which is completely at odds with the open nature the game is trying to have at the same time, simply because that core gameplay was never particularly fun in the first place.See, Metro games were never good FPS or stealth titles, if you boil them down to mechanics specifically. Those worked to create the tension necessary for the situation, for the story. Those worked in conjunction with the moral choices you had, with understanding that you must ration your ammo, your filters, your medkits. Mechanically, it was boring and basic. Stealth, as mentioned, was almost always the "intended" way to go, but it was relatively not annoying specifically because you just had to follow the "intended" path and everything will work out. Shooting was fine for short sequences, because the unorthodox weapons had neat little touches to them that made them unique. Metro 2033 and Last Light were great because these mechanics served a purpose of telling the story.Metro Exodus jumps between telling a genuinely atrociously stupid story and outright refusing to tell the story unless you beg it to say anything. The story, as it is, is just boring, but the fact that you essentially have an all new cast, while the main character is still a mute dummy isn't helping. The obnoxious "love interest" from Last Light returns and is, in fact, the main focus of the story in a way, her dad, redesigned completely yet again, returns as well. But apart from them, the rest of the cast are all new and all forgettable, all lacking personality. With Artyom being the biggest personality void of all. In 2033 he was just a guy who suddenly got an important task assigned to him and went on a journey that changed him and who managed to change the lives of those around him as he went. In Last Light he was closer to your typical soldier character, a "hero", yet it still fit the story. In Exodus, he is simply not a character at all. He has all these relationships, all of these desires, yet he, as a character, is just absent and nothing in the story or the gameplay builds him at all.What's worse is when you need to ask the game to tell you things. Do you know how most character developments, most critical expositions that build the locations you visit happen? You need to find a character who is willing to share those and stand near them. Just literally stand near them. Doing nothing. For up to 5-10 minutes. Listening to Exposition Podcast. With things mentioned there that are vital to understanding the situations and motivations. Who thought this was a good way to tell a story in a story driven game?But then again, Metro Exodus tries hard to not be story driven and to be gameplay driven and it just doesn't work. The joy of Far Cry, or Just Cause, or whatever other similar titles is in the fact that you can do really fun things with the core systems, the core mechanics of the game. Heck, even Gears 5, with similar open level design, is good because its core shooting is, and always was, good. Repetitive, but good. Very few things in Metro Exodus are mechanically interesting, yet the open level design forced the studio to cut down on the actions and the weapons, so they could reuse those in the most efficient way, as often as possible. And it's just boring to go through. And on Ranger difficulty, which is, as usual for the series, in many ways the intended experience, the scripted sequences feel about as fine as they used to before, except now in the open exploration you can randomly die to something unexpected and then learn that the last checkpoint was 10 minutes ago and before you did all of that boring "collect crap, craft crap, upgrade weapon crap" stuff that is common to the Far Cry games. No challenge, just annoyance.There are good things in this game, however, as little as there are. Some of the stories you encounter are genuinely interesting. The whole "morality system" is least obtuse here and feels surprisingly well integrated into the story. Visually the game is astonishing even without the Ray Tracing features and locations are consistently beautiful at any time of day that is dynamic as is the weather. And even though it's considerably less inventive with its storytelling than the original was, it still has some really good moments.Two story DLCs for the game aren't particularly exciting either. The first one, The Two Colonels, feels closer to what Last Light and especially its DLCs were about, but otherwise tells a rather unimportant part of the backstory. It has some interesting moments, it has a flamethrower as a main weapon, but otherwise it's not very good. Also extremely poorly optimized for Ranger difficulty where you will most likely often randomly die to something. The second one, Sam's Story, does the same open level design as the main game, but its story is as bland and unimportant as of the first DLC. It is essentially just "more of the same", except with an even stupider story.Oh yeah, also the game can still be incredibly buggy. I personally encountered mostly animation bugs, with characters and things randomly teleporting around or things getting stuck in other things, but a few times things went completely off rails and I had to restart the checkpoint. Also, it's been 10 years, and the PC settings in the game are as basic and crap as they were in 2033 - just a couple of presets and no manual control over what enables/disables what. It doesn't even say what each preset does, which is especially obnoxious since it seems that the last 2 presets are basically the same in terms of settings and its just that the highest one uses supersampling (renders the game at a higher resolution and downsamples from it).I didn't actively dislike Metro Exodus, but unlike the previous two entries in the franchise, I didn't enjoy this game at all. Most of the time I just wanted it to end so I could move to something else. It looks great, it has a few good moments, its post-apocalyptic world, while expanded, is still curious and Tihar is still one of the most interesting guns in gaming history, despite its simplicity. But it's also primitive and bland as a story driven game, rather limiting and linear for an exploration focused open level game and not particularly exciting for a stealth action title. Also, the music is downright terrible this time around. How far from the wonderful music of 2033 we have come. Honestly, instead of playing Metro Exodus I'd suggest checking Metro 2033 again, in original or Redux versions. I kinda wish I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated series, all 3 games are nothing short of masterpieces of the modern times. With that said, this time Artyom and his crew finally break out from the haunting dark tunnels of Moscow metro and travel all over Russia (or whats left of Russia) to find a place to call home. The base game is 25-30 hours long if you are like me and prefer listening to every conversation and checking out every corner. The DLCs too are definitely worth the money and made with the same effort as the amazing base game. The Two Colonels is completely linear (veterans of metro will feel more at home) and tell a great story which I am sure nobody wants me to spoil here, its around 2 hours long and you can easily finish it in one go. Sam's Story is more like the base game in the sense that it gives you a map to explore. It follows the journey of the only American crewmate of Artyom who's trying to get to his home country, its around 5-6 hours long. Sam's Story starts right from the point where the base game ends, so its definitely better to play the base game first before jumping into any of the DLCs (even though Two Colonels is mostly set in past. it does contain massive spoilers for the base game). I still can't wrap my head around the fact that this game wasn't even picked as a nomination for GOTY. Single-player shooters aren't dead. Thanks 4A Games. <3

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the Metro series, I feel I must unpleasantly post a negative review of this game. I think it was a big mistake to strike out so significantly from established norms of the series. The abandonment of the metro proper for, primarily, the countryside of Russia was a mistake and not in keeping with the atmosphere of previous Metro entries. The times I had the most fun with Exodus were in those relatively rare moments that you were in more tightly enclosed confines or ruined cities. The open world elements did nothing but pad the play time with uninteresting journeys through the wastes and with side encounters that were generally uninteresting.Additionally, dealing with the factions of the Moscow metro and the effect the previous games had on the metro itself were the most interesting aspects of the series but, of course, this was completely abandoned for new factions and situations that were entirely unenthralling.Here is hoping that subsequent entries will return to the roots of what made the Metro series uniquely interesting.Oh, and ♥♥♥♥ EPIC.

I didn't get to play this game until 2021 because I didn't have a good enough PC to run it.  I was aware of the developers taking the game off Steam upon its release to be sold on Epic.  Which I thought was a real jerk move and clearly done for money reasons.  It pissed off Steam users, me included. Remastered" version of this game now.  Stating that it is for high-end PCs.  Which just made me laugh.  The game as it stands is for high-end PCs.  I ran this on an RTX 2070 Super with max settings. I constantly had this glitch occur where I would be in the truck/van and go to look at my map.  The viewpoint in the vehicle would shift way up so I couldn't drive properly.  I'd have to get out and get back in to fix it.  Pretty game-breaking actually when you're getting your ass kicked because you can't see.It plays like Evil Within 2/Dying Light, mostly.  Leveling, crafting, side quests, open world, etc.  Although to me not as engaging or fun.  I guess I prefer a linear/tighter experience with Metro.  Having played my fair share of the Stalker series.  I feel that is what this game should have been and not a Metro game.  If you like Stalker but find it too hard, then I guess this is for you.  The game's ending was not satisfying to me either.  The game felt padded and just somewhat bland in areas.  I felt a real lack of a horror element too which may be because of the openness of the game.  It looks and sounds great aside from the Ray Tracing issues.  I do have to mention the AI again.  Not that the other games have super AI either.  I just wanted more from the enemies than Exodus provided.  I've played the Two Colonels which was fine and all, it was more like the original games.  Short and sweet, also surprisingly easy.  Not sure about the other DLC yet till I play it.  I am sure it will be decent.As for this Enhanced/Remastered thing that is coming out.  Just seems silly to me.  This game doesn't need a Remaster, it needs more updates/patches.  It just says to me that it was released too soon.  I haven't heard whether it is gonna be free to people who own the game already or not.  It's not something I will be buying.  It just makes you feel like you were taken advantage of.  A point of concern is... Unless you are really into Metro and this style of Metro.  You may only play this game once or not for a long time, due to the game's length.  So if you just played the original of this game then you are getting a lesser experience.  So no, it's not a bad game by any means. The NPCs always seemed to feel like they were stating the obvious.  The means of telling you what you need to do and how to do it.  It's better than being confused or lied to I guess... lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro games are made with passion. The series expounds on what was previously derived from the novel  by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, that was later produced into a movie, , by Andrei Tarkovsky, that inspired the Metro book series, before it finally making its way into video games. Metro Exodus is the third entry in this series. And it might be the greatest.Whether it checks that box for the consumer depends on if returning players, or newcomers, can handle the holistic changes that come packaged within Exodus. It’s a different game from its progenitors. It provides fundamental Metro gameplay, but it is now expanded within the context of open-sandbox environments. Which is a stark contrast from the on-the-rails story beats returning players might expect. Metro Exodus elected to give the player the power to create their own set pieces. And it was a risk, but a calculated one.The creators were most certainly attempting to broaden their consumer base while also being mindful of those returning (although Epic Store–timed exclusivity kind of screwed that up anyway). But alterations from the norm were a success. Metro Exodus is fantastic.  In the wake of apocalyptic nuclear war, the Metro series follows the surviving inhabitants living in the old Moscow Metro, or subway system. Metro stations have become towns and the remaining populace has formed collectivist ownership over these towns. Over time, each station established its own unique identity. Some friendly, some not. Previous Metro titles (Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light) tasked the player with navigating the metro, warring with self-radicalized stations, and dealing with irradiated monsters that now stalk the tunnels.Exodus is about Artyom, the series’s protagonist, leaving Moscow with a squad of series regulars on a year-long journey across Russia. The game opens remarkably similar to previous entries. The player traverses a frozen Moscow landscape, journeys through a metro station, and is otherwise exposed to linear narrative threads. None of this is tedious though. The Metro series has already showcased how adept it is at handling linearity. Mostly, it does it through atmosphere and mood, which continues to be exhibited in Exodus. Artyom has always been a silent protagonist, the exception being his journal entries that are voiced during loading screens. Exodus keeps the same format, and in doing so, handles expository information well. It is difficult to competently and realistically disseminate exposition in a meaningful way with a mute character, so it’s amazing how effortlessly Exodus does it. The player naturally learns of the events that happened between Last Light and this current story, the most important of which is that Artyom’s lover, Anna, remains as such.Events take place that cause Artyom and his crew to leave Moscow for the Russian countryside via locomotive. After that, familiar linearity of old metro systems is mostly abandoned in favor of successive, unique sandboxes that change as each chapter progresses. And they’re all astounding.After leaving Moscow, the story proceeds through four unique chapters that all feature different playscapes. Mostly these areas offer aesthetic differences that revolve around the seasons in which your crew visits them. Basically, expect the summer area to feel hotter and the autumn area to feel colder. The first three sandboxes, in particular, elect to give up control to the player to create their own action within the various locations constructed. It is obviously an enormous risk to create a Metro game that doesn’t take place in, well, a metro. But they had reason to bet on themselves.The creators were able to split the difference between their typical, linear narrative structure and popular open-world exploration. This was achieved by not making any one area have  much to do or be  big to explore. Artyom has a map of each region, and that map is highlighted with areas of importance. Some of these highlights feature a monster’s nest to destroy or a bandit’s camp to clear, while others contain pertinent story points.  It really works.  Exodus swapped tunnels for open landscapes featuring a day-and-night cycle. The same emotions that the player previously felt exploring the darkness of the metro is again achieved through this approach. It is still extremely immersive, and surprisingly eerie, to traverse Exodus’s landscapes in intense darkness, surrounded by things that want to kill you. The environments are different. The atmosphere is the same.An absolute must when developing sandboxes is that there exists an inherent mechanical reason for the player to explore them, in addition to narrative motivations. If not, the game is just as on-the-rails as before, only now watered down with unnecessary fluff. Fortunately, Exodus does provide a reason. Not only do the environments look interesting, they usually contain important crafting materials within. These resources are used to upgrade, modify, and clean Artyom’s equipment. And equipment can degrade rapidly depending on the situation. Which means nearly every collapsed building, dark tunnel, or campfire in the distance is worth checking out. Occasionally Artyom will run into members of his own squad while exploring these ruins, which adds to player immersion. The world just feels alive.Exodus tells a wonderful story. It features terrific characters, some of which were introduced in the previous games, and expands on their personas. There is, admittedly, a trope-ish element that exists here somewhat—there are tough characters, funny characters, and sweet characters. But if the player spends enough time listening to their conversations, they will eventually observe personalities that exist beyond their archetypes. Especially with Anna. Anna engenders immense pathos by the story’s conclusion, partly because the player is granted so many different, immersive ways to interact with her. All of which are extraordinarily additive. Maybe you’ll put your arm around her, or hold her hand, or brush her hair back. And while all of this is completely optional, it is hard to imagine any Metro player electing not to. Their relationship feels honest. Which is doubly an achievement when you consider that Artyom never utters a word. When certain circumstances arise that place Anna in extreme danger, there is an emergent need for the player to deliver her safely and as quickly as possible. By the time Exodus’s train reaches its final destination, the player will have experienced one of the more immersive stories in recent years. A story that, much to its credit, features multiple endings to increase replayability. I have beaten the game twice (once on console), and both endings were different, excellent finales. One of the endings was the  ending. But it didn’t seem bad to me; more like good storytelling.Metro Exodus is the third part in the Metro series. It is a mechanically sound, first-person shooter that takes place across a litany of areas that the player will explore. It is a blast to play. It contains a strong story that perfectly balances gameplay with narrative beats. While it may lack some of the spectacle seen in more well-known franchises, it more than makes up for it in its polish and atmosphere. In fact, Metro Exodus surpasses nearly all of its contemporaries with relative ease.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is awesome. But not as good as the previous two games.It has most of the elements I love from previous games like, pretty fun combat, fantastic atmosphere and level design, great story.There are some things that sucks though:- Pretty poor stealth.- Awful movement physics, possibly the worst I've ever experienced in a video game. It is very unsmooth, you stumble on everything, sometimes you move freely, sometimes you slow down heavily (not counting walking through the spider webs), you can slow down by walking on as tiny things as cables and wires too... Often you can stumble across a tiny rock and shoot a few metres forward often landing in a water and drowning or in some hole and fall to death. Or even worse, sometimes you run and then suddenly shoot yourself like a rocket into the air like 60 metres and then fall to your death... These happen very commonly.- Once saves got corrupted for no reason at all. Fortunately, the previous save worked and I lost like only a minute of progress.- Sound mixing is awful, couldn't make the game sound right no matter how much I played with the volume settings, it was always either the background effects too loud, the speaking too loud/silent, the music too loud/silent... It's as if every sound in this game has different sound volume on its own. Even in the same dialogue of two people standing next to each other sometimes there's like a 2x volume difference between the both of them.- Night/day cycle can be annoying. It changes way too often and sometimes there are no beds anywhere around.- Sometimes it is hard to tell whether you can walk on something or is it muddy water in which you can drown. What is even worse, sometimes an enemy can grab you in the water, you break out with a quick time event and then still drown...- Poor optimisation, at times it runs extremely smoothly, but most of the time it performs poorly.- Some of the worst product localization I have ever seen (for a big budget game that is). Most of the writings on the walls which are in russian, aren't translated (a few of them have translation pop-ups, but very few), also some of the russian dialogues aren't translated in English as well, they're just written in Latin alphabet in subtitles...Anyway, this game is an awesome journey with tons of nuisances.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: At this moment, I'm both angry and sad to had to write this review but I must to. Metro Exodus is a very interesting game, way superior in features compared to the other two (graphics, music, gameplay in general) but the amount of bugs you can find are stupid.    Some of them can be fixed on your own (like exiting and reentering a vehicle or switching to the map 2 times if you get that camera bug at some place) but what made me stop playing this game is a single dead ass one that clearly is game breaking.    One npc is supposed to go with you, and at certain point, give you a lift so you can reach the next area, but guess what? the AI is so broken that the npc gets stuck and doesn't do anything. Since the game doesn't have a manual save slot system, only "quick" auto saves, I couldn't go back to retry that specific scenario.Searched through the web to get a possible fix for it (since the official stance of the devs is to restart the whole chapter, which means you have to reexplore the whole map again and finding everything again, which is a big NO if you tend to be a completionist) but nothing useful that could find. Tried the cheat engine method, tried to force the npc to teleport to my location, tried to get another player save file, nothing worked.   I must recall, this game was the one in which one of the devs in charge got so mad that he threated people that this game would not come to PC if gamers ended up revolting... It is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DISGRACE that quite some time has passed since its launch on Epic and Steam, and game breaking bugs like this one didn't get fixed at all. It killed my joy and having to replay a whole chapter (exploring, gathering collectibles, gun parts, lore, etc) is just bs. So long Metro, way to get an experience ruined. 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel Metro Exodus is a step forwards and two step back....For those who love open world exploring then you're in a treat, because Metro Exodus offers that. But at the same time I feel this in't Metro anymore. When I first play Metro, it's because it's literally inside a Metro, it was so unique and mind blowing how people built their new life inside a Metro system. There was nothing like this even till today. Only Metro game you get to see it. Now having an open world is nice, but I feel the developers were lazy, because the world is fun to explore yet at times feel dead and dull, since there's no real form of missions or any sense of requirement for you to explore. Sure it's better to explore it and get all the best equipment, but you don't actually need it to complete the game. It's like you have to use your own imagination to have fun with it....if I were to do that I wouldn't be playing a game, I would learn to be a game developer instead. Battles / gunfights are lot more mediocre too....even on the Main Story line, It's not as epic and engaging as the previous two games. Hard to put it into words, but as I said when I play Metro Exodus it doesn't give me that sort of engaging and sense of a SP, but rather more like a MMO RPG Online game...It feels " dull " yet the game have so much potential....I actually had more fun in the DLC called Two Colonel...that's the easiest way I can explain my dissatisfaction with Metro Exodus. In a Nutshell, the game is great, I had fun, but It could have been better. And If I were to recommend a Metro game, I most likely would easily recommend Last Light / 2033 Redux instead, not because those are the Prequel, but I find those overall a better Metro games. Even when it lack the mechanic and gameplay Exodus offers. But I'm still gonna thumb it up. It's a Good game, but definitely not a Masterpiece or the Sequel I was expecting.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the previous two games and the books, I can without a doubt recommend this game. If you're a fan of the previous two entries, you owe it to yourself to see where the story takes Artyom and his wife in this Russian post-apocalyptic epic. If you haven't played the previous games, you could still enjoy this one but I urge you to play the others first as all three of them are part of the same story. I've played the game twice now, once on normal difficulty and once on Ranger Hardcore with all the hud turned off.Unlike Metro 2033 & Metro Last Light which were known for their linear gameplay and claustrophobic levels, this one has much wider and more open levels since our crew is leaving their life in the metro behind  in order to to persue answers about what life is like outside Moscow. The game still has underground levels that made metro so good in the first place, but the majority of the game is spent up in the unforgiving Russian Wasteland in what could be described as a Semi-Open world game.This is the most refined version of the gameplay that we know and love from the past games. The survival mechanics have been turned up to eleven. Mask filters are rare and  ammo is scarce. You're forced to count every single bullet and think before getting into an encounter. You wanna sit far away because you saw a mutant and you're scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Too bad, doing so will use all of your remaining gas mask filters so you have to man up and get it over with.  The gunplay itself has been improved drastically since Last Light. The guns feel much more real and impactful and you can really tell that you're firing a Kalashnikov when the gun starts to kick like crazy. Take care of your guns because if you don't do so, they'll get damaged overtime and they will jam. There's a huge amount of attachments  that completely change the identity of each gun.The bullet  economy has been changed this time around. In this game, there are no bullets that will get you anything. You'll have to make due with  the stuff that you find on the surface. Only then will you be able to craft things like bullets and so on.The AI itself is quite questionable. On my first playthrough (normal) I found both killing enemies and sneaking past them rather easy, while on my second playthrough(Ranger hardcore, hardest difficulty) the NPCs would grow a third eye and always spot me. They were also super deadly in combat and would kill you in 2-3 shots. If I had to choose a difficulty for someone who plays the game for the first time, I'd without a doubt choose "Hard". The number of enemies felt way too low on normal and way too high on ranger hardcore, so I feel like hard would be the best balance out of all the things that I mentioned.As far as mutants go, this game easily has the most variety out of all three games. You have your usual flying demons, you have your lake monsters, our friendly watchmen patrolling the wasteland, creepy underground spiders, mutated animals and of course a few others that I'll let you explore on your own.The maps/chapters are very varied as well. You have the huge caspian desert that feels like you're playing mad max, you have an underground bunker that feels like playing Wolfenstein, a far cry-like forest level, or the Volga level that Stalker fans will love. Dont get me wrong though, the final level of the game is classic metro on steroids. Absolutely mental.The replayability of the game isnt too bad either. Without getting into spoilers, the game has multiple endings that require different playstyles. Also, thanks to the non-linear levels, there's different ways to approach each objective and many things that can be easily missed on your first playthrough.The story of this game is loosely based on the Metro 2035 novel but 90% of the story is new. It only borrows some book plot twists in its first hour and thats it, everything else is new. It's a continuation of Metro Last Light and you see the effects that the ending of the second game had on this world and its characters.The plot itself sounds like a typical post apocalyptic Odyssey on paper but the subtle political messages and the characters are what make it special. My biggest complaint is that just like the previous games, our protagonist, Artyom, does not speak. He speaks in loading screens so you can hear whats going on in his mind but he does not speak in the actual game. That's really immersion breaking when people talk to you and ask things of you and you dont say anything, but they somehow get on with it anyway. What I dont understand is that since Artyom is already a very established and interesting character in the books, and since he already speaks his mind during cutscenes, why shouldnt he speak in game ? The other characters consist of Artyom's wife Anna from the second game, her father Colonel Miller from the first game and a few comrades from the Spartan order and people that you meet along the way. I was pleasantly surprised at how much of a backstory each one of them had. You can read your journal and learn more things about them and confont them on the aurora to hear optional dialogue that builds their character. All in all, great.The story itself with all the plot twists and stuff I thought was great, although I did see a few twists coming from a mile away(But again, I had read the book which the game drew inspiration from). The game slowly builds towards the big finale of the game which had me on the edge of my seat and was truly breathtaking. I legit had no idea what was going to happen in the end.Another thing that I feel like I have to mention is the lack of supernatural elements in this game and the story. If you've played the previous games then you're  familiar that the games can get pretty nuts with all the supernatural stuff but for better or worse, they are mostly absent from this game. Which, again, is because the same thing happened with the 2035 novel. The game though focuses on some political messages that were present in the book too which I enjoyed. Its a story of how you can best manipulate a nation, conserve it underground and make it follow false leaders who all they have to do is point their finger at a plausible enemy so you can blame them for your failures and be doomed in an eternal war. The 2035 novel itself is dedicated to this theme and how man needs enemies to find purpose in life and identify himself. It's a story about being afraid to look at the truth and take actions.TL:DR: This is a great entry to an already amazing series that thanks to its survival mechanics, gameplay and unforgetable story make Exodus a must play.+Great Story+Interesting Characters+Immervise survival gameplay+Shooting feels amazing+Satisfying ending+Very detailed Journal about the world and its characters with lots of lore+/- A few nice plot twists that might feel disjointed if you can sense them coming+/- AI can feel uneven+/- Silent protagonist (Which is a personal prefference)NoneScore: 8.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those titles that stuck with me long after I finished it and that I kept thinking about for several days.The game is set 2 years after the events of the previous chapter.Our protagonists, Artyom, Anna, Miller and some former Spartans, tired of life underground and after discovering that there are other survivors living on the surface, embark on a journey on board a train in search of a place where they can settle a colony and start a new life outside the metro.This "exodus" will mean that throughout the storyline we will visit a variety of different places, each characterized by its own peculiarities. The bombings occurred about 25 years earlier and therefore a large part of the territories are still highly irradiated, inhospitable, infested with mutants or in any case difficult to inhabit.The game will let us discover many small settlements, each of which, following the wars and the absence of a central government, has had different events and has evolved and adapted to the circumstances as best it could.This allows for a very varied narrative that is free from the setting of the tunnels, which bored me a bit after Last Light. And towards the end, when we’ll have to return to another subway and visit its tunnels, we will discover that even there events took a very different turn compared to what happened under Moscow.Initially I didn't appreciate the first "open" level (The Volga), coming from the linear gameplay of the previous chapters I found it a bit distracting. However, once I got past the first adaptation phase, the game hooked me. In fact, it is not so much the gameplay that popped, but rather the various stories that we will gradually discover. Each chapter is somewhat comparable to one of the Fallout vaults, and so the thing I found most exciting was trying to understand what happened and how it got to the current situation.The environmental narration also helps a lot in this, very carefully crafted, full of visual clues as well as the classic fragments of diaries scattered around. All this captured me and immersed me in the stories, I felt right there, sometimes inside and sometimes alongside Artyom, while I explored All the characters have endured extremely hard stories, and are the often tragic fruit of their experiences. Despite everything at the end of each episode, however dramatic, there sometimes remains a glimmer of hope, perhaps reflecting the vision of Dmitry Glukhovsky (not having read the novels I can't say for sure, but I can certainly say that I felt like to read them while playing this title).To all this I would add that aliens are not present in the main plot, unlike the previous chapters, and this makes it in my opinion much more linear and simple to follow, and ultimately I appreciated it much more than that of 2033 and Last Light.Speaking of pure gameplay, however in this chapter we will have more freedom of movement thanks to the introduction of semi-open world hubs, where in addition to being able to decide whether to have a stealth or more aggressive approach, sometimes we will be able to choose the order in which to face the objectives.This might be a bit reminiscent of the immersive sim genre, although in reality everything will be much simpler and more linear. The result, in my opinion, is quite balanced and enjoyable, and contributes to immersion in the general atmosphere.Moving on to the graphics section, I must say that I also found this to be exceptional. I played the version with Ray Tracing and I found everything really well done, non-repetitive and with great attention to detail. As already mentioned, the environmental storytelling is really effective, also thanks to the beautiful graphics. The artistic direction is excellent, all the settings had a strong visual impact on me, without ever boring me, really managing to immerse myself in the atmosphere.The same thing I can say about the sound, whose well-crafted effects amplify even more the emotions gradually transmitted by the environment, the tension of walking alone inside radioactive tunnels full of corpses or in a sandstorm. The soundtrack is also excellent, discreet and effective.In conclusion, a game that I approached because I felt the need for a bit of a post-apocalyptic “fix” and which definitely exceeded all expectations, leaving me more than satisfied, and above all intrigued to finally read the novels on which it is based. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: After a few weeks I was finally able to get through the bugs and finish this game. The gist of the story is that after years of living in the metro, Artyom discovers theres' life outside of the metro and looks for a new radiation-free place to live. As a conclusion to the metro trilogy, I feel like it leaves off on a satisfying note, but I'm left with the feeling of "what ever happened to X". The Spartans have a lot of personality and don't feel like generic NPCs travelling with Artyom. I actually like and care about his companions. You will only get to know them if you actually go out of your way to interact with them and listen to their dialogue though. As for the gameplay, it's pretty much identical to the previous two titles. You can go in stealth or guns-blazing. Bullets are not very scarce this time around, however I only played on hardcore. Hardcore Ranger may be different. There's a decent amount of mutant variety, but they're not as dangerous as human enemies. Gun customization is pretty insane. You can get a variety of scopes, magazines, barrels, etc to customize guns as you see fit. The graphics and environments are phenomenal. This is definitely the best looking FPS I've ever played (sorry Crysis 3). The game itself would be solid if not for the atrocious bugs. The biggest one is hard crashing at the Desert lighthouse. Sometimes when sneaking up on enemies you aren't given a prompt to stealth kill or knock them out, resulting in death or being discovered. Random crashes can result when enemies discover and engage you. The game sometimes auto-saves when near hostile enemies or doesn't auto-save at all, resulting in having to redo 10 minute sequences. You are not able to create hard-saves, only quick saves. You can load up to 5 previous quick saves, but if you want to load one further than the most recent you have to quit to the main menu.I enjoyed the game, but the bugs can make it completely unplayable. I'm not just saying to say it. There is a high chance that you will not be able to finish this game. It really is jarring for a game of this quality to have these kinds of bugs, especially considering 4A has made two other Metro games without any issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus: 2 years later. Spoilers ahead.Intro:After two long years I have finally picked up this title. Once I was hyped and refused to buy it on the Epic Game Store so I needed to wait another painful year while reviews and spoilers made their way to me. But in the end I did it myself.Story/Gameplay:The game is not like any of the other 2 (or 4) Metro games and misses a major thing: the actual Metro.As much as I liked travelling through whole of Russia with the Aurora I must admit that I missed the claustrophobic tunnels of the Moscow Metro. Knowing that the tunnels are a maze for it's own (lore wise) instead of an open plain in the Caspian desert.The gunplay is amazing, we see old classics like the Bastard Gun or the Kalash return with many new attachments. New weapons also made it's way to the collection like the bullpup based Bulldog or the stealthy Crossbow: Helsing. Attachments, medkits and ammo are less frequent in the instanced open-world in Metro Exodus, yet can easily be crafted with scrap parts and chemicals you collect through out your journey.The story sends you through different locations where you need to face different enemies and problems. May it be desert bandits in the Caspian desert, hungry cannibals in Yamantau or light sensetive mutated spiders in webbed bunkers. The enemies feel unique to their zone and gain a progression advantage like the player itself with newer weapons like modified long-barrel snipers or shotguns with extended mags.Performance:Metro Exodus runs with an average of 70-80fps on 4k high-ultra resolution with a 2080ti. Minor stutters were expectable and noted yet I have encountered but -one- major bug during the Caspian Lighthouse mission once you leave the cave. The game render engine crashes once you take a look at the ocean + it's cliffs with flying demons. Shoutout to my friend Ray who helped me solve the issue at 2am. (Fix: Look at the ground and manouver blindly to the next checkpoint 20meters away.)The controls were clightly questionable and most likely designed for a controller. You throw your grenades etc  with "c", swap the grenade for a throwing knife with holding down the same button and cursoring over the wished throwable. Taking your iconic bullet lighter out is once more on "L" while the flashlight is on "F" and so on. Playing different games makes one  scream in agony to get used to the controls.Conclusion:Metro Exodus is a game clearly worth the 60€ mark. 18 hours shall be in without doing too many bonus objective and searching for collectibles. Per usual we get two endings: a good and a bad one. The player himself chooses indirectly which one he get's while collecting invisible "karma" points for rescuing damels in distress or killing slaves.Overall it's based more on games like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. than the original Metro's but still a Metro by heart.Rating:  9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Would buy if you have any interest in Stealth games or Survival Horror.Atmosphere 9/10Levels are a great mix of open-world travel and metroidvania-esqe missions. Dystopian storylines are a dime a dozen, but this one still oozes the nihilistic yet hopeful personality of everyone's favorite badass subway dwelling Ruskies.Story 8/10Solid storyline, bolstered by the great atmosphere, points off because it doesn't show it tells. You need to sit for minutes at a time between missions to have the narrative explained to you by the various npcs. Graphics 10/10Ultra-realistic graphics. Demanding (~58fps on 2070, 1440p w/ raytracing med), so you need a solid rig. That, said, this one of the games that will make a powerful rig worth building. They aren't just for show, watching the light from a headlamp approach down a distant tunnel is a great way to track enemies.Gameplay 9/10The game does a great job of letting you be powerful, yet punishing you for a mistake. The right gun aimed carefully from stealth will oneshot all except mini-bosses, but that same enemy can kill you in one second, or sponge 4 bullets if you spray, quickly leaving you with no ammo. The levels and AI are designed well. Open world sections funnel into linear missions nicely. These missions reward stealth and carefully planned runs and makes this feel more like a 3D metroidvania survival game with 1st person marksmanship being a valuable skill, rather than a traditional shooter. The gun-play feels good and the customization is simple but works.Stability 9/10No major bugs as of review time. There was one spot that consistently crashed to desktop when I was shoveling coal on the train in the intro level, but that was optional so w.e.Sound: 9/10 Audio design could've been better, some audio cues seem slapped in on top of the rest of the sounds, but the directional sound works, the metro radio station tracks are back, and there is some nice acoustic guitar as well. Good enough to not detract from the great visuals.Overall: 9/10 I gotta say this is a great game. It does so many things well. The game feels intense and immersive. The visuals, especially the lighting, are AAA, and rather than just being pretty, they support the core stealth mechanic, by clearly marking shadows and reflections. There are no bugs or goofy immersion to break immersion, only the personalities of the crew. The combat is snappy and rewarding while punishing, and the stealth/horror survival aspect is strong enough that you can get through most areas without firing your weapon. The best iteration yet of Metro yet. I can't give 10, since Metro's evolution ultimately is too similar to other franchises, like last of us & tomb raider, to be considered groundbreaking, or a classic. But it does what it sets out to do so well, its hard not to recommend this one to add to the wish list. Metro titles usually go on steam sale for cheap, so pick it up!

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus, the final game in the post apocalyptic, survival shooter series made by 4A Games. And without a doubt this is the premier Metro experience. From action to world design, to crafting, and customization this title really brings home the core ideas of the metro series to a satisfying conclusion. With a jump to an open sandbox style experience similar to the original Crysis, and retaining the survival aspect of the first two games is frankly sublime to play. Semi open sandbox type experiences are my personal fav way to play FPS games. So when I realized Metro Exodus was doing this, lets just say I was very, very excited! Full props to 4A Games, because they really pulled it off with a large verity of locations, events, and side content to play. This time around Metro's story is decent with the iconic choices that the series is known for, and surprisingly some really decent emotional moments. Not something I was expecting from a title such as this, so it was nice to see some decent dramatic payoff. Some criticism I have is that some of the dialog is a bit cheesy, and sometimes the dialog would overlap in scenes breaking my immersion. Really kind of nit pick issues in my opinion. But the one noticeable flaw is that the game has glitches. While playing I noticed quite a few small bugs that weren't game breaking, but enough to be noticed. So would I recommend Metro Exodus to a friend? Of course! If you PC can handle playing this game, its a strong buy. Really a new high point for the series! Both the main game and DLC are fantastic. 9/10 Incredible!

This time they tried the "OPEN WORLD" formula but did they succeed ?:, many said this is one of the only game pulling an unreal engine 5 type of performance on Unreal 4, and they arent lying! Maxed out; the lights, particules, smoke and so on, are really, really well done. And all of that with excellent performance on a good PC. (RTX3070ti / i5 12600k 4.2ghz / pcie4 SSD / 4x8gb DDR4 3200mhz), Metro keeps its truely unique aesthetic with litteral tons of attention to details. Recharging the flashlight to make it brighter, pumping my tikhar rifle to send those pellets at deadly speed, wiping the gas mask, patching it with a piece of cloth in an emergency, GOD I SWEAR I LOVE THESE LITTLE QUIRKS AND FUNKY MECHANICS SO MUCH !!!, every sound is near perfect, satisfying, makes sense. Don't care much about music but the SFX ? Omg, great stuff ! are top notch.. , the 2nd act in the sandy desert feels weird in the serie's context but that's what they were going for. The game picks back up after that, but the middle part of the game feels a bit out of place for what you'd imagine a metro game to be like., specially in the caspian sea level.  Even on a blind hardcore difficulty 1st playthrough! _childDocuments_.review: The story is engaging, the switch from a linear game to an open-world one felt natural. All the characters are incredibly human and even likable (Even Artyom on loading screens.) So why the thumbs down? Two reasons: First, the crafting system. While not strictly  per se, it's an unwelcome change from previous metro games where you used ammunition as currency. Balancing your ability to deal damage against purchasing much-needed supplies. It's swapping something wholly unique for something everyone else does. It's a downgrade in every sense of the word and I find myself hating it more and more due to the following reason.The bugs. Randomly getting softlocked due to inputs not registering. Controls refusing to update. Filter time spiking down to zero in seconds rather than minutes. Hits just not registering. Guns jamming whilst fully cleaned. Frequent freezes for seemingly random reasons. Enemies detecting you through walls. Constant save corruption.Functionally, the game is a mess. Metro: Exodus is an exercise in form over functionality. The game can have the best story, the prettiest world and some of the most compelling characters, but all of that is naught but ash when the game itself plays like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: Note that I am not actually saying "don't buy it's a bad game", in fact I think it's a pretty good game but there's a few things about it that rubbed me the wrong way. I'll give an overview with possible minor spoilers but avoid major spoilers.First, the gameplay and movement is very clunky. It looks really clean but it actually handles like a truck. I also don't like how the inventory/combat/regions work. You'll be crawling around the map and exploring (it has limited open world segments as well as linear segments) to collect a handful of gear upgrades, gun attachments and the 2 ubiquitous resources that you can turn into anything. But you really only need these resources to craft more ammo/medkits/repair that you use up by searching for them, and most gear upgrades are inconsequential. You can buff the weapons up, but then at one point you just lose all your gear you built up! So overall the entire inventory segment of the game seems pretty wasted.Which is the next issue, is that as a metro game it has a karma system to get the good or bad ending. Now the way this game operates and portrays people and the situations it puts you in, you should really be gunning down most people unapologetically, right? I mean if they're hostile and trying to kill you, and they're cult wackos or slavers or bandits it should be no problem to kill them, right? WRONG! BAD ENDING! The way they implemented this was horrible and feels extremely forced. "Oh no, you didn't show mercy to the slaver scum that tried to kill your whole crew! Oh no, you knocked out some forest weirdos!" It's even worse when an ENTIRE REGION in the game forces you on this path of, "oh you gotta sneak around and can't engage anyone or bad karma". They also take your gear away for this part as a sort of *hint hint* thing to say "no killing". But it makes this entire sequence way less fun than it should be, and it's still one of the highlights of the game. And the game seems to equate nonlethal takedowns with lethal force, which is all the more annoying.And the last problem is, it's really not very true to the metro series. It's more open world style and takes place... not in the metro. The story and characters are not all that interesting, with a few exceptions. Many plot points feel forced or just nonsensical. The more funny and gallows humor side of the series is almost totally absent here, with only a couple nods. And the entire story just has no emotional impact until the ending sequence. Overall, it's a pretty good game especially by modern standards, but it's bogged down in many aspects (including some technical problems like crashes) and is a pretty weird (presumably) ending to the metro series. I'm mainly being contrarian with my downvote but I'm pretty annoyed having finished the game, which had more generic preachiness about "oh religion bad" and "blindly trusting military authority/ charismatic leaders can actually turn out horribly!" than any actual interest in the dialogue or story.
