_childDocuments_.review: Another great addition to the metro franchise. I can very well say that the game will be enjoyed by fans and relished by players those who will take their time to explore every nook and cranny the game has to offer. It took me 22 hours in single play-through with all the side quests, upgrade and collectibles completed, but would take around 8 hour only just to do the main objectives. From the game time perspective i wish the game was a bit longer. The story follows after the event of  the battle of D6. As usual of the series the game has an amazing story driven narrative. You will unravel backstory of your squad mates through small events in the train. The game nails the interactive moments perfectly (Won't spoil it for you these things happen in the train) that makes the characters feel alive. The narrative builds some sort emotional connection with each of the character.The world metro looks beautiful. This time we get to see how the nuclear devastated world outside metro and Moscow looks like. The game has multiple sandbox area that you get to explore throughout the story. There's only 2 original metro area players will get to explore (prologue and end mission). To me that was kind of disappointing. The linear gameplay is slightly changed to semi open world. There are some new weapons and better version of the previous weapons. This time weapon mods can be changed and few ammo and supplies could be made on the fly. To change loadout though you have to get to a workbench. Also there are some gear upgrades throughout the game to suit your play style.Moral system is kind of simple compared to the previous titles. _childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is just about outside of that "Masterpiece" range. There's just a couple of not-so-tiny things keeping it down.First, let's get the good stuff out of the way. The graphics and artwork are absolutely phenomenal, there's an insane amount of detail in every level, and that's especially stunning when you realize that Exodus now went out with some of the more open world type of levels, but there's no lack of detail in those either. Everything was carefully crafted to seem as immersive as possible. That's also supported by all of the tiny interact animations of Artyom, such as whipping out the map, climbing ladders, checking your geiger/compass and so on. All of this has tiny little animations which show Artyom physically interacting with the environment around him and it all adds up to create this insanely immersive experience.Add to this the epic music and all around quite immersive voice acting, whether you choose russian or english, it's mostly great, except for some of the characters. There's all this "russian-english" going on and it's kinda funny. The sound design itself is fine, but what's a little weird is some of the cutscenes, it sometimes feels like as if there's missing audio, or the voice acting overlaps in places, it's a bit off, as mostly it's good, but especially at the beginning it's rather noticeable how the cutscenes sometimes feel weirdly silent.Speaking of the beginning, make sure to get a few hours in before setting your judgement on the game, as the beginning is probably the weakest part of the game, once you get to your first open area - the Volga swamp, it gets better. And then by the time you get to the final level, you'll get all that classic Metro atmosphere you were starving for, trust me, the final level is epic and so is the ending, it's just the game starts a bit weak, then gets good, then a little weaker and then good again, kinda strange I know.But yeah the main two things aside from the weird audio at times, is the movement and the bugs. Artyom's movement is just extremely "floaty", jumping around or going down stairs has never been more dangerous. Artyom might slip or slide off at any moment and since the fall damage in this game is bonkers you might aswell break your leg at best. And these aren't a very good combination to have in a game where there's occassional platforming or very dangerous and slippery cliffs, roofs, floors and so on.As for the bugs, I personally didn't encounter any game-breaking ones my entire playthrough, but there still were a couple of funny bugs, mainly regarding the NPCs, they sometimes teleport around, stutter, or their equipment starts floating, it's a rather common sight in games regarding bugs, but here it's kinda everywhere, so try to not look at the NPCs too much, it might break your immersion lol. But I've read people encounter countless game-breaking bugs, such as NPCs getting stuck, the inability to interact with some core elements and more, so hopefully most of it was fixed now and you're good to go, as I didn't encounter anything fatal, no crashing or errors either.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This is no longer a Metro game. Worth playing once, wait for a sale. Or watch a Let's Play on Youtube, you won't miss the gameplay much.Although I had some criticism towards the former two Metro games, in general I liked them. I was looking forward to play the third game, especially given that it was supposed to be very different from its predecessors. And that it was. Unfortunately, I can't say all changes were welcome.First, what I liked about the previous Metro games is the atmosphere of the metro and remnants of humanity. There was a fine balance between spending time in the underground and on the surface, there were quality horror moments with a dose of mysticism. And for the most part, all of this is lost in Metro Exodus. Except for the last chapter (which, I think, is the best part of the game), most of the time you spend on the surface, underground bunkers are rare and optional and are not even close to replacing the metro. The suspense moments are simply nonexistent. The authors tried to set the mood by the post-apocalyptic scenery on the surface, but that is a poor replacement, especially given the gameplay. The game feels and plays as an open-world survival, with lots of resource hoarding and crafting. Looking at another crumbled shack or a rusted shipwreck you're thinking what kind of resources you might find there, not what kind of story is hidden in there. This simply kills that depressing atmosphere I was so fond of.Second, the first two games had reasonably good stories. The first one was especially good, it even had a moral choice in the end. But I can't say there is much of a story in the third game. Basically, at the beginning of the game Artyom and a small crew of spartans leaves Moscow and travels around the country with no real goal. Sure, at certain points the game offers a reason to move forward, then, at the end of the chapter, it gives you a reason for the next one, and so on. But there isn't an ultimate goal or a feeling of progression towards it. Besides the simple kill/don't kill decisions, there aren't any moral choices in the game. What's worse even, there's no moral of the game, at all. In Metro: Last Light, there were kill/don't kill moments too, but you had a moral obligation to the Dark One, and the characters in M:LL were more complex and more familiar. All that made those decisions not so trivial. In Exodus, you barely even know the characters beside your crew, and there's barely any reason to make one choice or the other. Barring some details, the ending is more or less predictable, and, given how unattached you are to your companions, is mediocre. There are good and bad endings, depending on your choices during playthrough.Speaking of the characters, they are one of the weakest parts of Metro Exodus. Some of the main companions are straight annoying in their sheer blind stupidity. () Every character in the game is 1D, shallow, straight as an arrow stereotype. You know them for 5 minutes, you know them to the end of the game. No shades of grey here, we are the good guys, most of them are bad. Aside from a couple of obvious main companions, the rest of the crowd are so unremarkable that you can barely tell them apart, if not by appearance. The dialogs, with the speechless Artyom and these dummies quickly become a farce, and you wish you could skip them. I have to say, stereotype characters were bad in the previous Metro games, especially M:LL, but even there they had some depth to them (remember Pavel?). In Exodus, it got much much worse.What is good about this game is visuals and sounds. The game is beautiful, and in that regard it continues the Metro tradition. Although level design has bugs in quite a few places, like grass or objects hanging in the air or objects you can clip through. The game has dynamic day/night cycle, although at key points in the game time goes non-linearly, which can be apparent.In conclusion, should you buy and play this game? If you're a fan of the Metro series, you don't need my answer - you will likely buy and play it regardless. And you might be slightly disappointed, like I am. Still, I think the game is worth playing once, especially if you like the more open-world direction the game is taking. Just don't get your hopes up and maybe wait for a sale on Steam. For the ones new to the Metro series, it is difficult to recommend starting your acquaintance with Exodus. I'd recommend playing Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light first. Having played those first you'll have better understanding of the story and background of Metro and you can then decide if you want to play Exodus.

_childDocuments_.review: My God 4A, you really hit it out of the park. I absolutely fell in love with this game; it just exudes beauty and depth in every square inch of game play. Movement has never felt so smooth, and balanced with the absolute JUICY weapon mechanics makes this one of the best feeling FPS titles I've ever played.The world building is done with impeccable attention to detail, making it come across as a finely polished hand-crafted experience. The amount of professionalism displayed in the artwork is staggering. I haven't felt like a kid in a candy shop in a VERY long time in video games. The closest might have been 2016's DOOM. This game knows what it's doing. Every character has their own unique personality and I find myself growing more connected to them as I play. You can really feel the struggle and comradery between your fellow survivors. Your decisions matter, and they play up to the ending of the game. The horror elements also come up later through the story and Exodus delivers the same anxiety inducing tension that we've experienced in 2033 and Last Light.I really cant express how much I appreciate Studios like 4A. From watching the developer commentaries and tracking the release, I couldn't help but feel a strong attachment to the team. These guys put their noses in the grindstone, toiling for years over every line of dialogue, every line of code, every texture, every polygon, to produce the best experience they are capable of. It ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ worked. I have so much respect for hard working artists that craft such an amazing vision like this. I had an absolute blast.I hate endings. They make me sad.I cried at the end. I did. This project connected with me as an artist myself and I experienced a swelling of emotion as the credits rolled in. What a culmination of talent. I really wish luck and success to 4A, despite the controversy created by their publishers. They are a group of people unanimously devoted to their craft and it shows. I can't wait to get my hands on whatever they come out with next. I hope the story of Artyom doesn't end here, and even if it does, Exodus will most certainly suffice as a book ending.Thank you 4A.

_childDocuments_.review: Played through the enhanced edition which doesn't have it's own steam page. The extra ray tracing made a great looking game look even better and i appreciated the implementation of DLSS 2.0 and an FOV slider. As for the game itself, it's great. It has minor flaws which hold it back from being amazing to me and i do think Last Light is still the best in the series because of it's strong pacing and well written story. The open level design in Exodus allows you to take in the environments more and be more immersed but i do think the pacing slightly suffers compared to the other games. The slower moments where you are looting, exploring and travelling between areas were never boring because of the amazing atmosphere the game has but it's not that tight concise adventure that the other two games were. The crazy amount of dialogue in the game is a little extra in my opinion and it doesn't help with the pacing. You can listen to these characters babble on and on for hours, some of the dialogue is good and adds extra world building, but a lot of it feels like padding and just pointless. The worst offenders are all the one sided conversations between a character and the protagonist because artyom doesn't speak in game, so the characters feel like they are just talking to themselves and it's not engaging or interesting to listen to. I thought the story was good but it's heavily segmented into mini plots between each area while having a very loose over arching plot in the background. It doesn't have that one big story it's trying to tell. But i did think the story was a great way to end the trilogy and it felt satisfying. The gameplay is great, the customisation has depth, the shooting feels impactful, the stealth feels satisfying, exploring and looting is engaging and immersive. All of the small details help with the immersion too like wiping or patching the mask, checking the map or the compass which is all done in game etc. I appreciate games doing this and i wish more do it in the future. The little things make a big difference in getting you immersed in the experience. I also recommend playing all the metro games in Russian because of the added authenticity and the english voice acting isn't very good. I'm glad i waited for the enhanced edition to come out, i did play this game previously on the microsoft store when it came to game pass and it was a blast to replay this game.8/10 (Great)

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing Metro Exodus PC Enhanced Edition here, since it doesn't have a page by itself.First of all, this and Cyberpunk 2077 are the best-looking PC games I have ever played. Nothing comes close currently. And it's all down to the ray-tracing. It looks so bloody good I was in awe several times while playing. And I kept taking screenshots simply because I had to.Gameplay-wise the game is also stellar. I would have liked it to be even more open-ended, but what is there is pretty damn great. Didn't care much for the ending, but that subjective. It wasn't bad, I just wanted it to end differently. You might like it a lot. As I said, it was well done, just not what I personally would have preferred. Perhaps there are other endings, I don't know.I would have loved for the game to have more RPG elements. It has some weapon upgrade mechanics, and that's it. There's nothing else. So the only reason for exploring is to find crafting materials you need to make ammo and medkits. And finding the occasional gun piece that will allow you to customize your guns at a workbench. But it felt lacking and I ended up exploring mainly because the game looks so good that I wanted to see all of it.Loved the monsters and enemies in the game. Rarely does a game have this diverse a cast of foes. From human bandits to slithering slime monsters and giant apelike creatures. And all so damn well done! AI is also pretty good. Love how they often comment on where they saw you last: "He's behind that fence" or "He's hiding behind those crates". Works really well. Stealth isn't great, but it was adequate. I mostly liked to just kick their butts. But I got scolded by my team so much for doing so that I ended up trying not to. :DThe characters are great. And there's some good voice-work too. Unfortunately there's also some really bad voice work. At least for the English language. That forced accent just doesn't work very well. It sounds comical at time. Anna's voice worked really well. But the colonel's voice felt off quite often. Other times it was decent. But ultimately the voice-work overall just felt a bit comical. I tried playing with the Russian or Ukranian voices with subtitles. But I couldn't concentrate on reading it while I was also playing so... Bonus points to 4A for making so many different languages. But at the end of the day, I would actually have preferred them to dial the accent back a lot. Not remove it, just tell the voice actors to stop forcing it so much.But that won't taint my overall impression of this game. The PC Enhanced Edition is, together with CP2077, by far the best looking PC games ever made. And for the most part the gameplay also keeps you hooked. I was looking forward to each playing session I had. That's always a good sign.EDIT: Just researched other endings and as it turns out I got the bad ending. I kind of thought I did. The thing is, I was quite careful after the first open segment to not kill people the game told me were innocent. And I completed all the fetch quests and freed all of the slaves I could find. One instance though, with two fishermen in a cage. I freed them, and when the cage opened nothing happened. They just stood there. I felt that was odd. Looking at Youtube videos it turns out my game bugged out with those, and it probably didn't register me saving those guys.On top of that, the games enemies are a mixed bag and hard to tell apart. In order to get the good ending you pretty much have to play stealth the entire game it seems. Oh well. I could just look up the good ending and it's fine. In my mind I got that ending.It's just an odd choice for the game. The endings aren't really connected to any specific thing that happens. It's only decided by looking at how much good stuff you do. Don't do enough (even though I did A LOT), you will get the bad ending. I think that's an odd choice design-wise.But, it doesn't detract from my overall opinion of the game. I still loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: Man screw this game. I tried, I really did. I loved the previous metro games. But the bugs and constant crashes finally motivated me to give up on an already irritating experience. Nearly every system in this game seems poorly thought out or downright broken. You're free to customize weapons with tons of attachments! But because of their balance you'll end up sticking to a single configuration that dominates the rest, and ignoring the system past that point. Crafting was introduced so you can convert two resources into whatever ammo, or supplies you most value! But even playing on ranger hardcore I was absolutely rolling in resources and had more ammo, health kits, grenades, and filters than I ever needed. The game often places groups of monsters next to groups of human enemies. But if you trying to act clever and lure one group into the other the AI completely breaks down. Enemies will stand around, looking confused, maybe throw a half assed attack towards one another now and then like they're in some theatrical performance of Metro Exodus. Bullets are also you're currency, so you have to judge when a combat encounter is worth it and conserve ammo so you'll have enough to buy supplies later. Except, they're not! The bullets as currency mechanic, one of the defining and most beloved mechanics of the previous Metro games was just taken out for some reason.Combat feels pretty good, when you're fighting humans (and they're not shooting through walls at you). Guns are all fun to shoot and time to kill is nice and low. But the second you're fighting some sort of...weird swamp lobster that spits poison at you, or a mutated pokemon that charges straight at you and locks you into one of the hundreds of agnozing QTEs this game has; combat becomes a total chore. And if you don't want the game wagging its finger at you with all the eye-rollingly condescending moralizing it can muster, you'll need to stealth past half the fish zealots and mad max mercenaries you face along the way. Stealth in Metro has always been broken. You're always in one of two modes: visible to every enemy in the area, or completely invisible to enemies even 5 feet away from you. But in Exodus the encounters are seemingly designed around the absurdity of this, arround moving through a clearly lit hallway while multiple guards scratch their monkey brains as you crouch your way past them. Pure stealth in Exodus is just zero fun in my opinion, it's a ton of trial and error, it completely breaks immersion, and it doesn't have enough tools to make it interesting or interactive. Even the simple act of pressing the use key is aggrivating, as almost every interaction requires you to hold the button down for what feels like 2 whole seconds. Want to open a crate? Hold down the button. Wanna get in a vehicle? Hold down the button. Wanna open a door? Hold down the button. Wanna resume the game after a loading screen???? Hold down the button. Wanna swap your gun with one on the ground? Oh you can just press the button for that, but if you wanna loot the ammo out of a gun on the ground (which is what you'll want to do 99% percent of the time) you betta believe that's a hold down the button! This might feel like a nitpick but it completely ruins the pacing of combat when you have to spend 30+ seconds holding down a button to loot ammo out of the individual guns of 15 bandits you just murdered before moving to the next batch. This game just seems to have very little respect for your time, whether its the numerous unskippable first person cutscenes, walking accross vast lengths of empty game world, or the friggin button presses.There's also a preveiling sense of bugginess here (though I realize experiences may vary). I've had quest markers fail to appear, I've been flung 600 feet into the air while driving a vehicle. Ever time I've booted up the game I've been greeted with a save data corrupted notification. I eventually made it to an area that hard crashed the game every 2 minutes. Running things in safe mode and messing with the game files increased this time to about 20 minutes but it was this issue that got me to give up. TLDR: Almost every system here feels broken on both a conceptual or implementation level, lots of bugs, common of the game to crash repeatedly in an area half way through rendering it almost unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best semi-open world games, great story, controls, guns mechanics, survivor game systems like inventory, gun management, best gun customisation and armor upgrades. This game like previous Metro game immerses you into its post nuclear war Russia, its unpredictable, savage, and unlike sequels of other games Exodus doesnt drift from its original game style and no multiplayer story driven game (co op would be fun as a dlc mission) instead it improves it and adds more.One of very few AAA titles that adopts minimal ui (almost none, the only time you get reminded that its a game is when you pause it, how crazy is that) and a silent protagonist (this way your thoughts become Artyom's voice, drawing you further in). It is under-recognised despite its efforts for perfection and developer's solid steel dedication to give a wholesome game which is the only game this year that looked better than its E3 trailer. Sigh, its sad to see its not nominated for best game of the year or narrative or best graphics, and people say its not underrated. Comparing to other similar games, Metro comes out winner in every aspect, story, survival gameplay, graphics, characters, the dynamic environment, the voice acting, animation. Play it!

_childDocuments_.review: In the grand tradition of Russian apocalypse simulators, I've always been more of a STALKER than a Metro fan. I found the stealth mechanics of Metro 2033 and Last Light to be needlessly obscure and the shooting largely unsatisfying. The exploration of linear cramped environments was also rather dull, and the writing appeared to be either bad or lost in translation - or both.With Metro Exodus, 4A Games continues its crusade against the FPS mainstream with another grim-faced Eastern European epic. Given its underwhelming prologue with overly familiar metro crawling, lots of ham-fisted dialogue and a couple of rather silly (not to mention all-too-convenient) plot twists, it's fair to say that the game didn't make a very good first impression. But when the Aurora grinded to a halt on the banks of the Volga and Artyom got to explore the frozen wastelands around him, the whole game shifted gear quite dramatically.For a series defined by its granular approach to FPS design, it's more than a little ironic that the emphasis on (bad) storytelling and elaborate set pieces has so often drowned out the methodical, slow-paced gameplay which Metro actually demands. The fact that the new game includes expeditions into vast open areas (with a fully dynamic day and night cycle, no less) to be explored at the player's own pace makes a huge difference. While slowly making my way across the desolate landscape - constantly on the lookout for groups of scavenging monsters and enemy patrols - I found it much easier to take in the scenery and appreciate the exquisitely hand-crafted remnants of a civilization long since consigned to dust.Of course, it goes without saying that its ground-breaking graphical wizardry has something to do with my enjoyment of Exodus. In 4K on Extreme settings, the overall experience can be quite breathtaking. I found the introduction of ray tracing in and of itself to be quite subtle, but there are individual scenes (for examples, dimly lit indoor environments interacting with the daylight outside) which definitely stand out. Even if it's hard to put into words exactly what's going, it does feel like a rather seismic shift towards a new level of realism.Fighting bandits in a rain storm, discovering a gargoyle's nest on top of a water tower and sneaking through an abandonded factory to avoid being swarmed by a veritable army of mutants were some of the more memorable moments during my time in the Volga area. What really stole the show, however, was the exceptional design of the environments themselves. And while graphical fidelity can sometimes be dismissed as a superficial concern, the artistic integrity of what 4A Games has accomplished here is arguably inseparable from the sheer amount of polygons and layers of post-processing etc. which makes this simulation of Russian post-apocalyptic decay feel truly alive.While I knew Metro Exodus wasn't going to be an actual open world game, my sandbox instincts got the better of me and I broke away from the main quest as soon as possible. After having methodically explored the frozen Volga wasteland for several hours on my own, I finally got back to the train and started picking up the actual assignments associated with that region. This resulted in a lot of backtracing, since all the quests were naturally associated with places I had already cleared out. The pacing thus got somewhat weird towards the end of my Volga expedition, but at least the game recognized my deviations from the intended path with some additional dialogue (and also mercifully refrained from repopulating said environments with fresh enemies!).Making my way through the following sandbox area (the Caspian desert) was associated with a not insignificant amount of gameplay-related frustration, as my stubborn and mostly failed attempts at stealth resulted in a lot of protracted trial-and-error. A few times it was legitimately the game's fault, when the situation suddenly went from bad to worse as a result of some minor glitches combined with the lack of hard saves (only quick saves and autosaves, which at least is an improvement on earlier titles in the series). Also, the enemy compensates for their unstable AI by being unrealistically excellent marksmen, even at absurd distances (at least on Hardcore difficulty).On balance, though, the second large environment in Metro Exodus still provided a more memorable experience than the majority of first person shooters and open world games out there. The more linear sections related to the story missions were all quite enjoyable (while never overstaying their welcome), and thorough exploration of the region's many ruins was consistently rewarded with genuinely useful gear and weapon attachments.After having lived and breathed the Volga region's sublime desolation for an extended period of time, I was ready to declare Metro Exodus one of the best action games in recent memory. Alas, my enthusiasm slowly diminished - albeit never completely disappeared - during the remainder of the campaign. By the time the last level turned out to be a tedious and claustrophobic chore pared with a clumsy narrative climax, I just wanted the game to be over. But despite unsatisfying stealth, bad dialogue and some technical annoyances there were still lots of memorable moments during my intense 35 hour playthrough. Exodus represents a radical step forward for the Metro series - and in some ways even for the FPS genre itself - and 4A Games has clearly moved from scrappy underdogs to industry heavyweights with their latest release.

_childDocuments_.review: A good follow-up to Metro 2033 and Last Light. All characters have motivations and feelings, they feel human. The balance between fun and realism feels right. The soundtrack is alright; there are a number of tracks that are memorable. Graphically it either matches or surpasses the competition and the artstyle is unique, noone does "realistic post-apocalyptic irradiated wasterland" better than Metro.Sometimes the voice acting feels off, characters try to do their "Russian accent" a little bit too much, but if you've already played the other Metro games and got used to it/it didn't bother you, it's servicable. It's short if you rush through it on an easier difficulty (10-12 hours) but if you explore everything and choose a higher difficulty than what you're used to, you'll get atleast 30 hours from it.It's my pick for GOTY 2019 or atleast Best FPS 2019.Edit: It's November 2020 and I have chosen this as my GOTY 2020 for Steam Awards because apparently it counts.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Game, i personally felt the chapterwise divison and inclusion of a few open world levels in between linear levels really made the gameplay shockingly refresing, especially since almost no area overstays its welcome and most encounters are well designed and varied mini sandboxes inside the giant sandbox of the level itself, except for the final are but that's to be expected, and it stays far more ludonarratively coherent compared to games like Far Cry and most other open world games. The Story and Graphics were my main driving force, which is very rare for me personally since i usually get hooked to gameplay, themes, music etc. Having Playing the Previous Metro Game, I had ideas about how the game will go and it exceeded expectations, especially when you actually genuinely started caring about characters. Having a small ragtag team go on a Train Trip is as fun as it sounds. My favourite part was the train rides section between missions - Very nostalgic, the scenes were very similar to what i used to see when i used to travel a lot on trains as a kid and i loved every second of those looped scenes. For those scenes alone in various different biomes, i feel like the price i paid was justified. This was a Constructively short review based on a Purchase of the "Gold Edition" of the game at 75% off on a steam sale, that would be about $10(US). After completing only the base game as of now, i can recommend anyone to pick this game at nothing less than a 40% discount, ideally 75% or more. I feel like the game genuinely justifies its price even on full price, especially since according to SteamDB they have implemendted Regional Pricing so nobody's getting ripped off with unfair prices either. Game's Pretty Demanding though, both on your PC and You, as the game can get quite stressful and difficulty can be over the roof if you're not careful. I played on Hardcore and Mutant encounters were fine for me as an fps Veteran, but gradually human and other enemies got stronger and i had to tone down it to normal in certain parts to finish the game. Also, Better make good use of benchmarking tools provided with the same and i also suggest talking a look at the requirements before making a purchase. Being a single player game, some performance drops didn't bother me and the few bugs i saw were mostly animation related, and i found them quite funny tbh. These 26 hours were well spent, i got at least 3x the value of what i paid for the game in the first place. A AAA Studio made a complete game on launch, we all steam gamers scrutinized the publisher a lot for the epic exclusivity back then, but looking back its easy to see why they took the game from steam for a year. Even if the Publishers made questionable choices, there is no denying that this game oozes love and respect for the source material, the previous games, the playerbase and its own legacy to deliver a quality game and the marketing trailers of the game match so well with the actual game. The Immersion is surreal and gameplay is fantastic. I'll be trying out the DLCs too at a later date, but i have feeling they hold a high regard for quality just like the Metro Series has always been. Thanks for wasting precious hours of your delicate life reading this. I appreciate your ducking time and hope you have a ducking nice day or night or evening or afternoon or whatever the hell your time dictates.

_childDocuments_.review: First, ignore my hours. The original and the enhanced edition of Metro Exodus share a Steam page, but reviews only show hours played in the original version. Any hours in the original were just me leaving the game running for cards. I put 17.2 hours into the enhanced edition.Overall, the best thing about metro is the graphics. They really are pretty. Being the first ray traced only game, I was surprised at how well it ran. At 1080p with DLSS on quality mode and ultra settings, my 2070s averaged about 80 fps, with some areas as high as 130 fps, and basically no where dipping below 60. Unfortunately, A large part of the game takes place in dark areas that require the use of nigh vision goggles, painting the world green. While I really like green, the night vision goggles really made it hard to appreciate much of the beauty.Another thing the game did really well was the AI. Enemies would regularly tell others where I was, for example “over there! Behind the barrels”. I thought that was really cool and made them feel much more like real people.Unfortunately, the gameplay didn’t live up to the graphics. The actual gameplay consists of a lot of slow walking across vast landscapes with limited supplies, which at times got really annoying. I get what the game is going for, it just not something I liked.The characters are another area where the game fell flat. After spending almost 20 hours with them, other then the 2 women, the leader, and the driver, I could not tell you who was who or anything unique about them. They just weren’t memorable or unique, but maybe that’s the point since they were all soldiers.Overall, I enjoyed the game enough to finish it, but I wouldn’t really recommend others try it unless they want to test out their new ray tracing card or really enjoy slow paced games where you spend a lot of time wandering around.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed the game with in 18.4 hours (non-DLC) and now I'm depressed.This is the only series of games I have ever played where the next game is better than the last. Normally, this is not the case, but Metro is a no ordinary game. The story really makes you feel a part of Artyom's family. Over the course of the series you bond with Artyom's mates in a way that feels closer than family. You care about everyone's well being and you want to play through the story to make sure everyone remains safe. Not only that, but the development of each and every individual character is wonderful. There's a lot of depth to them and you hear it in random conversations when you stumble upon them or smoke with them on the train ride. Hearing every word that everyone has to say any time really does mean a lot. I honestly rate this games story line 10/10 and I've already restarted to replay it This is the best game I've played in a long time, I 100% recommend this game. You will not regret.You will actually feel sad when you complete this game.

_childDocuments_.review: takes players on an unforgettable journey through a beautifully crafted post-apocalyptic world, offering a fresh and immersive experience that captivates both newcomers and long-time fans of the series. Developed by 4A Games, this enhanced edition serves as a remarkable upgrade to the original game, showcasing stunning visuals and improved gameplay mechanics.One of the standout features of Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition is its breathtaking graphics. The developers have painstakingly created a visually striking world that is both desolate and hauntingly beautiful. From the dark, claustrophobic tunnels to the vast, open landscapes, each environment is meticulously detailed, bringing the post-apocalyptic setting to life. The enhanced lighting and ray-tracing effects further enhance the atmosphere, making every moment a visual treat.The story of Metro Exodus continues the narrative of the previous games, following the journey of Artyom and his companions as they seek a new home in the devastated Russian landscape. The game successfully maintains a sense of tension and desperation throughout, as players encounter various factions, mutants, and environmental hazards. The well-paced storyline keeps you engaged, with emotional moments and unexpected twists that add depth to the characters and their relationships.Gameplay-wise, Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition introduces a more open-world approach compared to its predecessors. Players are given more freedom to explore the vast environments, complete side quests, and scavenge for resources. This change in design adds a sense of exploration and discovery, allowing players to make choices that impact the story and the world around them. The survival elements, such as managing resources and maintaining weapons, add an extra layer of challenge and immersion.Combat in Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition has also received significant improvements. The gunplay feels more refined and responsive, making each encounter thrilling and intense. Players can choose between stealthily eliminating enemies or engaging in all-out firefights, adding variety to the gameplay. The AI has also been enhanced, making enemy encounters more dynamic and unpredictable.While Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition offers an exceptional gaming experience, it does have a few minor drawbacks. Some players may find the pacing a bit slow, especially during the game's early stages. Additionally, occasional technical issues and glitches can detract from the overall immersion, although these are relatively rare and not game-breaking.In conclusion, Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition is a must-play for fans of the series and anyone seeking an immersive post-apocalyptic adventure. Its stunning visuals, engaging storyline, and improved gameplay mechanics make for a truly unforgettable experience. Despite a few minor flaws, this enhanced edition showcases the dedication and craftsmanship of 4A Games, solidifying the Metro franchise as one of the best in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhh where do I start with this...First of all, the game is amazing, the weapon animations, shooting mechanics, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics are beautiful! Faces look photorealistic most of the time, and the global illumination looks so natural and real. The sound and atmosphere shines big time too, the developers took big notes of what made the STALKER games so good, Shadow of Chernobyl in particular, and implemented that into the Metro experience. I really like the game, I really do, loved Last Light that even played through the entire campaign it three or four times.That said, Metro Exodus doesnt play like previous Metro games, not even the Redux versions, this game is sometimes a very good enjoyable experience and some other times a complete rage inducing mess. Remember when you played Last Light Redux on Hardcore Ranger mode and only had trouble at the beggining? Remember how enemies were as fragile as you were during firefights? Remember how well the stealth system was? Well now forget all that because in Metro Exodus Hardcore Ranger the enemies take 6 AR boolets do die and sometimes take 1 shotgun blast to the body or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 6 SHAMBLER ROUNDS TO THE FACE TO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AT THE VERY LEAST FALTER BACK. Seriously, my biggest complain about the game is how easy shotgun enemies popup in one corner and instantly blast your ass back to Moscow with a single shotgun shell. Or how they can snipe you with a barebones bastard from 20 meters away with perfect accuracy, putting 10 bullets in your skull before you had time to acknowledge their position because they have this pseudo STALKER Anomaly ultrahardcore aim. Their field of view changed from like 100° wide (Last Light) to 200° because they can ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ see you when you're behind them, oh and they instantly start shooting your ass when they see you, no more alerting their friends or giving you a window to run up and perform a kill to shut them up. Sniper rifle bullets somehow dont connect to your telescopic sight reticle, they go off a little bit enough to either side of the reticle to avoid headshoting an enemy. Artyom has this weird moon-like gravity that causes you to stay on air for more than half a second after performing a jump, pair this with the stupid low height that kills you if you surpass it and you'll be reloading an AWFUL LOT of checkpoints. I've died from jumping off the top of a car (without pressing the jump button), died from flying over the place i wanted to jump on (sometimes the game speeds you up when you jump forwards), died because got stuck on the geometry while jumping, died because i jumped into a chair and somehow fused with it preventing me from landing and instakilling me. This game has serious issues that can kill the experience for some people (i raged many times but it didnt killed my experience, i guess), just be mindful of said issues when buying the game. Oh and if you never finished previous Metro games on the hardest difficulty (i did, many times) stay the ♥♥♥♥ away from Hardcore Ranger mode, just play the normal mode, or else you'll suffer from how unfair and broken it is.

_childDocuments_.review: For as much as I do want to recommend this game to others as a very fresh take in the Metro franchise, I can't do it with a good heart because of all of the technical issues I encountered in my time playing it. I think about 1/4th of my playtime was troubleshooting the issues I ran into which had some of the most maddening and odd fixes to them. I encountered: A bug at the mid part of The Caspian Sea when you exit the cave and have to reach the lighthouse by the boat. For some reason, crossing the boat would lock up my game. The only way I fixed it was by forcing the game into "Safe Mode", looking down at the ground when exiting the cave and walking forward hugging the right side. The hitrate isn't 100% (I think it took 3-4 tries before I got it right) but I got pass it after a lot of headache.A bug at the end of The Caspian Sea where the level transition would crash my game. I noticed some missing dialogue at the final cutscene for that part and knew my most recent auto saves were corrupted by  so I had to go back to my most recent auto save  Also... _childDocuments_.review: When I played Exodus for the first time last year at Gamescome, I thought: It looks great, but ... is it still Metro? No more dark tunnels in the bowels of Moscow, no more abandoned busy, no anomalies, transfer stations turned into small settlements or, in most cases, burial grounds full of horror. Nevertheless, the uniqueness of the series, as well as its name, drew the most from where it was situated - into the post-apocalyptic metropolis, more precisely, its underground train system.But now I realize that Metro is much more than just ... metro. Glukhovsky's bestseller describes the morbid and violent renaissance of humanity, the rebirth of civilization, which, however, is basically only a return to the primitive era, moreover full of repetition of old mistakes. While Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light revealed that man's need to stand over others is alive in a corpse, where governments have taken over the revived Nazi and Communist factions, Exodus goes further. During one game year he will transfer the player not only to different parts of post-apocalyptic Russia, but especially to cultures that arose - or only returned after hundreds or thousands of years - after the bombs hit. Sectarian religion, cannibalism or slavery; wherever you move, as the Christians in the new Subway, there is a separate, very sad, and convincingly drawn chapter of the human “book of survival”. And it is full of horror, often not even horror intestines of the Moscow underground full of corpses, monsters and huge spidersEach part of the game, which is stylized not only to different locations, but also to different seasons, is associated with the previous and following predominantly linear story. The 23-year-old Arťom, now an experienced and respected member of the elite Spartans unit, as a combat group's main explorer, is being broadcast to unexplored parts by a nuclear shootout of a mutilated Russia. The game starts in the subway, but it is only a fraction of this sandbox visual feast. If there is something that impressed me after just the first ten minutes, it was the great atmosphere of post-war Russian mother wrapped in luxurious graphics. Visually, Metro Exodus is a beautiful ode to destruction and disintegration, plus you don't need strictly high-end cards.It's hard to tell if Metro Exodus is the best game in the series, but it's definitely a great post-apocalyptic title. It is different from the previous parts, much more massive and less solitary, but at the same time it is a sharp departure from the atmosphere of its predecessors. Luckily, however, the game is closer to titles such as Far Cry, Rage or Mad Max, fortunately, without boring cotton pads in the form of casting camps and basic or revealing the map. It is a linear but profound experience and a natural evolutionary step in the chapter of the amazing stories of the Moscow metro settlers. All thumbs up.I personally rate the game 9/10Postive+ impressive atmosphere of the world+ very good story telling+ nice variety of environments and types of gameplay+ visual ballad with great, alternating atmosphere+ an engaging, albeit predictable story+ diversity also in the case of weapons and their adaptability+ sympathetic main characters to whom you create a relationship+ dynamic weather and day / night cycle+ large sandbox maps including Madmax Caspik+ stealth option for most missions+ game lengthNegative - it would want a more varied range of enemies- the environment is large, but besides the story deaf to activities- often labyrinth design of levels- there could be more open environments

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks absolutely gorgeous, even at 1080p non-Enhanced edition. Even on a dated PC it runs well at Ultra quality. The production quality is through the roof, AAA stuff. It's very apparent that this is the most ambitious game they have ever developed. The wanted to create an epic conclusion, grand in scope.Two major areas (Volga and The Caspian) in Exodus are semi-open world, i.e. there isn't one huge map, but several smaller which can be explored. It's also a game where having no ambient music during exploration actually works. For example, in Dragon Age Inquisition, it made exploration a bore. Here it builds atmosphere. However, the gameplay loop of the open world is painfully average and serviceable. Though there are a few elements that were just plain bad: using the boat in Volga is slow, cumbersome, and being attacked by the fish creatures is a chore.Gameplay wise:Finally! Quick saving, huzzah!... but it's a single slot shared with checkpoints... also still no FoV slider, boo! At least the default is 90 degrees, which is perfectly acceptable.The physics are weird. You can accidentally bump off of the environment or slide off a cliff while walking. Jumping is very floaty.Ladders are contextual now, so no awkward "aiming for the ladder when trying to go down" moments. Stealth is virtually the same from the Redux versions. It was fine there, but no improvements at all should be pointed out: - You cannot move bodies. - Enemies either don't know you're around or know exactly where you are at all times, just - because somebody saw you for a split second.- Using a flashlight even for a moment is a coin toss. You either won't get noticed, or everybody goes into instant alarm.Additionally, the hitboxes sometimes just do not work. You will shoot them in the head but nothing will happen. Except, of course, a building wide alarm.Story wise:I'm surprised at how much dialogue there is in this game. In 2033 and Last Light there was a lot of talking, but in Exodus it's just too much, especially in the first few hours. The dialogues just go on, and on, and on, for several minutes at a time. What's worse, Artyom STILL does not talk outside of loading screens. This makes the dialogues extremely awkward.Mind you, there are some great scenes in the game, primarily on the train, but overall it's just talking. At times the NPCs are even talking over each other.Anna comes off as overbearing. I understand she loves Artyom, but sometimes it appears a bit creepy, and if she had any doubts, she'd cut Artyom's junk off for perceived cheating. Read: it's unhealthy.DLCs are much better than in Last Light. The Two Colonels is short, but serious. Sam's Story is longer, but very lighthearted.Overall it's good, but a bit overrated.

_childDocuments_.review: This for me, was the very first single player FPS game that finally surpassed the general feeling I had when I played Half Life 2 for the first time, long ago.Both the gameplay and story pacing were handled very well. The level variation of the open world maps was very prominent, whilst maintaining incredible levels of details. Every single spot in the open world sections felt as carefully handmade, as their counterpart, underground or "Metro" sections. This however did not subtract from how vast these open world sections were. I genuinely appreciated the levels of balance the developers have made between these two different aspects, simply because the iconic, claustrophobic underground Metro sections only gained in every aspect, in Metro Exodus.I feel like people don't give enough justice to the immersive aspects in similar games. Metro Exodus definitely excelled in both the day/night cycle and weather systems. The only time I felt similar levels of immersion during a storm for example, was when I played Red Dead Redemption 2 last year. This is without even touching on how all of these immersive factors also greatly affect gameplay, especially when it comes to stealth.The gunplay and gun customization definitely did not feel left out in Metro Exodus. Each gun had a ton of modifications for the player to choose from, some of which could even fully alter the effectiveness and way a gun could be used. Shooting said guns felt incredibly satisfying, the weight, recoil and impact each shot had were carefully considered, to spectacular results.I never wrote a steam review before, nor do I think I could give this game enough justice with words alone. For a Metro fan, or generally speaking, all the immersive simulator fans out there (big shout-out to STALKER fans!), this game is an absolute must buy. Without a doubt, 10/10.

Stealth and combat are both viable options and there are plenty of tools and weapons to make use of. As for the structure of the game, I am still unsure as to whether I like the closed corridors of the previous games or the now open areas you visit more. Both have their pros and cons. Finally, it would be silly of me not to mention how great the game looks, just be aware that ray tracing is a resource hog.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start out this review saying that this game is amazing and a great continuation of the Metro series but the same old bugbears that bothered me in the previous games have come through: Namely the moral system and its fetish for stealth runs and I've just kinda had enough f it.Yes, you can blast your way through an area of murderous cultists with the guns you have spent ages collecting resources for to upgrade; you can but the game will make you feel like a total piece of ♥♥♥♥ for doing it or trying to enjoy some of the new mechanics and this I have finally lost my patience with. Imagine! A post-apoc shooter where it's -1000 goodboy points for killing, (or even knocking out in some cases) a Neo-Facist or Cultist! Thereby dooming you, your party and the entire Metro to a smug, 'I told you so!' ending, sealing the fate of humanity. The Ranger's motto should be, "If not stealth, then what?"

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a long time Metro fan, i've been around since the original 2033 released. I managed to grab Exodus before the whole epic games store ordeal, so hopefully I can be helpful to folks that have been stuck waiting a year.Overall, the game gets a solid thumbs up from me. It has it's weak points though, I'll elaborate on that in a moment. The same old 'metro' feel is definitely there, but with various improvements over even last light redux. Plenty of immersion is to be had with the interactions and comfy downtime onboard the train. I found myself growing quickly attached to the new characters in the game. You'll likely also notice that the gunplay is significantly improved, with weapons having far better animations, sounds, and character. The downside? There aren't as many weapons in this game compared to previous Metro games. Don't fret though, most of the old weapons from previous games still technically exist, just as modifications for the relatively small selection of weapons in this game.One of the weakest points of this game is definitely the open world sections, namely the caspian desert. The first hour, the middle point between the two open world zones, and the finale (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the finale was amazing) are all very good. The open world segments fall short though with dragging on too long and just not being all that interesting. Metro has always been a linear experience, and the linear portions of this game are absolutely the best parts. If you end up losing interest around the desert I won't blame you, but you should definitely try to stick it out because the entirety of Novosibirsk is definitely one of the most memorable moments in the entire series.Overall i'd have to give the game a 7/10. The opening and the last two hours gets a 9/10 but unfortunately the open world portions hold the game back a bit.Side note: You can edit various game settings such as field of view, removing mouse smoothing, motion blur, and more by editing the game's config file. Look up the pcgamer wiki page for this game for more info.

_childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is hands down the crowning achievement of the Metro franchise. It brings Artyom and company out of the claustrophobic metro tunnels of 2033 & Last Light, and into the daylight of POST-apocalyptic Russia, in all its glory. Never before has a game so effectively blended the polish of a linear FPS with the freedom of a reactive open world, while capturing a Slavic atmosphere which rivals that of blin-kingpin S.T.A.L.K.E.R. itself. Exodus takes Metro to fantastic new heights while cutting out nearly all the lows, whether that be in gameplay, world-building, or storytelling. As a fan of the series for years, I’m happy to report that this  the sequel we were waiting for.Metro Exodus begins with the protagonist, Artyom, plagued by the suspicion that there is still human life left on the surface beyond the Moscow Metro system. You, as Artyom, have been making frequent dangerous excursions to the surface since the end of the previous game in the hopes of finding a radio signal to validate this theory. This causes strife with your wife, Anna, who is fearful that one day you won’t arrive home still breathing. As a consequence, she decides to come with you on one of your trips to the surface to watch your back. On that fateful day, Artyom and Anna discover; not a radio signal, but actual people who claim to hail from outside the city… as well as an operational locomotive train, capable of taking them – and the Spartan Order – across the country.Shifting to the graphics of Exodus, I have to say that they are entirely up to series standards. The art style is identical to that of its redux-ed predecessors, but every visual detail has been tweaked to breathtaking fidelity. Textures are photorealistic, faces are way beyond the uncanny valley in a positive direction, animations are fluid and numerous, the lighting is gorgeous to the point that its beauty exceeds real life, and all other technical components are practically flawless. The soundscape is noticeably (mostly) unchanged from the previous games, however there is a whole new soundtrack which accompanies Exodus’s atmosphere terrifically. As for performance, the game is demanding, but still well optimized. All in all, I’m absolutely taken by Metro Exodus’s presentation.Exodus is divided into roughly three separate maps throughout the course of the game, as well as a few more linear levels. While the settings themselves are gorgeous to the eye, from the swamps of the Volga River to the deserts of the dried up Caspian Sea, there’s also a lot to do. Each region has multiple objectives and locations, with secrets to uncover and loot to seize. There is a disparate theme to the individual provinces too, giving Exodus a real sense of variety. Notes and audio journals dot the world-space as well, revealing the history of a place and its people following the war. The several environmental stories told are enlightening, and sometimes even heart-rending. Altogether, Exodus’s environments are impeccably designed, and reward intense investigation.Metro Exodus, among other secondary features, utilizes an all new crafting and modification system, which I’d say is… a mixed bag. The crafting component of the game feels lazy, as there are only two materials to work with: metals and chemicals, which (annoyingly) functionally constitute 90% of the games lootable items – meaning most valuable consumables must be crafted. On the modification side of things, there’s a lot more to like. There are roughly ten base guns in the game, but each can be radically altered to work more effectively in different scenarios. Gear modification serves as the progression system, so it’s important to stay up-to-date with your weapons and accessories. There are a few more gameplay mechanics such as stealth, radiation, and vehicles, but all can be roughly summarized as ‘well implemented.’The Metro series is known for its atmosphere, and the immersion of its combat is a central element. I truly believe Metro Exodus has perfected the first-person impact of firing a gun; between the recoil and sound design, and even on down to the stopping power of each individual weapon. And good news – from bandits to mutant beasts, and slavers to the eerie humanimals, there’s a whole host of new adversaries to blast away across the scarred face of Russia. The AI of human enemies is quite sophisticated too, being able to call out your position to their allies if they spot you; relative to the objects around you. It’s also worth noting that you can defeat humans non-lethally, and that combatants will surrender if routed. Intricacies like these nested within Exodus’ combat system are what drive the gameplay, and make it uniquely satisfying.Refocusing on Exodus’s story, it’s a much better tale than that of the previous titles. For reasons I won’t spoil; you, Anna, Colonel Miller, and the rest of the Spartan Order travel eastward through post-apocalyptic Russia in the train found at the beginning of the game, which is quickly coined the . As the crew trek across the scorched earth of the motherland, seasons change, and new societies are discovered. The survivors of the nuclear holocaust have become vicious luddites, bandits, cannibals, and slavers – but a rare few have preserved their humanity. Eventually the Order’s goal becomes to find an untainted land to call home; a place where a civilized society can rebuild, and Artyom and Anna can raise a family.Whereas in past Metro games the supporting characters were side-pieces or even something of a nuisance, Exodus is much more character-driven in its storytelling. The blank stares of Bourbon and Khan are gone; replaced by the sensitive compassion of Stepan, cockiness of the impressionable Duke, and the  love of Artyom’s wife, Anna. The Aurora’s crew grows and changes with time, developing through the experiences they endure and the trials they overcome. If you care to bend an ear, your comrades will talk it off, expressing their thoughts, plans, hopes, and fears. While the translation of dialogue to English can be clunky at times, the character writing itself is just magnificent. The inspiring humanity of this small group of characters truly bring your goals as Artyom into perspective. The people of Metro Exodus are what make the whole experience.On a quick narrative note before my final verdict, I’d like to clearly express that Exodus tracks your moral status throughout the course of the 25-odd hour campaign. There are particular actions you can complete that will give you positive karma, and specific crimes you can commit that will accrue negative karma. How you interact with the game world and its characters will have consequences – not only in the form of separate endings, but in a cascade of different narrative outcomes. The Order’s exodus is a treacherous one, but the most perilous war is that of the one which rages .I feel my opinion on this game has been made fairly obvious by this point, but that doesn’t mean I won’t praise it further. Metro Exodus is one of the best games, period, that I have ever played. Its the culmination of what already was a phenomenal series, and Exodus pulls no punches in giving the trilogy a stupendously vast, enjoyable, meticulous, touching, and downright impressive send-off. I couldn’t have imagined a better way to conclude Artyom’s journey.

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5 / 10 ( 8-8.5/10 if they fix the numerous bugs ). A great game that I will certainly play again. Depending on who you ask this could be the best or the worst metro game to date so opinions are varied. Personally don't think it is better than the previous 2 games, but it is certainly worth playing. Most of my issues with it come down to personal opinion or ( i think fixable ) bugs but some things just felt average. Pros:- Graphics are great ( though heavy on your system so be sure to have decent cooling )- Nice variety of maps- The story was solid but not as good as previous games - On the spot crafting was a nice addition- The unmarked side missions gave areas a bit more back story and never felt like a chore. You can skip them without problems but some do impact the main story.Minor complaints for elements that are generally good:- Audio was generally good though I found that the audio certain areas not as good as it was in previous games as I found it lacking atmosphere that the audio is often responsible for. Audio had some bugs in some areas too but that could be due to the fact I turned on the Dolby Setting.- Didn't like some new creatures like the "zombies".- Some elements felt a bit unpredictable which could result in annoying one hit deaths ( at least on hardcore difficulty ). Luckily the new save system avoids losing a lot of progress with the game generally auto-saving every 3 minutes. - New save system, while in a way a great addition as you never lose much progress, it removes any real feeling that a wrong move might lose a lot of progress and that feeling of stress or panic that might come with it. It does change how you would play the game in a minor way. - Personally felt that many area's didn't have that metro vibe I was hoping to find. I think peoples wish for more open areas have not resulted in more enjoyable maps. Other people really loved those so its really down to personal choice.Cons:- Bugs. So many different ones. From failing to start to enemies shooting through walls to screen overlays being smaller than the screen and human enemies that couldn't be killed with stealth and failing to start sometimes. My biggest immersion breaking bug was that adjusting the FOV ( no ingame slider ) resulted in screen overlays being smaller than the screen and thus looking buggy. So like the binoculars or damage overlay would not fit ( aka be smaller than ) the screen as well as some others. - Save system: While quick save is a nice addition, the automatic saving is buggy. It can result in horrible situations where it saves while you are being attacked. In some cases people have had to restart the level as the save game was unusable.- AI isn't too great. While it wasn't perfect in other games I feel the AI had more issues in this game. In one specific situation the AI said they saw me, but they never even came to attack me.

_childDocuments_.review: The Metro Series is based on the novels of Dmitri Glukhovsky. It is clear to me that the writers of this game took the origin of the story very seriously. You can tell that they didn't want to just insert a story into the game just because - they want the player to care about it as well. The characters themselves, as well as the dialogue alongside pretty much everything else is written , you can really tell that they treat their source material with outmost respect. While Artyom is mostly silent (except for loading screen dialogue/diary entries), his role as a passive protagonist isn't as bad as I orgininally thought it was going to be. Rather than just getting told what to do by every NPC, he has moments where the plot is developed through his actions - or rather through the actions of the player.This is outstandingly done by the "karma" system of the game, which means the story will follow a different path, depending on the players choices. You can choose whether to mercilessly kill everything that stands in your path or carefully approach the situations given by the game and respect its virtual residents These choices are done not by merely pressing a button, as in "Would you like to be bad? Y/N", rather it's done through action - or even the lack thereof.This way it doesn't just feel like Artyom defines the story that is told, but that the  is pushing the plot forwards.In short, a beautifully told storyline with interesting characters.Let's get to the juicy stuff. It's a FPS so naturally you'd expect a fair size of shootin' action. While that is true (and it's good shooting, we'll get to that in a bit) it's not the only thing you do and depending on how you play, might even play a rather subelemental role.The levels that the players find themselves in are not a linear row of corridors, which was a point of criticism of the predecessors (2033, Last Light), but are big, open and fully explorable areas that differ wildly throughout the game's journey. You get the usual dark and atmospheric metro tunnels, as expected, but you'll also get desert areas, swamps, citys, forests, etc. It's a huge step up in scope when compared to the previous titles.These levels aren't just big for the sake of being big  but are carefully crafted to The game is a realistic apocalypse; you're not running and gunning, spamming the "E" key to pick up loot.I played on hardcore and every mistake I made was punished accordingly.  - Shot down in seconds. - That's on me. - Crafting stations are plenty, ya dummy. Your guns are heavy and feel powerful, while avoiding pinpoint accuracy and unnecessarily big magazines. Doing maintenance on your guns is crucial if you don't want the aforementioned gun jamming to happen to you.Another mechanic to further immerse you in the apocalypse.Metro: Exodus is not without flaws though:- While guns have a natural inaccuracy to them and it's mostly fine, sometimes you'll just get these Your crosshair is right on target but your knife throw still misses.- Minor bugs here and there, such as a buggy POV driving a car. These are mostly rare and minor inconveniences though. If you care about story, have played the previous titles, enjoy a slow paced FPS based on immersing you into the beautifully crafted world and its environments: It's a no brainer, this game will provide many blessed game hours.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, Metro: Exodus (MEx) might seem like a typical FPS with a couple of twists, and while it doesn’t really offer anything groundbreaking, it is a perfect example of a whole package being greater than the sum of its parts.::Unless you want yet another FPS with some extended features, you should most definitely play this game on . Having played through the game twice, I decided to try Normal and, let me tell you straight away that this is most definitely not the way you should experience MEx.Not only is the game too forgiving but , which makes it stand out in the oversaturated FPS crowd, become basically non-existing. Just imagine if Dark Souls had Skyrim’s quest pointer.If you’re uncomfortable with a very challenging setting, pick the one that you’re OK with and go a step above in order to maintain the pressure and the idea of a harsh and unforgiving post-nuclear world. I’ve heard someone saying how , and I could not agree more. With that being said, let’s dig in, shall we?The Franchise previously known for its predominantly claustrophobic and linear levels becomes very open-ended in its latest iteration. From this, it’s easy to assume that there are going to be some big changes, and, I for one, welcome and absolutely loved those. Thematically, this is still a Metro game. There are even a number of linear sections and levels, such as the game’s opening, where you have to play as it is intended and have little to no say so in how things develop. Gameplay-wise, the foundation is there, just that it has been expanded and improved upon, but the overall feel was quite different for me. Being dubbed the best scout in the unit, Artyom, the game’s protagonist, has a lot to live up to, and MEx provides plenty of opportunities to do just that. Wandering the outskirts and the wilderness, scouting for points of interest and noting them down on your map for later exploration is a very important and big part of the experience. In fact, depending on your playstyle, scouting, exploration, and scavenging might as well be the major part of your MEx playthrough, and this is actually pretty cool.Now let’s add a high level of immersion to this. I’m talking about no HUD. This means no objective tracker on your screen, or a mini-map full of colorful icons to pop. No distraction whatsoever while exploring. You go where you think that something of interest might be. Of course, you can still access the map and check the objective tracker. You have your visibility indicator for stealth and the Geiger counter as well as many other indicators. The thing is, they’re presented in a very immersive way. They’re all gadgets, mostly on your wrist, audio and visual cues which are a part of the game world, and when you see or hear those, nothing is reminding you that while all of this is cool, you’re still playing a video game.Even though MEx puts you on an open level, it is still not an open-world game. In fact, these open areas are big levels that, once you’re done with, you may never return to. This is why you might want to let your FOMO take over and take your time to make sure you’ve visited every nook and cranny. Why? Because this is how you progress, for the most part. The game will  so pay attention to what your comrades are saying!You don’t exactly level up in MEx. There are no perks to unlock or XP to grind. However, there are still ways to improve your character, like gadgets, suit upgrades, and weapon parts. Finding new weapon parts is a big deal, as the game lets you customize guns in the field. Considering various enemy types, different weather conditions and the impact that the time of the day has on the world of MEx, this is quite useful. Need a medium-range rifle instead of a silenced pistol? Strip down your revolver, and make a couple of adjustments! Swap the silencer for a long barrel, add the 2X Scope on it's rail, and you've got yourself a rifle. If you've searched thoroughly, you will have everything you need, and can improvise to adapt to any given situation. Once obtained, these upgrades can be used through the entire game.Others are given to you as the story progresses. You might actually want to stick to the main objective until you’ve obtained the binoculars, at which point you’ll be properly equipped and have everything you need to explore the world on your own.When it comes to the story, perhaps more than the content of it, I like the fact that it’s rather believable. Listening to the Artyom’s comrades speak about what was going on is what I enjoyed the most, as they were all lovable characters with a lot of personality.The adventures of Aurora’s crew and their objectives feel like they are happening spontaneously. They were logical conclusions and decisions based on the current events and situation that I never found to be forced on the game simply because the developers needed some excuse to blow things up or shoot someone.  Player choices and their consequences, which the game always had (to an extent), are done better and more clearly telegraphed to the player this time around, although there’s still room for some improvement.  The exploration, which I’ve brought up so many times already, also extends to the story as some story-related things require to be found first. It is also the best way to gain additional Karma points which will determine how the story unfolds and eventually ends.  Of course, I am recommending this game. I’ve played it multiple times and actually plan to give the recently released raytracing-only version a go sometime down the road.  However, keep in mind what I’ve said at the beginning: unless you make this game unforgiving, you’ll be mowing down enemies and playing a post-apocalyptic shooter, which is not really that impressive nowadays anymore.  My impressions are based on the very specific Ranger Hardcore mode with Minimal Interface. This made the game slow, methodical and unforgiving, which is something that I very much enjoy. Ammo was scarce, just like the resources, I had to make every bullet count, and when I made a mistake, it was punished severely. At times it reminded me of the good times when I played Metal Gear Solid 3 back in the day on my PS2. When I scoured around for resources and ammo, waiting for the perfect opportunity to strike. MEx is, in many ways, just like that, and if this sounds like something you’d like to experience, then, by all means, get it, play it, and love it.

from the main game. it introduces a new weapon which is really fun to use and the dlc itself gives some backstory to the main game. the characters actually have some personality instead of just being the stereotypical love interest or the irritating child that you're suppossed to find cute and care for.  sam's story adds some additional story to one of your squad members and adds a nice new locations that's different from what you've experienced in the base game. new enemies. new allies and more conflicts to solve with new characters with their own personalities. this time around the dlc is more focused around doing a task. yes there is a story but the dlc focuses more on gameplay. the new weapons also bring a nice change. it's nice to have something other than AK's or homemade weapons to use. the ending was quite nice too. as i mentioned before having a voiced protagonist is a really nice change from the base game but i have to say. sam is just the stereotypical "badass brodude" american shouting oneliners all the time which can make it insufferable constantly having to deal with his idiotic insults and stereotypical 80's american actionmovie oneliners. this games approach to morality is also a nice change. there's no counter or bar to tell you how good or evil you are. you have no idea if you've been a good boy or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ untill after you're done with a character likes to just barge in guns blazing and it just feels so pointless to carefully move through a level when your control gets taken away and the game forces you into a gunfight. even if _childDocuments_.review: Metro Exodus is an amazing evolution of the Metro series. While it's still a linear game, the levels themselves are very open and contain a lot to explore and quite a few side missions to do. The environments in each level are pretty different, but very well designed and just beautiful to look at. I love how every encounter can be approached non-lethally or you can just run in guns blazing and how this does have an impact on how the levels themselves progress. The crafting system is a nice change as it allows you to customize your weapons while you're exploring.You can just power through the story in a few hours, but to really experience everything Metro Exodus has to offer, you should take it slow, explore and listen to all the dialogues. The NPCs talk a lot with each other and often hint at more background story, making the world feel very alive. You're missing out on half the story if you don't stay and listen every once in a while in my opinion.It's sad to see how the publisher decided to exclusively sell it on the Epic Store and removing it from Steam. I still can't leave a negative review for that as the developers did an amazing job with Metro Exodus. It's already the best game of the year so far and it's going to be pretty hard for anything else to beat it. I can only recommend that everyone buys and plays it as soon as it returns to Steam next year.
