_childDocuments_.review: Minimally improved from the previous game, for a sequel it largely fails to add much more to the experience; being heavily recycled conceptually.The overall presentation remains polished and comfortably stylish, while the gameplay is quite satisfying and engaging to interact with. Unlike the previous game however the story makes absolutely zero sense, and many conceptual elements of the world have been outright recycled for no explicable reason. Which only renders the story even more nonsensical due to said repetition.Unfortunately many problems from the previous game are still here, and in this regard the system has seen almost no improvement. The game has zero protection against stun-locking and many hazards that will exploit it, numerous hazards that instantly knock the player out regardless of their health, hazards that will instantly strike the player from off-screen or ambush them as they enter a level, hazards hidden behind objects in the foreground, completely random item and resource acquisition that will sometimes deprive the player of crucial gear, mechanics designed to punish the player for certain actions will be triggered by things other than the player, numerous underpowered items that simply are not worth using unless nothing else is available; and more.The controls are tight and precise but players are randomly put into overbearing situations that require unreasonable split-second levels of finesse to survive. Most of the time the game rewards the player for being reasonably dexterous and obstacles can be overcome through such, but randomly an overbearing situation will arise that requires an instantaneous and completely exact reaction to survive. These situations are so random and specific that players have zero chance of anticipating or learning from them, which makes surviving those encounters even less plausible for any player that does not have literally perfect reactions; or luck. Beyond that certain elements of the controls are entirely contrary to dexterous gameplay. Such as the wall and ledge grabbing mechanics that players cannot fully control or the finicky grab and crawl mechanics.As the game has many difficult, nuanced obstacles a massive amount of trial and error is needed to memorize how every single thing works just to avoid instantly getting knocked out by a single threat. The game makes an extremely obvious point of punishing players for their lack of knowledge in regards to any conceivable thing. However this game is filled with mechanics that operate in extremely specific yet variable ways that only become more volatile when they happen to randomly be combined with other things. This results in countless hyper-niche situations where players are punished for not knowing the single answer to a rare problem that will never manifest again for potentially dozens of hours in playtime due to sheer randomness. Which actively serves to contradict the act of learning since by the time players actually encounter that threat again, they will potentially have forgotten the one counter that it has.Every single time the player makes a mistake, is unlucky or gets presented with an unfair obstacle their entire survival hangs in the balance. It is completely random whether a given mishap will knock the player out, or simply wound them. Thus even the act of failing this game is arbitrary. Sometimes the player will make one mistake during the course of an hour long run and survive, other times they will be completely obliterated. The exact same applies to luck and unfair obstacles, like those mentioned above.The design of this experience is so incoherent that it simultaneously has zero tolerance for mistakes while absolutely rewarding dexterity and memorization but also randomly forgives mistakes while producing obstacles that explicitly undermine dexterity and memorization. Resulting in an experience that, while appealing in its presentation and satisfying in its gameplay, ultimately comes down to random chance when it comes to whether the player actually survives a run or not.Players do not beat Spelunky or Spelunky Two, Spelunky and Spelunky Two allow players to beat them; randomly. These games have all the tools necessary to guarantee the demise of the player in numerous moments throughout the course of a run. Whether that happens is just entirely random, which is ultimately the result of incompetent balancing.If you're interested in finding some games that I do positively recommend they can be found on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: Spelunky 2: Electric BoogalooSeriously, this game is Spelunky HD turned up to 11, including the deaths. You will die a lot, and have nothing to show for it. This is a true action roguelike, just like the original Spelunky, albeit harder, a bit more punishing, and occasionally unfair.Overall, Spelunky 2 feels a bit unbalanced, at least compared to the first game, and has a few kinks the developers need to work out. Online multiplayer is not currently present, but in development. I can't really think of any other cons at the moment.Pros are abundant. There's more content here (items, enemies, levels, secrets, and plenty of familiar stuff from Spelunky HD as well), the controls are tight and responsive, the core gameplay loop is ultimately satisfying, and there's a high level of polish to the music, art, and overall game design that, despite my frustrations with the difficulty, warrant a recommendation.If you want a game that truly challenges your skill, look no further than Spelunky 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Six years of practice in Spelunky 1 has finally paid off. I don't die to bats anymore! Now, I die to lizards and moles. Damn it, Derek!EDIT: After beating hard ending on around 230 hours mark and many great QoL updates, I can safely say that this is the best game ever made for me. It hits everything that I love: randomly generated levels each run that always keep me on my toes, no in-game progression that makes my win purely based on my skill and a little bit of luck, and simple mechanics that chain together into a hard, but winnable challenge.What I dislike on many modern roguelike games are in-game unlockables that makes the character stronger, thus giving an illusion of the players become significantly much better, even though their skills only increase a little. Spelunky will make sure that each challenge that you overcome are the result of you learning from past failures, correct threat identification, and correct response to such threat. You will feel your own skills increasing as you beat the seemingly insane and impossible challenge.This game may frustrate many players. I can understand that. Due to random nature of the game, sometimes Spelunky just throw a few bullsht at you that you can't respond in time. I too had my fury with this game's bullsht in the past. It's also because it's the first time someone encounter a particular threat. But, most of the time, it's due to the players' own folly. Taking things slow (most importantly, by changing the default movement into "walk" instead of "run"), identifying threats, and act accordingly, are the only things that you need to beat normal ending every time. Hard ending is entirely a different thing, though, and only players who truly enjoy Spelunky will attempt doing that.If you can't imagine enduring Spelunky by yourself, good news, Spelunky online multiplayer is ready and great to use. Find yourself a friend or two or three and try to beat the game together! It may make the game slightly easier, but everything is much more fun with friends and you can all laugh at your undoing together. You don't have friend to play with? Go to  and find someone to play with there.In conclusion, Spelunky 2 is a worthy successor to Spelunky HD and a testament to Spelunky's game design. This is the best game ever for me and I truly recommend it for anyone looking for a pure challenge.I still hate moles. I hate witches. I hate cats. I hate curses. I hate trap blocks. I hate egg. Derek Yu, bless your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ soul for making me pass all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: I understand, and appreciate what the game is about.  It's very challenging, and was made to be challenging which harkens back to the old school 8-bit/16-bit games.  However, the difficulty in some of those games were due to technical limitations, poor design choices, port from an arcade game trying to screw you out of quarters, or other issues.I am  like these so please be aware of that when seeing my recommendation and review.  In terms of positives and why I got this game?  Simple!  For the co-op play.  I found the co-op with friends to be .  Going through the challenges and running around was a blast!  Graphically this games is great.  The art style is easy on the eye, and overall very smooth on my increasingly aging computer.  I am of the belief games with art style such as Spelunky 2 will age better than those who go for realism.  Especially since technology is so fast and realism dates itself quickly. What I distinctly didn't like about the game  was the fact that once you lost all your lives you start at the .  We'd reach level 2-1, lose all our lives, and start at level 1-1 all over again.  At first it's funny but, after the 10th time playing with 2 other people of various skill level  it quickly loses its appeal.  The 8-bit era had memory issues hence why progress couldn't be saved in some games.  We don't have those issues today for games. So not being able to save my progress showed how little patience I had.Another issue?  One hit deaths or worst - fall deaths on blind corners / platforms.  The stages were procedurally generated so this meant you can die in the most tragic, unlucky way.Like I said just not my kind of game.+ Fantastic artwork, and style+ Co-op mode+ Simple gameplay mechanics and controls- One hit deaths, no continues, and no saving progress- Frustrating gameplay (which many may see as a positive)- Very difficult- Having start all over again once you lose all your lives Not a fan of this frustrating, "git gud" type of game 4 /10

_childDocuments_.review: carries with it much the same spirit of its prequel, being a 2D platformer with roguelike elements. In comparison, it comes with a more expansive world and more secrets. The baseline difficult exploring platforming remains. There are perhaps a bit more predictable spawning of certain items/creatures on certain levels with the way the game is set up, but there's enough variety and sudden death opportunities to always keep the players on their toes. Once again, expect to get frustrated from all kinds of different mechanisms, just so that you can start over again with more knowledge about the game.At baseline, it's a 2D side-scrolling platformer where your goal is to progress from level to level --entrance to exit, and deal with the enemies along the way. You will explore different biomes and deal with a variety of enemies, each with predictable patterns of movement and reaction to you. You will run, jump, whip or throw climbing ropes or bombs, both limited in supply. You will come across money that you can use at shops for additional gear, or you can steal or kill shopkeepers for them if you truly want to not play by the rules. At the end of the day, you will die many times trying to make it to the end, and occasionally you might just succeed.The game is hard, because of the way it's set up. While you can unlock some shortcuts through playing and fulfilling certain requirements, many players will start from the beginning and work their way through each time. Every time you turn the corner, you could face an unexpected event that completely destroys your run, and you will have to start over. Even using shortcuts you will face certain variety in level generation to make the individual levels feel different.There are also more ways to die in this second  game because of a lot more aggressive enemies, more traps, more potential explosions, etc. Derek Yu heard all of our complaints about how long it took to spawn the ghost and how slow its movements were. Instead, now the ghost (plus other enemies) are on steroids, coming after your very life.There are more bosses in this game as well, that's probably why the game sometimes feels a bit more predictable. This doesn't make it more easy, you can just be sure to expect certain things to always show up in specific locations. I remember playing through the first game and always thinking that it was odd to only have one boss, unless you took the string of secrets through various pathways in order to get to Hell. Of course there are still secrets and pathways to string together in  but there are a lot more branching pathways to make life interesting.Anyway, I have one win under my belt so far, after 77+ hours, and who knows when I will get my next. I have done almost all of the exploring on my own, because that discovery and trying to piece things together has been incredibly fun. Having played the first game a lot, I was definitely keeping an eye out trying to discover any potential secrets. I found some, but not enough. The biggest draw for a lot of people to this game was the promise of online multiplayer. This is not yet available, but we are all hopeful that it will be soon. In the meantime, there's been a lot of tweaks here and there, so it's been interesting to see the game get some major and minor changes during its infancy based on player critique.What stood out for me about  was its platforming, with such responsive controls, predictable movements, and precise actions, everything felt so right. With  that feel has remained the same. There have been other tweaks to the smaller details that people will noticed between the two but they both work well and are responsive in their own ways. Once you get used to the control scheme and become comfortable with expected movements and outcomes, you will find that everything feels to be more or less within your control--a small percentage of the time. That feeling is good and brings me back to these games for repetitive playing, even though I know I will likely fail.2D platforming with roguelike elements.Very responsive, some people prefer keyboard, others prefer controller. You definitely want to experiment with both to see which one works better for yourself. I personally use a controller.More child-friendly artwork compared to the first, deceptively so. I do not think this game is easier, in fact, I think it's more difficult. Animations are really awesome.Music is quite good, though not quite as magical as the OST from the first game. Sound effects are mostly okay. (I personally think that there was one major change in one important hidden-pathway sound effect that got almost muted and hinders my own game a bit.)For those who want a hardcore 2D platforming experience and every run being different. For those who don't mind dying repeatedly in order to learn the game's mechanics in order to have a better chance at further progression.Absolutely worth the price. made a lot of people wait, and it was worth it. It's such an enjoyable experience, and Derek Yu delivered on the promise of a game that can be fun and refreshing for new  players and returning veterans alike. No matter who you are, get ready for an exemplary and hardcore platforming experience. It will be frustrating at times, but you will ultimately learn the mechanics of the game through repeated deaths so that you will give yourself the best shot at winning against the odds.Absolutely recommended for the single-player experience alone. I cannot wait for online multiplayer to be implemented, to be able to play with friends.

This alone isn't so bad, but given how annoying and poorly designed Dwelling, it's really not fun to have to go through it in order to get back to where you died before. The levels also are more generic - 1-4 is always a miniboss and there are no things such as the snake pit from the Mines. The player character also feels less responsive and tedious to control - it feels harder to grab on a rope, being frozen in place after getting hit, or falling off ropes after firing the shotgun.Also, with the amount of the content that was copy-pasted from the original Spelunky, it sometimes feels more like a DLC than a whole new game.Were this to be someone's first encounter with Spelunky games, I'd much rather recommend to get Spelunky HD, as I think it offers a much more fair and enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: I do not recommend this game to anyone who loved the prequel.Long version: I've been playing the prequel (Spelunky HD) for years (just shy of 2000 hours on Steam) and love it. I still play it a lot, try to beat the daily challenge every day and use it to kill time and hone my skills still. This Game does a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ job as a successor in my opinion and this is due to various causes. For instance, the controls are wonky and awkward. Where the prequel allowed you to precisely control your character, use every millimeter of every movement, this one is just different. It always feels like the character is drunk or kind of "sticks" to the ground, every jump feels awkward and just wrong. Enemies' hitboxes seem all over the place, sometimes the whip misses although you're standing right next to your target which is really annoying. I bought this game enthusiastically when it came out and expected a worthy successor to one of my favourite games ever, but I was very disappointed to learn that Spelunky 2 is a completely different game. I do not find it hard from a difficulty point of view, but it next to impossible to do anything right with these wonky controls and game design.All in all, I am very disappointed and would not recommend this game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Spelunky 2 is probably my favorite game on steam. It's the game I have the most hours in, the game i play most with friends, and the game I enjoy the most, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.Spelunky 2 is a difficult game, and in the 60 hours that I have played this game, I have never beaten it in a non seeded run. I was able to beat it once with this seed: 2EDB3B4F, but that doesn't matter. The dwellings (first world) is brutal, with moles that come out of the walls, and lizards that can send you flying into corners just to get hit again, as well as bats, which are hard to hit from below, unless you know the backswing of your whip. I don't remember how long it took me to consistantly be able to get out of the dwellings but it was a while. The game doesn't have permanent upgrades, other than shortcuts to help you get to later parts of the game without going through the earlier parts, although if your going for secret endings and collectable stuff, you're going to need to start from the beginning either way. I think the level generation is alright, to me dwelling has too many repeating structures, but the rest of the levels all feel unique in each seed. Speaking of seeds, the game supports a seeded run mode (as mentioned earlier) but there is no current way to find what seed you just played in a normal run, so if you want to discover new seeds, select a random seed in seeded mode and just do that on repeat until you get a seed you like. The controls feel great, it's just fast enough to feel quick and fast paced, but not so fast that you feel like you're losing control of your character. The whip feels nice and heavy, with a small backlash behind and slightly above you before the main hitbox comes out, and it's really satisfying to time it right to hit bats above you, or maybe block incoming arrow traps. You can run, jump, pick up and throw stuff, and use ropes and bombs, all of which are fun to do.Overall, I think the game is great, and only has a few low points. I think compared to the original, this game has a lot more BS. The hit stun is much longer, making it MUCH easier to get combo'd to death no matter how much heath you're at. The moles are just annoying in my opinion, and same goes for those stupid lizards, but hey the BS goes down after the dwelling. Getting past that first world may be annoying for new players, but once you do, you'll get the hang of it. I think the BS of the dwelling readies you for the game, really punishing you for pretty much everything, giving extreme examples of stuff that could happen in the later levels, and teaching you to be careful.Overall, I'd give the game a 9/10, if it weren't for that kinda dumb first world, it would be a 10 in my opinion.Before I go, I'd like to mention one thing, mods are really fun, and you should checkout spelunky.fyi for tons of fun mods, whether it be simple custom characters, or full on randomizers, although some do give you achievements you didn't actually earn. I only got the cosmic ocean from a randomizer, but steam still thinks I did it :|

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't played Spelunky 1 or Spelunky 2, my best recommendation is to play Spelunky 1 to the fullest and only even consider acknowledging this game's existence until you get completely bored of Spelunky 1. When this game was just a trailer and a couple of gameplay demos, I couldn't even imagine writing a review not recommending this game, but it's clear that after playing for as much as I have that Derek Yu doesn't understand the magic and fun that came with Spelunky 1. The main issue is that the game is needlessly antagonistic towards the player for no reason other than what seems to be, "Hey, you! Player! Stop having fun!" Why is it that the jetpack now must explode with contact with fire? In Spelunky 1, the jetpack is far from a victory guarantee and despite its utility, there's still plenty of opportunity to find yourself with another loss with it equipped. Yet, regardless of the result win or loss, the jetpack is such a joy to use. In Spelunky 2, the jetpack retains its familiar maneuverability, but the "contact with fire and it explodes" gimmick leads to removing much of the enjoyment of encountering it in a run. And I think that's how I'd describe most of Spelunky 2's additions from the first game: player-punishing gimmicks. In Spelunky 1, the game is completely up front with all hazards and really the only re-occurring element of surprise is enemies in pots or damsel-disguised enemies (but these are only found in a secret appropriately difficult alternate world). In Spelunky 2, we've got enemies hiding behind scenery, run-ending traps hiding behind scenery (although, thankfully, after an update there's now a small gold piece to make bear traps a little less blending into the background), and enemies in pots that poison you. Poison takes one damage at regular intervals until you rescue a damsel (and good luck finding one after you get poisoned usually), which is a far harsher punishment than taking one damage from being surprised by a hidden enemy in a pot in the first game. The first time I encountered the poison and curse debuffs I thought they were interesting additions, but then when you really think about it/try to deal with it in game, you realize they just don't really mesh at all with the core gameplay. The only thing that even comes close to being a constant burden like curse or poison in the first game is getting the ball-and-chain debuff from destroying too many Kali alters, but for the most part, you have to purposefully go out of your way to make this happen. Even with a random alter being destroyed by something out of your control, I always either had enough favor with Kali for it to not matter or quickly rebuilt favor to avoid the harsher ball-and-chain punishment (and the odds of alters being destroyed twice by RNG are extremely low anyways). Either way, I think I only got the ball-and-chain punishment maybe twice in thousands of runs. Meanwhile, I don't know how many times I've gotten cursed or poisoned in this game, but frequent enough for it to really sour the experience of playing.At some point long ago, I started playing Spelunky 1 with the music muted and I've resumed that with Spelunky 2 after many hours playing, but I will comment that the music in Spelunky 2 is highly repetitive and not nearly as enjoyable to listen to as the first game. This is more of a disappointment than something that I wouldn't recommend over. I think the adaptive soundtrack is an interesting idea, but hearing the main dwelling song again and again with little variation on every run shows how badly this works in practice (it doesn't help that the main dwelling song is probably the worst in the soundtrack). I think my return to Spelunky 1 one night after many lackluster not so fun attempts at Spelunky 2 runs says it all. That night, I managed to get a victorious alternate ending run in Spelunky 1 less than ten playthroughs and I had a load of fun in the process in spite of the hundreds of hours I've had in that game. I sort of walked away with the feeling of, "Oh, I forgot there is a version of Spelunky that's actually consistently fun to play." Perhaps the only good thing I can say about Spelunky 2 is that online co-op is a lot of fun because most of the player punishment I discussed above doesn't really matter as much since dead players can be revived on the very next level. However, personally, my main interaction with Spelunky 1 or 2 is through solo play, so I hold with my opinion that I don't recommend this particular iteration. I'll continue to play Spelunky 2 if only to get to one of the game's endings, but after that, I'm not sure I'll play that much aside from co-op and the random one-off session.

_childDocuments_.review: Spelunky 2 is a game that as sadistic as it is satisfying to play.  I died nearly 1,000 before completing the game and that was with shortcuts.  Spelunky 2 far more difficult than its predecessor from the very start.  I'd like to say that all my deaths felt fair but I'd be lying.  The amount of cheap ways to die surpasses Spelunky 1 by quite a large margin.  I was often frustrated by deaths that came without proper time to even react.  I've had shop-keepers come after me for seemingly no reason, and on occasion, I've died without knowing what even happened.  Dying never has felt so punishing especially when I have traveled so far just do die so cheaply to something that would have been impossible to avoid without further warning.  So much of this game relies on you understanding what can or can't kill you which isn't always obvious.  This means you must die quite a bit before completely grasping all the myriad of ways death can come to you.  This is fine for the first few levels since there isn't so much on the line but this becomes infuriating later when, for example, you die to your own shotgun blasts that were reflected back at you because you shot at an late-game-enemy that happens to reflect bullets.  Shortcuts help mitigate this frustration once they're all finally opened but they can be quite frustrating to unlock as well.   Anytime shortcuts require hired-help as a means to unlock is absolutely maddening.  Hired help, a.k.a., cave men, are dumber than a brick and always manage to die before ever reaching the area I'm taking them to.  All of these flaws add up to what is a pretty frustrating experience.  That being said, I've had so much fun playing this game.  Despite my frustration, I came back over and over again because the general gameplay loop of Spelunky has never felt so satisfying.  Despite the sequel being less balanced than the first, I still prefer it by quite a large margin.  Spelunky 2 is more grounded, more imaginative, and far more beautiful than its predecessor.  The game gives you so many options to enjoy the game in your own way.  Want to ride a turkey to gain an additional jump? Go ahead.  Want to blow the turkey up and eat its cooked meat for extra health? That works too.  Want to throw the turkey to set off dangerous traps?  Have at it!  Any single object, creature, or item always suggest numerous different possibilities at your disposal.  This kind of emergent gameplay makes each run feeling fresh and interesting again and again. I loved Spelunky 2 and I recommend it to anyone who is willing to look past some amount of obvious frustrations.  I absolutely think it's a much better game than its great predecessor and that its positive qualities largely outshines its negatives.  Spelunky 2 is terrific and one of the best examples of emergent-game-design, period.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me question whether I ever actually enjoyed the original.  The original was challenging, but here everything has been cranked up to 11.  The first set of levels, which in the original were a way to ease into the game, are now a nightmarish slog, ultra dense with traps and enemies, including new enemies that are far more difficult than their predecessors.  They take multiple hits to kill (which cannot be done quickly as they are invincible during stun) and have fast, erratic movements.  Then once you graduate to the later levels, your health effectively becomes meaningless because 90% of your deaths will be 1-hit instakills, or effective 1-hit kills where you are stunlocked, thrown around the screen, and juggled to death.  The game does not even appear to be aiming for the "tough but fair" label that Souls games often get.  I experienced many deaths due to bizarre enemy interactions halfway across the map, or objects flying at me suddenly from offscreen.What all of this added difficultly results in is a game that is at odds with itself.  It must be played with extreme caution if the player wants to have any chance of success, but this slows the pace of the game down to a crawl and draws out the length of each run.  This being a roguelike where all progress is lost upon death, this makes every death as painful and disheartening as possible.  The balance between fun and frustration has been completely lost here.

But the fact that I've spent so much time on a game that I'm clearly incapable of mastering in reasonable time says a lot about how much fun this game is. I know I'll probably never be able to devote enough time to this game to become good enough to even see level 2-2, let alone area 6. Yet for reasons that I can't explain, instead of this making me want to kick Derek Yu in the nuts, it makes me admire the fact that he had the balls to make the general public pay to experience such unrelenting cruelty. It also somehow makes me want to spend even more time playing the game. Is this the feeling that drives people to throw money away on the lottery every week? Whatever it is, it's such a unique experience in my game playing history that it's moved me to write my first review.I recommend it to people who have no interest in progress.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I would say I have a mixed opinion of Spelunky 2, so I'll start with the complaints I have about the game so far, and this list may grow or shrink depending on how far into the game I get.These are all factors of the game that I don't entirely agree with or like due to how they function or occur in game.   And I overall think each of these needs some kind of addressment as they all feel like carry-overs from an earlier version.Now with what I dislike about the game out of the way, I'll get onto the positives of this review (and hence my rating of positive), I would say despite these numerously spanned flaws the game is still fairly fun and much of a blast like the original game, with dozens of new areas, items, and characters for you to find and unlock.   The gameplay feels alot more fluid and quicker than the original - and it generally feels smooth, while still having that Spelunky-esque difficulty kick we all know it for in the first game.   Restarting in this game is one of the most common things out there, but one of my favourite parts is how shortcuts allow progression and no longer disable it, making it easier to discover new areas or practice them aswell as unlock new content without being punished for it. I would also say I really enjoy some of the new mechanics/changes like being able to whip-kick off of walls, and bombs/ropes being infinitely more common, it feels less like a sacred resource and more like something you should use when you need to use it or want to use it.   I also like some of the progressional landmarks this game has as it really makes you notice how far along you've come.In general, all Spelunky 2 needs is a bit of finetuning and minor improvements but otherwise it's a fantastic game that's soon to have co-op!If I had to rate Spelunky on a scale of 0.0 - 20.0, I would give it a solid  - it's got it's flaws but it's by no means a mediocre game, and will be one you return to numerous times even after completing it.   This review score is prone to change as I have yet to beat the entire game.   But as of now, this would be my review for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I'm all that great at playing games in general, so know that going into this review, but to be fair I did manage to beat dark souls (after a lot of dying) and enjoyed it too.This game on the other hand has a serious learning curve going in, and the problem is that they took ALL of it and stuffed it into the first level. Give me SOMETHING new, or a boss that I can beat and then PROGRESS past.  That's what dark souls did and that's why I stuck with it.  Replaying the first level of a game until you puke is not fun.I will probably keep playing until I've met the arbitrary baseline skill threshold I have to reach to be able to consistently beat the dwelling, but this is ridiculous.  Expect mastery to come in roughly six hours, if you're an average gamer, and really ask yourself if you want to play the first level of any game for that long before you buy it.  One mistake and you're pretty much dead, no matter how petty.  Oh, and god forbid a bat hits you once.  Enemies don't get knocked back when they come in contact with you, so if it hits you, it's going to burrow into your skin and stay inside you until your iframes are gone and then hit you again.  But you can't run, because moving fast means you'll hit one of the 1 million arrow traps that liter every bit of the level.  That's the only part I'm going to nit pick, otherwise I'd rather just whine about the first level as a whole.Anyway, I'm going to "get good" because it's a really good game otherwise. _childDocuments_.review: I can only speak for myself but I feel that Spelunky 2 certainly lives up to its expectations. The art style is quite different both visually and musically to its predecessor but the game, to me,  retains the atmosphere and overall feel of the experience. As a whole, the game seems to be a step up in difficulty from the first, making it a challenging experience even for veterans of the first installment.The mechanics are very similar to the first Spelunky, albeit not identical. For instance the famous whip moonwalk move that allowed to move over 2-tile gaps is no longer possible, but it has been replaced with the ability to bump your head to cross the gap anyway. Whipping arrow traps has different timings and is generally a bit easier. I wouldn't say the game has suffered from the mechanical changes, the differences aren't necessarily better or worse.The game has many areas with their own striking visual styles affecting the enemies and environments that change up the experience as the player goes along. Of course, these areas will be visited many times as the player inevitably dies but they serve well to break up the monotony nonetheless. There are many new enemy types as well as some enemies returning from Spelunky. The players will be able to use their aquired knowledge from the first game while also needing to learn new behaviors based on the new additions. This seems to be a good balance for people fond of the previous game.The addition of multiple layers to a level don't appear as much of an important change as I'd assumed from the trailers but they do help make the game feel much bigger in scale regardless. The second layer areas are usually rather limited but can be worth exploring. I have more to say about Spelunky 2 than my motivation will allow me to type out but overall I'd say Spelunky 2 is one of the best rogue-lite splatformers in existence, bringing out the best out of the concept of procedurally-generated levels and well realized game mechanics that allow for a smooth yet strongly challenging experience through and through. For those who enjoy this type of game I have to say it's worth a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Spelunky 2 is an absolute triumph in the world of roguelike gaming, delivering an exhilarating experience that surpasses even the lofty expectations set by its predecessor. From the moment I delved into the treacherous depths of its procedurally generated caves, I was hooked, and the game's relentless charm and challenge kept me coming back for more.The level design is a true testament to the genius of Derek Yu and his team. The intricately crafted environments are not just visually stunning, but they also create an ever-changing landscape that challenges players to think on their feet. Every run feels fresh and unpredictable, with hidden secrets and dangers lurking around every corner. It's a testament to the game's design that even after numerous playthroughs, I continue to discover new surprises and challenges.Spelunky 2's commitment to difficulty is both punishing and rewarding. The learning curve is steep, yet the sense of accomplishment when overcoming each hurdle is unmatched. The game constantly demands skill and strategy, making each decision a crucial one. Whether it's avoiding devious traps, outsmarting enemies, or navigating the intricate puzzles, every move requires careful consideration, adding layers of depth to the gameplay.The addition of new characters, items, and environments enriches the overall experience, providing players with ample opportunities for experimentation and strategic planning. The expanded roster of playable characters brings diversity to the game, each with their own unique abilities and playstyles. This not only enhances the replay value but also adds an extra layer of complexity to the already challenging gameplay.Multiplayer mode is an absolute blast, fostering both cooperation and competition among friends. The chaos that ensues when navigating the caves with a group of friends adds a whole new dimension to the Spelunky 2 experience. The shared victories and inevitable mishaps make for unforgettable gaming moments that will be recounted with laughter and excitement.In terms of visuals and audio, Spelunky 2 excels on all fronts. The charming pixel art style is a treat for the eyes, and the dynamic soundtrack enhances the tension and excitement as you explore each level. The attention to detail in both the visual and auditory aspects of the game contributes to its immersive and engaging atmosphere.In conclusion, Spelunky 2 is a true gem in the roguelike genre. It not only lives up to the legacy of its predecessor but also surpasses it in every conceivable way. With its challenging gameplay, ingenious level design, and a plethora of content, Spelunky 2 is a must-play for fans of the genre and newcomers alike. Brace yourself for a thrilling journey filled with surprises, setbacks, and triumphs – Spelunky 2 is a five-star adventure that will keep you coming back for more!

_childDocuments_.review: Spelunky 2 has, at its core, flawless gameplay, flawless graphics and music. It's one of the few true roguelike platformer, where  your progress is not shown on an XP bar, but in your growing skill as a player and your knowledge of the maps. On paper, it has everything I love in video games. So why don't I recommend it?It's rather simple: it's the ''rng bullcrap''. One of the main feature of the game is also it's downfall. This was an important feature in the first Spelunky, but I found that in Spelunky 2, it's out of control. Though getting killed the second  you enter a room by your NPC ally because he went berserk after seeing an enemy can be "funny" in a slapstick kind of way, it's less so when it's extremely frequent and you find yourself not even being able to get out of the first level without dying and starting over 5 times. You can take shortcuts, but the requirements are often a huge pain in the neck to get. I played nearly 40 hours at the time of this review and I feel like I haven't even progressed that much. It was definetly NOT the case when I played the first one, in which I made great progress and discovered tons of secret in barely 14 hours. When I play a game, I don't like to go on reddit or YouTube to figure out how to play. I like to do that myself. I strongly do not recommend you do this with Spelunky 2. It's clearly a comunity based game, which is not bad in itself. It's a very valid design choice that has been widespread with the rise in popularity of hardcore games. But after finally looking at a few videos, I realized that this game was going to take a long time to learn all it's secret and techniques. I wouldn't mind to do that normally, but the thought of following guides for hours while I get unfairly killed by enemies, traps and allies sounds like something I don't have the patience for anymore. If someone would come to me and say the love the game as it is and that it's a masterpiece, I certainly wouldn't reject their opinion or question their tastes. As I said in the beginning, It's fundamentally a great game. Who knows, I might go back to it one day and maybe it's gonna finally click for me. But even if it does, I would never recommend it to anyone but the most patient, hardcore and (most importantly) dedicated gamer.EDIT: After an additional 15 hours of play, the help of a few guides, I managed to finally beat the game and get to the basic ending. My opinion on Spelunky 2 was only reinforced, as much for the negative aspects as for the positive. If I can end this review a positive note, I must say that despite everything, it did manage to have me go back to it untill I finally reach one of the final boss. It's a testament to the rock solid gameplay that is so good that it keeps you coming back despite the infuriating nature of the RNG. I still wouldn't recommend it to the vast majority of players.

_childDocuments_.review: After finally getting all the achievements in the game, I think I can effectively say I've experienced all that Spelunky 2 has to offer. To summarize my thoughts: this game is fantastic if you're looking for an extreme challenge. Just like the original (Spelunky HD, that is), this game will beat your butt no questions asked. Just like the original, you'll feel yourself getting better every run. Just like the original, it has near infinite replay value. Unlike the original, Spelunky 2 expands upon that feeling of discovery and strange locations. The introduction of backrooms, as well as split paths was an excellent choice, and really added a lot to make this game stand out from the first.That being said, with more content comes more issues. I'm sure it is evident to anyone who has played the game for more than a couple of hours, but the dwelling is certainly not all that it could be. The addition of a special level on 1-4 is a great idea, but some of the new enemies that weren't in the original really should've stayed out. The magic of Spelunky HD was that when you died, it was ALWAYS your fault, and you could only really blame yourself. But in Spelunky 2, some things just feel unfair (moles, horned lizards). That sense that the game is unfair is most concentrated in the dwelling, but it can affect you in other areas, too.Don't get me wrong, though. I still absolutely love this game. I wouldn't keep coming back to it if I didn't. The challenge that Spelunky 2 brings is addicting. If you loved the first game, chances are you'll love this one. If you have a lot of time to be frustrated at yourself, but slowly get better, chances are you'll love Spelunky 2. However, if you get easily annoyed at occasional unfair RNG, this may not be for you. While I think I can safely say that just about everyone can enjoy Spelunky HD, this game takes the difficulty to an extreme that many players would avoid. Even still, this game is a thrill, and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but it just feels... tedious? There are a ton of items, maps, secrets, and so on, but the actual game itself just isn't engaging to me on a moment-to-moment basis. The actual act of moving, jumping, and navigating doesn't really involve much skill at all - about 90% of the game is just about looking around, taking note of your surroundings, and being careful, but once you do that, executing your moves isn't particularly fun or exciting. And consequently, about 90% of my deaths came because I walked into an arrow trap I didn't notice, a spider dropped from off-screen onto my head, or I broke a pot that had a snake inside, and not because I mistimed a jump or reacted too slowly to a new challenge. Maybe that sort of slow, methodical style is fun for some people, but I personally just found it frustrating and artificially difficult.Really, Spelunky 2 feels more like a "meta-game" about discovering secrets and fooling around with interactions than an actual platformer - it's a little like Fez, if you could also die at any moment because the game is full of contrived threats that are only dangerous because avoiding them is so tedious that you'll end up getting too bored to properly defuse them. I just didn't find it that interesting, honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface: I have thousands of hours of playtime in many of the most difficult rogue-likes around. This game is a mess. There are other reviews that mirror my feelings on this game, so I'll be general. Scores of enemies that give you little to no time to react, especially when you must constantly scan the entire screen for threats. Wonky hit/hurt boxes. General punishment for strategic thinking (You have a good plan to get by? Oh, here's a mole out of nowhere or a skeleton that does not animate until it's too late for you to react). Abundance of inaccessible areas paired with a lack of resources. Juggled to death for making one mistake, which more likely due to the clunky controls more so than a lack of planning. The moles can be tracked as they dig, but I have 20/20 vision and no other visual impairments, and I have a hard time seeing them as they dig (I can only imagine how impossible it could be if you were, say, colorblind). Beyond gameplay, the music is soooo repetitive. A few more tracks in each area would make the repetitive attempts at the mines a little more tolerable.  This game just does not want to be played (this is coming from someone who plays games like Nuclear Throne and FTL regularly). I liked the first game well enough, but always thought certain things like hit/hurt boxes and controls could be a lot tighter. I hoped this game would improve on those things, but it's pretty clear at this point that the creators were not interested in making a game for fans of rogue-likes, and instead focused on catering to the .0001% of people that are known for streaming/doing Spelunky let's play videos. I hope for a patch, but doubt we'll get one. Was hoping this would usher in a second renaissance for the rogue-like genre, but I really think it's going to put a lot of people off while only attracting slews of "git gud" edgelords.

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect sequel. Spelunky 2 finds the perfect balance of:"Oh, I remember that from the first game, I know what that does,""Okay, that was in the first game, but it's waaaay different now," and"WHAT THE EFF IS THAT?!"I think Spelunky's greatest downfall is that I have no idea how a new player could get into it. The game is one of the most difficult games I've ever played, and a lot of that comes from the immense amount of knowledge required. I can't recommend this if you're the kind of person that gets mad at video games, but if you're willing to sit there, learn from hundreds, probably even thousands, of little mistakes bringing your demise, and push forward through it, Spelunky 2 is a fantastic game and my nomination for Game of the Year.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could I'd give this game a neutral review. Spleunky 2 is a very different game from the first one in very subtle ways, certain controls will feel different, certain approaches to enemies will be different, but it is fundamentally quite similar to the first game.From the perspective of someone who played the first a lot, the 2nd feels oddly foreign and even a bit rough to work with, my chief complaint is the first zone is overwhelming with how many things it has going on, there's an ungodly amount of mobs, traps, etc, however the game improves a lot once you leave the first zone.Overall though the game still has a lot of flaws that needs to be hammered out, I think the mob spam in the first zone isn't a good choice, it makes moving through that zone a pain, and i found myself doing nothing but throwing rocks at enemies when there. Map generation in the first area also leaves much to be desired, with there often being areas that will make you stuck unless you use rope to backtrack. Many QOL changes could be made as well, the chest containing the eye treasure cannot be moved, unlike the previous game, which makes doing the mini-quest for it annoying. The soundtrack doesn't sound as interesting as Spelunky's either, about 2 hours into playtime i had turned the music off in favor of just whatever background noise I can play.There's a few (possible) bugs as well, if you get an NPC companion there's a chance they may try to steal from the shopkeeper, instantly making them all hostile to you. This is a really good game but it has a lot of flaws that makes it a questionable buy right now, the lack of online multiplayer also makes it a difficult game to recommend, but I trust the game developers will improve it over time.

_childDocuments_.review: I have over 500 hours in the original Spelunky.  I've beaten that game multiple times, know all the secrets, and have almost all the achievements for it (the last two don't look fun to get, so I've not really tried).  I played the original, OG Spelunky before that...though I didn't start coming into my own with the game until the more modern version.  I'm no master level player, but I know the game well.  I adore it, and it's one of my favorite games for relaxing.   Win or lose, I find most of my playing really engaging; I laugh at my deaths and take glee from my successes.  As a result,  I had my eyes on Spelunky 2 for a while, and the pictures made it look like just what I wanted.Then I played it...and I kind of wish it had stayed on my wishlist.Spelunky 2 isn't a bad game so much as it is a sequel that is at odds with the game play of the first title.  Strong among the first game's qualities were, as you got good, you were able to take your time and really build yourself up.  The level layouts rewarded mastery, while still being stuff that greener players could traverse and get to the end of.  Traps were designed in such a way that the vast majority of my deaths in the original game felt like my fault and only my fault; it felt fair, while still being cut-throat.  I was the one who failed, the game didn't 'trick' me.  The end of the level ghost was a problem, but a more clever player could circumvent it and even kite into gems to increase their value, creating this interesting risk/reward dynamic...making the end of every stage a calculation of what you could do safely...and what you could do if you were willing to risk it.All of that is gone now.The traps are much more frequent, and feel designed for cruelty rather then a rewarding game play experience where the challenges feel designed to create a good time.  The physics have changed, meaning you can throw a stone in front of you and not hit what is in front of you....so not only does that make no sense?  As a vetran of the first game, I have to unlearn what the previous game taught me for what feels like no good reason.  The ghost isn't something a skilled played can circumvent and avoid...and even use for profit; the ghost is much faster, so it's so much closer to a standard time limit without the nuances of the original title.  The money is now more sparsely laid out, so building yourself up is harder and more challenging....without actually feeling more rewarding; I never feel like my inability to buy things and build myself up is a fault of my choices...but a fault of level lay outs that now spawn less money.  You used to be able to cling to ladders and ropes and fire a gun, allowing the methodical and thoughtful players a chance to use the terrain; now the kick back shoves you off...presumably to make game play more "interesting".I'm not interested.The game feels like it wants to just be harder for the sake of being harder alone, when the original game was still very challenging and engaging as it was.  The design was pretty flawless.  What I came to Spelunky 2 expecting was that core design, while getting new content, stage lay outs, and concepts.  What I got instead was Spelunky for the irritating and toxic "git gud" crowdAnd there are lots of fun things in the game.  The little fire beetles are brilliant design.  The Boarcupine boss is well designed, and fun to try and figure out.  The cave systems are great, and how doors interact with bombs presents fun challenges and interesting options.  The new level short cuts are well designed.  I'm just upset that all these fun, new features are now in a core game experience that I nakedly despise.I would have returned this thing, but I accidentally missed the cutoff window by letting the game idle while picking up a family member from their job.  So I stuck with it longer then I would have otherwise....I started being able to get into later stages, and facing the traps there.  The problem is that it isn't fun or rewarding.  It's a miserable slog. Even when I succeed...I never get the sense of triumph the previous game give me; my reward is only ever a new piece of tedium to throw myself at.Honestly, I wish I had my money back instead.  This game just misunderstands what made the previous game fun, and I sort of hate it.  It represents all these ideas that I wish I could bring back to the original Spelunky.  Until someone makes a mod though, Spelunky 2 just represents a waste of my time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a huge fan of the rogue-like genre for many years now, starting all the way back with the Binding of Isaac. From there, the genre has exploded into many different variations of randomly generated levels and perma-death level difficulty; where the stakes are high and the rewards of succeeding feel that much sweeter. Spelunky was a title that, in certain variations, has existed even as far back as Isaac and it was a game i had always heard about, but never really knew if I would enjoy it.With Spelunky 2, I decided the time was right to take the plunge; this quirky little platformer could be a bit of fun. Little did I know, this game would bring me immense frustration, laughter, elation, anger, excitement, and feelings of discovery. This game is unforgiving and doesn't hold your hand; it drops you in and leaves you to find your own way out. Maybe that's not for everyone, but at this point in my life, this game has become my favourite in all of the rogue-like genre.Being able to overcome a level or boss brought me incredible satisfaction; being able to discover secrets and secrets within secrets probed me to dig deeper; getting to a point in the game when you think it's all over only to discover that there's much more. These are the things I've experienced from this game and being able to play with friends and seeing their exact same emotions as mine is something that makes me want to share this with everyone.With most rogue-likes, there is usually a large slew of items you can pick-up that gives you a unique "build" for each run you do of the game. The lack of items in Spelunky means that most of the variation exists in the way the levels are generated; and sometimes, that variation is cursed. I've found that having a small pool of items makes almost all them useful in some way, so no matter the seed that is generated, you know that when you pick up an item, it will prove to be helpful to you in some way.In regards to the level design, you're fighting against the RNG; sometimes it works in your favour, sometimes you're left to figure out the best escape route possible. Sometimes, the items you need are generated and easy to pick-up or purchase from the shop. Sometimes, the only clean way out is to go down a route and avoid traps and enemies. The more you play this game, the more you are able to navigate the variations in levels better than you ever thought you could.In almost 100 hours played on Steam as of writing this, and not to mention the time i've spent on the Switch and PS4 as well, this game is an experience for those looking for a meaningful one. If you are patient and determined, I feel like this game can reward you for the time you put in and will keep you coming back to see if you can beat it again and again. I would recommend this game to everyone and hope you, too, can beat this game, even if it's just to say "I did it".

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy if you are planning to use a gamecube controller.You will be hardlocked on the tutorial without having to do workarounds. The game requires you to open the journal to complete the tutorial, but the button for the journal does not exist on the gamecube controller, and for whatever reason, you -cannot- change the keybinding via in-game settings. You also cannot just keep a keyboard nearby to press the Tab key to do this mid-game, because the game refuses to allow you to have both available at the same time. In order to use the keyboard bindings, you have to disconnect your controller and maybe even restart the game.There are workarounds(complete the tutorial with keyboard, or use steam controller settings to change bindings around), however it's kind of silly that you have to do this in the first place.Just don't waste your time unless you're really into the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorites. First of all, rogue-likes appeal to me because of their easy to pick up nature from whatever point I am at. I don't need to remember the story or what I was doing last time I played the game or have a series of tasks I need to do before I can get to the core game play. I just pick it up, dust the rust of my skills, and see how far they take me. This is why I keep coming back to this challenging game.I'll never forget the charms of mass murdering shopkeepers in Spelunky HD, but Spelunky 2 is simply an improvement across the board. The polish of mechanics and level design are cleaner, controls feels smoother- superior movement controls(higher fps less input lag), and it also retains the same charm as Spelunky HD through the music, settings, characters, etc. Not to mention the net-code works!If you are playing with friends, expect to kill each other a lot and not make much progress but the fun you'll have will be well worth it. Also, highly recommend Spelunky 2 Death Match. Death Match with friends is a a great past time of mine that I've continued even from Spelunky HD, going to a friends house and playing LAN XBOX and PC. Throwing 99 consecutive bombs at my friends ragdoll body will never get old! Anyway, with the net-code on steam play being pretty good, playing Spelunky 2 online is a near painless process(compared to HD) and is loads of fun with friends. 10/10 would steal from shopkeep and get forgiveness 2 floors later again!

All around, Spelunky 2 is an amazing game, and a worthy sequel to the first entry in the series

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is one of those hundreds-of-hours negative reviews, ha ha.  Are you also familiar with the "this RPG is great you should play it, the first 50 hours suck then it gets good" trope?  Well, my first 160 hours with Spelunky 2 were mostly miserable, so I can't rightly recommend a game that I expect someone to hate for 160 hours, can I?  There's no middle ground for Steam recommendations, so consider this a very conflicted review.Originally I wrote this review around 30 hours, then updated it three times over the next 170 hours.  I've replaced that with this to make it a little more concise:The reason I stuck with Spelunky 2 so long was that I played classic Spelunky to the extent I would see it when I closed my eyes, and knew what Spelunky is at its best: a series where, with enough proficiency, a player can learn the game and react to situations before they actually happen to overcome incredible odds.  I thought if I stuck it out and got gud I might actually get to enjoy a one of a kind game, and all the wonderful new content this installment brings.  Fortunately, I was right, but with some caveats.The problem with Spelunky 2 compared to the previous games, is that Derek Yu seems to have bought in to the meme about how hard his game is like a Dark Souls 2 dev.  The chaos has been ramped up to a completely unfun and unfair extreme.  Enemy and trap spawns can be out of control, the number of instant deaths has been cranked up, tiny mistakes are usually punished with death, and an already notoriously dangerous late game area recently got a rework that seems to have made it even worse.  Players new to the Spelunky series will face hundreds of frustrating hours, at least.If you consider yourself an average player like I do (around 170 hours in I started making it to CO consistently, for you elitists), and you put in the time to break through that barrier and start having fun, you'll still occasionally find yourself variably angry and disappointed with the game.  The best players you can watch on Twitch and Youtube will just have runs ended completely out of their control; skill (mostly caution) only decreases these instances.  There are far too many egregious design flaws, but here are a few of the major ones:Classic Spelunky's ledge grab mechanic was so flawlessly intuitive, it's dumbfounding it was ever changed for Spelunky HD.  Automatic ledge grab is still here, and still not optional.  Even more glaringly, the Climbing Gloves were changed from the HD style, which seems to admit automatically grabbing surfaces sucks, but we're still stuck with it for ledges.  This also means there are two control schemes for essentially the same action.The Jetpack now explodes, which is fine as a counterbalance to what is still a great item.  The other packs also explode, because internal game logic is more important to the developer than balance.  This makes the other backpacks a straight downgrade from the Jetpack that you will never touch if you have any other option, and most people won't take anything else but the Hoverpack, even when there's no other option.  The Powerpack is a fun item I never use.There is now a fetch quest of items the game expects you to take if you want to go the distance, and at least the first of them can't be subverted no matter what.  This means you'll never carry an item through the certain area, and anything fun you found is just temporary.  Couple this with the increased number of near- and worthless items, and Black Markets are often just landfills of junk.The level generation often sucks.  I could spend 10K words on this so that will have to suffice.There aren't many games at all like Spelunky--the closest I can think of is Rogue Legacy--and none that have their charm.  I wouldn't have this series without Derek Yu, but I think these games would be leagues better if he was strictly an ideas guy, and left the design to someone better at the fundamentals.  I never would have stuck with Spelunky 2 long enough to get to the light at the end of the tunnel if it hadn't been for the better, if less ambitious, games in this series.  And even though I'm out of the tunnel, the game still hits me with plenty of trains.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is both magnificent and the worst imaginable gathering of unfortunate events that are 100% out of your control.Spelunky 1 was a breeze compared to this clustertruck of weird, BS moments where no matter what you do you will get stabbed in the shins by 3 moles in a 1 tile-high corridor outside of a door. There is no way to see it coming, there is no way to dodge it, and you will get hit at least once. And yeah, sometimes in Spelunky one, you enter a new level, and something happened, and the shopkeeper is mad, or you die instantly. Sure. it happens.But in SP2, EVEN if the shopkeeper doesn't get mad at you for unrelated accidents (most of them anyway), and EVEN if there are more ways to get HP now, guess what? Doesn't matter. because 50% of your runs are ruined from the start. Hell, one time I restarted, and a skeleton spawned right next to me. Sure, I should have spammed the whip right away like a pro speedrunner, but also HOW ABOUT TUNING IT DOWN ON THE 40 ENEMIES ON FIRST LEVEL?I don't mind Dying. Dying is fun. Dredmor taught me that, and Dredmor killed me a thousand times more than this game ever will (probably) but at least in Dredmor, 95% of the time it's my fault. This is not difficulty. This is cheap.  It's engineered to kill you. It will kill you. and half the time, you won't even know what hit you.My pet peeves (in no specific orders)-Moles being invincible when they emerge and being able to move INSTANTLY after said invincibility phase.-Moles emerging under you in a 1 tile high corridor-Stages with many moles. By that I mean 3-4-Lizards hitting you 3-4-5-6-7 times in a row (see 1-tile high corridors where you come out of a door for additional rage)-Cavemans tripping over something. That's fun. The following 0.8 seconds stun phase right after that is not fun at all. make it longer. 2 seconds is all I ask. but no.-having 5 ragdolls in one spot, and having anything happen to it with you being close to it.-Having the pet behind a 4-wide wall, in a corner way up there-Having the key behind a 4-wide wall, in a corner way up there-Having the ghost jar behind a 4-wide wall, in a corner up there (you get it)-Having any important area completely isolated by the level, inaccessible behing walls, usually by a shop as well.-Having the drill over a shop, or any other important areas. -5 enemies behind a door, literally 2 feet away from you. -Any of these scenarios, but with a ghost jar.-Ghost jar getting broken when you enter a stage (how about making the jar indestructible the first 5 seconds? I mean come on man!)Any of these (and there are a tons more trust me) will usually put you in a horrible spot, or straight out ruin your run or kill you. And there is NOTHING you can do about it. I don't mind you cranking the difficulty to 11 out of 5, that is perfectly acceptable, I eat Dante Must Die runs for snacks, but just like there shouldn't be unavoidable instant hits in beat em alls or fighting games, there shouldn't be situations that are 100% out of your control THIS OFTEN. having 1/10 of my runs ruined is understandable in Spelunky. Not half of them. Some of these shouldn't be impossible to fix as well.The balance issues by itself is also wonky. In the first 4 levels, there are snakes, bats, scorpions sometimes. these are understandable threats. The scorpion poisons you now (the poison status effect shouldn't do what it does IMO, but whatever) but okay, that's fair somewhat. Then you have cavemans, moles and lizards. In order:-Cavemans: slow, dumb, can't jump or stop running once it does. Abides with the rules of the game and is understandable. Has 3 HP.-Moles: Fast, digs in dirt. Unpreditable, incoherent, an absolute threat. invincible when emerging from said dirt, difficult to deal with. Also has 3 HP.-Lizards. Attacks on sight. Cannot be stopped once it goes, except by stronger weapon or throws object. Will murder you if in a 1 tile-high corridor because you can't stop it with your whip. ALSO 3 HP!so when the game spawns 4 cavemans in your face, at least you can stop them with your basic attack or do something about it. If 4 moles spawn in your face you might as well expect to trade 3 HP to get away or fight them, depending if the game boned you on level generation as well. Because sometimes it does, thank you for your money. At the very least, it makes for some excellent entertainment watching. Waving at you Vinny Vinesauce Man! Watching you turn into a duck out of frustration in spelunky is always the best times. For us, sorry for you.I could rant for ages. So should you get the game? Niuhg. Like I said it's awesome, but it makes me bitter every single times I boot it up. I have fun, but I feel worse about it. Every streaming session I did of it so far has been pain, no exception. So despite the high praise the game gets (and I really understand it and agree with it), let this post and review be a warning for you all. Because this game is unfair. it is infuriating. it is ABSOLUTELY BRUTAL!!!! I CANNOT recommend it as I would other difficult games, because it is an unfair mess of garbage scenarios that will test even the most hardcore of Spelunky veterans, except the kids who eat raw coffee beans for breakfast. However, if you read all of this, and the pain you imagine excites you, then by all means... This game is pretty dope.

_childDocuments_.review: Spelunky HD is my most played game on Steam as of this review and after all the hours i've put in I still love that game.Spelunky 2, on the other hand, feels unfinished,unfair and frustrating.Keep in mind it took something like 30-45 days to patch in AI helpers knowing that lava = death, one of the major bosses has been reworked like 3 times because going afk while he killed himself was optimal and online co-op is only being rolled out now, so this game is definitely still a work in progress.Given all the oddball design choices the only reason i've stuck with this game for so long is that i wanted to get every achievement out of respect for spelunky HD.With that said if you really like platformers and dont mind the game deciding that "you just die now" you'll probably get enough hours out of this game for it to feel worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't beaten the original Spelunky, it shouldn't hurt your experience with this game.With Spelunky 2, Mossmouth has been taken the original game, broken it down to its individual parts, and tweaked those parts to make them different, better, or more expansive, then assembled them all in a much different way, filling in the cracks with brand new content. There is a lot to like here, especially for die hard Spelunky fans who have squeezed as much enjoyment as they could out of the original game. Mossmouth saw what you were capable of, and built this game to challenge YOU at its very highest levels of play. At its most basic level of play, it is a bit more difficult than Spelunky in many ways, while offering new ways to survive. At its most complex level of play, it is a brutally difficult, complex, and nuanced challenge with many ways to get to the very, very end; one that few players will get to. It is a much bigger difference than the two endings of the original Spelunky; the multiple endings of this game are of vastly different difficulties.This variety is what leads to this game's biggest strength: more ways to play Spelunky. Even if you haven't beaten Olmec in the first game, the amount of things you can do in this one is remarkably refreshing, and gives you more ways to enjoy the Spelunky experience. It can be easy to experience burnout when playing a one of a kind game such as Spelunky, and giving you more ways to enjoy the experience will allow you to improve much faster at the overall skill. Playing Spelunky 2 greatly improved my ability to play Spelunky 1 after going back to it, and, after playing Spelunky 1 for a while with a much fresher mindset, suffering less burnout from repeated plays, I went back to Spelunky 2 and discovered that I had gotten much better at it. It's a neverending cycle that probably would occur even if Spelunky 2 didn't have the variety it did, but is greatly helped by the fact that it DOES have that variety, and it improves this game's experience as a whole, even when playing it on its own.It is with all this in mind that I highly recommend playing this game, but probably after playing and getting familiar with Spelunky first. You don't have to get good at it; you just have to get a feel for what its all about. That being said, it's perfectly possible to play this game first, enjoy it, and then play the first game. There are no rules; I can only verify that, in my own experience, playing and watching other people play the first game really allowed me to appreciate Spelunky 2. That's another thing; read up on, discuss, or watch others play these games; it really improves the experience.Just remember that the joy of the game should be how you tackle each run; not your ability to beat the game. If you concentrate only on whether you beat it or not, you will just end up dissapponting yourself. You will get there eventually.
_childDocuments_.name: Spelunky 2

_childDocuments_.review: What is the one difference between Spelunky 2 and Spelunky HD? Probably the appeal to different demographics. Spelunky HD was hard from the very beginning. I didn't unlock the jungle until my 20th hour in HD. Spelunky 2 may not be easier, but it has a better difficulty curve. For casual players, Spelunky 2 is a godsend for anybody that wanted to get into Spelunky but lost interest after many deaths. There's even an online multiplayer for those who want to play with friends. For the hardcore gamers however, you may find Spelunky 2 to be unbalanced. If you want to get to the first ending, the game is fine, but if you want to get to the hardmode second ending, the game restricts your choices to where you can only go a certain route, making the playthroughs boring. Only a handful of earth's gamers have had enough patience to beat the third ending, that being the Cosmic Ocean. I recommend Spelunky 2 to any players who play the game to see how far they can get over players who play the game to get the farthest. In my book, though, this game is one of the most entertaining action roguelites to date. Even after 92.2 hours I'm still making stories to tell to my grandchildren! 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Spelunky 2

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously if you liked Spelunky 1, you're going to like this just as much. Basically the same thing, but way more fleshed out and a lot of fun.For someone who didn't play the first game, this is also still good. Just very hard, but there's something addicting about giving it one more shot, because maybe this time you'll be able to steal the shotgun without getting your ♥♥♥♥ pushed in, and with the shotgun you're basically invincible. If you like a fair but difficult challenge, this is a must buy.If you like platformers or rogue-likes, this is a must buy. If you like 10/10 games, this is a must buy.
