It's a fun automation game and you can just leave the game running to collect resources once you have robots. There's always more to do!
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: The devs summarized the game pretty well on the store page, so I recommend reading that.You manage a factory that you build up by yourself, the emphasis is on automatization rather than manual labor like in other gathery-crafty games, although you have to do some of it at the beginning. The options for buildings and technologies are pretty deep as they are. It is pretty fun and challenging to optimize and to keep your factory running. Expanding a production lines, merging them with new ones, building train lines to supply your factories with basic resources and keeping the technologies rolling gets difficult to handle.On top of the whole factory thing there’s a nice mechanic, where the alien native lifeforms get angry if you pollute too much. Meaning they'll get harder to kill and be more aggressive as you continually pollute, so you have to defend yourself and your base while you work your way to build yourself off the planet.I played around 50 to 60 hours with the game in a short amount of time a couple of months back and stopped playing entirely after I researched/built everything I could. Like other crafty-buildy games the end goal is pretty weak, you have to make a building and fill it with lots of resources and you'll get a message that you've won. The game was very fun at first for me, but there isn’t much else if you get bored from the basic concept (although I guess I got burnt out from playing it too much, which speaks about how good this game is). There's more content in the scenario pack to challenge yourself, the game has plenty options to set up a newly generated world and there’s good mod support too, so there are things to try out.The devs updated the game steadily in the past and I didn’t have a single technical problem with the game yet. I played a bit of the multiplayer too a couple of months ago, it worked okay then and based on the blog post I read, they improved it a lot since.The game has a nicely detailed and animated isometric look to it too, kind of like in Cossacks or Commandos, which I like very much. The UI is barebones, but it gets the job done. The controls of handling the inventory and the items work nicely too, it’s well thought out and the different actions can be rebinded.There’s a demo on , which I assume is outdated, but it’s free if you want to try out how the game plays.P.S. to the devs: MUH TRANSPORT BELT REPAIR MAN SCENARIO PACK!
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: This is not related to what the game itself is worth, on its own it is a pretty good and polished game. The issue is the attitude of the developer, who has said multiple times the price was final, has done some moral grandstanding about why they won’t do sales only to go and do the opposite. Here are some examples:Inflation is something "unforeseen"?Why are sales not worth it in the long run, besides greed, is anyone's guess. Apparently they are under financial pressure now. Notice how both times they have increased the price, the narrative is almost the same: “buy it now, or it’ll be more expensive later!”. So they won’t do sales, but reverse sales are all right. Ok.The game hasn’t got any big new content since before the final release. Mainly bug fixes and very minor changes, but you don’t need a big dev team to do that. The game is very polished anyway, so I doubt it requires a lot of attention in that sense. They are developing an expansion, yes, but it won’t be free and apparently it’ll be priced close to the full game. If they are in need of cash, releasing small DLC would be something your established player base would support. Instead, increasing the base price of the game and going against what you’ve said is just a PR disaster.Many other developers are still updating decade-old games without increasing the price and most of the times said games currently are at a way cheaper than release. Wube Software apparently has special needs.Games work like movies, there’s an initial inversion and developing cost and once they release, studios break even or even get pure benefits. I’m sure Factorio has more than broken even since it was released. Studios then move on and work on new projects. Inflation is just a poor excuse for greed. Congratulations, I won't be buying the expansion. Hope it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to say anything that hasn't been said by everyone else, but this scratches the OCD organised optimisation itch like pretty much no other game out there. If you like the idea of starting with nothing and ending up with a sprawling automated system of finely tuned production where everything is about finding that next bottleneck, fixing it, and then working on the next level of complexity, just to rip out half of what you've done when you find a different way of doing it that would be about 20% more efficient, this is the game to play.Sure, there's monsters you shoot, and with the recent updates you can turn them from being "minor inconvenience" to "pain to stay alive", but the game shines in the way the complexity is steadily added from simply "mine stuff and turn it into other stuff having transported it on conveyor belts" to managing liquid production, using wires that turn stuff on and off with logical conditional statements, making new bases and building an automated rail network to send large quantities of stuff over large distances, then robots capable of carrying stuff through the air, then ... etc etc, every time you get a bit further you get faced with new opportunities, new problems, and new complexities to incorporate into whatever spaghetti network you've alread got.It genuinely takes a long time to get through a game to completion, and even when you feel like you've basically seen it all some of the mods add huge amounts of additional layers and tiers of complexity (such as the Bob's mods collection).SummaryIt's like a dynamic and evolving randomly generated puzzle game mixed with a colony builder, where a single playthrough can genuinely take tens of hours (the higher level achievement for speed play is to complete within 8 hours of game time, which gives you some idea of how much there is to do). Replayability is mixed (lots of settings you can change, map is randomly generated, but essentially you'll still be doing the same thing), but I've come back to it time and time again to try doing things differently or have more aliens attacking me or less resources to work with and so on.Very highly recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.  You can really make stuff happen in it, by putting together factories that build equipment to put together further factories.  It runs well on my slow computer; I've played through twice to the end of the game, which is launching a satellite into orbit, though I haven't really tried to build one of the "mega-bases" I've seen, nor join an online game.  My winning strategy tends to be to save the game, build something, blueprint it, then go back to the save-game file, and use the blue-prints (from the alternate future) to build it in a fraction of the time.  That way I have things built in time before the inevitable bug-attacks.I enjoy using the "combinators" in the game, which is like rudimentary programming language, though I've come to realize that too many such devices will lag the game, and most things that can be done with combinators have other solutions.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10Although it's still in "early access", the game already give full experience better than many other so-called "completed" games.  The only missing part, IMO, is the military aspect, since the enemies (aliens) are quite dumb to invade along the same tracks, and not enough variety, so the offense/defense can get boring after like 200 hrs.This can be, however, be compensated by an important feature of this game: modding.  There are tons of mods available on portal, ranging from quality of life (QoL) mods, minor additions, vanilla-friendly mods, post-game extensions, to complete overhaul mods.  Finding and installing mods is very easy, either in-game or on mod portal.  Build your own mod is also easy.  Actually I have published a tank mod and some auxiliary mods to complete what I feel lacking from the vanilla game.Think you have achieved "everything" in vanilla single player game?  Browse the mod list a bit, I am sure you will find some interesting mods to install.  There are also some active public multiplayer server going on, with other players 24/7.  So it is really quite hard to get bored here.Be warned: this game is a MASSIVE time sink.  I have now played 1160 hrs (OMG!) without even noticing, and it is very likely to grow even more, since I haven't lost any tiny bit of interest yet in the game.  There seems nothing in saving me from the one-more-hour syndrome...One more thing: the game is constantly updated.  Though it is still in "early access", it is way more polished than most other games.

_childDocuments_.review: Review:🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟 10/10 - Would become a sleep-deprived engineer again!Graphics: 🎨🖥️Who needs breathtaking visuals when you can feast your eyes on the most beautiful assembly lines ever created? Forget realistic graphics; Factorio brings you the ultimate pixelated wonderland where factories thrive like neon-lit disco parties. It's like watching a Rube Goldberg machine on steroids. I mean, who doesn't want to stare at conveyor belts all day long, am I right?Gameplay: 🎮💡Factorio is not just a game; it's a crash course in engineering brilliance. From assembling mind-boggling contraptions to optimizing production chains, this game offers a blend of creativity, strategy, and insanity. You'll be hooked from the moment you start your first factory and spiral down into an addiction where time ceases to exist. My sleep schedule is a wreck, but my factory output? You'll find yourself dreaming about ratios, perfect throughput, and the sweet symphony of machinery.Difficulty: 🚧🤯Factorio doesn't hold your hand; it straps a rocket to it and launches you into an engineering obstacle course. _childDocuments_.review: The best indie game I've ever played. I only wish there was more content for me to explore, which I hope is coming soon with new expansion. Firstly, this game is so smooth to play, which allows you to be sucked in so easily. You know that annoying UI thing or road placement thing from City skylines or other management games that just doesn't allow you to place the road just how you like it, or just doesn't work the way you think it would for some reason? There is nothing like that in factorio. Especially when you learn all the hotkeys, playing this game is so smooth that it never breaks your focus. The progression of this game is great as well. Up until the late game, almost every technology you unlock is necessary for progressing in some way, and because of this the progression feels so natural. "Oh I need blue science, so I need to process oil to make plastics, circuits, and sulfer [all of which you need for other things as well, but the new science pack gives you the nudge to automate these things], so I need oil processing, fluid handling, maybe some dedicated trains since crude oil seems to spawn super far away on every map I play", then you keep going from there, snowballing into a bigger and hopefully more efficient factory. I would say that this game is targeted toward a specific audience, but if you like automation and management games, I can't reccomend this game enough. It is by far my favorite in the genre. My main criticism as I mentioned earlier is that I wish there was more content. There isn't much to do after launching your first rocket other then try to build a megabase, but that's a self derrived sand-boxy type goal rather than a design driven one I think. However, although the game is basically the same play-through to playthrough, I can't seem to get enough and I find myself replaying the game even though from the outside looking in it doesn't feel like there is a lot of replay-ability. I guess the replay-ability is similar to like mine-craft or something. "Oh I should try to build a megabase", or "I want to experiment with beacons and modules more this time", and I'm sure there are mods that add a lot of content as well. Highly reccomended. It's 100% worth the $30.00, and it's never going on sale. Try the demo, and buy the game, it's great.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is A M A Z I N G. Everything you do is satysfying and meaningful, almost every thing you automate pays off in the long run, and the devs are probably, the best of the best in the gaming industry. The game gets minor releases every week or two on average, devs actually listen to the community (when an issue gets reported it's usually fixed in the next two days), and IMO every update made to the game was good. There's also a very easy way to play in multiplayer (you can set host and join public servers) which can be fun.One piece of advice I can give you is: don't spoil the game for yourselves, but don't feel bad for looking stuff up online. Oh, and did I mention... THERE ARE OVER 5000 MODS ON THE MOD PORTAL WITH OFFICIAL SUPPORT YOU CAN PLAY THIS GAME FOR 10000 HOURS AND NOT RUN OUT OF CONTENT

_childDocuments_.review: I'm usually not a fan of 2D games, but I am so glad I gave Factorio a try! One of my favorite games now. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game that evolves in complexity more and more as you grow your base and production. Things that you would have trouble with in the beginning become more and more trivial as you progress through the technologies, but the game also rewards you for keeping the basics solid. It's rewarding to be able to go back through what you've done, upgrading and expanding as you find new problems in the flow of your machine, while presenting a challenge of keeping your pollution levels low enough that the hives evolution doesn't outpace your ability to defend the base you've worked so hard on.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Anno 2070 for a long time because I like the logistics element and the depth of the crafting trees. I've also played Rim World and Banished because I like the survival and automation element that comes with a well run and well equipped colony. Then I encountered Factorio. Never for the other games have I found myself out and about and suddenly been possessed by the need to write down and prioritize a list of all the things I can do to improve what I build in game. This happened with Factorio. As mentioned elsewhere, play at your own risk. The game may consume you.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my all time favourite games, it speaks to me on every single level (no pun intended): setting, style, graphics, music...and the gameplay...oh the gameplay.  I have played this for so many hours, all night sessions, weekend binges...and all before it even came to Steam.  I feel a deep connection to the developers as they quite literally took my soul, interrogated it, and made a game out of the responses.  I can't recommend it to everyone as it won't be to everyone's taste, but if you like building, design, processes, logic, tanks, strategy, process improvements (yes, I really meant that), and anything that requires using your brain, then you will love this.  You may love it even if you don't like those things... Maybe you should try it?  Of course you should!!  If you need any tips, be sure to check out YouTubers quill18, Arumba, Aavak, or MangledPork.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: This DLC is amazing, but not for the feint of heart. It was rather challenging, even for an experienced Factorio player like me. I pity the new players who will choose Gleba as their first planet. That said, it was absolutely great! Each planet offers a very different and new experience, and there are tons of design challenges. _childDocuments_.review: Really fun, some players stop playing not long after the introduction of oil and fluids. The oil stage is a step up but if you learn how it all works and how to use trains efficiently the late game is probably one of the best when comparing to other similar factory building games. Unlocking bots really marks a step up in your capabilities and in my opinion it is the real start of the game. If you're looking for a good late game oriented facotory game this is a good one. The introduction of biters and enemies that actually attack your base might turn some people off but for me it gives the game just a little bit more purpouse. If you dont like them you can always just turn it off in the settings.The game is not for everyone but if you've enjoyed other similar games you really should try this one. Great game, 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you seen all those praising reviews? Did you wonder how a game that looks so strange at first view could achieve something like this?The reasons therefor are multifarious.Factorio itself is a masterpiece and plainly the best in its genre and there is by far no other that could compete.The developers are genius. They deserve a monument for their transparent and responding behavior. Do you remember playing games where the community was toxic a. f...?The majority of people who play Factorio are helpful, friendly and interested in contributing their knowledge to make the game even better. How do I know you ask? I am constantly reading the forum entries on the website and here on steam. Even the controversial topics are exciting to read because of the many people arguing smart and reasonable. I already told you about Factorio being the incumbent in the genre and here is why. The gameplay triggers your brains to a level where it might even hurt a little bit and it has an incredible smooth learning curve. Something I find refreshing along all those mindless games. I have played quite some games in my lifetime but no other kept me engaged and thinking about it while not even playing. tl;drOf course this game isnt for everyone. No game can be that perfect. Factorio is nevertheless one of my favorite games of all time.I truly hope that everyone who is deterred by those first impressions will overcome their aversion and give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: You think it's simple, but then you realise it's been 8 hours and you're still trying to figure out where your supply line is being blocked and how to remedy it while future planning for new designs so you don't have to rebuild everything to be more efficient and you can't stop because your factory is your life
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: It's a wonderful game of managing construction lines and logistics with the backdrop of alien attack swarms.While it is certainly complex, I was pleasantly surprised how much thought was put into making the user interface seamless. I was given tools to manage the ever-growing complexity with neat little animated "tips and tricks".The game also appears to be some type of commentary on environmental issues. Your factory causes increasing amounts of pollution, prompting attacks from "biter" bugs. So you go and wipe out their nests to protect your factory. Definitely feels like being an eco-villain :)
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: The most played game in my library, and its expansion is number 1 on my most wanted list for a good reason.  Factorio is a wonderful game that is easy to learn but hard to master.  At its core it is all about automating previously manual tasks in increasing layers of complexity.  Each new improvement to your factory introduces a series of new problems while solving an old one.  The base vanilla game is nothing short of a masterpiece, and the mod support is absolutely excellent adding near infinite length to this game.  If you like sandbox builder games, this game is for you and will surprise you with its depth and complexity.  There is a certain joy to be had every time you turn on a new segment of factory for the first time and watch as engines of production roar to life.  I have angel's mod saves that exceed 200 hours of play and aren't even close to being done.  If you've played Satisfactory, its very similar to that (except 2d) only much much better.  The trailer is a very good representation of what the game is like.  I'll probably be playing this game until either Steam or I expire (whichever comes first).
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Factorio for two years now and the entire time it has been my favorite game! The simple game mechanics let a player start out with little practice, but it scales up as you become better and even with no mods I am still not bored after around 500 hours of playtime. I would easily pay $45 for Factorio instead of $20 and not have any regrets (apart from losing control of my social life) ;)

_childDocuments_.review: This is the ultimate micro-management, producer-consumer, tech tree, dependency management, automation optimization sim with a great sci-fi flavor. It starts simple and ends up with you in a giant machine of your making, fending off hordes of alien creatures while you tweak your megalithic factory to get you back into space stat. No game has ever had such an exhaustive dependency and resource stack combined in such an additive way before. Better yet, the devs have been pumping out updates for years, continually making the whole experience more fun, with better graphics, improving the tutorials, UIs, scenarios, etc.. Many, this game just keeps on giving!

_childDocuments_.review: For the love of god, don't buy this game; it's not a game, it's a curse.Sure, it starts out innocent.  A couple of transport belts here, a robotic arm there.  Oh, what's that? I can unlock more things to build, you say?  Sure, why not?  All I have to do is connect these miner thingies to a furnace array, then sort the metal output to a couple assembler factories and put the results on a train to go to another assembler factory, where the product will be taxied by drone to my rocket silo so that the resulting white stuff can be transported to my research facility and voila, my automatic missile-shooting train can now shoot 12% farther.Suddenly, it's daylight.  That 12 hours between shifts you were supposed to spend eating and sleeping to keep yourself well nourished was instead used to play this "game".  You reluctantly get in your car and go to work.  Your colleagues say they're gonna hit the bar later and ask you to join.  But alas, you tell them you've got to stay late to finish up this couple of assignments.  In reality, however, there are no more assignments-- no, there is only Factorio.You get home in a fit of panic, desperate for your fix.  It's been invading your brain the whole driver, thinking about how to optimize your main bus split-offs, making deadlock-proof junctions for the copper transport rail system.  You get a text from this girl you started seeing.  Asks if she can come over.  Exasperated, you pause your game, only for a minute, so you can come up with a lie about taking night classes at a community college 5 nights a week for the next two years.  She says it's cool, goes out to a bar alone, where she hooks up with one of your colleagues.Weeks go by.  Months.  You've lost complete track of time.  You've taken off of work for the past three weeks citing some sort of infectious disease.  You can't remember the last time you left the house, even your computer.  But alas, the day has come.  Your steadfast dedication and unwavering determination have finally paid off.  The inhabitant's of this alien world have almost gotten in, almost destroyed all your hard work on so many occasions.  But alas, their efforts were for not as their noble warriors lay by the hundreds, no, the thousands, at the foot of your base-- your megabase.  You have finally done it.  You are now launching 60 rockets every second, science coursing through your veins by the hundreds of thousands.  You control everything.  Not a tree stands on this red planet you can now call yours.  You exit the game, reminiscing over all the good times you had in that base as you watch the replay with teary eyes.  Then, back on the main menu, you slowly move your mouse towards the bottom to exit this "game" and return to the real world.Suddenly, something catches your eye.  That button.  You never really paid attention to it before.  How could you have missed it in your zombie haze?  What's this?  This game... has mods?
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: This game you make factory production chains using logistics networks of various types: trains,loader belts, liquid/gas pipes,barrels & robots. Think of how fun the chains are in games like Anno but without the worry of the needs of npcs, and instead you just satisfy the needs of your manufacturing. The game is relaxing & sports a host of map options you can set to make the maps harder or easier for your game play experience. Factorio looks  complex & it is however after you do the ingame tutorial you will be able to start and learn as you go smoothly. Luckily you do not "Need" to check the wiki for everything, you will likely use it for reference than anything else. It's a great game and next to the Anno series probably my favorite production chain sim.

And I did, for... wow, 35 hours... really?  Whatever, it actually was fun at times.  I loved to see exactly how screwed up I could make something work, especially because my friend is so OCD. _childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a game that I played for a long time now, during different periods of time. I can say, that it is the best automation game that I have ever played. It has this sort of uniqueness to it, with all of its machines, transport features, the added threat of biters and their evolution, and the different weapons that you can use to get rid of them (the late game weapons are satisfying). Also, multiplayer is a thing, which makes it more fun, in my opinion. Who doesn't love accidentally running your friend over with a car!? I won't even get started about all the different mods for this game, which add new weapons, resources, machines, enemies. Some even add new planets! If you are into automating everything, along with base building and fighting mechanics, then this is the game for you! Keep going, Factorio team!

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a wonderful game, it's all about being lazy, really. You spend 8 hours in early game, handcrafting a bunch of ♥♥♥♥, just so you can build a mall to get the very same ♥♥♥♥ without being handcrafted. After that, you can start developing even more research and progress towards the ultimate goal of the game: to build a rocket so you can fly off the planet, and in my imagination, crash on another planet because one of your robots ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up your first rocket so now you have to start over. _childDocuments_.review: Factorio: The game where you industrialize an entire planet, only to be greeted by the furious locals as you siphon away every last natural resource. It’s like SimCity but with more pollution and giant alien bugs actively trying to murder you for your environmental crimes.Side effects of playing Factorio may include:Losing all concept of time: You’ll sit down at 6 PM for a "quick" session, only to realize it’s somehow 7 PM... the next day.Developing a compulsive need to optimize everything: Whether it’s your factory layout, your fridge, or the flow of traffic in your neighborhood, nothing will ever be efficient enough again.Divorce: Because let’s face it, your spouse is going to want custody of the kids when they realize you love conveyor belts more than family dinners.Your spouse taking your kids: Mostly because you used them as part of your blueprint for a more efficient production line.10/10, would lose everything for the perfect factory again.

_childDocuments_.review: Well worth the $20, one of the more stimulating and fun games I've played in a long time. Do you like city builders? Railroad simulation? One can play it messy and inefficient and still enjoy it, or can get hyper critical and detailed with efficiency spending long chunks of time on a simple problem yet compelling problem. One can become obsessed with the defense systems to deal with the Zurg and their constant encroaching and attempted destruction of the primary factories. But it's also really relaxing too, no commitment with a game that pauses when you log out, you can turn off the enemy attacks, or play the multiplayer (which they fixed and is much much more stable and fun), and feel like you're missing out on building with friends. This game likely won’t appeal to everyone: but anyone I know that loved Minecraft and simulation games, even the space strategy lover and you know they will like the game. I’ve even turned a 50+ year old guy onto it 8 months ago and he hasn't stopped playing since

_childDocuments_.review: I think the fascination with this game comes from the many levels of challenges. On the surface it looks like it's about building, managing logistics, automating. But you quickly need to start automating the building, then further in you might need to start streamlining that automation. To build a megabase you are automating the automation of automating. Each of these levels turns into a new game, requiring planning, new strategies, new ways of thinking. You constantly discover new bottlenecks, new problems that need to be solved.The other fascinating part is the simulation, seeing that your PC is capable of updating millions of items sixty times per second. Each of those million items have a unique ID, age, health, and lots of other attributes that the game keeps track of. I often just sit and watch it run.Wube deserves a word for the implementation as well. Factorio runs on MacOS, linux and on that third OS (can't remember now, but apparently very popular despite its flaws). Either way, the game runs perfectly on the three major platforms, no workarounds are needed, users can exchange save files and blueprints, and play online with users on other OSes.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily as addictive as Civ 5. So this basically requires my refinery operations to be exactly aligned to a body of water if I need to transport water. It is however rewarding to figure out an efficient configuration for liquids-You guys should fully flesh out the campaign. I really enjoyed it and I feel like it wouldn't be difficulllt to make perhaps 8-10 more missions that walk players through the tech tree and different scenarios. Another improvement would be to add some touches to the existing campaign such as actually being able to drive down the coordinates you found in mission 2, or actually flying the airplane in mission 4.-I read your website for possible changes in the future. A cool idea might be having corporations that manufacture industrial or consumer products that are sold to markets. It could be competitive in that there might be other player/AI corporations competing with you for a short period of time, so this really necessitates maximising efficiency (just like in manufacturing IRL) whereas in the normal mode sometimes there's a lack of pressure. Factorio is, in essence, a puzzle game that adds more and more layers of complexity the more you play it. Currently, I haven't finished the game. What usually happens is that I finally reach a point where I have a lot of science going, I have things being made, and a massive swarm of monsters swoops in from a new angle where I haven't put my guns yet.If you want a game that will keep you thinking and will force you to find, if not the best option, something close to it, Factorio is for you.If you want to blow up aliens with rockets, Factorio is for you.If you want to build a massive rocket via a complex supply chain of belts, robots, assembly machines, miner drills, furnaces, trains, and more, Factorio is 100% the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio gives you a pretty straightforward challenge: build a rocket and escape the planet you are stranded on.  A rocket is pretty complicated though, and there are a lot of steps to automate to produce everything you need in massive amounts. The game is, in essence, a huge series of little puzzles that all fit together. You'll need to come up with your own solutions for raw material extraction/transportation, refinement (this includes smelting and oil refining), production lines, delivering materials to said production lines, researching, and electricity production, among many others. The game gives you the tools to figure these out for yourself, and there is no one correct answer. For every little problem you find you can be creative and come up with a cool solution, not something that's been done before. And there's nothing quite like zooming out, looking at your whole factory, and knowing that everything in it is uniquely yours.Since Factorio is primarily about automation, it respects your time like few other games do. The blueprint system means that you never have to build the same thing twice, just order your construction robots to do it for you. If you really want, you can use other people's blueprints, but I find that defeats the fun of the game.It's such an engaging game for me, because there's so much stuff to do to make my factory better. Some of the little puzzles that I've solved lately include how to best place railway signals on the huge intersection outside of my base that handles all of my trains, bringing in raw materials from all across the map, optimising electronic circuit production within the small space that I left myself, and designing an innovative way of delivering the 7 different science packs to my labs on only one conveyor belt.And once you finish one thing, you'll find another part of the factory that needs to be built, or optimised. There's always stuff the be improved. The factory must grow!

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio may well be one of the most successful of the videogame Early Access games that I've ever been involved in. While there are some very good games up there with it (RimWorld comes to mind), the creators of Factorio have consistently been producing and pushing new content, new underlying engine improvements, and new discussions about the game on an extremely regular basis for quite a while.The game itself has a familiar premise: you are alone on a dangerous planet with nothing but the basics of engineering, the will to extract resources, and a near endless supply of aliens. Do something cool. However, instead of the (now) traditional first-person shooter interface where you run around and punch trees, you have a top down, third-person interface where first you punch trees (and rocks, and iron outcroppings) before getting to the real meat of the game – building machines to punch the ground and get resources out of it for you. And then connecting those machines up to produce the more complex pieces of equipment that you need at every stage in order to build the tools, to build the tools, to build the tools, to let you build the tools, which will let you launch your first satellite and essentially "win the game."That sounds ridiculously tedious. In actual practice, it's a complicated dance of managing and increasingly complex factory system and getting the parts that you need to the places you need them at the right time involving a spider web of moving conveyor belts, robotic arms, fluid pipes, and trains which move from station to station schedule that you set.Factorio is not a game that you sit down and play for a half-hour. Oh, you can intend to sit down and play it for a half-hour. You can intend that every time you pick it up. What you'll end up doing is sitting down and playing it for a couple of hours then looking around in puzzlement as you try to figure out where your day has disappeared. Or why it's time for you to wake up and go to work.There is a bit of shooting and killing in this game as wave after wave of hungry, pollution-annoyed alien monsters which steadily gain in power and resilience decide that your facilities are really the thorn in their side. (Haven't they heard that they should unquestionably take migrants in and offer up everything they have?) You'll see to their needs by placing project outer it's, laser turrets, giant flame-gouting, oil shooting turrets, and packing your own destructive hardware in your upgraded power suit while riding in your freshly constructed tank.Sometimes you just have to pacify the natives. You know how it goes.Do you like understanding and implementing complex plans? Do you like looking at a well oiled factory moving things efficiently from one side to the other and producing all the products you need to continue to survive in harsh, alien world? Do you like murdering aliens?Factorio might be for you.

The development team has made an incredible experience with Factorio. The basis of the game is you start on alien planet and have to work through technology from simple pickax to full automation of the factory. The enemy in the game are little insect critters who do not take kindly to the players pollution. Factorio also features a peaceful mode where the aliens do not trouble a person if you prefer to just build your factory without the threat of alien attack. Although i suppose technically the player is the alien and the bugs are just home. THE FACTORY STILL MUST GROW! The vanilla factor will grow into space with the coming DLC update. Coming to an update in the future, space is not going to just be the final frontier.  Still an enjoyable time sink now that the DLC has released and the game has updated to 2.0.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for this game around three years before I bought it and I don't complain. The game becomes really addicting the more you play it that it doesn't seem long, but you've already spent 6 hours straight. Don't have yet that much on record, but this game has singleplayer, multiplayer, servers and many mods to try. Also, making own mods is simple for this game, just need to learn some Lua and Factorio itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: This game can seem a bit intimidating, but if you can get past that and have a little patience at the start, this game is truly captivating. Many hours of my life have disappeared as I tinkered with little aspects of my factory or thought out the best way to create my next big expansion. I have played through to the rocket launch (the default victory condition) a few times at this point, and I still feel the itch to start again so I can utilize new mechanics or just optimize my setup further.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Tekkit and SimCity mixed together in all the right ways. Basically, you achieve everything through the process of automation to create everything from basic resources to spaceships. And I guess you need to defend your base too, but all I did was make a tank and commit mass vehicular manslaughter. As far as variety, I can't say I'm impressed. It just feels like there should be a lot more. But this is very early access, so who knows what will be in future updates?Most of this game works around tedious processes and a lot of building. If you don't like those games that mostly feel like a chore, I cannot recommend this to you. This game requires patience and effort.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: After about 2000 hours played including my hours without internet connection I think its fair to say i'm addicted and trash at making logical factories that work but if it works it works you knowI really do recommend this game if you want to spend some time figuring out how to logically do something and then later on realise you need to change everything again as you forgot to future proof
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: There are few games that i find myself coming back to after years of not playing. This is one of those games. When I first found out about this game, it didn't look like a game I would find entertaining. I believe a friend gifted it to me and we played a few hours of the sandbox mode. I couldn't really get into it so it sat in my library for a few months. One day I was skimming for something to play and decided to give it another try. Decided to play the tutorial and for some reason it hooked me.Seriously, give this game a try. _childDocuments_.review: Factorio  Early Access  Wube Software LTD.  Wube Software LTD.  Niche Strategy  25th of February, 2016  Singleplayer & MultiplayerFactorio takes the cake and eats it single-handedly in front of you. Then orders you cook up a fresh batch since he’s always hungry for more. Playing this game, you’ll be able to summarize it almost like a love-hate relationship. Stressful at times, but too good to pass up or abandon. Wube Software managed nearly the impossible on Steam. (Re)Invent a subgenre I thought was long since been declared dead and buried. The kind of strategy game that features just the right amount of base management and resource gathering, without being tagged as “real time strategy”. Not by its classical definition, at least. You don’t control an army per se, even if you shall be forced to fight for your life and in defense of the machines you shall construct. Think Industrial Giant 2 except you’re not running a business, instead focusing on escaping a strange planet.Who said a game about in-depth industrial processes can’t be fun? Our story begins with the lone survivor of a crash landed spacecraft. The silent type of astronaut/engineer/MacGyver that shares some of these traits with every gamer’s favorite space engineer, Isaac Clarke. But I’ll just call him “Bob”. So what does out good pal, Bob, do once he finds himself within an inhospitable, foreign and far away place? Does he phone Home, fail and then crawl into a corner and weep at his sorry fate? Nope, he industrializes the living hell out of his foster planet, in the noble pursuit of building a new spacecraft capable of facilitating his escape. As you can imagine, the local wildlife ain’t too happy to concede defeat and allow our resourceful spaceman to revive and actually bring about what shall really look like the Third Industrial Revolution in regards to scope and complexity, if not in sheer size.Just take a good look at the game’s screenshots from its Steam Store page. If you’d been an alien lifeform inhabiting that planet, you’d probably try to kill Bob too. But our protagonist is both determined and crazy enough to let no one and nothing stop him from achieving his goal. While focusing on the rocket, he won’t hesitate to build and make good use of anything from drones, tanks, laser turrets and trusty ol’ trains, in his attemps to defend the resource greedy machines while tinkering away at the many crucial components required by a spacecraft.If you think the road ahead is gonna be both long and tough to complete, rest assured I’m here to…confirm your fears. You’ll be facing an uphill battle against increasingly aggressive aliens (which almost resemble the Zerg from Starcraft) and industrial machinery which requires some degree of automatization. You start off barehanded and stranded, but it doesn’t take long before you craft a pickaxe and start mining for the first metal ore pieces, stones and coal to literally fuel your struggle for survival. In-game tips are always present and the tutorial featured in the first few missions is more than welcome. You’ll need all the help you can get and creativity plus intuition will always play crucial roles, as you have to become as efficient as the machines you are creating.On some campaign maps, you’ll find space at a premium but at least you can easily deconstruct structures and assets with the option of repositioning them at will. In more than just one way, your battle to escape can be regarded as a metaphor for humanity’s own struggle to always evolve and adapt. You start off with the help of steam (First Industrial Revolution), then electricity (Second Industrial Revolution) only to move on quickly towards complex circuit boards and the increasingly independent machines that only lack true artificial intelligence, from being self-aware and able to build/maintain themselves without human interference. Are you kickstarting the Third Industrial Revolution or just creating a small scale Skynet? All of this while destroying the planet step by step with the rapid industrialization and its inevitable by-product, which is pollution itself. Congratulations!If all that sounds complicated or simply grim, that’s because it really is so. I glanced over the reviews written by other Factorio players here on Steam and simply looking at their playtime, I realized that I couldn’t reach dozens or hundreds of hours into this game, even in 6 or more months. It is an addictive game, I get it. I simply would lack that kind of patience which I sincerely find noteworthy, in those which possess it. And the title surely isn’t helped by the fact that it looks nearly like the tycoon games from 15 years ago and somehow with even fewer sounds. Before you start throwing rocks at me, understand that I’d never choose quality graphics over quality gameplay but a balance is needed in everything we accomplish. Take into consideration that the game for all its plain looks, still is feature rich, complex beyond its own good and offers a sandbox mode for truly passionate builders to quite literally unleash the mad genius lurking within them. I still find Factorio a bit on the overpriced side, since it’s an Early Access game. But as always, your choice counts in the end. It is humanity’s story in a nutshell. Relentless determination followed by greed and sacrifices in pursuit of bettering ourselves at any and all costs.+ Solid gameplay with in-deph industrialization/automatization.+ Well explained mechanics and natural scale of difficulty & progression.+ Steam Achievements.- Spartan looks.- Limited sound selection.- No Steam Trading Cards.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game even though I  often let it run in the background to produce stuff/finish researches whereas I did other stuff.Pro:+ You can practically automate everything+ Almost all achievements give you reasonable goals which you can achieve relatively easy + Different power sources with different pros and cons+ Different effective ways  to fight against the aliens (nukes, flamethrower, destruction capsule, tanks, power armor)+ Different ways to transport the ressources/products in your factory (belts, logistic robots)+ Different factory designs, for example a factory which only uses belts to transport items or only robots,         Factories which uses as less space as possible with productivity and speed modules but cost a huge amount of         energy or Factories that use a huge amount of space but no modules and far less energy than those with modules.+ You can blueprint your layouts (production of chips, smelting areas) and let construction robots build "new section" of     that layout Cons- Only purpose for the existence of the aliens is to be an obstacle, but they serve no other purpose and are only an    obstacle in the beginning. You can forget the aliens once you can build a good defense (laser turrets, walls,...) -  The game has no real replay factor. You can only win if you build the rocket.              The fight against the aliens and the building of the base becomes quickly repetitive.             The only reason to play the game a second or third ... time is to get all the              achievements or to try different factory designsTherefore I recommend this game to people which like to experiment, to test different layouts, designs.  I would advice people that only play it a single time or are not sure if they like this kind of game to wait for a sale, because you can easily finish the game in 10-15 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best game I have ever played. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. If you enjoyed the old Tycoon games such as Rollercoaster Tycoon 1/2/3, Railroad Tycoon, Transport Tycoon, etc, you'll love Factorio. Factorio is amazingly well balanced, you can get through all the content (and there's a lot of it) without any grinding. It has an great engine that can handle the ginormus factories you'll be building without any slowdown, even in multiplayer.I bought it before it was on steam so my hours played are even greater, and I'm hardly done with the game. The developers are adding all sorts of great stuff to it, but it was worth buying years ago and is even better now.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning! This game can be addicting. You will begin playing and glance at the clock and gasp when you realize 6 hours has gone by. Extremely fun and engaging. There are many great resources for beginners online, but the real fun begins when you figure out how to design your own systems to efficiently automate EVERYTHING.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: Damn this game is like crack!  Still haven't checked out the mods yet, but there are quite a few available now and the latest version of the game added some great new features!  Lots of fun stuff to play with.  Just gotta watch the clock or I end up spending all day playing and forget to eat!Update:  Mods are awesome, but not as awesome as this game's developers!  Years later and they are still adding updates to make the game more awesome.  Definitely one of my classic favorites from now on.Update 2: Another couple of years later and the game has only gotten better... seriously the guys over at WUBE are MVPs for all the hard work they've done on this game. I'm sure I'll keep playing it for years to come! THE FACTORY MUST GROW!Update 3: We have entered the SPACE AGE! I honestly did not expect this expansion to be so... expansive! It's like they added 5 huge mods into the game as official content (not really, but that's how it feels). This update and expansion have added probably hundreds more hours of gameplay to experience, and it really ramped up the complexity and difficulty in reaching the "end" of the game. I haven't got there yet obviously, but I'm well on my way! I probably don't need to say this, but if you've had a fun time with this game before and want to dive back in, be prepared for a looooooong trek. Each new planet presents additional challenges to overcome that require different solutions in order to properly automate. Best of all, if you have a recent save file from before the update, you can still continue it! The devs recommend starting a new game, but the old stuff is still quite compatible with the new changes and content. Once again, mad props to the devs on all their hard work!!

_childDocuments_.review: I still use belts instead of trains for most things.This game is great in that you can roll your own solutions, share them, or find other solutions online. For the most fun though I think it's best to figure out the problems on your own first. Comparing your work to everyone else's ends up being stressful. For hours 350-400 I was doing that and not enjoying the game as much as all the other times.I was still in that phase of discovery and fascination after 100 hours of playtime. I think handling oil was the biggest hurdle in terms of scaling and how to manage things. And once past that, things just suddenly ... took off so to speak. This is a great game of emergent problems that at first you solve by hand, then automate with machines, and then you scale up to mind-bending proportions. It’s super fun and I look forward to the next several hundred hours of play.

_childDocuments_.review: The true genius of this game is that it's actually a masterclass in logistics programming that tricks you into wanting to eradicate aliens for their resources. It's the agony of always being one part short to complete your fancy new subsystem that's connected to a main line of cargo that you've already spent hours carefully connecting only to realize that you could move something just 2 tiles and add one more inserter here or there to improve it by only 0.25%. That's a huge number in the world of this many moving parts and most players of this game would likely agree.The sense of progression is something akin to Civilization where the start of the game provides you with 2 sticks that you can rub together to make your first furnace glow that will have to be powered by fuel you hand gather. By the end you'll be in charge of a giant series of machines that spans across a literally infinite map that just simply wants more and more. Your robot army will help put fuel in your tank so that you can drive to site, destroy all of the aliens around it, design a new system on top of it, add it to a blueprint and plop it down with one mouse click right next to your new train depot that's piping ore into smelters 10 minutes (in train speed) away in the other direction.If you get lost, there's a lot... and I mean a lot of information out there from other players that also realize this game is as much of a theory and programming language as it is a game. I personally think experimenting until everything on fire is the best kind of science so I've spent quite a few hours now just hooking things up to things and trying to figure out exactly just how far I can take the programming circuits. Sure I could have played the game and won several times over, but this very much the hybrid between real-time strategy base building and Transport Tycoon I didn't know I really wanted until I just blew almost a whole week of free time playing it.Of course YOU can play this game exactly how you want, because after all it's multiple games at once. It's a formidble tower defense game and turtling is a viable strategy. You can turn the aliens off and just build a fancy factory that hordes resource, or you can play the game the "right" way and work towards building a rocket to get off of this alien infested rock. A very supportive mod community makes a ton of completely optional enhancements that do very minor things like improve quality of life, or add complete overhauls that seemingly have created expansions for the base game. I just experimented with a mod that overhauled how the game generates resources, which drastically changed my entire strategy. Again, I say option because the base game already offers 100's of hours of enjoyment if you find what it is that I personally enjoy: Destroying an entire planet.. 9.5/10 mechafistsside note: if this were an Early Access alpha standard, I may not regret 97% of the other abandoned trash fires I pointlessly invested in. This game is still heavily supported and maintained each week after FOUR years.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Addicting gameplay that generally provides you clues about what to build next. Nearly endless replayability thanks to a multitude of built in game settings, plus a huge modding community.UI - makes it easy to accomplish everything you need to do, provides good player feedback about current status, easy to read, and modders can hook into the UI to make all sorts of fun changes.Sound/Graphics/Music - all are top notch for this style of game. Rustling leaves of trees, waves of water, chemical plants whiring, biters angrily screeching. Little graphical details brought to life like parts of your base being destroyed are still visible, the glow of your laser turrets at night, and foot prints in the snow and sand. One of the few games I leave the music on because it is unobtrusive and really sets the mood.Devs - receptive to feedback, quick to fix bugs, passionate about the game, respect the gaming communityMods - this is why you play on PC right? for the mods? Unlike most games, the modding portal is built right into the game and the devs go to great length to support mods. They make it easy to add/remove mods and to ensure the right mods load with your save. No dealing with Steam Workshop, Nexus, et al. And the modding community was already huge before 1.0 release. Dont like some aspect of the game or wish something was easier, chances are there is already a mod for that. Try the game first w/o mods, because it is still very complete and bug free. Unlike many other games, there is no need for an "unofficial bugfix" mod with Factorio.Cons:Addicting - like "one more turn" in Civ, only its "I'll just reroute this real quick then goto bed" and next thing you know the sun is rising.Update: If you really liked the base game, the expansion "Space Age" is totally worth. A lot more complex, so if you struggled with plain Factorio, the expansion might be too much.

Amazing how this game just captivates you and doesn't let go.Got it gifted by my best friend and was one of the best gifts I've gotten in a LONG time. I'm usually bored with games after 5 hours but this is just addictive as ♥♥♥♥ !

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the most satisfying game I've ever played to date.  The concept is so simple when you boil it down to the raw mechanics.  Simply move a product to a machine which makes new products.  But in that simplicity it opens up the freedom of exploration and creativity.  You can focus on building things a million different ways.  Constantly tweaking the designs to get a better more efficient system going.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: I heard about it. I bought it. I've done nothing else with my life since.I started a world, it seemed easy so I restarted with twice the enemy settings. It got too spicy, so I left the default settings, it feels just right.My first world I walled in a small base... I could not expand easily. My second world, I walled in a bigger space, it was not enough for increasing hostiles later. I then bought Space Age, I started that new world; With my recent knowledge by trial and error, I walled off every inch of available map I could safely reach right out of the gate, and rushed automated ammo belts with turrets XOXOXOXO style across all walls... I lived comfortably for a while, then it got spicy. I now live comfortably with a solid line of lasers in front of all turrets, rampaging in a tank every time I expand the base approx 200%-400% every expansion. I've left my planet behind and am establishing industry on a volcanic world.... I still have at least 3 more worlds to explore.I've many hours in the game.... So many hours.... Too many hours... Factorio is love, Factorio is life.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games where you can pick up enough of it to have fun fairly quickly, but still be learning finer points after a very long time. _childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is the most addictive game I've played so far. It's very easy to just sit down and delete a whole day without even noticing.+ The process of building your factory is a never-ending positive feedback loop that keeps you constantly enthralled, and watching it all come together never gets old+ There are a ton of different ways to play and restrictions you can place on yourself to keep things interesting + Each world is heavily customizable before you even begin+ The music perfectly fits the lonely, mechanized, world-dominating atmosphere+ There are approximately 0 bugs+ Looking at the map and production graphs is fun on its own+ Highly addictive; if you can get past the negatives, you'll probably never stop playing+ It's the best optimized game in human history/ There is no story- There isn't a concrete goal to work towards after you "beat the game"- Fighting and fending off enemies isn't very interesting, but, in my opinion, it's required to keep the rest of the game from feeling empty- Player movement is very slow and there's a lot of it since the world is huge

_childDocuments_.review: Crash, explore, mine, build, mine, refine, build, build, research, ascend. Command a factory, expand its borders, its resource demands, mine up the entire planet, and when the entire world of crawling bugs comes knocking, defiantly defend your industrial bastion, your ember of engineering, surrounded by a sea of gnashing talons and hungering maws. Do not go down without a fight! Expand your industrial might! Let it be a factory! Let the seas boil, let the stars fall! Though it will take the last drop of my oil, I will see my factory free of bugs once more! And if I cannot save if from angry bugs, then let the planet burn!

_childDocuments_.review: When you see the wall of positive reviews and have discovered that this game is second only to (the equally brilliant) Portal 2 in the all-time-list of top rated steam games, you may wonder if a huge hype is going on, but Factorio really is that great!It is not a game of sophisticated stories, beautiful graphics or impressive action.Instead the setting is simple: You are stranded on an alien planet and your objective is to get a satellite into orbit and call for help while fending off aliens, who are not exactly happy about your not so environmentally friendly activities on their planet.The way to build your satellite is long. You have to mine, craft, and ultimately raise a factory that will produce what you need piece by piece, but things are getting real fun, when you start to automate things and try to draw your picture of the game. More often than not you will build parts of a production chain, see that they don't work as flawless as you have imagened and redesign them again and again until satisfied and it is not unheard of that people who wanted to "just finish something up" in the evening end up still "finishing up things" far into the next morning.Factorio needs a bit of time to get into but if you can muster that patience, you will be rewarded with an almost endless source "automated fun".

_childDocuments_.review: I got the game as a gift and i wanted the game for a while prior to that.Fun, addictive, problem solving (a lot of problem solving) (while keeping the fun), expanding (aka creating problems), improving, battling aliens with explosives and fire, what more do you want? And once you finish it, there's pretty much infinite replayability. Not only is freeplay just as fun the second time, and it's never the same, but if that's not enough, there's countless of great mods to make the experience WAY different. Different early game, different mid game, different late game, and with the correct mods one game can take 1000 hours to complete (from what i've heard) and I'm not exxagerating. Of course making the game take longer isn't the only thing you can do with mods and there's a ton of mods that just add more stuff and make the gameplay different, not harder. And once you're done with those you can move on to the challenging mods, and since a modpack both hard and easy usually contains a couple hundred mods, the replayability skyrockets to even higher than before. And did i mention multiplayer? Solving and building with your friends is fantastic and with mods it's just even better (should i shut up about mods??). There's a lot of fun to be had and worth all the money and time that's spent on it. And FYI there are both tutorials and tips so you won't have to worry about starting it and not knowing what to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is not merely a game; it's an addictive blend of engineering brilliance and strategic depth that hooks you from the moment you start playing. One of Factorio's greatest strengths lies in its gameplay loop, which is both simple to grasp and infinitely complex to master. You start with basic tools and resources, gathering materials to construct machines that automate production processes. The satisfaction of watching your factory hum with efficiency as conveyor belts transport materials and robotic arms assemble products is unparalleled.The game's design encourages creativity and problem-solving. You'll constantly find yourself optimizing layouts, adjusting production ratios, and designing intricate logistics networks to handle your factory's growing demands. The satisfaction of overcoming logistical challenges and achieving peak efficiency is immensely rewarding.Factorio's graphics may not be cutting-edge, but they serve the gameplay perfectly. The top-down view allows for clear oversight of your factory, and the minimalist aesthetic ensures that the focus remains on the gameplay mechanics rather than distractions.Beyond its gameplay, Factorio boasts a supportive community that contributes to its appeal. Mods extend the game's lifespan infinitely, adding new features, challenges, and improvements. The game's developers also provide excellent support and updates, continually refining and enhancing the experience.Factorio is not just a game; it's an education in logistics, problem-solving, and efficiency. It challenges players to think critically, plan meticulously, and adapt continuously. Whether you're a fan of strategy games, simulation, or simply enjoy a good challenge, Factorio is a must-play. It's a testament to how indie games can redefine genres and deliver unforgettable gaming experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: Trust me and over 40,000 other people: Pick this one up. If you are willing to trust the judgement of everyone ever, and you aren't just buying games for the eye candy, just scroll up  and buy this game already. You're still here? Maybe my rundown of the game will convince you: Factorio is a factory building game set in the distant future and on an alien planet. You are stranded alone (or with some other people if you have any friends who aren't afraid to sink hours on end into a game) and must build a rocket to escape, or at least, you USED to do that. Turns out most people, including me, didn't really care to leave the factory behind. Now you "win" by launching a satellite. "Win" in quotes, because you never really win, not when there's so much to optimize and improve.The game features a crafting system that can be fully automated with machines called "Assembling Machines" (we just call them assemblers, buildings that craft things) and a transport system using "Transport Belts" (conveyors), "Inserters" (robot arms that move things within their reach), and "Trains" (Metal wheeled carts on track that... nevermind, that one is pretty straightforward), along with flying robots, naturally. The game features materials like iron, copper, coal, and uranium, as well as fluids like water, oil, sulfuric acid, blah blah blah.The game is not without challenge, if you are up to the task. The game contains alien enemies who, being not very pleased with the pollution you're causing on their otherwise pristine planet, are, how can I put this... unfriendly. This is of course, togglable, and you could play the game without them (although, that wasn't always the case.), although they do provide an interesting dynamic and increase in complexity.The modding scene in the game is fantastic, with nuance created by each mod, although, the game is already nuanced enough I feel.Seriously, this game is beloved by all, what with a 98% positive rating on Steam, it's just an absolute treasure. Trust me and over 30,000 people: Pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is the game that did everything right, this type of game isnt for everyone but if you like the concept of running an interconnected factory it is a must have. It came out in early access with slow but consistent updates, taking gamers feedback and adapting their game. Sometimes they got things wrong but they came back and either updated it or talked us the gamers around to the new way of doing things. This dev cycle meant that when 1.0 hit several years later we had the best factory game of its time.Like all the best games it is easy to pick up and hard to master but what really shines is the customisation of difficulty and complexity. You start off building simple structures and processing ore into plates to build more buildings and with only 4 starting resources to mine its quite straightforward but then with each research you get another new thing to play with until 10 hours in you have a sprawling factory with dozens of different products all being made in different places and you having to figure out how to get your plastic from one side of your factory to the steel on the other side to make low density structures. The game on default settings will take 10-20 hours to play through the first time you manage to win, but why stick to the default setting?When starting a game there is a large amount of customisation for all of the things: * Want a nice casual game? Turn off the enemy invasions, turn up the resources and kick back tinkering with your base in a sandbox with progression. * Want an intense hell where you're up against wave after wave of merciless enemies where sacrificing one part of your factory to save another is a regular occurrence? Lets talk about the "Deathworld" preset* Want to play transport mongrel where a large long range railroad setup is must? "Rail world" has your back.* Think only having a half dozen raw resources and 50 odd things to build is too simple? Angles and Bobs mod packs will increase this (and the complexity and playtime) ten fold.* Want to play a game that will last 200-500 hours for a single run through with hundreds if not thousands of things to make, intense complexity, interconnectivity and a logistical nightmare? Let me introduce you to "Seablock".No matter which settings or extra mods you have running you will always be solving a single question: "Why dont I have enough resources?" but the way you solve it will be different every time and the journey and thought exploration as you progress and solve the same problem in completely different ways in mind expanding.Factorio already has a live and vibrant modding community where there are a number of complete overhauls to add new playstyles, items and technologies or extend gameplay. Some of these are of such high quality you may believe this is how the game was designed to be played and you can easily get a 1000 hours going through all of these without replaying a single game mode, but what about its official development?Factorio's slow but steady production has continued past its 1.0 release and they have recently announced a new DLC that whose content has already had multiple years of development completed in the background. Unlike other games where there is a new DLC every 3 months delivering minor improvements for a similar price to the base game this one looks to be huge, looking to be as big as the base game itself. With its release I have no doubt it will spawn another generation of mods to build upon the new ideas and technology presented within. I look forward to spending 20 hours completing the DLC when its released in a year or so and another 1000 hours playing the various combinations of ideas it instils in the community.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, I can't deny it. This game is a masterpiece.The gameplay loop is perfect. You automate something you need, immediately reap the benefits of automating said thing, then either diagnose and refine what you just did to improve it, or move on to automate the next step. Constructing a new section of your factory then turning it on and watching it work scratches some kind of itch in the brain that makes this game so engaging. And the best part is, there's always some way to improve or alter your design, so you never feel like you will run out of things to do. The game spaces out giving you technologies that radically change how you can build designs, so there's always something to retrofit or some bottleneck to improve. Pair this with probably the most open, humble and competent development team, a unique and clean art-style, and top notch sounds and music, and this game just works so well and feels so good to play.What people say about lying in bed and having your thoughts be consumed by your factory is true. _childDocuments_.review: This game is not for everyone, I'll just put that out there right away.But if you are into creating and managing gigantic factories, creating mind bending contraptions that work for you and automating every last thing in your life, BOY is this a game for you.TL;DR: Great, mature game, lots of content, basically no grind, modding for days, lots of fun with friends, free of any game breaking bugs. Totally recommended.First, lets talk about the GAMEPLAY: Your goal is to launch a rocket to get off the planet and for that you need resources. Like a lot of resources. These can be mined by hand, but this is a game about automation: Get some machines to do it for you! And then some for automated processing. And crafting. And logistics. These technologies can be unlocked through research, also requiring resources. And that's the basic idea of gameplay. If that sounds boring or grindy to you, I can assure you it is not. Since you have machines for automation, your main job is to devise the new contraptions for further automation. There is zero grind.So far so good, but all that machinery and automation creates a lot of pollution (e.g. our current World). Guess who doesn't like that at all: The natives. Introducing Biters, the monsters inhabiting this world that you will have to continuously fend off to continue expanding, with a small variety of weapons, vehicles and turrets.Time wise, if you already know what you are doing, a relaxed playthrough with two people from start to the first rocket will take you around 50h, but, if you are new to this game, you will probably take quite the time learning while figuring stuff out as you go. But if you have launched your first rocket, why stop there? It's a sandbox, time to scale up! Create your own Megabase with performance measured in thousands of science packs per minute! But what if that gets old? Answer:MODDING: This game has a native modding API and builtin mod manager, complete with search, updating and dependency management. The only thing missing is a manager for modpack presets. Since this game has been in development for quite some time now, there is a plethora of mods, ranging from simple QoL to indepth full conversion mods, taking the complexity of Factorio to a whole other level. You are pretty much guaranteed to find a mod of your liking that can further enhance your gameplay.MULTIPLAYER: Everything is more fun with friends, so if you have a buddy, try and get him into the action. Twice the people, twice the productivity, as long as you're not busy shouting at each other about how to properly set up that new structure or how you crashed into a power pole, taking out your entire bases power *again* :P Highly recommended.There is a lot more to tell about this game, but I think the three topics above are the most important ones. One more thing I wanna mention though: The stability of this game is INCREDIBLE, I have not had a single crash or even noticeable bug that I could think of in my entire 280 hours of this game. Also the devs are amazing at listening to their playerbase and maintaining a great relationship. All of this is a rare occurrence these days and deserves a mention here. This is one mature game.CONCLUSION: Great, mature game, lots of content, basically no grind, modding for days, lots of fun with friends, free of any game breaking bugs. Totally recommended.If you made it this far, congratulations and thank you for taking the time to read through this wall of text.The factory must grow.

_childDocuments_.review: While playing Zachtronics games such as Infinifactory feels like implementing an intricate algorithm, playing Factorio feels like system administration.  There are still elements of programming (this also includes micro-management of conveyor belts for e.g. lane balancing), which can be complicated if one wants to, but usually in Factorio I don't spend that much time on such things, nor does the game allow me to (unless I change difficulty settings by e.g. enabling peaceful mode).  There is a significant real-time element in Factorio due to the presence of enemies, so like system administrators, I have to find a balance among solving immediate problems (e.g. the factory breaking somewhere or running low in ammo/inserters), automating things properly, and longer-term planning.  Building a fully automated factory of green science packs can take quite some time for a beginner like myself, but enemies don't wait, so I have to automate things step-by-step, resorting to some hand-crafting at first and manual transportation of intermediate products among chests before I finally find a way to run a belt from the source to destination.  It is stressful having to take care of so many things at the same time, a lot more so for new players unfamiliar with the keyboard shortcuts and peculiarities in how things work; indeed, I stopped playing the game for two years after 3 hours of playtime (and in the third tutorial level) because I found it hard to cope with the stress with the biters attacking from time to time.  However, compared to real-time strategy games, Factorio is still relatively forgiving by default (e.g. chests are cheap and have a large enough capacity to feed early production lines for quite some time), comparable to the tutorial levels of Age of Empires at the easiest difficulty level.  Eventually I find biters manageable again once I give defense (walls and turrets) a higher priority.  It is still troublesome to keep the walls repaired and so many turrets fed with ammo manually (need more iron plate and ammo production capacity before I can afford transporting ammo on long belts), but at least I don't often find walls breached and machines destroyed now.After 20 hours of playtime (6 hours in the 5th level, some earlier levels played 2-3 times) I've now reached the 5th level in the tutorial campaign, with the train running automatically and the old mining/smelting areas started again, just when the local iron mines are running dry.  After spending quite some time cautiously advancing along the rail line near enemy territory, It is very satisfying to finally get these old stuff fixed and see them producing iron plates at a breakneck pace, but my own ad hoc, slow, buggy, incomplete production lines beside them are also lovely, because I built them all by myself in the past few hours.
