_childDocuments_.review: The complaints about this game are valid, and while the game is initially fun for a time it quickly devolves into something more akin to work and spreadsheet maintenance than 'a game you have fun with', the level of complexity and knowledge about the game needed to progress becomes a difficulty scaling on the terms of an actual job..which is sort of the opposite of what a game should be. Let me describe;Initially the game is very entertaining, mine resources, automate production of various units, gain an ever-increasing level of complexity of that automated production and the resource lines responsible for keeping that production going. Matching output of certain materials with their necessary input as ingredients into others is fun, coming up with creative belt placements, loops, and mining distant resources with outposts connected by rail to ship them back to your main factory, all while defending your main factory and those outposts from increasingly agitated hostile native life due to your wanton pollution of their planet is also fun...what isn't fun is that the level of complexity in the game grows to nauseating tedium if you wish to advance your factory past a certain threshold. Are you prepared to watch hours upon hours of youtube tutorials to figure out why your petroleum/oil production has stopped, only to find that fluid backup is why it has stopped (for some reason, why this game mechanic is a thing is beyond me) and then watch more tutorials on how to 'solve' this problem by convoluted means of setting up switch networks among pumps and storage tanks to ensure no backup occurs so that the useful liquids can still flow through to your production network. Why is that a thing that is even necessary as an in-game mechanic? Do not worry, this type of fun doesn't stop there, it only gets MORE fun.Want to use blueprints? Online tutorial, as nothing is described. Use robots for a logistic network? Online tutorial, as nothing is described and no tutorial covers this. The 'absolute basics' tutorials for things like your rail and oil networks are ~45 minutes in length, past just the simple one-way pickup/drop-off rail lines for simple movement of materials from point A to point B. Rail signals? Rail chain signals? More tutorials. Just the rail network.Logistic networks? No idea what those are. More tutorials. More hours on youtube. Passive logistics boxes. Roboports. Arithmetic combinators? No idea what those do, as the game tutorial doesn't describe anything this advanced nor does the tooltip description. Welcome to another 'just the basics' online tutorial of an hour. Does that sound fun? I hope it does, you'll need more online tutorials to teach you about whatever constant combinators are, how to use power switches, how to use a circuit network that you'll need to use in order to prevent that fluid backup from completely stopping that oil production earlier we'd talked about in a convoluted mess of a system when..the game could just not have the mechanic wherein all fluids in a refinery stop production if one of them is at capacity in a storage tank. The game is fun, for a time, but that time long passes with the hours of online tutorials you'll need in order to functionally 'play' the game past a certain level. Factorio is a 'game' inasmuch as adding levels of unnecessary complexity to a system are 'a game'. Purchase this with caution, it's worth some tens of hours of playtime until you hit one of those walls and just decide...nope, I don't want to spend as many hours watching a tutorial on how to build a circuit network into this system of assemblers/pumps/storage tanks/automated anything/functional rail networks in order to build the third type of module/processor/inserter/belt/anything because having three of them with increasing levels of complexity and interdependency is..fun, I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this game since the early beta releases, long before the Steam release, so I've watched this game grow and evolve into the single best damn basebuilding and resource-management games out there on the market. That's a bold claim to make, but the game easily proves itself worthy.On the surface, Factorio doesn't appear all that different from the multitude of crafting and survival games out there. The first thing you do is craft and axe (though this is actually going to be patched out) which doesn't really inspire confidence. But where Factorio suceedes is that it is not a game about crafting: it is a game about automation and production. Everything you do is with the single goal of making your life easier as a player. Tired of mining iron by hand? Set up a production chain. Sick of having to go out and kill enemies yourself? Build some artillery to do the job for you.The challenge of the game isn't grinding for resources, it's figuring out how to implement your goals. Which really what every single management game should make you do, but Factorio is one of the few to actually succeede in this.While the game does have a goal, that's more just to give players roughly something to aim for. And, at game start the end goal is so incredibly distant (you have to build a rocket when all you can do is chop down trees by hand) that it might as well not exist. More often than not you're going to be focusing on other, more short-term goals.If I had one criticism of this game, it's that it's very much "easy to learn, hard to master". It can be very easy to just blindly expand your factory, not paying attention to if you're using space and resources correctly. Unless you're playing on a hard difficulty, the game is pretty forgiving. But, when first playing this game I've found myself in situations where I unlocked a new production chain (such as plastics or robots in the mid-game) and I didn't plan my factory out for future expansion, meaning there's no easy way for me to expand my production. But, this is easily dealt with by planning ahead and playing carefully. So, if you're a fan of base-building games but are looking for something that will really satisfy your depraved needs for logistical complexity, then Factorio is your game. Don't let the "Early Access" tag scare you off, this game has far more polish and depth than a good number of "finished" games.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a factory-building game.  You are on an alien planet.  Your goals are: secure resources, clear nests of indigenous creatures, build a factory that produces the materials you need, build a rocket, and launch a satellite into orbit.  You can build mining drills, assembly machines, transport belts, power plants, chemical processors, trains, flying robots, and plenty more.  The only limit is your ability to organize such a large factory (and your CPU's ability to simulate it, but there is a continuing effort to optimize the game engine).Not enough?  Try some of the dozens of great mods that have been created by the community, from whole-game overhauls to minor tweaks to the UI, and many that add a single feature, like my personal favorite: the Orbital Ion Cannon.Downsides:  The game is not yet complete, and there isn't a satisfying end-game (you just launch the rocket and you win).  Also not complete is the multiplayer hub and an official mod website.  You can still install mods and play multiplayer, it's just more manual to set up.Did I mention trains? They're awesome, for expanding your reach to more remote resources, or organizing your factory in modules, also for getting around a large base in a hurry.

_childDocuments_.review: This scratches a similar itch as Rimworld does for me, but they are very different games and both are very fun.  Implementation of new techs and features as you move forward are like miniature puzzles to figure out, as is fitting it all together to make bigger and better things.  I always lose track of time while playing this and it's very addictive.  Multiplayer works remarkably well for building together, and you can add people to your multiplayer games at any point or play with less if you so desire.  Overall challenging, but manageable with decent tutorials to get you started (train tutorials need work IMO...but there's a youtube and Wiki which are much better).  Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is an exceptional game that stands as a shining example of the excellence that indie game development can achieve. From its humble beginnings, Factorio has grown into a masterpiece that has captivated players worldwide. There are several reasons why I wholeheartedly recommend Factorio:Addictive Gameplay: Factorio's gameplay is incredibly addictive. The core loop of resource gathering, automation, and optimization is executed flawlessly. The constant drive to improve your factory and make it more efficient is both satisfying and compelling.Deep Complexity: Underneath its seemingly simple premise lies a staggering depth of complexity. The game offers an intricate web of logistics, automation, and production chains that can challenge even the most seasoned players. The joy of solving complex logistical puzzles is a unique aspect of Factorio's appeal.Endless Replayability: With a vast tech tree and countless ways to optimize your factory, Factorio offers virtually endless replayability. Each playthrough can be drastically different, and the modding community has expanded upon this by providing even more content and challenges.Collaborative and Competitive Play: Factorio supports both cooperative and competitive multiplayer modes, making it a versatile experience. Playing with friends to design and optimize factories or competing against others in PvP scenarios adds layers of enjoyment to the game.Community and Modding Support: The Factorio community is one of the most passionate and supportive out there. The developers have also embraced modding, making it easy for players to customize their experience. This extends the game's longevity even further.Polished Graphics and Sound: While the game's primary focus is on gameplay, Factorio doesn't skimp on the presentation. The graphics are clean and functional, and the music and sound effects contribute to the immersive experience.Active Development: The developers have demonstrated a commitment to the game's ongoing development, with frequent updates and improvements. This dedication to refining the game ensures that it continues to age like fine wine.Educational Value: Factorio also has educational potential, teaching players about complex systems, problem-solving, and logistical thinking. It can be a fantastic tool for those interested in engineering and automation concepts.In conclusion, Factorio is a true gem in the world of gaming. Its addictive gameplay, depth, and replayability make it a must-play for anyone who enjoys strategy, automation, or puzzle-solving games. The combination of a dedicated community and developer support ensures that Factorio will continue to be a beloved title for years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is the king of factory games.  Simple on the surface, but incredibly complex as you get deeper into it.  No wrong way to play, you can focus on building the most organized efficient system, or go crazy on a death world fighting with biters and try to survive.  Now with the Space Age DLC, even more complexity spanning multiple planets.  That's right, the base game that many have spent hundreds of hours on is just the beginning to an increasingly intricate web of logistic challenges that you can approach in a billion ways.  Which planet should you travel to next?  How will you get back?  Should you even go back?  To say much more would spoil some of the game's interesting design, so I'll leave it at this:  If you know you know, give the demo a shot and see if you can stay away from it. I'm at 935 hours so far, and just scratching the surface of Space Age.  I dream in belts and splitters.  I hear the sounds of logistic robots in everyday life when there is a noisy environment.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels a bit weird to be unrecomm... disrecommendin... not-recommending? Yeah, let's go with that. It feels a bit weird to not be recommending this game because there's really not much I can complain about that isn't really kinda the whole point of the game.Some people have described it as "Programming: The Game", but I think that misses the mark completely. If I had to give it a similar name, I might choose: "Complexity-fetishism: The Game". This seems to me to be very much a game for the kind of person who, given the choice, would use kubernetes and 5 tiers of microservices to make a calculator. If that sounds like you, then you will almost certainly enjoy this game enough to never see your friends and family again because it has been fine-tuned for your particular mental illness.For me however, the ceaseless exercise in rearranging tangled masses of conveyors, wires, pipes in order to automate the process of building machines with ludicrously deep critical-paths so that you can use <1% of them to improve the automation process and feed the other 99+% into a blender to be turned into science-goo you can use to climb an absurd tech tree... well, it doesn't appeal to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is amazingly fun (in a way it reminds me of Spacechem). No you'll going to have to work for it and create an automated (mini)factory to get (and keep) it running.Harvesting resources, processing, assembling, making ammo, transporting the parts to their destiny, everything requires you to create a self functional automated system that only requires fuel to keep it running.It's like an advanced mechanical version of Lego, I'll be enjoying this game for many more hours. Very recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: So I went into this game very excited for a survival-esque game where you crash land on a planet and using science and machines, eventually build a rocket and escape back to space. So I began the very addicting process of mining, building, automating, and repeating. I spent many hours learning of locomotives and how to make the signals speak to each other to make a smooth system. I researched faster speeds at which to automate and move resources more efficiently. And most important of all, I researched increasingly deadly weaponry to fight back against the alien scum. Man those bugs are annoying. The fight to survive went on, sometimes desperate, but I always managed to pull through. The factory grew larger, I expanded for more resources, and the planet got sickly. My factory went nuclear and the rocket began to be built. Soon I would be able to leave this little planet and it's residents. Then the aliens attacked and destroyed part of the factory. Enough was enough. I took my tank and decimated the vermin. And out of spite I took my flamethrower and burned all the forests I could find. I pumped as much pollution I could into the water and air. (Imagine that song "How bad can I be" from The Lorax). It was at this time the rocket finished. After many hours, I was about to escape from this planet on the rocket and win the game. Preparations complete, I began the launch sequence. As the rockets fired up its boosters, I contemplated as the trees burned in the distance the sacrifice, dedication, and risk it had taken to get to this moment. I was victorious, I thought as I watched the rocket I would escape on launch into space...Turns out you don't actually leave on the rocket, it's just another way to get a lot of science for your research. I'm sure there is a lesson to be learned here as the planet burned around me... but who cares, the factory must continue to grow.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: In one word: addictive! One minute you're using your pickaxe to mine a few resources that'll help you get started. A few hours later you're automating your entire factory from resource gathering to building materials. There's a learning curve, mostly because of the expansive tech- and research tree. At the same time, the well thought out options and gameplay mechanics make it simple to explore new building patterns, features and tech. The Factorio team push out frequent updates, which fine-tune the game balance or just add new, fancier graphics. Haven't experienced any bugs so far, so Q&A is top notch too. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game; just be aware that it can quickly become a time sink! ;)

And enjoy games that mainly are about logistics.Factorio is basically the defacto factory game and it holds up extremely well even today and while the base game is a blank canvas the modding community is vast. _childDocuments_.review: The game starts with you crash landing on a planet, slowly build up a factory by gaining resources, first by digging them up yourself then eventually making machines to do it for you.  You then build factories to build better and more complicated products until you have basically a self sustaining factory that builds exactly what you need, which is basically parts for a spaceship. There is quite a bit of up front work for hours but eventually you end up with a factory that runs itself.  The spaceship parts keep flowing and the people in space are really happy with your work.After awhile though, you spend less and less time improving the factory until it basically just runs on its own.  Sure, you might stop in once in 2-3 years to add new things like a walking spider robot to ensure that you keep those space people happy.  But after awhile it gets a little stale and you have to promise those space people you’ll make more stuff to send them, but it will take awhile.Then one day you realize that an inflation crisis is affecting the world and its a perfect excuse to charge the space people more money for the same product you’ve been giving them for 3 years straight so you can afford a better cappuccino machine on your yacht.  Who cares that the factory runs itself, hasn’t been affected at all by inflation and you haven’t upgraded it in decades.  You are happy to charge people more for the same space slop you are feeding the space people, even though you promised you would never do it.  Then you pat yourself on the back and go back to oppressing the locals.  That’s basically how the game ends.All in all, the game is fun but for some reason it leaves a bad taste in my mouth every time I log in.I give it 2/10.  A little to close to real life for my taste.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, let me just state this right away:  If you're bothered by the game's price, dont be.  This is more than worth the $30, no question about it.  Frankly, for something this good, I'd have gladly paid double.  Factorio is something very, very special.  Incredible, almost unmatched depth and complexity and an absolutely staggering amount of content await you here.  And fun, lots of fun.The game's trailers do a good job in showing you what it's all about.  Stranded alone on a strange planet, you need to find a way to call for help.  And the only way to do that is to get a satellite into space, via a rocket.  But a rocket isnt something you can just craft.  Nor can you just build it out of blocks like in other games.  Such an incredibly complex thing demands far more than just that.  No, in Factorio, the only way to reach your goal is to design an entire factory to produce all the things you need.  A really HUGE factory.You start off small.  When you begin a new game, it's just you, and the surrounding landscape.  Grab a few resources, and make a pick, Minecraft style.  Gather a bit of iron, coal, copper, and so on.  You'll notice that this is an incredibly slow process.  This, though, is a game about automation, not mining by hand.  Right away, you'll start crafting and placing machines to do the mining for you, and fueling them with coal.  And you'll start to automate further than that.  Why fill each machine with coal by hand, when you can use conveyors to send it to where it needs to go, and "inserters" (robot hands) to grab it and put it in the machines?  This is where the automation begins, and where the game starts to show hints of it's brilliance and potential.  Getting even just this little, simple setup going for the first time feels great, and is the point where many players will suddenly find themselves hooked.From there, the complexity mounts ever further.  You soon have electrical power, and once that happens, the game really gets going.  You'll be setting up entire arrays of mining devices and smelters, with conveyors going all over the place to get things where they need to go.And by "things", I mean ALOT of things.  Something I found surprising was the sheer scale of this game.  Factorio isnt the only game to have you building a factory... heck, even Minecraft does it with mods and such.  But this game has a total focus on it, and factories are about mass production... emphasis on "mass".   At first, 100 iron plates might seem like alot.  But a couple of hours later, and you'll be going "I only have 2000 of these, I'm running out!".   You'll be producing items by the thousands, tens of thousands, whatever.  And chances are it still wont ever truly be enough.  It's extremely daunting when you're first starting out.  There's a sense of "oh wow, this might be too much for me".  But stick with it.  The tutorial is... lacking, to say the least, but I find that the game's overall flow works nicely.  You'll gain new things to make from an utterly monstrous tech tree, and each new thing will build upon concepts you've already learned.  You have alot of opportunity to experiment with each thing and learn what they can really do.And there's so many of them!  Mining devices, smelters, boilers, splitters, a whole array of different types of inserters, trains, and even things like assemblers, which take a crafting recipe, and repeatedly makes that item, provided you give it the components it needs.  Suddenly, instead of just crafting inserters yourself, you've set up an automated process to just make them for you.  You can even have the assemblers make more assemblers!  And with a game of this scale, you'll probably end up doing exactly that.  There are all sorts of things you can build and use, and a million different ways to use them, and this is where the game's challenge shows up.  A factory is a complicated thing.   VERY complicated.  You can see that even in just the trailer.  All sorts of situations will appear to challenge you.  You need some pre-made gears and copper wire going at the same time towards some assemblers, but you've already got lots of other machines around and conveyor belts going all over the place.  How can you fit it in there?  You'll puzzle through stuff like this constantly.  And you'll be constantly looking for ways to improve your factory.  After all, a good factory is efficient, yes?  The best part is, with so many different parts available to you, you have extreme freedom in how you go about things.  You can play the game YOUR way, come up with your own designs and ingenious builds.  And however good they may be (or not so good) there's always room to improve, always chances to try new things.   The depth here is astonishing.  As is the sheer amount of freedom you have.Better yet, everything is "smooth".  The game is freakishly optimized, for one.  But also, it's stuffed full of convenience and anti-frustration features.  For instance, if you want to craft an assembler directly, it needs specific components.  But you dont need to waste time making each individual one.  The game will automatically queue up every little thing it needs, and craft them, and finally put together the assembler.  And your character can still run around and do things while this is being done.  There are MANY things like this in the game, making sure you have a good time instead of an irritating time.And best of all... there are no dull moments.  There is ALWAYS something to do, and all of those things are engaging, interesting, and challenging.  You'll even be going to war against swarms of monsters who arent too happy about you being there.  While the learning curve here is very high, I think it's more than worth it.  You'll find yourself addicted quickly, and having a great time every step of the way.  There's very good reason as to why this game is rated #2 on Steam.  And hey, there's even full mod support!  Customize the game however you like!  A great deal gets even better, yeah?Overall, just incredible.  Absolutely incredible.  It's hard to find anything negative to say about this.  But I could praise it all day.  Easily one of the best games out there right now, and it's only going to get better from here.Just be warned, it'll eat your time.  There's another review somewhere that says something like "I had a family, now I have a factory".  You'll quickly grow to understand what they meant by that.  You've been warned!...Really though, just buy it.  You'll be glad you did.

To get there, you'll need to manage your resources and defend against the ever-growing biter threat. You can also continue the game after launching the rocket and build a sprawling mega factory. The devs are also very pro-modding; factorio provides an in-game mod manager that allows you to install thousands of different mods and modpacks. Some mods provide QOL mechanics, and others are massive overhauls that increase the complexity of the game. Overall, it's a 10/10 in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio has one of the most engaging gameplay loops - building automated factories to achieve your goals (there is an end goal that I have yet to achieve in 70+ hours of play). I'd compare it to a more polished take on one of those Minecraft modpacks with mods like Buildcraft and IndustrialCraft 2 and whatnot, where the loop is basically getting enough resources to automate mundane tasks so you just end up with a ton of materials to mess around and build with.I really dig the gritty sci-fi/steampunk take of its art direction. It's very satisfying to be able to stand in the middle of a whirring mess of robot arms, belts, steam engines, and machines and watch/listen to them work.There's multiple layers of systems to manage, from logistics for crafting/automation, to energy distribution, to train networks, to a heat distribution system for nuclear, to (on vanilla settings) a PVE element that you have to consider so your factory isn't destroyed by alien bugs responding to the pollution you generate. It's very easy to get sidetracked for hours when I log on planning to do one thing and shift gears to address some other issue that catches my attention.My favorite part is how the factory you make can arise organically as you plug machinery and whatnot into each other. While there's plenty of knowledge out there to optimize everything and plan in advance, I'm not in a hurry so it's entertaining to develop strange and wierd solutions without too much consideration for future-proofing a setup.Overall, strongly recommend this game. Plenty of entertainment in just its vanilla form and that doesn't even scratch the surface when it comes to custom scenarios, multiplayer, modding...

_childDocuments_.review: This game has to be one of my top games this year.  Bluntly put, if you like building things this game is for you.You start by having to do everything by hand, crafting and mining much like a standard 2D minecraft style game.  But what really seperates it all is your ability to automate literally everything.  Get machines to mine for you.  Get machines to craft for you.  You can get even lazier though.  Have a drone network deliver you items, because walking is hard work.  Create blueprints and copy paste entire sections of your base, placing things by hand is for chumps.  And in the end you'll end up with a giant industrial masterpiece that no one will be able to decipher, except for you because you build this all from the ground up.  The devs have made it clear that this game will always be $20, no sales, so its never a bad time to pick it up.  However, $20 is nothing compared the number of hours and immense satisfaction I've gotten out of this game (and will continue to).  In addition to the vanilla game, the devs update it constantly with new fixes and updates, and there is a huge amount of extra content in the form of some impressively high quality mods.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: At it's core it's a game about automation.First you mine with your hands. Then you mine with a machine. Then you mine fuel for the machine with another machine and use a machine to transport it to the other machines, which makes mining automated. So now you have an infinite amount of ore, so you make a system of machines to automatically smelt it into the metals you make the machines out of. Might as well make machines manufacture the machine parts while we're here, so it takes less time to make new machines. But now your mining machines are too slow to keep up with how much metal you're using so you make research machines to automatically design faster machines. But now bugs start attacking because you're making too much pollution for them to live peacefully by your side so you make killing machines and machines that make ammunition for those machines.This goes on for a couple hundred or maybe even thousand hours until you either make a machine god you can no longer bargain with or become one.

_childDocuments_.review: There's definitely a steep learning curve, and I've found myself progressing, restarting, progressing a bit more, restarting again, and so on and so forth, but I've enjoyed every second of it. There's a lot going on in this game and all of it is good. This is the truest form of factory construction and management simulation and easily some of the best money I have ever spent. As someone with a degree involving programming this scratches almost all of the itches that programming does; the desire for optimization, problem solving, one thing leading to another, and the feeling that something broken can't be left and must be fixed right now, oh damn I'm low on iron again.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio is a game about crashing on an exotic planet and trying to craft materials for your way back home. Now, this may seem familiar and, fairly so, quite boring, but Factorio puts a nice spin on it: In order to progress, you need to automate pretty much everything. The goal of your entire factory will be to create (4 different kinds of) science packs in order to progress in the tech tree, get new technologies which make your factory significantly more efficient and, eventually, reach the point at which you'll be able to launch rockets into space, in an effort to get back to your home planet.Making science packs requires sophisticated chains of production, the ability to think ahead and a LOT of trial and error. On your journey to be able to unlock all tech, you'll also stumble upon some unfriendly fellas which will, if angered, start attacking your base. The more you anger them, the more pollution of yours reaches their base, the stronger they will get, so it's not a bad idea to prepare for this BEFORE they get too strong, you do this by either destroying their bases, building good enough defenses or simply not producing any pollution and going on greener ways.All in all, Factorio has been in development for over 3 years now, being regularly updated by the developers. Before releasing the Steam version they have been hard at work at polishing and optimizing the game, so you can be pretty sure this won't be like your run-of-the-mill laggy, unfinished and bugged out Early Access game. Regular updates also contribute to the game staying bug-free while still adding content.All in all, this is an inherently great game and I would recommend it to anyone remotely interested into the idea, as long as they're willing to commit a lot of time and effort into learning the game and how to make a working base.

Just don't build conveyor belts. Couldn't recommend this game to people enough. The only person I wouldn't recommend it to is the gamer for which graphics are more important than gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: What can you say about factory games?  Well, how about the fact that most of them really don’t have much to do beyond building your factory.  Enter Factorio.  Initially this game will have you so twisted around that you won’t know which conveyer is going where and why the heck you built it that way.  You’ll be ripping and tearing your factory apart over and over again because you needed to get wire over here, or iron plate over there, and there’s just no way to do it.  Oh, did I forget to mention that you’ll be doing this all inside a self-crafted walled area that you’ll have to continually expand outward because you’re under constant attack?The main story behind Factorio is that you were flying along, minding your own business, when suddenly your ship crashed into the surface of a hostile planet.  A planet covered by creepy and crawly bugs.  Starting out they don’t really mind you being on their planet, as long as you leave them alone.  That said, you gotta get off the planet somehow… And you ARE a blue-collar worker.  So why not build a factory to create a rocket to get yourself back into space?  Seems pretty logical, but there’s one problem.You see, the bugs on the planet like their home just the way it is.  Then here you hop along creating a factory, sending pollution into their atmosphere, ripping down trees.  I mean, any wonder they get pissed off and want you dead?  There has to be some kind of middle ground here… and like the true blue-blooded human you are, it’s GUNS.  Well, walls and guns.  So as you build your factory and piss of the local wildlife it’s important you protect your investment with as many gun turrets and walls as you can.  That said, those guns need ammo right?  So let’s build another factory to produce ammo.  Or wait, how about we build a bunch of factories to produce better ammo!  More pollution, more guns, more ammo… It’s a vicious cycle.  Then again, let’s just build a tank and go take the fight to them.Anyway, Factorio is one of those games that gets complicated pretty quickly, but for us factory builders that’s exactly what we hope for.  Honestly, this is probably one of the best factory building games I’ve found.------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------For more no-nonsense reviews check out my curator page at;

_childDocuments_.review: Do you remember doing math in school? Or maybe you are still in school, doing math. Factorio will remind you that math is super satisfying when it has a purpose, and is a real ♥♥♥♥♥ when you are wrong.This game will have you inadvertently returning to those old notebooks and lesson plans in your brain to solve complex problems that you created yourself. The game has an end target, but you can set that up to autocomplete over a lot of time and never return to it again while recipe timers tick-down, and that exactly not the point of Factorio. It is always about bigger and better systems that you design yourself. The draw and motivation of this game is "the rabbit hole", you'll be consistently working both forwards and backwards. Forwards towards the inevitable goal of the game, to launch a rocket and escape the foreign planet. And backwards, going back and fixing the inefficient design sins you made before, or the holes in your poor boots that the biters have chewed open.Factorio (while having options and mods to affect, dissolve, or modify this) is a game that is simultaneously is a Tower Defense and Factory designer. You defend your machines and systems while they help you progressively work toward the technology and capability to leave the planet and win the game. The core problem is the easiest solutions for Factory-side of the game expose you to harder threats on the Tower-Defense-side of the game. Coal and Oil has a lot of energy stored in it and gives access to things you need for bigger and better machines like acid, lubrication, and plastic. But, it pollutes the air, which draws the native aliens towards you, making their bases grow and evolve, as well as making their attacks more frequent and dangerous. However, this is a necessary evil if you want to gather what is needed to win the game.But miraculously, nothing in the game feels broken or silly. Everything is a trade-off in one way or another, and the game gives you the tools and interfacing to easily detect and fix problems. You want less attacks? Less evolutions? Go solar or nuclear, but that means you are going to have to invest in more intelligent solutions with your designs, and you'll have a more sprawling base to defend.Want to design grand and easy to work with? Making your factory simple to build on? Go ahead, but this means more area to cover with turrets.There are many questions to ask along the way to the end when playing Factorio, all of which feel rewarding and important without having to throw some fatty dialog and narration like a RPG game. It is a game that can easily call for more than one play-through, its achievements requiring feats and its options giving many challenges. Additionally, it is slowly gaining a mod community that already adds to the lifetime of the game.TL;DR:The big question, is it worth $30?No. Not unless this game sounds like something you would very much enjoy. It is a niche title for sure.Can I recommend it?Yes. It is a journey for those that enjoy engineering design and blowing hordes of aliens to the sky. Neither of which is as fulfilling by itself. (Play time by most players is extremely inflated. Factorio is a game that can punish and reward being left running in AFK to function. Your machines keep working, but the enemies keep attacking; a flawless defense will be required.)

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty good.Some people might find it repulsive because of the stress caused by limited ore patches and the constant biters attacks, but I like to think I am more relaxed playing Factorio then one that is designed to be way less stress inducing: Satisfactory. In Factorio the ore patches and biters are not a huge treat except for the early game and you always have a ton of ways to customise both of these at your will.The bigest thing that makes this game so "chill" is that compared to Satisfactory there is no "perfect ratio" you can build at couple of miners and a bit of furnaces without being stress by caculating the exact proportions of items needed.I also think the 2d grid is way better to control my spaget belting and help me find exactly which belt lead to which.All of this not to say that Satisfactory is a bad game far from that, but just to say how much calmer and relaxing this game can compared to my expectations and maybe your's going in.

_childDocuments_.review: Does this game even need more praise? YES! At the point of this writing I have played exactly 333.3 hours and celebrate this fact by posting yet another colourful review. Well, Steam says it was 333 hours but this is questionable since Factorio is known to warp the concept of time. You login after a long day of work, start building and tweaking your factory and when you think it should be about time to go to bed you realize it's already early in the morning. But you don't care because your factory must grow!I am an avid gamer all my life and nothing has excited, stunned and hooked me like this since 2007 when Supreme Commander came out (with the notable exception of Project Zomboid but Factorio has thrice the number of hours meanwhile). It is not just the hyper addictive gameplay which earned the game the nickname of "Cracktorio". There is so much more: The very active modding community (and the game has full support and management tool for mods). The fact that with circuit logic networks you can basically start to program code inside the game.The hundreds of settings + full sandbox mode that allow me to tweak every aspect of the game to my liking even without mods.The way Wube (the company) communicates, supports and works - they are true professionals and do things how they should be done.It has never been on sale and never will be which I also count as a plus. It's fully worth it's price and your money goes to an indipendent developer that deservers to be around for ages, demonstrating you can be successful without malpractice, shady business models etc. It also ensures that a certain type of players I won't describe any further will not join and ruin everything. You know what type of player I am referring to.Finally, once you are hooked, check out Trupen's Factorio videos on YouTube, they are both hilarious and informative at the same time and thus very entertaining.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game for a bit, I started of thinking about refunding it, but I realised I already had spent 30 hours into this game already.And even after I turned off my computer, I was still "playing" this game while I was in bed. I just couldn't sleep, because I was demoralized I couldn't optimize my later-to-be confusing mess this game forces me to create.This seems like the downside of this game, but in reality it's the opposite. Factorio has a nice balance of progression, problem-solving and discovery through the game. It's the most fulfilling and satisfying feeling when your newborn frankenstein of a layout works like a charm. Usually remaking your facilities takes a while, and the progression of the game doesn't help at all at making your brain ache less, but it helps an amazing lot with the production of your factories.My biggest problem with Factorio is that after some time your factories get too messy to reorganize and recreate, and it pushes you into wishing to restart. Once you do get the courage to retry, you'll find out the start of the game is soooo slooow. It took me two years to rest from this game to come back after getting in this situation. There's a certain point of the game that there's too much for me to handle, man.But overall, Factorio is a blast of a game. It's slow to start, but a great rise. It's confusing, but satisfying. You'll make a mess, but you'll optimize everything. You'll have a lot of fun, and your afternoon's gone before you notice.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a builder game, but on a scale not typically seen. You start off small, chopping trees and digging coal out of the dirt by hand. You quickly get set up with a machine to automatically mine, and start smelting some iron. Then you make something that automatically moves the iron to your smelter. Then you research a machine to construct items for you. Then you automatically move your iron, copper, and stone through appropriate smelters, on to assemblers that make more assemblers, smelters, miners, and things that move items around. Then you make trains to supply your smelters from far away. Then you build robots that can simplify your supply chain within your factory by moving items between any two points as needed. Then you build power armor and carry the robots with you. Then you have them build entire solar farms in seconds, from components built automatically in your factories. Eventually you've built enough infrastructure that you're measuring your iron consumption in hundreds or thousands *per second* and start launching rockets into space on a regular basis. About the only thing you can't automate is deciding where/how to expand your base.It's rather telling that it takes literally millions of item crafts to launch your first rocket, but it can be played indefinitely with as few as 101 of those crafts being performed manually, and speed runners can beat the game in a couple hours.The way it manages to transition you between these stages without telling you what to do is rather fantastic, albeit rough at times as you struggle to figure out the best way to lay out your factory. My only significant complaint is that proper management of trains is decidedly unintuitive. Or rather, it doesn't give good feedback on *why* it's failing if a train can't find a path. But this game has already improved over time in so many other areas that I can't see that being a problem forever. And once you find a pattern that works, the game has built-in capabilities for copy-pasting your designs elsewhere so you don't have to worry about it anymore.Oh, and there are aliens to fend off the entire time you're doing this, so good luck with that (though you can technically choose to play with them on "peaceful" so that they will not attack first.)If you're worried about getting bored, don't be. There is a very healthy mod scene in this game, with mods adding everything from tameable aliens, to dozens of ore types, to entirely restructuring the tech tree to make them game 5 times as long. And the game itself isn't done yet, of course, with plans to eventually expand out beyond your initial planet.TL;DR - If you like builder games, you'll love this. Just be prepared to voluntarily lose some sleep.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: Did you play Open TDD? Buy this game. The rest of the review is for those that didnt. Factorio is a game that can suck your life away, it's addicting for all the right reasons. As the About This Game section says, you start by manually doing everything yourself, working up to massive automated factories that you never have to touch again. However, that's where the fun is. Learning how to be more efficient, learning how to use machines in ways you thought you couldnt use them, and the game is geared toward you experimenting. In my opinion, the one feature that facilitates creativity is the lack of any sort of penalty for picking up anything you place down. You dont have to demolish anything to get part of the resources used back, you just pick the whole thing up and place it down infinitely. This allows you to keep trying again and again to design factories that work best with the rest of your facilities. I've sunk nearly a hundred hours into Factorio and I'm only at the tip of the iceberg. So much to learn, and I can't wait.

I played it off and on over the years and maybe put in six total hours.  Then I started playing again.  I have put in at least 40 hours in the last couple of weeks alone.  It's THAT good. And it only Early Access.  Still.  My wife is going to Divorce me if I keep playing this game.  That's not going to stop me from playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming up to 5000 hours playing this game, and im still learning new things in multiplayer.  The devs are by far the best ive ever seen.  FFF (Friday Fun Facts) is a blog post they write up every Friday.  Every. Single. Friday. For the last ... 4 years?  look at them on their website, its not a 2 min blurb, its a full review of what they've done that week, and where they're headed, what their plans are, current iterations they're going over, complete with pictures and sometimes *chuckle* hand drawn graphs.  Their IRC channel (there is a link on their website) has someone on the dev team there pretty much 24/7.  Not just "community manager" nitwits (Trangar, te he), but guys like Rseding91 (their C++ guru) that are programming the actual updates.  Oh.  There are updates.Are there sometimes bugs in the patches?  Sure.  Which is why you sometimes see 2 patches in the same day.  Bugs get quashed immediately whenever possible.  While this review doesnt speak much about the game, the team behind it deserves the recognition - its amazing, thoughtul, and incredibly well done because of them.In a nutshell, its similar to RTS games like starcraft, where you build up and gather resources.  But instead of spending 20 minutes to build up a base to have the game end in 2, you keep building.Building Bigger.Making things more efficient.Tearing down and rebuidling.Im almost 5000 hours in and sticking with vanilla until I can personally say Ive mastered it.  Once I stop learning new things almost every time I play, ill start fooling around with mods.  And there are lots of them.  Is this game worth $20?  It absolutely was for me.  This single $20 purchase brought me thousands of hours of entertaintment, frustration - when things didnt work planned, and absolute delight - when things get fixed, and I can reflect on my orchestra of 500 machines working in harmony.  Whether or not it is worth it for you is up to you.  But I would be remiss if i didnt impore you to give it a try, get the demo, fool around, commit an hour or two.

_childDocuments_.review: Factorio: The Ingenious Symphony of AutomationRating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5)Factorio, developed by Wube Software, is a game that stands as a testament to the beauty of automation and the thrill of problem-solving. It's not just a game; it's a captivating journey into the world of engineering, logistics, and creativity.At the core of Factorio is the satisfaction of efficiency. The game challenges players to create sprawling factories that automate resource gathering, production, and transportation. The result is a symphony of machines and conveyor belts working tirelessly to fulfill your vision.The depth of complexity in Factorio is staggering, and it rewards those who revel in optimization. From refining raw materials to crafting advanced technology, the sense of progression is ever-present, making each achievement feel well-earned.The game's visuals, while not aiming for realism, have a charm of their own. The minimalist design prioritizes clarity and functionality, allowing players to manage intricate systems with ease.Factorio's sense of scale is awe-inspiring. You'll find yourself continuously expanding your operation, unlocking new technologies, and tackling more significant challenges. This sense of growth is what makes the game endlessly engaging.Moreover, the modding community surrounding Factorio is active and creative, offering an array of additional content and experiences to keep the game fresh and exciting.In conclusion, Factorio is a masterclass in automation and problem-solving. Its intricacy, scale, and sense of accomplishment make it a must-play for anyone who enjoys building, optimizing, and creating systems. Dive into the world of Factorio and watch as your vision of a perfectly efficient factory becomes a reality.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice fun game to either relax to or challenge yourself the mods help, but if you're looking for intense challenges you won't find it with the base game as the alien enemies are very few and the world is super simple. _childDocuments_.review: You ever watch How It's Made, and stay awake long enough to see those huge factories making stuff like cakes or lightbulbs? Hundreds of machines, all interconnected, conveyor belts snaking too and fro between them, devices performing task after task, all working in harmony to spit out the insane number of cakes needed to satisfy the regional demand on a daily basis...That's factorio. Only you cant make cake... yet. Sure it's simple enough on the surface. I build a machine here, to take item X, and turn it into item Y. Then I take Item Y, combine it with item Z, make item Q out of that mixture, which gets mixed with items C through F to create item B, which in turn gets used to build a solar panel, for a rocket you're building and launching into space. Definitely not cakes. It's a game about complexity, automation, and solving problems. This is not a game for everyone, and even those who like it usually shut it down in a moment of crushing depression after overcoming the first few hours with the game. But if you stick with it, keep working out the problems, and get your factory running smoothly, I can almost garauntee you'll be hooked. This game is rewarding in a way i havent seen in a long time, partly because it doesnt hold your hand at all. Everything in your factory is where you put it, set up the way you set it up, and it lives or dies by your decisions. But let me tell you, when you power up a factory block for the first time, and see it smoothly working, doing exactly what it should, the way you want it, it feels damn good....until you realise your iron output is woefully sub par and your new production branch is starving out the rest of your factory. But that's just another problem to overcome.TL;DR, It's a solid game for those looking for a real time sink. Stable branch is very stable. Bugs are very rare and I've personally never experienced a crash, even with 50+ mods running in the background. Not much end game, but just getting ot that point will take multiple hours. Would reccomend.
_childDocuments_.name: Factorio

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoys strategy and management games, Factorio has been an incredibly rewarding and engaging experience. The game offers a unique mixture of resource management, automation, and problem-solving that keeps me constantly thinking and planning. From the moment I started playing, I was hooked by its intricate mechanics and the endless possibilities it offers.One of the standout features of Factorio is its deep and engaging gameplay. The core objective of building and optimizing a factory from scratch is both challenging and satisfying. The game's complexity gradually ramps up, allowing me to learn and master new systems at a comfortable pace. Whether it's setting up efficient production lines, managing resources, or optimizing logistics, there's always something to think about and improve.Factorio excels in allowing players to automate processes and systems. The satisfaction of designing a fully automated factory, where raw resources are transformed into complex products with minimal manual intervention, is unparalleled. The game's blueprint system is fantastic for sharing and implementing complex designs, encouraging creativity and experimentation. I love the sense of accomplishment that comes from seeing my factory run smoothly and efficiently.The game's world-building and atmosphere are immersive, drawing me into its industrial landscape. The visuals, while not overly flashy, are clean and functional, which suits the game's focus on efficiency and optimization. The soundtrack is subtle but fitting, enhancing the experience without being distracting. The presence of alien creatures adds a layer of challenge and urgency, as I must balance expansion with defense.One of the things I appreciate most about Factorio is the ongoing support and updates from the developers. They are dedicated to refining the game and adding new features, which keeps the experience fresh and exciting. Additionally, the modding community is incredibly active and creative, offering a wide range of mods that can significantly enhance and expand the game. Whether it's new resources, technologies, or quality-of-life improvements, there's always something new to try.Factorio offers immense replayability. Every playthrough feels unique, thanks to the randomly generated worlds and the various ways to approach factory design and production. The game's open-ended nature means that there's no single "right" way to play, allowing me to set my own goals and challenges. Whether I'm aiming for the fastest production times, the most compact factory, or simply exploring new mods, there's always a new challenge to tackle.In conclusion, Factorio is a masterpiece of strategy and automation that offers a deeply satisfying and endlessly replayable experience. Its blend of complex mechanics, creative freedom, and continuous improvement makes it one of the best games in its genre. For anyone who enjoys problem-solving, strategic planning, and the joy of seeing a well-oiled machine in action, Factorio is a must-play. It's a game that continues to captivate me, and I can't recommend it highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This is is one of those games that's been in development for a while, but has actually been perfectly playable for quite a long time. But the great thing is that each update that brings it closer to 'release', is actually a worthwhile one. The devs are communicating with the community, and some bugs that have been part of gameplay for so long, have been polished into features. Some things are polished, some things are overhauled completely. While they try not to alienate existing players, they're not afraid to change stuff that's confusing or illogical, just because changing it would be annoying for existing players.It's also nice to see how some popular mods have actually made it into the game.But enough about that, on to the game itself.Can be summed up in a few words: Deceptively simple, amazingly complex and addictive as hell.

_childDocuments_.review: is a really fun casual mini-putt golf game!  If you like mini-putt you will probably enjoy this! It's the kind of game you can play for 20-30 minutes here and there without any other real commitment.  It comes with a lot of maps, and the ability to create your own maps.  Some holes are very difficult, requiring some skill (or shot memory) to get the lowest scores for each map (or play type).  The game customization options are very extensive too, you can use a ball, cube, puck, star, and a few other shapes. You can also set the ball size, bounce, jump mode, ball collision, and gravity to completely change the game up.It may be called "", but you don't need friends to play this game with, and you can find friends to play with by just playing online! So if you need friends, and especially if you like mini-putt, do not pass up on this game!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very quirky fun take on mini-golf that you play with your friends, strangers or even by your lonesome (trying to figure out the hole-in-one strats, you know who you are.) Currently has 2 courses available with more planned on the way, a few quirky modes currently on the experimental version and possibly some of the best devs I've experienced despite only being a 2 man team. They are very active on updates and have a roadmap in the forums if you want to see where they plan on taking it. They are very friendly and active on the forums and is taking community ideas and advice to make the game even better while also adding more to it in a fast enough manner.I highly recommend this to someone who wants a game that is more casual but has the options to make it a stressful race to the hole against others. There are plenty of Youtubers that have videos on it though they might be dated because of the constant tweaks by the devs but you can get an idea of what you'd be getting into from the videos, still though I think it's worth the price in it's current version with only 2 courses so when everything else eventually comes out it'll be more than cost efficient! :)

_childDocuments_.review: The best mini-golf experience money can buy.Pros:Multiple courses, All unique and vary in difficultyGreat physics (semi customizable)Custom set rules/settings (max shots per hole, ball shape, size, color, "jump" option, gravity, it goes on...The settings gives it a lot of replayability You'll never have so much fun getting frustrated with your friendsCons:Some extreme settings can make some holes impossible. (putting a cone a few places in candyland LOL) Very few ramps/runways/general ground areas don't match up perfectly which results in little bumps to crazy physics bugs. I really have nothing bad to say about this game at all, and as soon as the game starts it gives you a warning that the game is in alpha, there are bugs, it is what it is. It's not as bad as the warning makes it seem, in my opinion. The first "Con" is really on you, not the game. When you change gravity, use weird shapes, and have to jump a slightly bumpy spiral ramp, and can't make it... welll... duh. lol. The second is totally understandable, it's in alpha, and they are so far and few, it's just another thing for you and your friends to laugh and cry about, just adding to the overall experience. 100% Worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was pretty fun a few years ago, but it felt a bit under-polished. We still played it anyway, because of it's upbeat cartoony style and hilarious gameplay customisation. Over the years myself and others have played the game quite a lot, for a game that only offers very simple gameplay (shoot ball in hole to win). But the gameplay customisation adds quite a bit of replayability. Everyone hates the cone ball. Or you could have super low gravity and player collisions. Just to name a few things.They added some extra game modes, like hoops. And they slowly added new maps over the years. More official maps would have been nice, but we get by pretty well with what we've got. And there'e community workshop maps too (but they aren't as good as official maps). However, the game still felt a bit under-polished in some areas and not completely bug-free.But then, Team17 bought the developers out. Which wasn't a bad thing! They've massively improved the user interface, fixed bugs and added some cool new maps. Now the game really feels worth recommending to anyone - not just those who need their funny game fix. But I suspect there is still more content to come!It's a great game to grab a few friends with and have a reliably good time. Sure, it's not the most sophisticated game, but it offers pretty satisfying gameplay that should appeal to a lot of people.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want something like a more grown up version of Civilization that's more realistic?Do you want your games to (mostly) represent plausable alternatie histories?Well this is the game for you. It is not simply a wargame, but a "grand strategy" game that attempts to cover everything. It's like the Photoshop of grand strategy games.You can learn a certain amount about the complexity of real world political systems from playing this game. For example, attack that small country when you don't know what you're doing and suddenly you're in a massive war that destroies you because you didn't pay any attention to who their allies were. If only it had occured to you that you might be able to lure them away from their allies through other means and vassalize then possibly even diplomaticly annex them you might have done much better.Wondering what would have happened if the Netherlands had colonized Cuba? Well, start out in 1440 and you don't even have the Netherlands yet. Holland will have to invade other netherlandish kingdoms like Delft to form the Netherlands first. Once you've done that, you might eventually have a chance to colonize Cuba. But start out too late in time and Spain will have already done it.The game attempts to follow history as closely as possible without forcing you to do exactly what every country historically did. Unlike Civilization, which seems childish in comparison, nations are not simply cosmetic with a few balanced out differences. Some countries are at a major disadvantage, especially with technological development. Some, like the Ottomans, have some technological disadvantage but a major advantage in size meaning they could have conquered parts of Europe if they had focused their efforts differently and acted in time. Some are unlikely to conquer anything and have no chance at anything but colonization and trade, maybe not even that. For some, total victory would simply be maintaining their independence until 1820.While some mods let you play past 1820, certain historical events like Industrialization were literally game changing enough to require a completely different game, so the game mechanics don't cover anything past the beginning of the Industrial Era. That is how specific and detailed the mechanics are; they can't simply be generalized to all historical periods like Civilization attempts to do.Get this game on sale. It's one of those games where almost all new features are released as DLCs. The "core" mechanics updates are covered by the "Empire Founder's Bundle" of DLCs so if you want to start out with the important stuff that's the thing to buy. The others usually add features that aren't as significant or are specific to particular regions, or they just add cosmetic or musical content.But in any case, expect to take some time to learn this game. It's not casual and learning it seems like trying to learn Photoshop sometimes because, like Photoshop, it's difficult to stuff all of the necessary options into the user interface.

_childDocuments_.review: Tbh although this game is decently fun, i just can't give a thumbs up. There are too many things that could be fixed that would convince me to give a thumbs up, but I won't. First of all, once you play all the maps, the game gets kinda boring. so only a few hours of gameplay is needed until it gets boring. There's alot of things i want to complain about, but ill list the top 3. 1. The game has super unrealistic pars. The pars of the game are super low and could only be achieved by someone who knows exactly what to do on the particular course. Although this doesn't applky all the time, it does enough to where I'll mention it. 2. The location of the hole isn't always obvious. Of course in smaller courses, the hole is obvious, but there are many holes where the location of where you need to aim is unclear, resulting in a few strokes added. 3. the worst of all, the janky physics and hitboxes. The thing that angered me the most was how at many moments, My ball would be banked off of either something unrealsitic (that physics normally wouldn't allow) or I would hit a hitbox that is terrribly made(ex. a fish whose hitbox is a large cube.). I hope that these are fixed in the near future so others can enjoy it. 4/10 game, mostly because it's overpriced. I'd highly recommend waiting for a sale at least under 7 dollars, then maybe it would be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am really torn between giving this game a thumbs up or down, but I chose thumbs down for two big reasons.  The first is that there are only a handful of maps, and it simply gets boring fast, I am sure this will change with updates however.  The second and largest reason is that it seems to be too difficult.  Let me explain: as with every golf game the goal is to get the ball in the hole in as few moves as possible and each hole has par, anything less is a good score and anything more is a bad score.  The problem is that it's almost impossible to hit the ball with the right amount of force because the ball either rolls a lot or a very little and is hard to get the exact force you want.  Secondly you have to be a perfectionist when playing, there are several holes where if you make one mistake you'll get over par.  There are also some holes where it is almost impossible to get under par because the hole is seemingly designed to make you go out of bounds or get lost.  I'm looking at you egyptian level.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, if you don't have friends, then Golf With Your Friends might just be the perfect game for you! It's like having a whole group of virtual friends to play mini-golf with, without any of the real-life social awkwardness.And if you're anything like me, you'll find that the game's physics engine is almost as hilarious as your actual attempts at playing mini-golf. You'll watch your ball bounce, roll, and sometimes even fly off the course in ways that will have you laughing out loud (even if no one else is around to hear it).Plus, there's something oddly satisfying about sinking a tricky shot or getting a hole-in-one, even if there's no one there to high-five you afterwards. So why not give Golf With Your Friends a try? Who knows, maybe you'll even make some virtual friends along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: Golf with your friends, who ever thought golf could be fun right? Well it is.Golf with your friends is far from polished, the menu can break from time to time, there are some region and latency issues which present themselves during setting up your game, but once you're in a game things run smoothly. It's a ton of fun that you forget about the unfinished alpha-ness of this game and instead you start enjoying your time trying to figure out how the courses work, how you can cheat them with jump and having fun with friends. The game does need some work, animations, polishing on the graphics and the menus and just a general overall smoothness brought to it as a finished product. That being said, if I can have hours of fun on a first play on an unfinished game, that means the developers are doing something right, and I recommend you try out Golf with your friends for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: At first my friend and I had a lot of fun playing this and inviting others to join in some shenanigans - not even for good scores, just to mess around and do weird shots to see if we can make a new fun shortcut. The game works pretty fine from what we experienced, the odd lag/glitch here and there, sometimes our balls got stuck though we chalked that up to us getting it in unconventional areas. Then the new courses started to release as DLC where only one person needed to pay for others to play as well, and again we didn't mind *too* much because we were getting decent value for a half hour maybe of fun with each course pack of DLC. The problem is when the company announced price hikes for the previous DLC, and then priced their (at the time of this review) newest DLC for nearly $12CAD - WAY too much for a single DLC compared to the game's base price (about $17.50CAD). They've slowly started losing touch with their community and there isn't enough drive to want to support them if they're banking on those few folks who shell out for it/the achievements. It's a shame because it really was a lighthearted and upbeat game, but it isn't a *long* game you go back to very often and definitely not worth the inflated prices. Ultimately if you get this game on sale super cheap you'll find good value - or if they do a free weekend and you wanna dink around with friends. But I wouldn't recommend paying full price for the game, and ESPECIALLY not the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game. I really do. The courses are creative and challenging, the themes are fun, the physics aren't half bad, the AV is respectable...But...The camera controls are just atrocious. Playing multiplayer on a single screen is the very definition of retarded and infuriating.  I know it sounds trivial, but the camera needs to be manually moved by each player in order for them to view their next shot, because when a player's turn begins the camera may snap to their ball, but the relative camera position is carried over from the previous player. This, coupled with an aggravatingly persistent "Ready Player One" that must be manually dismissed at the start of each turn, means the beginning of EVERY turn consists of removing the turn prompt then manually correcting the camera view. Yes, I know this doesn't sound terrible, but after a while it becomes as maddening as a tiny flap of skin hanging from the roof of your mouth the day after you cut it while eating Cap'N Crunch.Another enraging thing is that all controllers are constantly active. Always. Regardless of whose turn it is. That's right, while your buddies are taking their turn using their controller, your controller is fully active as well! And there doesn't seem to be any way to disable it! I tried to come up with some rationale for why this would be this way, some explanation that might reveal a secret aspect of fun that I have never before explored. But I came up blank. It's just stupid.I honestly believe there is a possibility that this game came about because someone with a genuine and remarkable talent for min-golf course design was put in touch with a game design school dropout. If these glaring design flaws are ever resolved, I will gladly recant this review and purchase the game again. But in its current state, I simply cannot ever subject myself to this aggravation again.

_childDocuments_.review: Played through 4 18-holes. Visuals are bright, joyful, a bit crazy, but all in nice fun. The fact every course has its own entirely distinctive theme is simply awesome. Mechanics are relatively simple and clear enough, but there are a few issues. Notably, the camera seems to get stuck with objects at times and make you look much closer at the ball, making judging proper velocity a pain. Then there's the design of the levels. I was quite impressed by the first set of holes, which simply worked well and offered at times obstacles typical to what you'd find in a real minigolf course. Other levels were much more problematic, mostly in terms of difficulty. The first 9 is usually quite fun and shows interesting challenges, but the last 9 gets insane and too unforgiving at times, requiring way too precise inputs. I don't mind getting over par, but I do mind having to guess the almost exact force I must use for the ball to then roll on some accelerator platform and fly away through a ridiculously small hole in a wall, or on a minuscule platform. On the other hand, there is much space for the player to progress with practice. Thus, for anyone with the patience to go through those difficulty spikes that will certainly ruin your score sheet up until now, there's something really cool to play with. And then there's party mode, quite an original and funny concept that makes the unforgiving nature of some levels a tad more bearable, I suppose.I would recommend trying it at a rebate if this is your kind of game.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: get Tower Unite and play the minigolf minigame on that game instead.I played Tower Unite minigolf a lot before a friend gifted me this game and I was honestly expecting so much more from this given that its a standalone minigolf game and I'm so baffled by how much poorer quality it is in comparison.For starters, this game just simply lacks basic competency in many areas that have been non-issues in games for at least a decade (and not an issue in Tower Unite):- Basic graphics issues like misaligned textures, invisible or missing polygons.- A not very well crafted physics engine whereby if your ball goes into a nearby wall at max speed it will clip through it, and balls will repeatedly fall through the floor.- Very basic networking problems such as jittery views of other players playing.- Really rough UI (losing your text chat drafts in between levels, when you press Esc and you're the host of a lobby, it will close that lobby without warning).Then on top of that are all the gameplay problems:- Ball power that feels like it's on a curve rather than linear.- Really weird and awkward ball friction and physics in general.- The levels are so low poly that when you expect the ball to glide on a curved surface it ends up bouncing awkwardly instead.- So many weird little areas and nooks and crannies for your balls to get snagged on that feel like lazy inconveniences or form over function instead of part of a crafted level challenge.- So many gimmicks in so many levels that make too much visual noise and don't actually provide sufficient gameplay challenges to justify them (the Worms level possibly being the worst example of this).- The free camera isn't enough to explain to users what's expected of them and the 15 second allowed time is too short for many complicated levels.- The bounce controls are not predictable enough in water to actually make you feel like you're in control.Most of these are non-issues in TU. Tower Unite has quite a few gimmick levels but they were never as bad as the gimmick levels in this game.I really like the weird modes such as the dunk and hockey mode, but these never get integrated into levels so you end up having really awkward experiences like being under a hoop or on the side of a net and having to waste a turn to simply back out of before trying again. There are some cool ideas but it's buried under so many game engine and basic gameplay issues that they never really become joyful. For a game that's not in early access I am just so baffled by how unpolished and broken it is in many respects.If you want a good multiplayer minigolf experience, you should go for Tower Unite instead, especially when it eventually gets Workshop support for minigolf levels.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings as I hope all is well! Below is my Steam Review for Golf With Your Friends, thanks for reading as I wish you well in all your gaming adventures...STORY/LORE - N/ANo story or lore here ladies and gentlemen, just a fun amateur golf game that’s great with friends. If anything, each different course has a distinctive feel to it, so in essence, each course has its own unique little story. Does that count?GAMEPLAY - 8/10Golf With Your Friends is a pretty fun game if you enjoy amateur golf. Obviously, if you have a group of friends to play with, this is the perfect game to chill with on a Friday night. You know, grab everyone on Discord, sit back, and hit the amateur golf course. Golf With Your Friends has a good selection of maps and different ways to play by either using the Dunk or Puck mode, to add a little variety than just a traditional golf ball. You can also customize your golf ball with all sorts of fun different things from dinosaur bones to different kinds of trails. It’s not a whole lot but just enough to make it stand out when playing with others.GRAPHICS - 7/10The graphics are decent in Golf With Your Friends but keep in mind, you’ll find some clipping and glitches here and there. It wasn’t enough to ruin the game or anything but the graphics are fine here but nothing that’s going to look real or break your rig. This is a fun little amateur golf game to play with friends, it’s not real golf or anything like that.SOUNDTRACK - 7/10The music in Golf With Your Friends is fitting for an amateur golf setting as every course will have its own unique soundtrack to it. It’s nothing that’s crazy immersive or anything, just simple and good for background noise as you golf.MULTIPLAYER - 8/10At the time of this Steam Review, it does take a while to use Quick Play to find others to play with. This is most likely the case because it’s not an insanely popular game here on Steam. That’s why I recommend getting this game if you have a core group of friends that are looking for a chill kind of game to play with on the weekends or something. It’s very easy to host a game and you can customize it in a lot of different ways.FINAL SCORE - 8/10Golf With Your Friends is a fun little amateur golf game that obviously, is a lot of fun with friends. The golf courses are fun and unique with extremely simple controls to sit back and enjoy. The soundtrack goes well with this kind of game and overall, I enjoyed going through all the different courses, modes, and customization settings. I tend to play this every now and then with friends when we’re in the mood and it’s definitely created some funny moments when fueled with alcohol. I definitely recommend this game if you love amateur golf and want to get your friends together to try something different when you game.

Also, this game feels awesome with the trackpad on Steam Deck, with an added layer of tactility that enhances the whole package considerably. Feel free to check out my config!
