_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is an architect's wildest dreams realized. At it's core, it's a puzzle game about taking a plunge into an infinite abyss over and over, witnessing the architecture that looks like it came from the mind of Giovanni Battista Piranesi, without the torture devices and people. It's like a house that refuses all manner of scale, endlessly tall, infinitely long. And as a puzzle game, it is remarkably clever, even if it is mostly variations of block puzzles.Presentation of the game is simplistic, but simplicity itself can be used to portray abstract design. The world is mostly beige, with a fog covering the world that is vastly infinite. Colors are used sparingly, primarily for the blocks that are used to solve the variety of puzzles. The real focus of the presentation is architecture. William Chyr is an artist of sorts, and the way he presents architecture in Manifold Garden is important. Like with a previous game I reviewed, it's abstract, but occasionally there is something recognizable. Giant cogs of machinery locked behind impenetrable glass, fountains, and trees, but more importantly, buildings that seem to be so tall, their scale is hidden behind the fogs that hide the edges of the infinite abyss, giving this world a natural, looping abyss where each structure can naturally repeat.Music too helps sell the idea of exploring the infinite abyss. Composed by Laryssa Okada, the soundtrack embodies the wonder of witnessing an architectural dreamscape of infinity. It plays in the background, subconsciously telling the player how they should feel. The moment the soundtrack won me over was the very moment I stepped outside for the first time, and the song that played began to build, until entering the prison, where the scale began to set in. The song climaxes here, almost like it's saying "woah" as the prison extends endlessly above and below.The gameplay of Manifold Garden is a simple first-person block puzzle game with a unique set of twists. At first, the player is simply asked to place blocks on specific switches, but quickly shows how unique it gets. Each block is color-coded to specific sides of a cube, from red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. It ties into the mechanic of switching gravity on the six sides of a cube, as each block can only be moved if the player's gravity is in the same plane as the cube they are trying to move. More importantly, they stay solid, meaning that they can be stacked; even cubes of different color (and as such gravity property) can be placed on cubes of differing color, which is often used in a variety of puzzles to keep them in place or to maneuver a cube from one gap to another.If it was just that, it would be a fairly tame puzzle game, but Manifold Garden often employs unique twists to the formula. I won't list all the examples here, but some notable ones include growing trees for more cubes, to using the gravity switch mechanic to maneuver giant tentrinimo-like blocks around the world. Each mechanic is unique and exciting, but start off isolated from each other before the game decides to use all of them in clever ways that intersect the mechanics.Another major part of the gameplay that's important to discuss is the endless plunging into the abyss. There is no jumping; instead, it's a constant trust fall. Manifold Garden's dizzying heights are the same as its depths, so often it becomes efficient to instead fall towards the location from above. At first, it's disorienting, but later becomes the fastest way to travel the world. The recursive world is even used in some of the puzzles, meaning that sometimes solving certain puzzles requires another plunge into the never-ending abyss.Despite it seemingly being just an abstract art piece, Manifold Garden does have a story of sorts, though not the traditional kind. There are no characters, NPCs, or hidden notes filled with lore. The main character the player controls has no body or voice, and there is never a moment where the game says anything about what happens. The story itself is abstract, with many ways of being interpreted. It's thematic, beautiful, and has an ending that I can only describe as glorious and disorienting. It's an ending that deserves to be witnessed within its context, as even just talking about it does a grave disservice to its beauty and impact.Manifold Garden is the kind of artsy game I think more developers should try to make. The experience of the game itself perfectly encapsulates video games as art, in the most existentially terrifying way possible. If art is meant to disturb the comfortable and comfort the disturbed, then Manifold Garden is comforting in its lush and beautiful world, and terrifying in the existential dread of infinity. It's the sort of masterpiece where one screenshot of the world looks like it would live in an art museum, and I sincerely hope more people give this game the attention it deserves, from its incredible sense of scale, the beautifully realized architecture, the haunting soundtrack, and its series of interesting, challenging puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a simple puzzle game with no strings attached and I love it for that.It's visual style reminds me of Antichamber but the gameplay is nowhere near as obtuse. And that's no hate on Antichamber, that game is frustrating and unintuitive on purpose. But Manifold Garden succeeds in giving the player obtainable goals and reasonable expectations. It's a bit on the easier side if you know what you're doing, which I actually like: the "Talos Principle 1" effect where you remain stumped on a puzzle with no method of breaking through that hurdle, so you just sit there for minutes or hours contemplating why you're even playing the game? Not really present in MG. Some might say that's a critically missing feature for a puzzle game, but me personally I like that I always feel like I'm moving forward, even if the puzzles have got me...well...puzzled, I'm not sitting in one place doing nothing.This brings me to the main gameplay gimmick of Manifold Garden, and I gotta say it's one of the better ones:  Objects AND you are affected by  It adds a lot to the "liminal space" aesthetic, but also it makes tackling puzzles both intuitive AND fun because most of the time all you need is a change of perspective. Literally.  and you'll be able to get the hang of most of the puzzles. The other ones that are more complicated require knowledge of mechanics that the game gives you plenty of time to learn.The sound design is mostly atmospheric, not too much to say about good or bad. I'd say the  sound the best, can't really say why: you'll just have to play the game to see what I mean.And if all of that wasn't enough, Manifold Garden is beautiful. I'd say it's easily desktop-wallpaper material, and being able to move through these surrealist worlds is an experience I can't say I've ever really done before. Maybe in Hyperbolica, but not to this scale.Overall Manifold Garden is a balanced experience, and I can appreciate a game that knows what it is trying to be: the backrooms if it was good. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden sucks. I bought it because I like games that have impossible megastructures that make you feel feel tiny and mess with your sense of space and perspective, but this game is not that. Nothing ever feels big. There is no sense of vastness or wonder. You are trapped in a tiny box that when you fall through the bottom of the box you just come back out at the top. This is not NaissanceE, this is Portal. But worse, because there is no storyline. There are no hints or suggestions of what to do. The only mechanic is if you walk up to a wall, you can press space and now the wall is the floor. Also you can pick up companion cubes. But there are no slopes, you can't jump, you can't mantle, you can't fly, you can't do anything except walk around like a depressed, impotent Doomguy desperately wishing he had a spaceship like the one his buddy had in Descent circa 1995. After about 30 minutes of wandering around aimlessly I was bored. There is nothing to do except open doors and pick up cubes. What is this, Amazon warehouse simulator? If you're looking for grand, epic vistas, this is not the game. If you're looking for fluid, 6 degrees of freedom first-person movement, this is not the game. There are much better walking sims out there, games with better parkour, games with better zero-G. If you're looking for pretty much anything other than a slow, tedious, painstaking puzzle game, you will be disappointed. I sure was.

_childDocuments_.review: There’s a small selection of games out there that I just love being in. I’m not talking about enjoying the challenges or the gameplay, I mean I love loading up the game and simply wandering around in it. Games need a special aesthetic or atmosphere to draw me in like that, and among this unique subset of games, Manifold Garden may be my favorite. I’m a sucker for fantastical vistas and clever architecture to begin with, and offering that within the context of the sprawling infinite should make it obvious why I connected with this one so much. Mixed with the solid puzzling, it’s an experience that more people need to share.The story in Manifold Garden is very much open to interpretation, so I’m not going to try guiding your thoughts on it with my own suppositions. Instead, I’ll just mention that there are six colors from which a grand garden can be cultivated, and it’s up to you to make that happen. Making that happen involves navigating vast structures hanging in an infinite, repeating world, one that you can fall through indefinitely until you get bored and decide to land back on an iteration of the level. Adding to this mind-bending premise is the ability to flip your own gravity to align with any of the six directions that comprise the cubular architecture, allowing you to wrap around towers and explore the undersides of walkways, to name only a few of the incredible possibilities open to you.So there’s the infinite, and the ability to scamper all over or fall through it while orientated however you like. What’s one to do with such powers? Well, besides taking in the breathtaking scenery from all angles, you do have a garden to grow. Throughout the world of Manifold Garden you will find blocks of six different colors, and those blocks can be used for a wide variety of purposes, from opening doors to forming platforms to directing water, and so on. The trick is that these blocks have their own gravitational alignment as well, and you can only interact with them while aligned the same way. This, again, expands the puzzling possibilities as you start mixing different colors of blocks and working out how to get one to one place while the others are frozen in their alignments. The game does an excellent job of easing you into this mindset, and continues to do so as it adds more and more twists on the formula, but it does get devious in some parts that can leave you scrambling for some time.While there is certainly more ambitious gameplay to be found in this surreal genre of puzzler, I can think of few games that can match the visual flair that Manifold Garden has. The spectacle of a massive complex of chambers, windows, and platforms hanging in space, surrounded by an infinite field of itself repeated, never gets old. Every area feels so much more massive, so much greater in scope, than any other first-person game I can think of. And the simple color schemes give the aesthetic an even bolder look, drawing the eyes towards the shapes and details that comprise every structure. What’s even more impressive is how every few areas, the game manages to surprise you yet again with what it offers visually. I knew about the infinite staircases shown above long before I reached them, yet the experience of being there and navigating them still knocked me off my feet.Really, with visuals like these and clever puzzles dotted throughout, there’s not much more you can ask for. It’s a tight package, offering about 4 hours of infinite journeying before concluding in a way that was fitting, if not particularly revelatory. There are certainly secrets to find, and in fact there’s apparently a way to complete the game without doing any of the key tasks for each of the areas you end up in, so the replay value is there for intrepid types. Tied up with some excellent minimalist sound design, Manifold Garden is exactly what it sets out to do, and it does it incredibly well. As good as the gameplay part of this game is, it’s the experience of touching the infinite that makes this what it is, and it’s an experience I can whole-heartedly recommend.Did you enjoy this review? I certainly hope so, and I certainly hope you'll check out more of them at  or on my !

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game with interesting mechanics. The minimal texture style with complex, repeating architecture is truly a work of art. The music of this game perfectly fits with its visual style. This is a game that must be savored by all applicable senses.Taking the time to really consume this game as a work of art rather than something to be powered through is recommended as it isn't very long for those experienced with puzzle games. I consider myself better than average when it comes to logic puzzles, and I breezed through this one. This is my only real complaint about the title.While this game stands on its own as a uniquely mesmerizing experience, many may compare it to Antichamber which has a similar visual style and also incorporates extra-dimensional space. _childDocuments_.review: It's billed as a puzzle game, but it feels very much more like a linear pretty-visuals experience with a few puzzles mixed in. If you want some easy puzzles with pretty visuals for four hours? Sure, buy it. But it's definitely not a hard game.Don't get me wrong, the visuals are somewhat pretty. The 'water streams' basically look like a flat texture, but the whole 'infinite repeating tiny pocket of space' thing is visually interesting for a bit. There were around 15-20 puzzles that actually felt a little puzzling, but the overall difficulty is very low. At no point did I feel like I had to stop and truly 'think' about how to accomplish the task in front of me for much longer than a minute or two. And there were only six to ten that I DID have to think about for a minute or two (rather than hunt for missing info). Some of the sections that took the longest actually took time mostly because I was trying to FIND a tree/block/holder/path, rather than trying to figure out a puzzle. In a few cases, my struggle was through the lack of a decent perspective on the area so that I could see all the pieces involved, and the 'fix' was simply walking quite a distance (or falling) to stare at a few things and piece them together in my mind before moving on to the (now obvious) solution. There's no dialog or story. None was promised, but maybe you care about that. There are weird moments where the game just has you stare at the CGI equivalent of a kaleidoscope, with nothing else occurring and no way of moving things forward faster/skipping the thing. I was honestly hoping for more. The visuals are nice. The puzzles are easy. The audio is... okay? Clearly work went in to the audio, but there are some odd choices, particularly during one or two of the weird kaleidoscope sequences, that had sounds occurring that almost felt like sounds I'd associate with a slimy, decaying alien than ethereal, angular audio. I honestly thought that maybe I was playing a game with the classic trope of "you think you're doing the right thing, but you're making stuff worse" at a few points, including the very end. (Yes, I actually was left wondering if the ending sequence was somehow indicative of a 'bad' end.)

_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I dunno. It looks great. The sound design is spectacular. The concept is genius.But the puzzles are just sooooo weak, and have huge travel gaps in between them. So many of them were trivially easy, or designed so that you accidentally get the solution just by going straight forward, or hitting every button, or following the lines on the ground. All these incredibly powerful mechanics and yet they don't even scratch the surface of making any interesting puzzles.For example, there's one level where you learn that water (which is only active on a certain side) can flow along frozen water of a different color. A *hugely* interesting mechanic which was introduced very late. But rather than force you to learn this mechanic, they set up the level so that it happens accidentally and then *never use the concept again!*And the long journey to the next puzzle is sometimes grueling. Sometimes you will have four huge towers that you have to complete, each of which is a two minute trek to get to, but will literally have ONE PUZZLE inside. The ratio of puzzles compared to time in between puzzles is just criminal.[SLIGHT SPOILERS AHEAD] The only two or three puzzles which really have some difficulty are part of the hidden content, but not only is there not enough such content, but they also require you to essentially cheese the other puzzles to get the necessary ingredients. Like some hidden content puzzles required bringing the same blocks back and forth across 5 minutes of levels literally 6 different times!! Watching the speedruns was like watching people do their taxes![SPOILERS OVER] And like I said it's an absolute shame because the look/feel/sound of the game is SOOO good, but the gameplay is just downright boring/frustrating.

_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: wOOOOWOWWWWWWWIf the term "Psychonaut" means anything to you, you OWE it to yourself to play this game. The OST also WILL NOT disappoint!Manifold is the correct term for the settings you find yourself falling through. Don't be afraid to try things; make mistakes. If you ever need to get a block back you will be able to; pluck it once more from the tree of its origin.This game feels like someone took my brain and distilled it out into a game; into an experience that I can show to people external to myself. I found myself diving into new doors as soon as they opened, almost entirely unlike my usual playstyle of exploring anything and everything before allowing myself to progress. The movement and controls are both shown to you as you need them and fairly intuitive (once you let yourself realize that there Is No Down - except the one you make for yourself.) "The enemy's gate is down." vibes hardcore. After coming upon a huge plaza and scoping it out; seeing what I needed to do, I went through just one more portal, and completely forgot about the space for what felt like hours - until I found myself inexplicably standing back within it once more, but this time inside the room I needed to access all that time ago. It feels like a dream, but whether that's the lucid or fever variety I couldn't say. Perhaps a measure of both. I completely forgo any of my usual tracking of 3-dimensional space around my avatar, except what is immediately visible. Ironic, perhaps, in this kind of game, but it's just so much more intuitive to only use what I can see and forget about all the unusual closed loop spaces and non-ordered boundaries, again, except that I find myself constantly running 'up' walls like they were the inside of a hamster wheel, or flinging myself off into the void only to skim to a standing stop halfway 'down' the face of the building I was standing on. I walk upside down just to jump off the stairs I was about to have to climb, then catch myself and swing around, now at the 'top' only having dropped 'down'.Mind meltingly mellifluous; magical and mysterious. Haunting, horrifying, and holy all at once.I can't wait to have something similar to throw the visitors I get in VR Chat into. I never knew I could get something akin to gender euphoria from dunking people into what is.. almost like a Feywild, were it made by a harmonic resonance cascade between the subconscious emanations of Euclid and Escher.Give me more of this forever.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: One of the most unique puzzle games I've ever played. Stunningly gorgeous in a way that adds to the gameplay instead of getting in the way of it. You should play it It is hauntingly beautiful, and has actively made me a better person just through playing it. it's an advanced walking sim, where your whole goal is just to meander through the world and explore,This is like that, but they decided to cram an AMAZING puzzle game into the game too. I don't think I've played something else so strikingly beautiful while also so desolate in that backrooms, liminal way in years.I don't even regularly like puzzle games. Portal is amazing, and I've been known to pick up and play Myst, Witness, etc. but this one, I keep coming back to. I will probably replay this in the near future once my memory of it has faded a little, just so I can re-experience how stunning this game is and how it made me feel. I don't think I can heap enough praise on this game to anyone. This will forever be one of those games that'll have this place, stuck in my head, where I just can't forget it entirely, and I'll hold it up as a prime example of gaming as an artistic medium, not just entertainment. If you're reading this, and haven't played it yet, it's worth every penny. and then some.

_childDocuments_.review: Put simply, this game is a must-have if you are at all interested in puzzle games. I picked this game up in February 2020 back when it was an Epic Store exclusive after seeing a speedrun of it at a recent Games Done Quick event, and I fell in love with it after my first playthrough. I will explain why by dividing it up into a few factors:1. The EnvironmentsThe big "pull" of this game is that the environments loop infinitely, and have structures resembling those within paintings by the artist MC Escher. Exploring these environments and wrapping your head around them is a feeling of wonder that I think hardly any puzzle games after this one will be able to replicate. In particular, there's one location leading up to the second god cube that instilled a sense of grandness that pretty much stuck with me for the rest of the game, and the ending cutscene of the game was a very good way to finish off the main story.2. The Learning Curve/The MechanicsOf course, the other big "pull" of this game is that you flip gravity to solve puzzles. Something I think people playing this for the first time might struggle with or feel daunted by is keeping track of which gravity state you're in in combination with where you are in the game world, as some of the levels can be massive and very complex. While that is the case, the game is very good about herding you to where you need to go to either solve a puzzle or find a component to solving a puzzle, despite not giving explicit instructions. In particular, the fact that the levels are designed around the player falling infinitely allows you to get a vantage point to find whatever you need to more easily. Because of this, while I did get stuck plenty of times (my first playthrough on the Epic Store version took 12 hours in total), I never felt like it was the game's fault or that the puzzles were "too hard", and persevered to get to the end.I am a speedrunner of this game that has spent nearly 200 hours on it between the Steam release and the Epic Store release, and has a put a fair amount of research into the development that went into it, and after all that time, all I can really say is this: Buy. This. Game.You won't regret it one bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game. Fun and satisfying puzzles, interesting mechanics and themes, and fantastic visuals. For me, the first playthrough was just right in gameplay and difficulty - some thinkers, but nothing that stumped me for too long. A very enjoyable experience. One minor criticism is that it's very linear, whereas I was expecting something more in the vein of Space Hole.[Spoilers may follow, I'm making this a mini-guide to secret content.]However, if you only play it once to the ending, you're missing out on a significant portion of the game (including a second ending). And yet the game barely even prods you in that direction. I only knew to look because of the achievements and a couple things I noticed in my playthrough (not that I had any recollection of where they were once I was done). You have to really, really be looking and scour every nook to find the path through the second playthrough. I almost felt like I needed a map of the whole game - and I have no idea what that would look like, given the nature of the physics. Compared to the relative ease of the primary path, it's a big change. I personally did not want to spend the dozens of hours on it, so I used guides when I wasn't sure where to go next. The guide on Steam is too vague, so I recommend the video by Lilith LeBlanc.Once you're done the second playthrough, technically you will have 100%ed the game (or just have a couple achievements that are easy to mop up). But there's actually still more! Just after the , there's a well hidden alternate path leading . And then, in between the , there's another well hidden path that actually contains more puzzles and more paths. These are extremely easy to miss, especially if you think you're done after the second ending. I would really have liked for the game to give more direction and acknowledgement of them.(Please let me know if I missed any other side areas. I'd like to play them too :P)I recommend keeping your save files for easier backtracking. A significant missing feature is the ability to duplicate save files, so that you can explore alternate routes and mess around without blocking off areas by accident (or having to beat the whole game again). Thankfully, just copying and renaming save files works perfectly (e.g duplicate your main file and rename it from 1 to 6). They're stored in AppData/LocalLow/William Chyr Studio/Manifold Garden/Saves.Credit for some content in this review to The Sojourner for the guide on Steam and gelly for the speedruns and strategies. Thanks to Rychro for gifting me the game.

_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, it's adequate at best. It's incredibly visually appealing, but that's probably the only positive aspect.The puzzles simply aren't at all difficult - in fact most of them it's very hard to do anything other than the correct answer. This makes the game play tedious, repetitive, and boring. It also means that there's no sense of reward or excitement, compounded by the fact that you essentially have one path forward at all times and that new mechanics are scarce, it doesn't feel like the progress you make actually means anything. In 3 hours, I've completed 60%+ of the game while distracted and without having to think at all. The areas suffer heavily from unnecessary visual and hit-box clutter and inconsistency, where you simply can't walk up certain stair-like structures but you can walk up others, forcing you to find your way around something that shouldn't be there in the first place. Further, the visual clutter makes it incredibly hard to tell where you are, where you're going, and where you've been. I've heard it called the spiritual successor to Antichamber, but it feels and plays like a visual designer with some coding experience but no game design experience attempted to make a shallow copy of Antichamber. Then I looked it up and that seems to be exactly what the case is. I'll be watching what the developer releases next, as the concept and art are great, but as it is the game is like a rough draft or a first foray into making games without much thought of a complete product.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing puzzle game. It incorporates many of the "recent" trends: portals, non-euclidean spaces, fractal structures, variable gravity. However, it does it with excellence, so the end result is coherent and achieves more than each part would. The author also does experimental sculpture, and it shows: this game is what contemporary interactive art is trying to emulate, without even knowing it.A unique thing is that every puzzle is about building intuition of the weird spaces the game puts you into. Unlike, say, Portal, where late game puzzles rely on complicated setups and mechanical execution, even the hardest Manifold Garden puzzles have relatively few moving pieces, and usually don't even include every mechanic. That means you will never feel overwhelmed, and the puzzle solutions are satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, this should be a generic review template for all puzzle games from now on.There are ultimately two types of puzzle games: "Know what to do, don't know how" and "know how to do, but don't know what". (Bear with me for a second). You can call them Solution-oriented puzzles and Goal-oriented puzzles.Second type is where the method of the solution is trivial or does not matter and the focus is on achieving the goal, learn game rules or discovering some complex relationships of game internals, etc etc. Example of second game are things like The Witness, Myst, or, to a lesser degree Portal which is a mix of both but falls a bit to the later category.The first kind of games is where the goal is trivial, but solution is what you need to discover, usually by observation, planning or trial and error. The example of the first type are games like Talos Principle, Baba is You or Sokoban.I hate this type of games and usually refund them. Manifold Garden is one of them and in my opinion absolutely sucks. The game is about rotating the space and placing colored cubes atop of each other. That's it, there is literally nothing else. I technically consider this game as finished in 30 minutes cause there is nothing new for me to learn or discover. However I know a lot of folks who like this kind of games and for them game will be very fun and they can treat this review as positive.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know the feeling in a FPS or a first person puzzle game when you suddenly walk into an exceptional open space with enormous structures disappearing into the horizon, and you stop for a moment to take in the awe inspiring vista? This game not only takes that to another level, it does it virtually all the time.The game reminded me of both Antichamber and Fez, both games I also completed. Antichamber mostly because of the graphical style, and Fez because of placing cubes at the end of levels for great effect. But the game was definitely its own. It supposedly took William Chyr 7 years to make it, and it’s understandable. Apart from the tech itself, just creating those infinite levels must have been a daunting task.The game was a mixture of solving local puzzles and navigating infinite levels that wrap into themselves like a lithograph by Escher, repeating its structures as you fall through it. The direction of gravity changes when walking up to a wall and pressing space. Now the entire level tilts around, turning walls into floors. Falling not only doesn’t kill you, it’s often necessary to navigate the enormous levels since you can’t jump.See that ledge over there? Drop down for a while until the level repeats itself, then steer towards the ledge as it approaches again and land. The sound of wind and a fear of heights still makes it feel dangerous.Please visit my blog to
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a very pretty, atmospheric puzzle game that I'd recommend to anybody that likes the mind-bending puzzles of Fez, Portal, and Antichamber. The block puzzles tie very well into its central mechanic, and it explores its "world looping" and gravity rotating mechanics pretty thoroughly throughout its relatively short length. It's just a solid, well-constructed puzzle game that never felt too frustrating yet still managed to make me think. My only real complaint is that, much like the game's infinite locations, it's very samey throughout. There's no real standout moments here that blew me away, despite the cool concepts and mind-boggling vistas. But you could argue that this sense of consistency is Manifold Garden's greatest strength--there was never a dull moment, and I enjoyed every second. It's simple, elegant, and doesn't overstay its welcome. And it has one of the coolest photo modes I've seen in a game--this is basically a trippy wallpaper generator!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this. Very atmospheric. If you have a problem with heights in games you will may freak out. The puzzles are pretty good, although if you're looking for a challenge these never get that difficult under normal gameplay which involves obtaining and placing "God Cubes" (rainbow cubes/tesseracts that let you complete an area, doing this gives you an achievement). I looked up a guide twice not to solve a puzzle but to figure out where to go.There is a way to beat the game without "God Cubes"  However, doing that without a guide would be daunting to figure out and a huge increase in difficulty from normal game play and probably require a lot of investigation and trial and error. I used a guide.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game with gravity, non-euclidian puzzles and portals and more!! Really nice. Could a use a little more tutorial puzzles to introduce you to some mechanics, you will figure out most things easily enough though. Very fun so far, looking forward to the finale > It was pretty hard! Nice one. Play Antichamber as well, it is harder than this.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A really beautiful game, and a very calming and mind-tingling experience. The music and sound effects dress the game perfectly. The infinite expanse mechanics take a little getting used to, but other than that, switching gravity is easy to do and most puzzles are challenging enough to make solving them feel rewarding, Not a story-driven game, but more of a work of art, feels like stepping through the looking-glass and intro an M. C. Escher painting. 10/10 for me
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely beautifull! The design let me experience the same vibe that I did when I first came to Saint-Petersburg. Endless repeating space reaching horizon is not something you see everyday. Puzzles are interesting and not too complicated but still well structured. There are no too much details nor too little. That's basically how beauty is defined.The only issue I see in the game is tetramino. They feel alien. And I can't say puzzles with tetramino were designed as good as others. Great game anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best puzzle games I've ever played.Firstly, I must thank the developers for allowing me to save progress at any point. So many games these days use checkpoint saves, which take control over my game session, resulting in an immensely frustrating experience.  Manifold Garden allows saving at .This game is a beautiful and relaxing journey.  The feeling of being lost in an ever-repeating geometric space is strangely soothing.  There were times when I just wanted to either keep travelling in one direction or continue falling, knowing that I was simply repeating a pattern over and over again.The puzzles are not always easy but always very satisfying to complete.  The use of shifting gravity is clever and challenging.The audio design is stunning and flawlessly integrated into the visual experience.If you like rewarding and challenging puzzles in a first-person experience then I cannot speak highly enough of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Man, what did I just witness!!! At the beginning I got a little bored with the minimalistic theme but soon adapted. This game is like describing a mystical/religious experience, especially the ending. like WOW! It was beautiful! The idea of implying infinity in a game, as done masterfully here is very unique! I really liked it!This is the kind of games that I would love to see the future generations make!I think the reason I even got tired of gaming in the first place in general was because everyone is trying to make pretty much the same crappy games that are spiritually/intellectually/existentially shallow, related either to some kinda point system, weapons and enemies, loot and cliche lores. Even the AAA titles. They leave you with a headache and more anxiety, and It's not that interesting.THIS GAME though, is the kind of out of the box thinking that can elevate ones intellect, flirts with ones consciousness and brings one into a whole different dimension. Very nicely done! it was also very meditative while not bounding the player to one direction of gravity. Puzzles were nice too, not too easy but doable. Very nice! I'm looking for more game with a philosophical, spiritual, religious-experience theme! There needs to be a completely separate genre on Steam for games such as this one, Everything or Subliminal. Games that explore mystical dimensions of the human intellect, subconscious and imagination!Really liked it! 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful and infinite mathematical world of loops that is a lot of fun to spend time navigating and solving the puzzles.  Takes a while to get used to the gravity changes when selecting other surfaces but you'll eventually get it.  I find it relaxing to pop in here for a 20-30 minute session and enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The definition of open your mind. I love puzzle games. I definitely love them when I'm on a trip to no where, this one definitely is definitely worth the journey 100x over. The best thing too. It's just enough to keep my mind busy and off things that have been stressing me out.Would highly recommend to those that enjoy trips as your first run through if you can manage. But also definitely recommend to people that love visuals and puzzles in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Another great game in a genre that I like to call "mindf*ck first-person puzzlers" like Antichamber or Superliminal, with its main differentiating features being its "infinite" world with huge levels inside it, and your control over gravity (compared to the non-Euclidean design of Antichamber or your control over perspective in Superliminal.It's also worth pointing out its similarities in level design with the game Naissance, which comes from the fact that both games were influenced by the architectural art of manga artist Nihei and his most famous work,  "Blame!".So. I also recommend this game if you like those two as well (and vice versa).
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful mind-boggling puzzle game that will give you an amazing experience! The only thing that bothered me a little is that it is a little on the short side. (5-6 hours for my first playthrough)A fun little bonus I accidentally found at the end of the game is that if you press  `   you will get a debug menu. If you type show_debug_panel in this menu and go to the level selection, you can play through some unused content! (not all the levels work though, you'll have to restart the game)
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The word "awesome" has unfortunately lost most of its meaning over time. Which is a shame, because while  definitely has many interesting puzzles, inspiring sheer awe with each level's landscape is what it's best at, and it's very difficult to convey that feeling properly without sounding incredibly cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If you think you might be interested, it's worth it. I haven't finished the game yet and it has already given me everything I've ever wanted. The non-euclidean geometry is really fun to explore. Strong 'antichamber' vibes, very similar aesthetic, but of course with different content. If you liked antichamber, 100% you will like this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If I'm ever asked what is the most unique puzzle game I've ever played, this would be my nominee.While the puzzles themselves aren't particularly difficult, just the surreal environment you are part of made the experience so much more entertaining, and the puzzles so much more interesting to solve.This game was an incredible experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I would really like to play this (and the Overwhelmingly positive reviews support this view) however I seem to be in a minority in that the game is too buggy to play. I have menu issues where the mouse disappears, the screen will stay blank on occasion preventing the game start, and when I finally did mange to get to the beginning of the game the mouse sensitivity was so high I felt like a CS:GO player doing 180 no-scopes every time I tried to move.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Game......at least when you are not prone to vertigo, and are fine with thinking outside the box with multiple gravities and a moebius loop built in.Some players will definitely stop playing within the first 15 minutes, not because the game is bad but because their brain isn't able to cope with the visual input when floors become walls or ceilings and the perspective changes over and over again (not randomly but controlled by the player), inducing nausea in some.The graphics are simple and excellent at the same time. Simple in the way that there are not many moving objects or special effects or videos.Excellent in the way that the endless world never breaks and the tricks optics play on your mind are just astonishing.Concept:Some puzzles are easy to grasp and the player is slowly introduced to the different aspects but it becomes really challenging after the first few "levels". Until now I didn't find any logical errors but it nevertheless is not an easy game.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10 tripy game in a good way. trying to find puzzles is harder than actually solving themi would grab the game on sale45% trying to find the puzzle10% walking around lost40% walking to get from point a to b5% solving a puzzle- run speed could be faster- one time i got stuck unable to turn the game and walk on walls, quick reset fixed itjust under 3 hours to finish the game, the rest is afk card farming
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is worth the price of admission on the merits of its visuals alone. It follows in the relatively new trend of indie titles exploiting spatial symmetry to disorient the player and give a sense of the infinite, and is, at the time of writing, perhaps the most dazzling execution of this design principle I have yet seen. As for gameplay, MG's lack of instruction adds to the surreal atmosphere, and most puzzles have very intuitive rules and decently satisfying solutions. Nonetheless, I did find myself stuck a couple of times, not on the individual puzzles themselves, but on the transitions between areas, where the rules are less clear. These are the only points in MG that I found actually challenging, as the puzzles themselves are pretty simple once you get a grasp of the rules. The only major problem I can put my finger on is a product of its symmetry-focused design principle; at various points, the player is expected to preform the same task multiple times. While this is thematically resonant, it can be a bit tedious. With criticism out of the way, this is a must-play in my book.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly good exploration puzzle game. Very solid sense of identity and aesthetic. The audio is an absolute treat as well and always fits the theme going on.It's the first puzzle game in a long time where I not only compare it to portal, but don't immediately feel the need to say some other qualifier like "relatively speaking".There are some moments where it can be easy to get stuck and not be entirely sure where to go, but for the most part the game onboards you to new mechanics really well and is just the right level of indications and telegraphing to not spoil the puzzle but not feel aimless.Wholeheartedly recommended to anyone that even thinks they'd like it based upon seeing it. The only possible negative is that the perspective shifting could trigger motion sickness in some.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is a great puzzle game. It never got so hard that I found it frustrating, but I always needed to devote my full brain to it. It is always engaging and interesting, as well as beautiful to look at. I really enjoyed that the puzzles kept you moving forward, and that it seemed very well edited, with later sections taking less time than earlier ones. It does what it needs to do and ends, which is awesome. If you're looking for a chill puzzle game that you can relax and enjoy, then this is for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden isn’t a bad game, and I wish I could give this an “informational” tag, instead of a “no”. There is two problems about this game, one minor, the other major. The minor one is that this game isnt a puzzle game per se. Its not like you sit there, you got all the pieces you need for the solution and you just cant find the solution. All riddles in this game are trivial, if you have the knowledge. So what this game is about is walking and jumping through a room to understand where everything is, what is unique, what is a repetition, and based on that, come up with the solution, which in always very simple. The more major flaw (though this is also very much a matter of taste) is also a major spoiler: It is that this game gives you no information on what is going on. There is a white world with some dark blobs. You unlock colours. At the end the dark blobs get more and bigger, but then you unlock the rainbow and the game ends. You see fancy animations. There is no comment, no text, no pictures, no nothing. There are two endings and both are just fancy animations. The problem I have with this game is that the story did not hook me. So the gameplay should. But the gameplay gets stale as soon as you realise its just about understanding the room. I finished this game in 4.2 hours apparently, and I already grew tired of the gameplay loop. I guess this game is to be understood as a piece of abstract art. Its pretty, yet not fun nor informative, and as a side note, the music too isnt impressive. But 20 € for pretty, yet short and sort of boring, that didn’t touch, entertain or provoked my thought just isnt cutting it. Had there been some great story that would have kept me hooked, where every "Ahhhhh" moment that happens when you enter a new large room is paired with an "Ahhhh" revelation in the story, this could have been great, at least for me. But like this, I feel like the game should have been a 1 hour experience, not a 4-5 hour game. That being said, I do see a vision behind this, so again, this is not a bad game. And if you like abstract art that tells you nothing, then maybe this will be great for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a really fun puzzle game that centers around Gravity based puzzles, MC Escher inspired staircase infinity worlds, and a little bit of Portlan "Aha" moments. I don't recommend playing more than thirty minutes at a time unless you want to get nauseous. I've never had such a physical reaction to a game lmao.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like this game. This does not necessarily mean that you will dislike it as well, since it does have some neat concepts.So why don't I like it? Manifold garden is a puzzle game in a 3D environment, so it does require a lot of walking around to see what the puzzle is and then to implement its solution. This is fine and others like Talos Pinciple get away with it quite well (though to be fair, I didn't like having to backtrack, to fix a solution after thinking about how it should work, there either, so maybe this is juts a me problem). Here on the other hand I spend most of the time trying to find the puzzle and multiple times I ended up backtracking way too far (there is no room concept separating puzzles and preventing you to travel way back). As such I didn't make it too far in and most puzzles I've encountered thus far were fairly basic (which wouldn't be bad to ease the player into the experience, but when most time is spend running around, not sure where to go, I'd like the puzzles themselfs to pack enough of a punch to make me want to stay). The concept of repeating space with rotating gravity is nice and looks gorgeous, so if this were more of a exploration focused game with narrative, I'd probably be thrilled about it, but for the puzzles it more often than not makes navigation unnecessarily convoluted. The game also gives me slight motion sickness, which has occasionally happened with other first person games as well, but for other games that I liked, I have sat through it and allowed myself to get used to the way movement works, but here it just didn't seem worth the time.Why might you still like it? The idea is very neat and navigation does feel good (when you are exploring, when just wanting to get from A to B not so much). The visuals and the infinitely repeating world look great. The puzzles may very well become more challenging later down the line and maybe you are more adept at figuring out where to go to actually find the puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Solving puzzles by traversing impossible geometry and sometimes non-euclidean space by manipulating gravity, what's not to like?Similar to The Witness there's no hand holding. Every sort of (puzzle) mechanic is first shown in short discrete area by itself before the player is confronted with more and more complicated versions and combinations of them. Show, don't tell. The only "tutorial" is a minimal overlay that informs the player what key or mouse button to press.The graphics are somewhat minimal and might not be for everyone. Given possible amount of geometry on screen at one time anything more would easily end up in an unreadable, cluttered mess. You might miss out if this is the only reason you don't get this.The soundtrack is simply beautiful and I can see myself listening to it alone a couple of times over the next days or weeks. So far specially Trust Fall stood out for me, maybe due to some similarity to parts of the Blade Runner 2049 soundtrack. I was pleasantly surprised to find out that the download includes a FLAC version besides the usual MP3 and wish more games would actually give the buyer the option to get a lossless format. I was expecting to buy it again on Bandcamp to get a FLAC version before looking into the folder - now I hope for a Vinyl release so I can throw more money at this.P.S. I'm only one hour deep into this but honestly: Even if there's only 1-2 hours of content left I'm already absolutely happy with my purchase as the time so far has been a blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I would say this is a unique game to experience. You can do a lot of interesting puzzles with the fractal level designs that you'll have to readjust your brain to think out of the box. The puzzles do get pretty samey after a few hours especially since a lot of the non-fractal mechanics are mainstays in the first person puzzle genre, but it doesn't outstay it's welcome at about 3-4 hours of gameplay. If you like the genre pick it up on sale and you won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A three dimensional puzzle game where you can change the point of gravity, 90 degrees at time. The surreal "artistic" environments don't seem nor surreal nor artistic, more like confusing and empty. Story is absent without a parents' justification. Go play Antichamber and Portal, instead. This one is boooooooooooring.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with wonderful low-poly geometry and colorful shading.My only complaint is that it wasn't longer.None of the puzzles were particularly confusing or difficult but they were still complex enough to feel satisfying. One you realize they did a great job with the stage geometry guiding your next move, you can flow through the rooms pretty fast.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, wonderfully made. Very creative use of the properties of infinity, in addition to the intriguing ways the game handles spatial manipulation. Fantastic graphics in the... certain... areas, and the end was absolutely riveting in terms of the animation. Soundtrack was subtle, but added beautifully to the atmosphere of the game. Overall a very solid puzzle game that I would play time and time again.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: The main gimmicks shown within  may be simple, but the levels and their infinitely impossible structures scream complexity into this wonderful puzzler.  Each stage of the game presents new mechanics throughout, and utilizes them in many clever ways.  I did find myself lost in a few of the puzzles this game had to offer from time to time, but it didn't take me long to find the solution each time.  There are even some extra secrets buried within this game.  Not only that, but unlike other puzzlers, this game has no limits to what you can do to solve each puzzle.  This lack of a boundary, along with the extra secrets, kept me coming back to replay this game.  While there may be no dialogue within this game that tells a story, the breathtaking artwork speaks the story for itself.  While I may have finished this game in around 4 hours, replaying the game for the extra secrets will bring in a longer play time.  I highly recommend you play through the entirety of this beautiful game, as it offers a mind-blowing journey that's unlike any other.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to put into words, but what makes this game so great are the endless constructions that appear to be filtered through a kaleidoscope lens. It's out of the ordinary, but if it manages to entrap you within its perfect lines and infinite polygons, I guarantee you'll have one of the most unique video game experiences you've ever had. Manifold Garden goes beyond the realm of video games to become an artistic representation of impossible architecture, a brilliant adventure of exploration and puzzles, and a section of audiovisuals that is both minimalist and surprising.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I kinda came from Antichamber when I actually found out that I like this kind of game and that I wanted to play a game like that again: Weirdly build up where simple things dont make sense in the normal way, simple desing and puzzles that are more than bringing object A to spot B in a normal way. I also expected the game to be different from the pictures but I got defitly surprised by how the game works. Its such a simple concept but it got put into this game so well done that the game is really fun to play. The soundtrack is amazing, chilled background music fitting the desing.The desing was amazing, absolutly beautiful with the only FPS drop for me beeing in the ends of the levels where the effects are more extrem, nothing thnat bothers me. During the gameplay it always worked fine.The idea of the game is really good executed. Switching gravity in whatever way you want and the infinite levels. I needed to look arround often to understand what to do and then it was just a matter of time until I figured it out.It is confusing and orienting is difficult but when you understand how things work you can orient yourself more easily.One thing was I wished the last level was a bit more complicated, like using all gravitations maybe or more complex puzzles, instead it felt like going through all colors while some of the puzzles where extremly easy, but that is not too bad.The last few achievements are brutal in my opinion, you can propaby find them out if you play the game really carefully if you want to get them by yourself, I personally didn´t. I found the 2nd ending achievements (I would call it that for here) really complex. I´m sure if you go this route you can propably end up with the win, for me it was way to complex and I think I would not have gotten the solution in the end. Nothing bad from the game, it´s just hard.But I can defitly recommend the game, it had a challenge that is not too extreme and you can easily understand it while still having puzzlefun.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on a whim and didn't play it until like, a year later.  If you like slower paced puzzle games this is pretty solid and the visuals push it to pretty great.  The trailer makes it look overwhelming, but you start understanding how the game looks pretty quickly and it's overall pretty intuitive after the first few tutorials parts.  My only issue with the game is that those tutorial parts are kind of long and they don't really show what the rest of the game is like.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: This is by FAR the most beautiful game I've ever played. From the visuals, the audio, the mechanical smoothness, everything. The visuals are stunning and intriguing, the audio is immersive and enthralling, the worldspace bends your mind as you bend with it. 11/10, my top gaming experience of the year.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the open world exploration and no hand holding feel of Outer Wilds, this game is for you.Puzzles will test your problem solving skills, and for impatient gamers, they'll become frustrated and resort to looking at guides. However, play the game you want, there is no fail state unless you completely bug out the game. Enjoy this gem because you only get to play it blind once.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm several hours in and loving the game very much. I'm a huge fan of puzzle/adventure games, with many titles under my belt. _childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is visually stunning. The MC Escher-type fractal environments are incredible to fly through, and are worth the price of admission alone. The audio design and music also elevate the experience even further. That said, the puzzles leave a lot to be desired. They often include a somewhat tedious "find the cube tree in the giant fractal maze" and tend to be much more focused on giving your eyes a "wow" factor and not really caring too much about your brain. I wasn't really ever stuck on a puzzle - you kind of just stumble through them. The majority of your time will be spent just looking around for the key puzzle elements - what door do I need to get through, where's the thing that opens that door, where is the key for that door. Once you have the elements, the puzzles tended to become very trivial (with a few nice exceptions).Overall, I still absolutely recommend the game, but I can't help but feel let down by the puzzle design. There is a LOT of things they could have done with these mechanics, but instead the puzzles and gameplay take a back seat. At the end of my 3 hours playtime, I felt like the overall experience was somewhat imbalanced, even though there was clearly so much artistry put into this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Manifold Garden is what happens if Portal puzzles took place in a M.C. Escher painting that you could explore in any direction. What sets this apart from similar games is how you manipulate the environment: instead of mobility tools, you simply rotate the entire world. Each side of the world matches a color, and interactive objects will stay locked in place when you rotate away from them. To put it even simpler, physics are locked outside of your axis; for example, you can walk up water and then switch back to its color at the top and redirect the flow.Everything is well-paced to introduce new concepts, interactive objects, and complexity over time so you never get bored. Most puzzles appear to have several solutions, and there's even an achievement for playing straight through without "completing objectives correctly". It's difficult to explain this game's actual gameplay without getting into spoilers... Not only because it's relatively short, but also because almost every new puzzle introduces a new concept or teaches you a new way to approach a previous one. The only real issue I have with this game is that it's the only desktop game I can think of that's given me vertigo, not only when looking down, but also when looking up. I have no issues playing VR so your mileage may vary, but some people might physically be incapable of playing this. Although I'd never finish it, I wish there were a 1:1 VR option so I could feel my brain trying to escape my skull every five seconds. It's definitely a unique visual experience, but the puzzle element is on-par with Portal, and significantly less complex than 2D games in the genre. The only puzzle I was really stumped on was the last one, and that was because the area had two "layers" unlike all the previous zones. It's worth playing but the asking price is definitely way too much. As usual, recommended on a discount if you haven't already finished Portal 1 & 2 yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: What really sets the game apart aren't the puzzles but the atmosphere. The fractal based visuals and the atmospheric soundtrack make this one of the most unique puzzle games out there. The endless repetition isn't just for show either since most of the puzzles will require you to fall onto the next iteration of the same level. This might also be triggering for some people because even though most of it is only really happening on a 27 inch screen in front of me, I had goosebumps from my fear of heights almost throughout. Some trippy sequences and areas also gave me this weird fight-or-flight feeling and I was tense through a lot of it but not at all in a bad way. There's really nothing that can hurt you in the game though some of the visuals are meant to be somewhat unsettling. The dev really found an incredible theme here and executed it perfectly. The way the geometry just fades out into infinity makes for some thrilling sights almost every step of the way.On the puzzle front, the game isn't particularly tough. You're mostly trying to navigate and find the puzzle or execute what you know you want to do more often than figure much of it out. You're mostly interacting with blocks and trying to get them into the right pads and other mechanics that I don't want to spoil. It's a fairly short game and I finished it in about 4.5 hours with minimal help at one point cause I forgot a mechanic but otherwise the most confused you'll be is when looking for what to do next.I'd recommend this to anyone looking for an FPS puzzler a la Antichamber which this seems to use heavily as inspiration for the structure. The visuals and atmosphere alone are worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: This game could have been great but it is just far too easy and I feel like a lot of the "I don't know how to solve this puzzle" is not based on you not knowing how to solve it and more to do with you just not being able to find the one red block shoved in some corner of the far too big maps.  The maps are huge to facilitate the idea and visuals of a repeating infinite landscape which look great but just make a lot of the "puzzles" a trek of 10 min to stumble upon the last cube and the second you see the last block you know how to solve the puzzle, of what I played I can think of one puzzle that I had to think about and it was not for long. The thing that really killed this game from me was when I spent 30 min after coming back to the game after saving and quitting and apparently I left a cube that you need right after finishing the red levels that I did not bring with me through the door and could not for the life of me get back to the red cube, I looked up a walk-through and it seems the door I need to go through is ether closed and I can't get through or I just can not find it in the too big maps.  A lot of the map design almost feels like padding to add to the run time of the game with the puzzles being so easy, If you just had the parts in front of you to do the puzzle there just would not be a puzzle to begin with because you would just be moving a cube onto a pedestal and the game would have lasted an hour.I also want to say that one of the things that got me to buy this was all the people saying "It like antichamber" and that is only in the non-euclidean world structure, this game has nothing on antichamber in terms of puzzles and respect of time and the non-euclidean world of antichamber is far more fun and intriguing to explore and when I finish a puzzle in antichamber I can just go do the next puzzle not spend 20 min looking for the last block I need. If you have not played antichamber buy that, it sometimes goes on sale for 2 buck but is worth the 20 it asks at full price if you really need a non-euclidean puzzle right now and if you have already played antichamber play it again because this ain't it. This game was over hyped.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to put my finger on exactly why I dislike this game as much as I do. For context, I love puzzle games, and walking simulators. Portal 1/2 and The Stanley Parable are some of my favourite games of all time, and another favourite is Monument Valley (on IOS, but SO much better than this - seriously) which I suspect this game was partially inspired by. Maybe the problem is that aside from the nice visuals, this one is really lacking in substance.The spaces are big and often infinitely repeating, which is cool - but they feel really lifeless. Navigation is a real slog and feels confusing in a not-fun (as opposed to wonder-filled) way. You sort of float along, and it takes ages to reach anywhere, and everything's so big and empty there's no reference point of how fast you're even walking. No headbob, no jump button to fool around with - literally just walking (and falling). There's graphical glitches from time to time, and sometimes I 'died' somehow without any real explanation of what caused it. I guess sometimes you can fall too far? The game also forgot my progress on a section a few times when I had to put it down.The biggest failing of Manifold Garden is it doesn't really have good puzzle design. Compare it to Portal: Portal introduces mechanics and then slowly, methodically introduces iterations that allow you to be challenged but not frustrated, before putting everything together for complex but fully comprehensible grand finales. This game's puzzle design feels amateurish in comparison, and either abandons its mechanics before they become compelling or skips to the convoluted bit without any of the natural progression you're supposed to do beforehand.Lots of the puzzle solutions also really feel like exploits, because the rules of the game are so murkily defined, it feels like you're in this unfinished tech-demo/test level where you're half-breaking the game and the designer hasn't really thought about what you can or might do. When you solve a puzzle you often don't know if you were even supposed to do it that way but the game lets you progress anyway. Really unsatisfying, depressingly unfinished feeling and ultimately a giant disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Manifold Garden

_childDocuments_.review: Utterly stunning aesthetic, but the puzzles are nowhere  as challenging or clever as they look at first glance. Manifold Garden is a spiritual successor to Antichamber, building on its minimalist art direction to great effect, and running with the infinity mechanic that Antichamber briefly showcased. Occasionally it wanders into Portal's territory, but its visits feel more like a respectful nod rather than a shallow usurping of Portal's ideas.The pacing's a little inconsistent in that you'll finish some areas in literally a single puzzle while others keep you running around for much longer. Where to go next is often vague as well, such that you'll find yourself falling around randomly looking for the next puzzle, which you'll discover but still not be sure you're in the right place. I remember one area in which I finished a puzzle only to wonder if I even needed to do it in the first place, as the piece I needed to finish that section was already available.Some games try to be "art first, game second" (Inside, The Turing Test, Little Nightmares), and, while I wholeheartedly support the usage of gaming as a medium for other arts/ideas, this particular genre often runs afoul of making the game elements bad enough that they don't justify the art that rides on top; almost like the game elements were an afterthought or merely an excuse for the designer to peddle their true passion (notably, The Turing Test is an absolute shocker for this). However, I feel Manifold Garden passes this hurdle as its game elements are clear and strong enough to support the real beauty of the game, which is the showcasing of infinite space and the environment that comes with that.Overall, I wouldn't recommend it at full price unless you want the visuals, which are truly something. Puzzles initially look daunting, but you'll solve them with a little tinkering. Turns out you can't do much with the "infinite space" concept as a puzzle prompt, but it doesn't half make for some amazing visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, relatively short game. Initially thought that it's supposed to be a successor to Antichamber. Later I found out that it's made by someone else. The similarities between the two begin and end at both using a non-Euclidean game engine. While Antichamber is significantly more difficult, Manifold Garden is more visually impressive and intuitive in its design.+  allows for interesting puzzles and spectacular level design. It's technical complexity wonderfully complements the developer's art direction.+  the game only gives you the minimal keybindings that you need to know. The rest is taught through gameplay alone. This being said, there is some kind of hand holding implemented in the level design. If you need to take  steps to complete a level (especially an "outdoors" one) and you just finished step , then step  and its solution are staring you right in the face.+  4-6h is adequate for this type of game, in my opinion.-  may be a bit confusing at first. Orange can be misinterpreted as yellow, and purple as blue. Once you know what to expect it's not an issue. Note that you can change the color scheme in the game's settings.-  there is a huge difficulty disparity between some levels. This may be only my opinion and others may find themselves struggling in other areas of the game, but the level with Tetris blocks was murder... The next two took 20m and 15m respectively.-  why not?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything superliminal is not.That sentence comes from having played the games rather close together and having thereby a pretty good comparison from the genre. My praise will therefore reflect my grievances with the other game, consider it a 2 in 1 review.Exhibit A: Manifold garden is beautifully consistent: any rule you learn once stays that way for the remainder of the game, never flinching even if a puzzle would be easier to do without it or even if it´s presence may confuse you about how to actually go about solving a puzzle. Now that might sound either duh or mildly inconvenient if you have little experience with physics bending puzzle games, but believe me, it´s crucial. It´s what makes portal so enjoyable, aside from the characters. Every single puzzle you feel like you had all the tools and all it took was a bit of ingenuity to put them together correctly. Furthermore, you might be asking why that is praiseworthy, aren´t game mechanics supposed to be consistent? Well, it is praiseworthy because of how far the game goes outside of normal physics. Portal manages to stay consistent with, well, the titular portal. Other physics puzzle games manage it with the tried and true cube, beam and occasional light platforming. Manifold Garden manages consistency with 1. changing the direction of gravity 2. infinitude in basically every direction at almost all times 3.flowing water and 4. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ timestop mechanics (I´ll elaborate later) on top of the standard boxes! Not to mention ...Exhibit B: It never feels gimmicky! I cannot stress enough how natural the rules of this peculiar little (actually infinite) world feel. You have multiple opportunities to encounter mechanics before they become crucial for a puzzle, like encountering the flowing water and thinking at first it might just be decorative, but uuh boy it sure isn´t! Whenever expected to learn a new mechanic you are put into a situation where trying it out is designed to feel just plausible enough to not feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but presentet ambivalently enough to not feel like the game is trying to hold your hand. Later on, old mechanics (with arguably exactly one exception) do not get forgotten but are expanded or made to interact with the new ones in increasingly creative, fun and frankly mind-blowing ways. The consistent feeling adds to the world´s authentic ...Exhibit C: Atmosphere. From the graphical presentation strongly reminiscent of Antechamber to the subtle yet fitting and all the more impactful when intensified musical score, this world is pure Art. You feel like contributing to the creation or at least cleanup of a hyperdimensional  art installation, or the titular garden. You are rewarded for completing each "gauntlet" of puzzles by jaw-dropping sights so beautiful you will sometimes actively stay in a "solved" room and infinityfall through it some to look at what your work has amounted to. Not many games of this genre manage to make rewards for puzzles more than the inherent satisfaction and the ability to continue, this one does. This feature is also strongly supported by ...Exhibit D: The freedom. This game, except in obvious cases where your further manipulation with the world prevents it, basically lets you backtrack or get anywhere within it you were or can see (except for glassed machines but hey, them´s the breaks). You do not have a path charted out, you do not have to go on, you can and will loop back again and again to some places, changing some each time you visit and you start looking forward to visiting again! At one point the game had me searching feverishly for a sollution to a puzzle, backtracking to somewhere I was 2 hours before in seconds, before realising that 1. there was no way i could solve my present problem with any material in the previous room and 2. the fact I even thought this might be the sollution to a puzzle shows just how interconnected and, just, whole this world with quite alien geography and geometry to our own feels. EDIT: While writing I wanted to backtrack to a specific point way back and found out i couldn´t for no obvious in-universe reaseon, guess there had to be some issue, eh? After all the designers are still only human...The last bit is somewhat spoilery, therefore only read on if you want to hear about something that might quite possibly makes the dicussed elements feel way less authenticbecause you heard my vague description of it. You have been warned!If you made it to the end, I both sallute you and am sorry for making such a wall of text. The game has left a genuine impression on me and I had to vent somewhere. If this review motivates a single person to get the game or finds some resonance in another player looking for other´s experiences, it will have achieved more than enough to justify it´s existence.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of physical puzzle games, don't think - just buy. Manifold Garden is a masterpiece - at once terrifying and spectacular in its design. The feeling of immensity is breathtaking and unique among puzzle games. For that alone, it's worth a purchase. While the puzzles themselves are on the easy side, the experience of the game is something amazing.The basic mechanics are simple. Essentially, move the colored blocks to the correct locations to unlock the next area. The twist is your ability to rotate the entire game world, changing gravity to help you traverse the Escher-like, infinitely recursing levels in different directions and move blocks. Overall, as puzzles go, they are on the easy side. It took about 5.5 hours to complete the main game, and no single puzzle took more than about 20 minutes. I'd estimate the total number of puzzles is about 50 - so some of them are quite trivial. But, it can be easy to get disoriented, especially on some of the larger levels, which to me is part of the experience of Manifold Garden. I noticed only one bug:  Unfortunately, unlike some other physical puzzle games, there is only one way forward. If you get stuck on a puzzle, too bad. You can't go to another puzzle and come back later. Given the structure of the game world however, I can't imagine how it could be any other way. It's easy to imagine puzzles in Manifold Garden that would have been deviously hard, and perhaps that would be an excellent extension of the product at some point. There are certain game mechanics that, strung together, would have been truly mind bending. Actually, most of the puzzles can be solved in only two or three "moves" and near the end, I did feel like the game could benefit from one or two truly challenging levels, combining some of the more space-twisting mechanics together with a more complex series of operations required to solve them. But really, I can't think of another puzzle game that captures a similar  while playing it. Manifold Garden is truly a one-of-a-kind game, more than just the sum of its puzzles, a game worth experiencing just for the sense of immensity, the technical accomplishment, and the opportunity to explore a kind of 4-dimensional space in a satisfying and unique way.
