_childDocuments_.review: An awesome remake of the original game that lived up to my expectations. Although there are moments that are outdated and that could be changed according to modern standards, the game still feels damn good and refreshing. My deepest regards to the developers of the original game and the remake. I hope the System Shock 2 remake will not disappoint either.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original, but System Shock 2 is one of my favorite games ever. And I say that without nostalgia googles, since I discovered the game just a few years ago. When I've heard that they were doing a remake of the original, I decided to wait until there to try it.And I waited, and I waited, and I waited... Finally we have it here, and is it worth the wait?Let me cut the crap: hell yes, it is. Again I was able to fully immerse myself in this world of claustrophobic hallways, dark corners and mangled corpses. There wasn't anything quite like SS series after it. Dead Space? Bioshock? Good games in their own, but, although the settings may be similar, the atmoshpere isn't. Too much action/shooting, too much jumpscares/setpieces. What makes SS unique is that its focus is actually on slow, tense exploration. Combat is important, but you won't be shooting dozens of enemies at once, the ones you meet are really thought, and conserving your resources is actually important (besides cyberspace, but that really sucks). That may not be everybody's cup of tea, but also makes it stands out from most FPSs. Play on Combat difficulty 3 if you like more shooting (I played with everything on 2).Knowing that Nightdive's remake is very faithful to the original, I can see how much SS2 owns to its predecessor (to the point of feeling just an upgraded version sometimes). The progression through the decks is very similar. However, SS1 (or at least the remake) doesn't have all those little secrets, nook and cranies to discover. It's a maze, but a more straightforward one. Moreover, the lack of RPG elements lowers replayability by a lot. Finally, I wish there was a difficulty slider for resource availability. Besides one or two moments at the beggining, I never ran out of resources, while in SS2 literally every bullet counts.I also liked the way they managed respawns, one of the most contentious points of the originals. I particularly dislike it, and one seemingly buggy moment at the beggining almost ruined the game for me (all killed enemies respawned at once at the same room in Medical). But the game gives you ways of disabling respawns, which are achieved pretty organically during gameplay. Light spoiler: Said the good things, we have to deal with the bad ones. After all, isn't System Shock if isn't as irritating and is enticing to play. Yes, the game is extremely disorientating and you'll have to break your immersion several times to check online what you are supposed to do. Play on Mission difficulty 1 if you want to avoid this. I preferred to just play my way and explore the levels, and look for help only when I'm stuck. Even knowing what you are doing, there is too much backtracking sometimes. Not the "good" one, when you go back to a previsous level to do something new, but when you have to retrace your steps just to find  something that you missed before (another very light spoiler, but truly a friend's advice: . As noted above, Cyberspace is the worst part of all game. Looks good, but it's boring, repetitive, and some sequences you'll have to replay half a dozen times and lost a lot of time until you get through it. This is the only difficulty setting I wish I could change after starting a game, but when you realize how bad it is, you'll probably be ten or more hours already in your game. On the technical side, enemy AI in this remake still could use a lot of improvement, since I won many battles by having the power of World's Geometry by my side.But all in all, it still was an awesome gaming experience. And, by the way, the final sequence is terrible. Truly terrible. But again, it won't be System Shock if doesn't have a bad enging. Well, at least it's better than "nah!"...
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a zoomer that has a problem with directions and zero attention spam, don't play this, this old school game design with modernized combat. _childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an incredibly pretty game that does an amazing job at upgrading citadel station graphically to the original, overall game play however I believe is a downgrade. Guns look great and have good animations but the act of shooting and the enemy getting hit does not feel all that responsive. Melee feels clunky and it doesn't feel like I'm hitting anything while swinging. There's also a few other gameplay things that are changed like "bosses" removing the ability to regenerate after you die which feels cheap in a bad way especially since they tend to do way more damage than enemies resulting in a quick and off guard death resulting in unnecessary time loss. I also feel like the inventory management feels like it's only there because it was in system shock 2, I don't think it fits the game all that well and feels like it only slows the pace of the game and serves as an annoyance. Another huge loss I personally feel is the music, while whats in the game is not bad on its own, it fails to give every floor any kind of unique atmosphere. It ends up making a lot of the floors end up feeling the same in terms of atmosphere which was the opposite in the original. Maintenance always stood out in the original because of its dark hallways and its droning song, now it reminds of the other floors, missing its dark hallways and having minimal soundtrack, like all the other floors.Also there's a handful of rather annoying bugs and soft locks I've encountered from energy draining when all the left modules were off, and to what killed my play through, items not staying in the elevators and not appearing the trash chute in reactor which is where I kept all my key items needed to progress which I didn't realize till 5 hours later in my play through.Overall, the game has an incredible presentation but lacks beyond that, it looks and runs like a 60$ game should but it plays and lacks the some of the atmosphere the original had that will cost only you 10$ on steam so I'm unsure to say what price this game should be, 40$ felt like too much but anything under feels like too little for how much effort went into the remake.Note: Also I will mention cyberspace is a big improvement over the original although I feel some of the sections drag for a bit and it's a bit mindless
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah good game....BUT there's a lot of little tiny things that kind of annoy me when I play it:-default controls are a bit strange IMO and I find I'm constantly tweaking them as a TON of things you'll use a LOT aren't even bound to a key.-some of the UI stuff seems messed up control wise (see media section of MFD)-auto-saves being practically non-existent later in the game after lulling you in to a sense of security by having a bunch on the first 2 floors-scrolling through media section for passwords is stupid, game needs a "known passwords" section-a ton of icons on the map aren't labelled at all and doesn't get any info when you mouse over it, the legend has like 5 things in it, yet there's well over a dozen different map icons, This drives me INSANE.-game just completely lacks an overall ammo counter which seems like an oversight.This stuff can and should all be fixed with a patch or two Nightdive, please.MAYBE some of this stuff is due to it trying to be like the original? But the original is still playable + there's the enhanced edition, a full remake is supposed to fix issues like this and add QoL improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Look at you, hacker.Excellent remake; it's authentic to SS1 where it counts, bringing back the same level designs, objectives, and (lack of) hand-holding. Plus, the retro, pixel aesthetic is a nice ode to the original. However, it's also not afraid to bring in new ideas and systems, better bridging the gap between this game and its RPG, horror-oriented sequel.SHODAN's sound design is as great as ever and her new (and rewritten) audio logs are fantastic (save for two that are a tad too melodramatic). Same goes for Lansing, Diego, and all the other crew members.I do wish cyberspace was a bit faster (and more meaningful); after you experience it the first few times it starts to become a bit tedious. Regardless, that does little to diminish what a fantastic experience this was. Here's hoping Nightdive remakes the sequel.

_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really cool and straight up my alley as it is just a really well put together immersive sim. Actually the grandfather of them all basically. It is just so neat going around trying out what works, hacking (ok cyberspace is not that great to play through but alright), looting etc. It is absolutely not the deepest immersive sim I have played as the toolset can be surprisingly limited as it is a very faithful remake of a 20+ years old game (you will not be stacking boxes or really complete tasks in drastically different ways here life Prey for example), but what is here is fun to use. The combat also feels pretty good but not amazing and the different enemies are all fun (bosses are a bit mixed though and the final one was super underwhelming). Exploring the space station is so much fun and there are so many little nooks and crannies with different loot and info about what is going on. The presentation of the game is spectacular. I love this retro future neon style that they have put together and I especially like how the textures are all intentionally pixelated on high poly models. Sound is also great, music as well and SHODAN especially is absolutely incredible how they have made her sound. The story is also very interesting and feels very organic in how it is presented through both environment, logs and audio files. Awesome stuff.The only complaint really that I have is how information is presented to you. I get that it is intentionally very hardcore as you have no objectives or anything like that written down in a log (sure, you can search through your logs for info) and it makes it pretty difficult to understand what you are even doing. I am managing mostly fine with completing objectives as I usually go through these games scouring every corner, and I do understand the main objective of the game, but most of the time I feel like I am completing objectives without even knowing how or why. I have had to google a few times as I just felt completely lost at times, especially when at the executive level (and everything that followed until engineering) as it got pretty frustrating that I just had no idea what I was supposed to do or what to even look for. It is sort of a minor complaint though as like I said I am managing mostly fine by just playing the game, and I respect the game in a way for doing this, but I do not think it would ruin the hardcore experience a lot by just having some sort of page with objectives. I am not saying it should even say where to complete it as exploring the station is the core of the game, but just some better info to give some more context to what you are even doing so that you avoid just running in circles for hours. Other than that complaint, that a lot of people may consider a great addition which is fine as well, this game is absolutely stellar. If you like immersive sims like Deus Ex or Prey (or basically any Arkane game lol), you should really experience this remake of a legendary game as it is where it basically all started. I would not say it is the best one I have played as Prey still holds that title I think and others have improved on certain parts of the formula (which you would kind of hope would happen in 20+ years), but it is fantastic either way.8.5-9/10
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game! Not the most accessible, but there is something refreshing about older games with the are just about the gameplay and story. No enemy level-scaling, tutorials, quick-time events, DLC, multiplayer, or microtransactions. The game doesn't try to force you into a particular play-style and you can go where you want. You are just a person on a space-station trying to survive. You can heal as and regenerate energy as much as you want (if you find those locations and are willing to run back to them). You can revive, but only once you unlock the story-appropriate points.I never played the original, but I love being able to experience the story in a more accessible form. Imagine the original Doom, but with the beautiful graphics you remember, not as it actually looked. And then imagine that someone set the game in space and wrote an engaging story for it! Sure, the enemies don't have great animations and it's sometimes hard to tell if the weapons/bullets are having an effect on them. But it's all about expectations and that's perfectly suitable for a remake like this.The game ran rock-solid for me, I loved the environment/level design, and the movement and shooting just felt good. Heading back to my surgery machine to heal up after exploring on another level started to feel like coming back to my home base. My favorite touch of the game is the light switches. There's nothing that quite makes the station feel like a real place as much as a simple thing like being able to turn the lights on in some of the rooms.

_childDocuments_.review: It is because of insects that Shodan survives. I was there, Xerxes. I was there 30.. years ago ... when Shodan first took Citadel Station. It should have ended that day, but evil was allowed to endure. Shodan kept the station. The connection of hacking was broken. There's no strength left in the world of meat and bone. They're scattered, covered, and smothered.

Get it, you won't regret it... insect!

_childDocuments_.review: Good but occasionally frustrating and not in a fun way. (e.g. SHODAN manifesting a gank squad to ♥♥♥♥ you up is fun, the map being a maze you initially have to navigate is fun, the map being a maze that you have to back track through while there is a trickle of enemies occasionally spawning to just get in the way, isn't)There was a point in the game where I had to search a level for an objective. Unfortunately the map hadn't registered that a door I had walked past earlier (as it was locked at the time) was actually a door and not a wall so when looking at my map it looked like I searched everywhere. I spent ages and all my health supplies looking over and over. After that the game had given me a headache that wouldn't go away, especially as I had used all available health kits doing this repeated search meaning that I had to resort to just dying and re spawning removing any stakes I had in trying to stay alive.There is a fair amount of backtracking in the game, which is fine but when some levels have areas that are just mazes that require you to slowly crawl through, it's just annoyingForcing the player to take note of codes is neat however the game doesn't give you a means to do this, meaning you either need to go find a pen and paper or tab out, ruining immersion. It shouldn't have been hard to add a notepad into the cyber UI.On the topic of codes, there is a code which, looking at the original game, went from obvious to it being important, but having no context until later, to being just another part of the background noise. meaning you're much less likely to take note of it until later.The economy is ... bad. The ammo economy is pretty much never an issue as the enemies spew them out, especially at the end. My problem is with vending machines and health.  Vending machines having limited stock of health items disincentivises healing and incentivises save scumming or just dying repeatedly, granted this was only be a problem because I got stuck and might become one on harder difficulties. That said I only struggled for that one part, the rest of the game I was swimming in the stuff and later on just throwing them away, something which could be mitigated by having a proper economy.The AI is terrible, half life 1 did it better. Peak, shoot, peak, shoot. (EMP grenades and laser rapier are cool though)cyber space, the hated part of the original game still sucksThe ending is also pretty bad6/10 Prey(2017) is better and Nightdive should've taken a couple more liberties in changing the game for the better similar to Crowbar Collective on Black Mesa
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't play the System Shock when it first came out in 1994, so I cannot compare it to the remake, but I did play System Shock 2.That said, this game has this old school feeling I was looking for, with labyrinthic level design, unforgiving enemies (most of the time) and menacing atmosphere.As a huge fan of immersive sim, its great to be able to (re)discover one of the first (the first?) that started this genre.So maybe we will finally see System Shock 3 one day?
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up playing System Shock 2, the mysteries of the first game were never really revealed to me until later on. By that time, I was unable to play it; just due to the fact that I found everything, especially the UI, to be incomprehensible and impossible. Thankfully with this remake, I can see what the original System Shock was trying to do, trying to be, and it is amazing.This game will not hold your hand, just like the original. If you choose a harder difficulty, be prepared to suffer. The game will also not tell you where to go or what to do. You better explore the levels well, and hopefully find the audio or text logs that tell you what you should do. While at times I found this to be obviously frustrating, I also immensely enjoyed it. It was extremely rewarding to figure it all out. Not having markers on the map pointing where to go, or a dozen journal entries with areas that were mentioned to go to, or secrets that have been revealed, or just what to do, was actually fun! You have to use your brain, and do some thinking. I don't think that is a bad thing to have in a game like this. I think this sort of thing should be done more.The graphics were pretty good, especially considering that my computer is decently old. The only problems I had was that enemies frequently would get stuck in death jiggle physics. Even after a patch came out that was supposed to fix this, limbs would still bounce up and down endlessly, wires would flail around, etc. It was a bit annoying, especially when I walked back into a room and thought there was an enemy and had a heart attack; but it was just a dead guy jiggling about.While I understand why they didn't go with the exact music from the original, I do wish that some of the more iconic tracks had been remade. What I don't really understand is why there isn't more music in general. There were a few times when really creepy and eerie tracks came on, or heart pounding action tracks, but they were all extremely few and far between. I appreciated being able to creep around and hear my enemies walking/talking so I could prepare myself and take action with the right gear and weapons, but the wonderful atmosphere that they created for this game really could have been spiced up by some more music.The gun-play in this game is pretty good. You want to slowly explore and peek around corners to nail an enemy with an EMP grenade and finish them with a rail-gun blast? Wonderfully done. Want to run around like a crazy person with the speed boots flinging explosive mines and using a laser rapier to disassemble your enemies into their component parts? Perfectly acceptable and well implemented. You hit hard in this game, but enemies hit harder. When I had secured the med-bay and restarted the reincarnation machine, I finally felt safe. Before that happened, or on levels where there was no machine, damn that death cut scene man...The final boss fight with SHODAN was... interesting. I definitely understand and agree that there needs to be something there as a culmination to the game, but I don't understand why it was done the way it was. While the original was janky and Cyberspace was awful, SHODAN literally erasing your screen and replacing you and your self, with her, is such a crazy and evil idea. I don't know why they changed Cyberspace for this one area in the remake, or why it went on for so, so long. I think that only one of those three 'stages' would be necessary. On the topic of Cyberspace, I think the way they changed it was wonderful and massively improved the game, completely, full stop.I think that also describes my review for this game: Wonderfully and massively improved. A complete and extremely high recommendation. Play this game, enjoy the horror, and let the 90s (and SHODAN) consume you.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: Think of it as a bit like an 'FPS Metroidvania' and you'll be on the right track. I've never played the original, so I can't speak to its faithfulness, but it is an *excellent* game.That said be aware there is a lot less hand-holding compared to modern games. For the stations complexity it is remarkably hard to get actually lost, but it is easy to get confused about your next objective, especially if you're coming back after a break.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely pristine remake with a TON of love and respect for the original with tweaks that make the experience better and more inmersive. _childDocuments_.review: A remake like this is a fine line. Change too much and you wont' have the sense of history, change too little and you end up wondering why they bothered. I think Nightdive did an admirable job here. Are there oddities? Sure. This isn't the perfect game that will cause the heavens to open and lead you to the promised land.  But they nade a game that has been too clunky to really play for decades accessible and enjoyable. Worth a pickup if you enjoy this kind of game, especially since its been a drought for the genre lately.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful re-contextualization of a classic, the system shock remake is the proto immersive sim and a great shooter. You, a rat trapped in a maze have nothing but your wits to explore large maps to locate better weaponry, ammo cache's and lore the discern the true depth of SHODAN's depravity in her delusions of godhood. as compelling as it was back in he 90's. System shock as of now is a remake worth your attention. Even now the devs are working to iron out what they had yet to add. the 7 years of work shown off with this small dev team. Definitely worth every penny even as of now. Despite how some ideas havent aged well. most notably cyber space.  Everything else works like a glove and itches that bunch of neurons in your brain thats all about scavenging and making trade offs that end with you earning more. Give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Link to full review:Find angrier, more unfiltered thoughts below. I don't hate SS(2023) overall, but I definitely don't like it. ---do you like floating around in a terrible 0g hacking minigame? do you like awful flip phone puzzle minigames? do you like inventory management minigames? and do you like environments that are more square and blocky than Minecraft? do you enjoy bulletsponge enemies? do you like labrynthine levels where every corridor uses the same texture and shares the same blocky shape? do you like infinitely respawning bulletsponge enemies, who will often drop in directly on top of you while you're trying to explore? and how do you feel about stealth? I hope you don't like it, because there isn't any in this game: every problem is solved with violence. System Shock 2 is old, but it holds up. I was expecting this remake--especially one that took eight ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years to make--to bring System Shock 1 up to at least the standards of the second game. At least. But it doesn't. Instead we get level design from 1994, and gameplay that has only two tactics: murder, and run away.The other reviews are right. This is a faithful adaptation of the original System Shock. It lacks any and all innovations of the immersive sim genre over the last thirty years, most notably including those of its own sequel. I hate the cliche of "there's a reason games aren't designed like that anymore," but come on. This is nothing but walking around clicking on everything, hoping it's an audiolog to pick up that'll tell you what to do, or the correct thing that you were supposed to click. Audiologs are the only guidance you receive, by the way, and finding them is your main incentive to explore; unfortunately, almost none of them actually contain important or relevant story information or objectives. Instead they're all, almost to a one, some idiot ranting about how he's turning into a mutant, or musing if the evil AI is actually evil. (Spoiler alert: she is.) I like being let loose without my hand being held, but some things, like, for example, on which of the fifteen floors should I start my search for the code that will let me reach the reactor; or, what do those giant red things do in the horrible pipe dream hacking minigame? Withholding this information doesn't actually accomplish anything except forcing me to waste time with trial and error. What has decidedly killed this game for me is the environmental design. Citadel Station does not look even remotely like a place where real humans once lived. At its best, it's a strange, ugly, confusing labyrinth of corridors, that feels more like a rat lab than a space station. At its worst, and unfortunately the worst is usual, it just looks like a level from Doom. I don't mind the low-fi art style, but SS2 feels significantly realer and more lived-in than this. This is just nothing. It's a video game. Somehow, even worse, if that's possible, they've opted to make interactable objects all green--and also make every wall and every electronic device green, so you can never spot what is or isn't interactable at a glance. It's some of the worst art direction I've ever seen in a video game--one of the most basic things, totally failed at here.My five hours of play today have made me want to do nothing but get a refund and go play the second game instead. I do not know what these other people are seeing, but I can't think of any explanation but that they are blind from nostalgia. I could bear a lot of small problems were it not for the minigames, which are what have pushed me over the edge to write a nasty review. ♥♥♥♥ these minigames. They all overstay their welcome; none are entertaining; all are miserable. If I ever have to enter cyberspace again, I'm going to destroy humanity with a laser drill. Let's bring out the cliche again: there is a reason why System Shock 2 got rid of this garbage.

_childDocuments_.review: I have never played the original and have no nostalgia for this game.It's freaking phenomenal. But it is certainly not for everyone. You really should take notes, you backtrack sometimes, the map is maze like and almost all halls look the same. It's a challenging and slightly dated design. The gun play feels good and once you get the lightsaber melee gets much better. I will definitely be replaying this game it feels like a game to be replayed.There are some things I wish I knew that I think people should know:1. TAKE NOTES. Dialogue will give codes, write those down. People will tell you tasks, write those down. I didn't and some stuff got confusing midway into the game. I know some people say you shouldn't look stuff up but I honestly felt like I really needed to for certain goals or what to do.2. This honestly feels more like a metroidvania than a immersive-sim. I think once you understand that certain design decisions start to make more sense and how you should progress.3. MAINTENANCE SUCKS. Maintenance's level really really wanted to make me quit. It's not clear how you should progress or what you need to do. The main problem stems from every other floor you can complete without having to go to other floors. Maintenance is only one where you need to go to multiple floors and then backtrack. I looked up probably six different guides and I had no clue how or what to do. I think it's important for new players to know that they should beat the executive floor, then backtrack to complete maintenance.This game is a 9/10 for me but I think people need to know what they are getting into and know it's not for everyone.Edit: I loved this game so much I tried 100%. As it turns out last achievements to get are broken. It's taken about 7 months to get some news about this. I guess they are still working on a patch. This is a little infuriating because they should've just fixed the numbers on those achievements and then work on patch 1.2. Pretty pissed now because I've tried 100%ing this game 3 times now and was so lost as to how I wasn't getting these achievments.

_childDocuments_.review: "We are dead and this is hell." - Nadine Cross, Stephen King's The Stand (1994)And yes there's a reason I picked that quote as I feel it's fitting for the game I'm about to go over. Before I do? Little history! It's 1995 and I've got some money in my pocket and I'm over at Incredible Universe here in the Phoenix-Metro Area. I'm over in the PC Games part of the store and picking up a copy of The Ultimate Doom as I never did get a chance to play the other Doom episodes and hey it's $20 bucks. I'm also looking at the discounted rack that just happens to be right next to the rack of EA CD-Rom Classics, for those of you a bit younger? That was the *Steam Sale* back then, you could grab something like Wing Commander 2 with it's expansions for $15 bucks. Granted you just got a CD-Rom with all of the manuals in PDF format, but hey you could get some pretty good games. Anyhow I see on the rack and in a bin next to the rack System Shock. There's the classic on the rack for $15 bucks, and somebody took the old System Shock Enhanced CD edition big box and put threw the same price tag on it. Now I had seen the review of it in PC Gamer a year back, and hey I'm a fan of Cyberpunk stuff, as me and my friends ran Shadowrun and Cyberpunk 2020 games.  I end up picking it up, I mean hey it's made by the same folks who did Ultima Underworld and it got a good review so why not?After getting home and installing it? It's hours later I'm in my room on my old Pentium 75 digging around in Medical some how being able to get some more ammo for my 9mm Mini-Pistol when SHODAN sends me an email screaming at me about how I will suffer her wrath as she sics a bunch of Cyborg Assassins at me. I forgot all about Doom. I'm trapped on this space station of the damned fighting an insane AI that reminds me every chance it gets that she will make me suffer and pray for death. I am dead and this is hell, and I'm loving every moment of it.And needless to say I was not only happy that Nightdive was able to bring back System Shock 2, but redo System Shock 1 with *vastly* better controls, and then I heard about the remake and now it's finally here. So how does it hold up? Perfect.**Story**I'm sure you've all heard this tale before, hell maybe some of you took elements of it and threw it into a Cyberpunk 2020 or Shadowrun game like I did. It's 2072 and a Hacker is able to break into the computer network of the Mega-Corp TriOptimum. He's caught and arrested (by folks who look very much like a Silencer from Crusader: No Remorse. BTW Nightdive if you are reading this? Beg EA to do something with Crusader please.) He's hauled up to Citadel Station and given a this time around one sided offer by TriOpt Executive and Corpo scumbag Edward Diego. Hack SHODAN (Sentient Hyper-Optimized Data Access Network) the AI controlling the station and remove her ethical subroutines, and he won't throw you out the airlock. Oh and he'll even throw in the military grade neural interface and the surgery for you... Real nice guy up there with good old Saburo Arasaka or the heads of the Renraku and Aztechnology corporations. Anyhow he lives up to his word, you get the interfact and six months down time in a healing coma. You come too six months later, and are contacted by Rebecca Lansing a TriOpt counter-terrorism consultant. Citadel has gone to hell, the crew on board are dead or much worse, SHODAN is now seeing herself as a goddess and wants to wipe out life on Earth. Stop SHODAN and you'll get a pardon for making this mess.And unlike the old 1995 System Shock? There's no intro video that tells you this, you get to play all of that out right from the start.**Gameplay**Ultima Underworld was the start of the immersive sim, System Shock was the refinement of it, with System Shock 2, Deus Ex, BioShock, Prey following up on it. System Shock here? It's a refinement of the refinement. You wake up and have *nothing* just a pipe to defend yourself with. You'll be checking everywhere for everything from medical items, weapons, ammo and upgrades for your cybernetic interface. Unlike System Shock 1? The remake now makes use of a grid inventory system, so you only have so much room to carry things. Also unlike the old System Shock there have been changes. There's no more useless weapons like the Dart Pistol or Stun Pistol. Each area of Citadel has a 'goal' of some kind besides surviving. This is the game that came up with the idea of fully voice acted audio logs, thus you will be grabbing those to find out how to move on.It's the little changes so far. Weapons now have upgrades to them, you can pick up junk and scrap them or haul the garbage over to a recycling bin and get credits that can be spent on supplies. You still have to do things like lower the security level of the level of the station you are on. The game doesn't play like an OS like it did back in the 1990's, but now more like a modern day title like Prey. And then there's cyberspace.See kids! Back in the 1990's we believed we'd be plugging or "Jacking In" our brains into the internet. And cyberspace in System Shock is generally what we believed it would be. Hackers would fly around stealing data and battling ICE programs and screwing around with the network to help our fellow mercs or Shadowrunners in the job. Those players in general hating the Netrunner/Decker player as they had their own 'game' to play if you will in Shadowrun and Cyberpunk. But yeah here? You fly around fighting ICE programs to gain access to new areas. Going to say... Part of me sorta misses the old VR Cyberspace from Cyberpunk titles, glad they kept this in even if I find it to be one of the weaker parts of the game.**Sound, Music, Graphics**Going to start with Music as the soundtrack is just wonderful this time around! System Shock in the 1990's had me flipping the old MIDI soundtrack off and putting on Stabbing Westward or Nine Inch Nails due to it being a bit of a mess. Really Zircon and Jonathon Peros did a great job with it, it's creepy has ties to BioShock but a bit of that techno flair at times.Sound? Pretty good, you can hear some sounds that are from System Shock 2. But lets talk voice acting and oh god lord it's good this time around! Not that the old 1990's System Shock was bad, but keep in mind a number of the 'voice actors' had been programmers and the like, thus the 90's System Shock sounded like you and your friends in a game of Shadowrun. Terri Brosius is of course SHODAN and while I don't know if they had her do new lines for the game? Well... SHODAN still can send a chill down your spine.Graphics wise? I sorta like what they did here as to me there's a bit of this modern 'retro' feel to it. Things look good, at least for me anyway. The game looks much more modern but you can see pixels and the like when close up to something. Also I'll give them credit there are things from the 1990's System Shock still in place. When coming down off a Berserk? I started to see the old System Shock 1995 Mutant sprites.**Overall**So far my time spent playing System Shock has been like seeing a very dear old friend from the 1990's again. We're both older now and not the same people from 1995. They made some changes for the better, I'm not the 16 year old kid who while he's enjoying himself, is a little mad that I can't just run around and treat the game like Doom or that Quake game I hear that's coming out next year.It's a throwback and a remake of a title I did love the hell out of. Going to warn some of you right now, this isn't a Boomer Shooter like Civvie 11 talks about. You are not going to be running around and playing it like Dusk or Boltgun. It's well worth the money, and I am happy to be back in the nightmarish hell that is Citadel Station. Outstanding job Nightdive.

_childDocuments_.review: This version of System Shock is hands down the definitive way to play not just System Shock 1, but to experience System Shock as an IP. Easily a 9.5 or 10 out of 10. Buy this game if you liked System Shock 2, Dishonored, Bioshock, or anything else vaguely immersive-sim related. You will not be disappointed.I think Nightdive modernized this game pretty much perfectly while still keeping the same vibe, enemies, levels, and even a lot of the same codes as the original System Shock. As someone who played through the DOSbox version multiple times, this is about as faithful as a remake can possibly be.Apparently Nightdive got flak from some review outlets for being so faithful to the formula and not taking more risks, but I think that's kinda stupid. Nightdive suffered from mission creep during this game's development and when it came right down to it, they decided to make sure the game they made was faithful and brought System Shock into modernity, and I know that wasn't an easy decision to make.Thanks for the hard work Nightdive; because of you guys, more people can experience one of my all-time favorite games.

It has enough surprises to ensure even veterans of the original don't get too complacent, while still demonstrating a deep respect for its roots - visually, musically, and conceptually.My only real criticisms relate to the poor sound propagation - very noticeable on surround headphones - and the extremely jank corpse ragdolling which is either inappropriately hilarious or alarming enough to waste one's ammo.When playing the original, I scoffed at the idea of anyone being idiotic enough to want an AI's ethical constraints removed. _childDocuments_.review: The original System Shock was one of my favorite games when younger, an interesting take on the fledgling first person shooter/exploration genre that was a bit overdesigned but a very memorable experience.  When a remake hit up Kickstarter, I threw some money at it, and over the years since basically came to accept that it was probably going to be one of those campaigns that didn't amount to anything.  I was pleasantly surprised to find out that not only did the remake actually end up coming out, it was pretty good and worth the wait.System Shock is effectively one of the progenitors of the Immersive Sim genre.  As a formative member, it lacks a lot of the enhancements that came with titles over the years, but it's still a game full of interesting interlocked levels, objectives that span multiple areas and are more complex than "find the key", resource management, environmental and audio storytelling, and puzzle solving.  SS Remake takes the core of what worked, expands on that some, makes some largely sensible redesigns, but still leaves the clunky-but-charming core intact rather than design it as if it was a brand new 2023 title.It's certainly not perfect, and some of that is due to the legacy design inherent in a game almost 30 years old. Some of the design changes don't add to the game in any particular way (especially the overly strict inventory limits), and the periodic boss fights tend to be tuned so high on the default difficulty settings that a deliberate and controlled journey around Citadel Station can suddenly morph into a quickload bonanza due to extreme damage spikes.  Also, unlike a lot of games that came later in the genre, there's not much replayability here as there's no character building to experiment with.If you've enjoyed titles that have come in the years since, like Deus Ex, Dishonored, Prey, or Bioshock, it's worth taking a look at System Shock to see where a lot of the genre originally came from; if you have fond memories of playing it before, then this is as good a way as any to take a trip down memory lane. I'd be happy to see Nightdive give System Shock 2 the same treatment in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a MUST PLAY remake, it is absolutely fantastic, needs next to no configuration at all to just get right-into play.  (i had to turn the audio down just a hair in settings so i could hear the voice chat of those who were in stream with me.) its so much better then the original, yet it pays respect to the second one (system shock 2) lining-up things that are all too familiar from that game. It adds little bits, not seen prior, that will make you recolect this version, when you proceed to play System Shock 2 afterward. Without making those little additions the Focus in this game. Easter eggs that you, if playing system shock 2, will get excited to see are brought more into focus in the second game.  That subtlety is HARD to achieve. It really is. Its often not even noticed by the player base. But those who become avid fans of their nostalgia later in life, progressing forward into the series, will appreciate the references. And it contributes the the whole experience of the series later on.Now The Original SystemShock was hard on the eyes.  This one can be difficult too, but less so, and for different reasons. Flat textures and LED's made the original difficult to view so much saturation and things looking similar, it was easier to get visually lost. In this version which is so much better, the strong saturation is reminiscent of the original as are the contrasting LED's on everything that are so strong. But 3d surfaces shadows and texture make it feel real.  So all the same feelings of the original are back. but with shading and darkness, making it much more horror and exhilarating then before. This might be the best Remake in HISTORY.This is better then the original, and better then the second game. yet balances that magical edge of not taking over or disrespecting either of those prior to it. This is some of the best work i have ever seen in gaming history poured into making the original game sooo much better, making it so much more real. For all its Draw, its maybe a bit Harder then the original., which works well, because there is a lot more drawing you in to keep playing and trying.  Kinda like Darksouls in the way that for as difficult as it may be, its fair and worth it, with enough interesting draws and pulls, that new players and old, will want to keep at it.  Which lengthens the play experience. Meaning you get a lot more out of your cost-to-game'time ratio.  Replay value is high.  Even though I've not reached the end yet, I almost don't want to. Because playing it, is whats fun. the Lore, is whats fun, Collecting and upgrading, hoarding, is whats fun. And trying the paths again even more efficiently then your first re-spawn, is whats fun. You know sometimes i consider leaving a negative review just because its what EVERYONE focuses on and reads.  Everyone wants to see why its bad. why its not recommended to play...  this gets a 5.5 stars out of 5.  this game is 120%. Because it was built based on something ALREADY great, and lovingly modified over a long thoughtful time, excellently and RESPECTFULLY reproduced, to improve on greatness.  Your group meetings and dev-socials paid off guys. Really!The original had flaws, and left me wanting for this or that. But only because of the limitations of the era and the hardware/software of the times.  It left me imagining my whole life what could have been better, or what would be taking it too far and detracting from the feel of the original with all the modern flashy-focus... the original was good, but limited by its era, They say copy-pasta is how we evolve and improve.  This team of devs, made that a matter of Fact. Clearly they discussed what taking it too far astray would be, and knew how to reel it in to maintain the original's experience. Bravo!I cant even express how much i am enjoying Panting and Sweating as i run through these Corridors.  It won't matter if the ending is short unepic or abrupt. I almost don't want to beat it, because how can anything compare with a perfect immortal Classic?I so much want to give this a bad review, just to get more cautious buyers to READ THIS REVIEW and give the game a shot. But i just cant click that 'not recommended" button. You devs have devoted time and torment to perfecting your respectful reproduction and making it even more emotionally impacting then the original, without damaging -anything- of the original. Breed and Reproduce you devs. we need more of your genes in the pool, Your lineage will prepare us for the day System Shock becomes reality.  Your magnificent grand children, will be the hackers that save humanity from something like Shodan!I cant even.   I cant even imagine better praise then this, You deserve it!

_childDocuments_.review: Spoiler free review- The game play, story, and environments are near 1:1 to the original from 1994. System Shock has returned to the world through a successful kickstarter by Nightdive Studios. This remake pays homage to the original while sprinkling in modern sensibilities and quality of life improvements. This ends up becoming a adrenaline pumping experience that will captivate new players and veterans to the series. Despite running on Unreal Engine, the visuals are stunning. Atmospheric and tense environments appear reimagined in the remake. Citadel Station looks terrifyingly pretty compared to the 1994 original. Retro-futuristic touches were added to hearken back to the original too such as grungy pixelated textures when viewed up close. Gameplay has been updated to fit modern standards and it feels like a modern action adventure FPS. Animations are smooth and detailed. Controls are simplified in a good way as to make it feel less light a flight simulator and more like a first person shooter. Personally I loved how atmospheric the sound design was. Going between combat and tense exploration sent chills down my spine and my heart couldn't stand it. Despite this, there aren't any jump scares or stand out horror moments. The ambient and combat tracks blend together seamlessly enhancing the experience even more. As for performance, the game had little to no frame drops, no bugs or glitches, and no game breaking issues. The only thing that isn't really much of an issue is that the ragdolls for each dead enemy seem to reset when you return to a level later which is quite hilarious and distracting. In summary, the System Shock Remake is an outstanding achievement, successfully modernizing a revered classic without sacrificing the essence of what made it special. With its stunning visuals, refined gameplay, captivating narrative, and immersive sound design, this remake serves as a testament to the power of preserving and revitalizing gaming masterpieces. If you have a taste for cyberpunk adventures and a love for atmospheric storytelling, System Shock Remake is an absolute must-play that will transport you to a dystopian world unlike any other.

_childDocuments_.review: The first  was way before my time so I cannot compare the remake to the original. Though I consider System Shock 2 and its spiritual successor Prey to be two of my favorite games therefore I was thrilled to see where it all began and my expectations were high. Especially after the game was delayed so many times.Without diving too deep into the story it is the year 2072 and you're a hacker who gets caught red-handed but given another chance to stay out of prison. The stakes are high because part of the deal is being transported to Citadel Station and removing all ethical constraints of the game's antagonist the AI SHODAN. As you awake from a coma you find Citadel Station and all of its inhabitants being hostile cyborgs due to your reckless attempt at self-preservation. Now it is up to you to make things right.From a gameplay standpoint the game is a hybrid FPS. Shooting and bludgeoning are your main ways of staying alive but there are also puzzles and hacking involved. The former is reminiscient of Bioshock's grid-connection mini-game and in the latter you commandeer a spaceship shooting viruses and cyber cores. The difficulty is highly customizable. Do not underestimate it. With the mission difficulty set to the maximum you're not only on a tight schedule to stop SHODAN but you also have no mission markers or objectives. What to do and where is only relayed to you by radio. There are some RPG elements such as upgrades to your neural interface and suit as well as weapon mods but there are no stats to distribute as it is with the sequel.Graphically I found the game to be gorgeous. Up close the textures get pixelated but it didn't bother me. On the contrary I thought it gave the game a nice touch. Where it really shines are the environments. As much as I like dark sci-fi the colorful and moody lightning never got old to me. The different floors of Citadel Station have distinct atmospheres. From the once sterile medical station, to the pompous executive suite, the industrial reactor core or the flourishing, leisurely groves.While it didn't perturb me too much I'd like to reiterate that the remake is very true to its almost thirty years old roots. There is an insane amount of backtracking involved, your inventory space is very limited and the game is extremely unforgiving. Some enemies respawn between level transitions to keep you on your toes and you better not forget where you dropped an important item to make room for that hefty railgun. I kept a piece of paper on my desk because access codes are randomized through every playthrough.What else is there to say? I had an absurd amount of fun even though the game has a tendency of being frustating due to its sheer difficulty. The game deserves the praise it got and I would put it on the same level of other brilliant remakes such as Resident Evil 4, Dead Space or Mafia. The developer is also working with community collaborators to bring the enhanced edition of System Shock 2 to Steam. I'm not sure if it will be free for owners of the remake or only customers who pre-ordered but it's worth to keep an eye out for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game sat in my Steam Wishlist for about 6 years. There were times when I thought it was never going to be released. Now that I have played it a little I have to say that it was well worth the wait. I played the original System Shock back in the 90s and it remains one of the best games I have ever played. That game was well ahead of its time with lots of little things that gamers take for granted now. For example, it was the first game I ever remember playing with a "lean around corners" feature. Now, all these years later, it's very clear to me that this remake was a labor of love for the developers. I am really enjoying the game. The visuals are good, but retain the feel of the original game. The soundtrack is really good; very cyberpunky, techno, and creepy. I am so glad that the devs, while upgrading the visual and audio technology, decided to leave overall gameplay mechanics of the original game in tact. The game does no hand-holding. You are in a huge, yet claustrophobic, enviromment, with a HUD map and compass, but there are no "quest markers" to show you where to go or what to do next. You simply have emails and audio recordings from the dead crew of the space station you are on to give you info and clues in an in-world narrative way--passwords, objectives, locations of ammo and supplies, etc. I admit that some modern day gamers with little patience may have trouble sticking out out with this game, but from my perspective, it adds to the immersion of the experience. I am enjoying the circuit breaker puzzles for opening doors and taking down shields, and the couple of times I have "jacked" into cyberspace have been pretty enjoyable. I like how the visually protrayed cyberspace in the game, again with modern tech, but the old school aesthetics. I'm only a fraction of the way through the game, but I am guessing this will end up being my favorite game of 2023. If you've played any of the Bioshock games and enjoyed them, but never played the original System Shock, you owe it to yourself to play this progenitor of those games.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake does a great job bringing System Shock to the modern day by making it much more accessible and easier to control, while upgrading the visuals with a retro cyberpunk style that does a great job retaining the feel of the old simple graphics but making the blocky interior work in a higher fidelity. That must have been a hard balance to find, but it is struck incredibly well.System Shock wrote the dictionary of game design principles that countless later games tapped into. This brings a problem with it: everything that this game does, has been done by games that came after it, and often better. It is not going to break new ground now in 2023 because it built most of that ground in 1994.But this is also its charm. Playing this game feels like going back in time, and seeing the genesis of the immersive sim and survival horror shooter genres. So many modern games can trace their lineage back to System Shock. You are playing 30 year old game design with some modern conveniences introduced to sand off the sharp edges, and this way it holds up surprisingly well.A word of warning: this game does not hold your hand. At all. Even when you flip a switch or solve a puzzle it is often unclear what you have changed. It is up to you to explore the claustrophobic corners of Citadel, listen to and read logs, and pay careful attention to your surroundings to figure out what you need to do and where to go next.But this is part of the challenge. The game expects the player to contribute a lot, and provides just enough tools for them to achieve their goals. Your secondary gameplay loop is to slow down, look over your collected logs, study your map, count your resources, and think about what your next step should be. To me this greatly increases the immersion of the game, because it makes me feel like I'm truly lost and alone with only my wits to save me from SHODAN.

_childDocuments_.review: The System Shock Remake is finally out, around 7 years after it's Kickstarter campaign. It's evolved a lot since that original demo, and I personally really enjoyed it.The story is almost the exact same as the original game, but with more fleshed out characters due to there being (if I recall the original correctly), over 10 times more audio logs. The original's animated intro cutscene was replaced with a short gameplay segment which tells more or less the same story, but with a small interactive portion at the start. The protagonist, a hacker, hacks into TriOptimum's servers and steals confidential information regarding cybernetic augmentations. He gets caught and captured by TriOptimum, and is transported to Citadel Station. There, a corrupt executive named Edward Diego offers to drop all charges and give you the military grade cybernetic augmentations free of charge, in exchange for the Hacker hacking into the stations systems and removing the stations AI's, Shodan's, ethical restraints. The Hacker accepts, does what he was asked, and is put into hibernation for 6 months. In the meantime, a now free to do whatever she wants Shodan developes a God complex and causes chaos on the station. That's all I can really say without spoiling the story.Shodan deserves her own little paragraph, because she's a great villain. She's always one step ahead of the Hacker, while you stop one plan she's already half way through executing another. She's more than aware of that fact, and will often communicate with you to mock you for it. She sees herself as a goddess, combining flesh and steel to create what she sees as perfection, and isn't willing to let humanity get in the way of her plans. During the game, you'll progress through Citadel Station with the goal of stopping Shodan and getting back to Earth. Citadel Station is a maze, a very dangerous one. If you just look at the automap, the different levels all seem like incomprehensible mazes, but actually navigating the environment is surprisingly easy, as each level is filled with landmarks. It's not always obvious where to go, System Shock really requires your attention. Key information is often hidden in audio logs, which isn't a big deal, but it's made slightly more annoying in the remake considering how many unimportant audio logs were added. Enemies respawn in places away from the player, so you're never fully safe. To fight enemies, you're gonna use a variety of weapons, mostly guns as there are only 3 melee weapons (all of which are weak). Unlike the original where only a couple weapons were good, here I felt like each weapon was useful. Most guns consume ammunition (which you can find around the station, loot from enemies or buy from vending machines which are one of the additions in this remake), but some use energy (which you can recharge with one time use batteries or recharge for free at power stations). The guns generally feel really good to use, and you can upgrade most of them with weapon mods (which weren't in the original game). The original game made you switch from interface mode to game mode constantly. Instead of just pressing R to reload, you'd have to press the button to go into interface mode (which would unlock the cursor), you'd have to go into the weapon menu, and click on the ammo type you wanted to load into the gun. Despite sounding weird, it was easy to get used to, and allowed you to do some cool things like shooting anywhere on the screen. The remake replaces this with a more traditional control scheme, which I'd say is probably an improvement.The only way to infinitely heal yourself is with surgery machines, and there are only 3 working ones in the entire game. Since there are 10 levels and only 3 have a surgery machine, you're often going to heal using one time use items, which aren't exactly rare but you're unlikely to ever have enough of them to truly feel comfortable.The original game used MIDI's for it's music, it was actually some of the earliest adaptive music in gaming. As cool as it was from a technical standpoint, 99% of the players didn't notice as the music often sounded like a child hitting random notes on a piano. The sound effects also weren't great, after a while of playing the original I was very close to muting it. This is one of the bigger improvements in the remake. The music is now way more atmospheric, and sound effects are way better. Some enemies can speak now, which in my opinion adds to the atmosphere.The remake is really faithful to the original, in both good and bad ways. Some issues with the original have been adressed, like making junk items useful (you can now recycle them for scrap which you can exchange into money, which you spend at vending machines for healing items, ammunition and weapon mods), and cyberspace isn't awful anymore (it turned from a headache inducing wireframe 6dof shooter with awful controls to a decent Descent clone) but some things are still just as tedious. I think the main change I would make is I would add something that would keep track of the red numbers. The player finds these on levels 1-6, but they don't stand out as much as they did in the original, and the player isn't informed about their importance until the moment they're needed. Keeping track of them somewhere on the HUD would save a lot of pointless backtracking.In short; the System Shock is a great remake of a great game. I'd definitely recommend it to fans of the System Shock franchise, fans of immersive sims like (Prey 2017), and fans of dungeon crawlers

_childDocuments_.review: Move over Deadspace. The Graddaddy of sci-fi horror wants its crown back.For those that enjoyed the original, this is a must buy. 9/10. There are some problems and there are some segments that are....weird.For everyone else, probably an 8/10. A competent shooter and a good, although obscure, story.The lighting and general atmosphere are amazing, minus some segments where the music is absent and others, forgettable.I would really have liked to see some basic objective remembering/tracking panels. Also, a Hud element to track remaining ammo in inventory vs what is just in the gun would have been nice. Plenty of other QoL features would be appreciated but altogether it works pretty well.
_childDocuments_.name: System Shock

_childDocuments_.review: suffers from the same bs as the orginal:-no waypoint markers, no feasible map system-awful map layouts-labyrinth-style exploration is just frustrating. Metroid prime 1,2,3, dread, hunters, fusion, zero, etc. all did this far better over the past 20 years.-same old over-exploration until you randomly come across what you are supposed to do, if you don't already quit after hours of not knowing what to do unless you find a guide or played the original.-still no context for objectives, even audio logs and texts do not tell you what you are supposed to really do past very little hints -enemies hit like tanks and gun-wielding ones have insane aimbot - will kill you in less than 10 seconds, especially turrents and the beefier enemies-pushes boss enemies almost instantly after the first level-take fall damage from falling 1 inch above jumping height in 2023 lol-terrible hacking sequences-melee is useless immediately after finding firearms-coin system for upgrades and items is boring, why not change this to just skill trees/leveling/loot?there is a ton more to add but not worth my time. They should have just made a whole new game instead of doing a 1:1 replication of a game that is known to have not aged well worth s***. There was so much potential to give this game the treatment it deserved, to modernize and update the awful parts of SS1 and make it worth buying. IMO, not worth even 40 dollars for the amount of frustration and intolerable laziness of this remake for just a copy-paste with better graphics.
